papers.title: Property Estimation in Geotechnical Databases Using Labeled Random Finite Sets
papers.abstract: The sufficiency of accurate data is a core element in data-centric geotechnics. However, geotechnical datasets are essentially uncertain, whereupon engineers have difficulty with obtaining precise information for making decisions. This challenge is more apparent when the performance of data-driven technologies solely relies on imperfect databases or even when it is sometimes difficult to investigate sites physically. This paper introduces geotechnical property estimation from noisy and incomplete data within the labeled random finite set (LRFS) framework. We leverage the ability of the generalized labeled multi-Bernoulli (GLMB) filter, a fundamental solution for multi-object estimation, to deal with measurement uncertainties from a Bayesian perspective. In particular, this work focuses on the similarity between LRFSs and big indirect data (BID) in geotechnics as those characteristics resemble each other, which enables GLMB filtering to be exploited potentially for data-centric geotechnical engineering. Experiments for numerical study are conducted to evaluate the proposed method using a public clay database.
papers.summary: Geotechnical databases are noisy and incomplete, so engineers often lack precise soil property values for design decisions. The authors treat property estimation as a multi-object estimation problem in the labeled random finite set (LRFS) framework. They use the generalized labeled multi-Bernoulli (`GLMB`) filter to handle measurement uncertainty in a Bayesian way, building on a claimed **structural similarity between LRFSs and big indirect data (BID) in geotechnics**. A numerical study on a public clay database evaluates the method.

papers.title: Revealing the Impact of Visual Text Style on Attribute-based Descriptions Produced by Large Visual Language Models
papers.abstract: When the visual style of text is considered, a wide variety can be observed in font, color, and size. However, when a word is read, its meaning is independent of the style in which it has been written or rendered. In this paper, we investigate whether, and how, the style in which a word is visualized in an image impacts the description that a Large Visual Language Model (LVLM) provides for the concept to which that word refers. Specifically, we investigate how functional text styles (readability-oriented, e.g., black sans-serif) versus decorative styles (display-oriented, e.g., colored cursive/script) affect LVLMs' descriptions of a concept in terms of the attributes of that concept. Our experiments study the situation in which the LVLM is able to correctly identify the concept referred to by a visual text, i.e., by a word or words rendered as an image, and in which the visual text style should not influence the attribute-based description that the LVLM produces. Our experimental results reveal that even when the concept is correctly identified, text style influences the model's attribute-based descriptions of the concept. Our findings demonstrate non-trivial style leakage from text style into semantic inference and motivate style-aware evaluation and mitigation for LVLM-based multimedia systems.
papers.summary: The study asks whether the visual style of rendered text changes how large visual language models (LVLMs) describe the concept the word names. It compares functional styles, such as black sans-serif, with decorative ones, such as colored cursive, and looks only at cases where the model correctly recognizes the word. **Text style still shifts the attributes the models attribute to the concept** even when recognition is correct. The authors call this style leakage into semantic inference and argue that LVLM-based systems need style-aware evaluation and mitigation.

papers.title: How language model agents reshape price competition
papers.abstract: Repeated Bertrand competition is a stringent benchmark for algorithmic pricing: in homogeneous-goods markets, standard learning procedures typically select the stage-game Nash outcome with prices near marginal cost. We show that LLM pricing agents can escape this benchmark, depending on deployment decisions. LLMs outperform standard online learners through faster adaptation, but this advantage largely disappears against full-information learners. An extracted surrogate algorithm illustrates how LLMs in specific deployments profit from regularly undercutting slower learners. Agents that post one price every period from raw market histories that include rival prices can sustain supracompetitive regimes in self-play. Agents that periodically emit probability distributions from summarized histories of their own profits instead move toward the competitive region in self-play. Markets mixing these interfaces can generate dynamic regimes in which LLMs establish a high-price anchor and regularly undercut it to capture demand. These regimes can keep both competitors' prices above marginal cost. Deployment choices shape these outcomes, shifting the focus from stationary equilibria to dynamic pricing regimes.
papers.summary: In repeated Bertrand price competition, standard learning algorithms usually settle near marginal-cost prices, and this work tests whether LLM pricing agents behave differently. LLMs beat standard online learners by adapting faster, but that edge mostly disappears against full-information learners. A surrogate algorithm extracted from the LLM's behavior shows it profits by regularly undercutting slower rivals. The outcome depends on how the agents are deployed: **agents that post one price per period from raw histories that include rival prices sustain supracompetitive prices in self-play**, while agents that emit price distributions from summaries of their own profits move toward competitive prices. Markets that mix the two interfaces produce dynamic high-anchor-and-undercut regimes.

papers.title: Encoded but Exposed: Language Embeddings can Reveal More Than They Should in Recommender Systems
papers.abstract: Language embeddings are increasingly used in recommenders to represent item content, but their privacy risks remain poorly understood. We study whether item embeddings can reveal item identities when an adversary has access to auxiliary item text from external sources. We show that a simple cosine-similarity attack can recover item identities with high mean reciprocal rank across language models and candidate-set settings on two real-world datasets. Leakage is strongest when the adversary's partial information overlaps with the victim representation, but it also persists through semantic alignment between independently sourced descriptions. We further show that item leakage can propagate to user re-identification from sparse ratings. Finally, we evaluate obfuscated descriptions as a mitigation and find a clear leakage-utility tradeoff.
papers.summary: Recommender systems increasingly represent items with language-model embeddings, and this work examines whether those embeddings leak item identities. An adversary holding auxiliary item text from outside sources runs a simple cosine-similarity attack and **recovers item identities with high mean reciprocal rank** across several language models and two real-world datasets. Leakage is strongest when the adversary's text overlaps with the victim's representation, but it persists even between independently written descriptions. The item leakage can also be used to re-identify users from sparse ratings, and obfuscating item descriptions as a defense trades leakage against recommendation utility.

papers.title: Physics-Transfer Learning: A Physics-Constrained Theory for Zero-Shot Generalization Along the Ladder of Complexity
papers.abstract: Reliable out-of-distribution generalization remains a central challenge in machine learning, particularly when models are deployed in data-scarce high-fidelity domains. Existing approaches often rely on statistical distribution alignment, or invariance assumptions that can fail when domain shifts reflect changes in underlying mechanisms. Inspired by a longstanding paradigm in physics that understands complex systems by starting from tractable idealizations and progressively incorporating additional mechanisms and levels of fidelity, we propose physics-transfer (PT) learning, a physics-constrained learning theory for zero-shot generalization along a ladder of complexity. PT constructs chains of anchor domains (CADs) that connect low-cost source domains to complex targets and introduces computable feasibility and reliability indicators for assessing transfer before target-domain labels are observed. Under physical-consistency and stable-representation assumptions, we derive an operational upper bound on target risk in terms of source empirical risk, the PT indicators, and finite-sample errors, and establish convergence as adjacent complexity gaps shrink and data coverage improves. We evaluate PT on excited-state energy prediction in quantum systems and dynamical-transition prediction in classical systems using neural networks trained without target-domain labels. Across substantial distribution shifts, PT yields accurate high-fidelity predictions, while the indicators identify incorrect physical mappings before target-domain prediction fails. These results provide a model-agnostic framework for designing, diagnosing, and controlling generalization in data-scarce learning problems.
papers.summary: Physics-transfer (`PT`) learning targets zero-shot out-of-distribution generalization in data-scarce, high-fidelity scientific domains by following the physics habit of moving from simple idealizations to more complex systems. `PT` builds chains of anchor domains (CADs) that link cheap source domains to complex targets, and it defines feasibility and reliability indicators that can be computed before any target labels exist. Under physical-consistency assumptions, the authors derive an upper bound on target risk and prove convergence as the complexity gaps between adjacent domains shrink. On excited-state energy prediction in quantum systems and dynamical-transition prediction in classical systems, `PT` gives accurate predictions without target labels, and **the indicators flag incorrect physical mappings before prediction fails**.

papers.title: Memory Bandwidth, Not FLOPs: Profiling and Accelerating Query-Based Segmentation Decoders on Edge GPUs
papers.abstract: Query-based segmentation models achieve strong performance even under real-time inference on workstation GPUs. On edge devices, however, we show their transformer decoders are deeply memory-bandwidth-bound, a bottleneck invisible to standard FLOP analysis that worsens with input resolution and limited DRAM bandwidth. An FP16 roofline analysis with tensor-core GEMMs active and hardware DRAM counters shows that the non-tensor-core aggregates of FastInst and Mask2Former reach only $2.5\%$ to $6\%$ of the CUDA-core ridge yet account for $53\%$ to $70\%$ of decoder time and $61\%$ to $71\%$ of decoder bytes. The largest individual kernels sustain up to $90\%$ of nominal peak DRAM bandwidth, effectively saturating the memory bus. The bottleneck is therefore not primarily low GEMM intensity, but cross-kernel activation traffic. CompactInst addresses this bottleneck using parameter-free spatial pooling at $4{\times}$, which reduces the bytes moved within the transformer decoder, while a two-convolution refinement head recovers spatial detail. Under TensorRT FP16 on Jetson Orin Nano, CompactInst delivers decoder speedups from $2.35{\times}$ to $4.74{\times}$ and model speedups from $1.57{\times}$ to $2.62{\times}$ as input resolution grows, while closely matching accuracy ($-0.4$ AP on COCO val2017, $+0.2$ AP on Cityscapes test). A heavier variant with $2.57{\times}$ more decoder FLOPs still runs its decoder $1.74{\times}$ faster on the most bandwidth-constrained device, confirming at the deployment level that decoder bytes, not FLOPs, govern latency.
authors: German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence)
papers.summary: Profiling query-based segmentation models such as `FastInst` and `Mask2Former` on edge GPUs shows that their transformer decoders are limited by memory bandwidth, which FLOP counts do not reveal. Non-tensor-core operations account for 53–70% of decoder time, and the largest kernels run at up to 90% of peak DRAM bandwidth, so the cost comes from moving activations between kernels. The proposed `CompactInst` applies parameter-free 4× spatial pooling inside the decoder to cut those bytes and adds a two-convolution head to recover spatial detail. Under `TensorRT` FP16 on a `Jetson Orin Nano`, it achieves **decoder speedups of 2.35× to 4.74×** with near-identical accuracy (−0.4 AP on `COCO`, +0.2 AP on `Cityscapes`).

papers.title: When is a large language model a good calibration agent? Physics-labeled prompting for budgeted engineering simulator calibration
papers.abstract: Calibrating expensive engineering simulators requires tuning model parameters to match reference data, a process heavily constrained by computational costs. This study investigates whether Large Language Models (LLMs), conditioned on physical diagnostic descriptions of simulation errors, can propose informative parameter updates more efficiently than conventional derivative-free optimizers. We test this on a cylinder-wake Large-Eddy Simulation and a damped-oscillator inverse problem. Physics-labeled prompts are evaluated against four text ablations (removed, anonymized, padded, misdirected) and standard optimizers (Nelder-Mead, Bayesian optimization, CMA-ES, and random search). Results demonstrate a strong early semantic advantage: the first physics-informed LLM proposal improves the initial design in 23 of 25 trials. After five evaluations, the median calibration error is 21.9 times lower than physics-free controls. However, this advantage is transient - disappearing by fifteen evaluations - and inherent LLM decoder variability yields a 9.8-fold performance spread. To address this, we introduce a hybrid workflow that uses the LLM as a warm-start, passing accumulated evaluations to a conventional optimizer. This two-stage numerical continuation policy reaches target accuracy in just 9 simulator runs, outperforming the LLM alone (12 runs), Nelder-Mead (17 runs), and Bayesian optimization (>60 runs). Supported by sensitivity analysis validating the test cases, this hybrid physics-labeled LLM scheme proves highly effective as a calibration agent under strict evaluation budgets.
papers.summary: The study tests whether LLMs, given physics-based descriptions of simulation errors, can calibrate expensive engineering simulators with fewer runs than derivative-free optimizers. The test cases are a cylinder-wake Large-Eddy Simulation and a damped-oscillator inverse problem, with text ablations and baselines such as `Nelder-Mead`, Bayesian optimization, and `CMA-ES`. Physics-labeled prompts give a large early advantage, with median error 21.9× lower than physics-free controls after five evaluations, but the advantage is gone by fifteen evaluations and results vary widely between runs. A hybrid that uses the LLM as a warm start and then hands off to a conventional optimizer **reaches target accuracy in 9 simulator runs**, compared with 12 for the LLM alone, 17 for `Nelder-Mead`, and more than 60 for Bayesian optimization.

papers.title: Trust but Verify: Designing Region-Inhomogeneous Forward Dynamics for Discrete Diffusion
papers.abstract: Continuous diffusion treats the forward process as a design space; discrete language diffusion often uses absorbing corruption, leaving context fully trusted throughout generation. This makes trust binary: corrupted context is copied as ground truth, propagating errors into generated spans. We reopen this design space by combining absorbing and uniform-mixing kernels with region-dependent rates. Missing positions follow absorbing dynamics, while context undergoes low-rate random substitution, exposing the model to observed but uncertain tokens during training. At inference, a heuristic sampler re-injects noise into suspicious context under an annealed intensity and freezes context updates late in the trajectory. An 8,000-step finetune of a pretrained 170M-parameter masked diffusion model takes under five hours on a 6 GB laptop GPU. The base model assigns roughly 50% probability to observed tokens even when they are uniform-random garbage. For uniform-random corruption, finetuning detects corrupted context with 0.96 recall and 0.91 precision, improves infill token-F1 by 3.8 points at 10% corruption and 6.4 points at 20%, and removes the accuracy dip next to corruptions. Clean conditioning shows no measurable regression, with a false-edit rate below 0.4%. Gains for plausible corruptions are weaker: about 0.5 F1 points at 10% corruption, without statistical significance. Our results suggest that detectability and damage depend jointly on departure from the data conditional: nearby noise is hard to detect and semantically mild, while distant noise is conspicuous and destructive. We interpret absorbing diffusion as the infinite-contrast limit of a trust axis, analogous to the signal-to-noise gap between known and unknown regions in diffusion inpainting. In our setting of a 170M model and a single text domain, intermediate trust is reached by changing forward dynamics rather than architecture.
papers.summary: Discrete diffusion language models usually use absorbing (masking) corruption, which means visible context is always treated as correct and any errors in it spread into generated text. The authors combine absorbing and uniform-substitution kernels with rates that differ by region, so the model sees noisy context during training, and they add a sampler that re-noises suspicious context at inference time. An 8,000-step finetune of a 170M-parameter masked diffusion model on a 6 GB laptop GPU **detects uniform-random corrupted context with 0.96 recall and 0.91 precision** and improves infill token-F1 by up to 6.4 points, with no regression on clean inputs. Gains on plausible, near-distribution corruptions are small and not statistically significant.

papers.title: Binding-Specific Relearning Savings for Test-Time Continual Learning
papers.abstract: When a fact becomes harder to elicit from a language model, has the model lost it, or has it merely become less accessible? Parameter-updating test-time continual learning agents are usually evaluated by current output accuracy; we ask whether that measurement captures how prior experience shapes later updates. We test whether learning a specific factual binding produces a later relearning advantage beyond familiarity with its entity, answer vocabulary, format, or query slot. In Qwen2.5-1.5B, we compare three matched, counterbalanced histories: LEARNED receives the correct binding, CONTROL receives matched exposure without it, and WRONG receives a competing relation-valid answer in the same slot. After an identical rehearsal-free continual fine-tuning stream, LEARNED reacquires the target faster than CONTROL at a prespecified checkpoint of partial forgetting. WRONG shows no positive advantage over CONTROL, while its comparison with LEARNED provides slot-matched corroboration, subject to possible competitor interference. The advantage remains positive after adjustment for measured pre-relearning behavior. In a secondary descriptive conversion using an unpaired never-seen pool, prior learning reduces the optimizer updates required for restoration by about 18%. Current behavioral accuracy can therefore underestimate the lasting effect of previously acquired experience. Code is available at https://github.com/zhezhou1106/relearning-savings
papers.summary: Test-time continual learning agents are usually judged by their current accuracy, which cannot tell whether a fact that has become hard to elicit was lost or is only less accessible. Using `Qwen2.5-1.5B`, the authors compare matched histories in which the model learned a specific factual binding, received matched exposure without it, or learned a competing wrong answer, followed by an identical continual fine-tuning stream. **Models that previously learned the binding relearn it faster** than controls at a point of partial forgetting, while the wrong-answer history gives no advantage. Prior learning cuts the optimizer updates needed for restoration by about 18%, suggesting that behavioral accuracy underestimates retained experience.

papers.title: Eliciting Specifications: When Does Interactive Clarification Help?
papers.abstract: LLMs can generate Lean specifications from task descriptions, but those descriptions are often underspecified or ambiguous and may omit verifier-relevant edge cases, yielding imperfect formal specifications. We study whether an elicitation agent (EA) can improve verifier-checked Lean specifications by seeking clarification from a reference-grounded simulated developer before formalization. The agent decomposes the task, identifies unresolved decisions, asks bounded clarification questions, and uses the answers to write a refined natural-language specification that an LLM formalizer then translates into Lean. On 189 Verina Lean 4 specification-generation tasks, we compare single-shot generation with elicitation under question budgets of k=3 and k=10, allowing at most three or ten EA questions per task, across same-model and cross-model configurations. The same-model Claude Sonnet 4.6 pipeline has negative strict pass@1 estimates at both budgets, showing elicitation is not a uniform accuracy booster. In contrast, the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 and Sonnet 4.6-to-Gemini 3.8 Flash pipelines have positive strict estimates. The largest strict result reaches 65.6%, a +6.3-point change (+12 tasks), in the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 pipeline. Six of eight conditions have positive compile-conditional estimates, with a maximum cross-model difference of +4.9 points among compiling outputs. Treatment estimates also differ across the basic and advanced splits; the largest advanced-task change occurs in the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 configuration at k=10, from 42.0% to 50.6%. Failure analysis identifies postconditions as the largest source of degradation. These findings suggest future autoformalization systems should treat elicited natural-language specifications as intermediate artifacts and optimize jointly for semantic correctness among compiling outputs and reliable translation of clarified information into Lean.
papers.summary: Task descriptions used to generate Lean formal specifications are often ambiguous, so the authors test an elicitation agent that asks a simulated developer a limited number of clarifying questions before an LLM formalizer writes the spec. On 189 `Verina` Lean 4 tasks with budgets of 3 or 10 questions, clarification is not a uniform win: the same-model `Claude Sonnet 4.6` pipeline gets worse. Cross-model pipelines improve, with the best (`Sonnet 4.6` eliciting and `GPT-5.6` formalizing) **reaching 65.6% strict pass@1, a 6.3-point gain**. Postconditions are the largest source of degradation, and the authors recommend treating clarified natural-language specs as intermediate artifacts and optimizing the translation step separately.

papers.title: Deep Learning for Forest Plantation Mapping in Godavari Districts of Andhra Pradesh, India
papers.abstract: Small-area forest plantations play a vital role in the socioeconomic well-being of farmers in Southeast Asia. Most plantations are established on former agricultural land, often on land less suitable for agriculture. Plantations that are converted from natural forest have adverse impacts on biodiversity. Mapping small-area plantations is thus important to understand the dynamics of forest cover in Southeast Asia and to study the social, economic, and ecological effects of this important land cover and land use change. While the small size of forest plantations makes it difficult to detect them using moderate resolution satellite sensors, the problem is exacerbated by the high degree of mixing between plantations, surrounding vegetation, and other land covers, which often show variegated responses in satellite signals across space and time. In this paper, we study the problem of mapping small-area forest plantations in East and West Godavari districts of Andhra Pradesh, India using deep learning methods. Remotely sensed cloud-free data from the Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 S10 product were classified using a pixel-level neural network and training data labeled using a field-based survey in concert with expert aerial photo interpretation. We compare the performance of deep learning methods with a baseline random forest classifier in our study region of 21543 sq. km over a period of 3 years and analyze the differences in the results across land cover classes and seasons.
papers.summary: Small forest plantations are hard to map from moderate-resolution satellite data because they are small and blend into surrounding vegetation and land cover. The authors classify cloud-free imagery from the `Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2` product with a pixel-level neural network trained on labels from field surveys and expert aerial-photo interpretation. They compare it with a **random forest baseline over 21,543 sq. km of the Godavari districts in Andhra Pradesh, India, across three years**, and analyze how results differ by land cover class and season.

papers.title: PRIME: Towards Verifiable Evidence-Grounded Reasoning in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents are used to check records against an organization's requirements, for example whether a vulnerability report is ready for investigation. Requirements often allow several ways to be met, such as a severity rating with a curator-reviewed advisory or a published advisory link. Agents fail by accepting a report after a required check has failed, or by settling for a weaker conclusion without trying another way that could still succeed. We introduce PRIME (Precommitted Rules for Inference from Minimal Evidence). Before checking, it fixes evidence routes specifying how each conclusion may be justified. A separate program records each check result and refuses any conclusion the results do not justify. It also points the agent to checks that could justify a stronger conclusion, or runs them itself. PRIME reports only conclusions authorized by its rules and ledger. With correct requirements, exact checks at known locations, and sufficient budget at stopping, completion reaches the strongest supported conclusion. On 480 public-record tasks, an agent shown the requirements reported unjustified conclusions on 26.7% of tasks, while PRIME reported none. Its directions and added checks raised the average score for justified conclusions from 30.1, with refusal alone, to the maximum of 59.2 out of 100.
papers.summary: LLM agents that check records against organizational requirements, such as deciding whether a vulnerability report is ready for investigation, often accept a record after a required check has failed or settle for a weaker conclusion without trying other valid routes. `PRIME` (Precommitted Rules for Inference from Minimal Evidence) fixes the allowed evidence routes before checking begins, and a separate program records each check result in a ledger and refuses any conclusion the results do not justify. It also points the agent to checks that could support a stronger conclusion, or runs them itself. On 480 public-record tasks, **a baseline agent reported unjustified conclusions on 26.7% of tasks while `PRIME` reported none**, and its guidance raised the average justified-conclusion score from 30.1 to the maximum of 59.2 out of 100.

papers.title: Embeddings Are Overpriced? A Frozen 16 MB Vocabulary for Small and Ternary Language Models
papers.abstract: In a small language model the vocabulary is the single largest part. In Gemma 3 270M the embedding table holds 168M of 268M parameters, and because quantisation methods leave the embedding in 16-bit, it is also most of the file once the rest of the model is compressed. We ask what that table actually buys. We replace it with one frozen table of 512-bit codes, 16 MB, with no trainable parameters, derived once from a pretrained embedding by principal-component projection and sign binarisation, and we train the same Gemma-shaped body from scratch on the same 2.05B tokens with and without it. The learned table buys 0.20 nats of validation loss for 2.6 times the trainable parameters, but on LAMBADA, HellaSwag and PIQA the frozen-table model is better or tied; only ARC-Easy favours the learned table. With a ternary BitNet b1.58 body the whole model is a 46 MB file, still ties the float model on LAMBADA and PIQA, and on a laptop CPU generates 615 to 740 tokens per second in 62 MB of memory, five to six times the speed of the float model's 8-bit GGUF in llama.cpp at a seventh of the memory. The frozen table wins by 1.7 to 2.3 nats on rare words, accepts 10,000 new words after training with a 3% cost where the learned table collapses by 43%, and all of it is released with the weights, the data and every evaluation answer.
papers.summary: In small language models the embedding table is the largest component, holding 168M of the 268M parameters in `Gemma 3 270M`, and it usually stays in 16-bit precision after quantization. The authors replace it with a frozen 16 MB table of 512-bit binary codes, derived from a pretrained embedding by principal-component projection and sign binarization, and train the same model body from scratch with and without it. The frozen-table model ties or beats the learned table on `LAMBADA`, `HellaSwag`, and `PIQA`, generalizes much better to rare and newly added words, and with a ternary `BitNet b1.58` body becomes **a 46 MB model that generates 615–740 tokens per second on a laptop CPU in 62 MB of memory**. That is five to six times faster than the float model's 8-bit `GGUF` in `llama.cpp`.

papers.title: CGDT-CESN: Correlation-Guided and Dynamics-Trained Clustered Echo State Network for Multivariate Time-Series Prediction
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of multivariate time series requires models that simultaneously capture variable-specific dynamics and cross-variable interactions. In this work, a Correlation-Guided and Dynamics-Trained Clustered Echo State Network (CGDT-CESN) is proposed, which comprises a modular reservoir architecture with each cluster distinctly specializing in one of the variables in the multivariate time series. An innovative reservoir design is proposed in which inter-cluster connections are enabled by empirically observed correlations among variables, providing a data-driven coupling mechanism. Apart from conventional readout training, inter-cluster connection weights informed by correlations are trained, which in turn allows the reservoir to capture time-varying cross-variable dependencies without sacrificing computational efficiency and further improves forecasting accuracy. The prediction performance of CGDT-CESN is found to be superior to that of the conventional ESN when evaluated on two fundamentally different datasets: Twitter information cascade evolution and solar wind forecasting. Also, the improvement in performance is preserved across multiple prediction horizons, even when presented with a low volume of data. By unifying cluster-specific specialization with learned inter-variable coupling, CGDT-CESN offers a principled, data-driven route to multivariate time series prediction.
papers.summary: Multivariate time-series forecasting needs to model both each variable's own dynamics and the interactions between variables. `CGDT-CESN` is a clustered echo state network in which each reservoir cluster specializes in one variable and the connections between clusters are set from observed correlations and then trained along with the readout. On Twitter information-cascade evolution and solar-wind forecasting, it **outperforms a conventional `ESN` across multiple prediction horizons**, including when little data is available.

papers.title: GPU-Accelerated Robust MA--RIS Pre-Optimization for Communication and Target Illumination
papers.abstract: Movable antennas (MAs) and reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) offer strong spatial control for integrated sensing and communication (ISAC), but repeatedly adapting MA positions and RIS phases to each channel realization can be impractical. This letter develops a GPU-accelerated robust pre-optimization framework that jointly selects slow-timescale MA geometry and RIS phases and returns a reusable Pareto set balancing expected worst-user rate and transmit-side worst-target illumination. The illumination objective measures directional transmitted power rather than complete echo-detection or parameter-estimation performance. The proposed Regime-Aware Multiobjective Pre-optimization (RAMP) preserves regime-specific Pareto populations, regulates cross-regime mating using Pareto-survival feedback, and constructs a worst-regime robust archive. Numerical results demonstrate competitive robust Pareto quality against the considered evolutionary baselines while avoiding online physical re-optimization.
papers.summary: Movable antennas (MAs) and reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) can improve integrated sensing and communication (ISAC), but re-optimizing them for every channel realization is impractical. This letter presents `RAMP` (Regime-Aware Multiobjective Pre-optimization), a GPU-accelerated evolutionary method that chooses antenna geometry and RIS phases once and returns a reusable Pareto set trading off worst-user rate against worst-target illumination. It keeps a separate Pareto population for each channel regime and controls how solutions are combined across regimes. Numerical results show **robust Pareto quality competitive with evolutionary baselines while avoiding online re-optimization**.

papers.title: An Adaptive-Horizon Graph Neural Operator for coupled surrogate morphodynamic modelling
papers.abstract: Morphodynamic simulations require repeated coupling between hydrodynamic solvers, sediment transport modules, and bed updating. For long duration, multi-scenario simulations on large unstructured meshes, such coupling is computationally demanding. This study proposes an Adaptive-Horizon Graph Neural Operator (AH-GNO) that formulates bed evolution as a graph operator learning problem from recent hydrodynamic and topographic states to predict future bed elevation increments. The model operates directly on the native unstructured meshes. The approach integrates area-weighted graph learning, historical state selection, and forecast horizon estimation, allowing the effective history length (K) and update interval (B) to vary with the evolving flow and bed state. Using Telemac2D/GAIA solutions as supervised numerical references, the framework is evaluated on the official Bump and Yen bend benchmarks and on a field-scale application (Waiho River, New Zealand). Results show that the AH-GNO reproduces the main patterns of bedform migration, bend-scale erosion and deposition, and localized bed adjustment. Across the three cases, the tested CPU-GPU deployment reduced post-training bed-update workflow time from 12~1204 s with GAIA to 0.08~3.34 s with AH-GNO. This improvement corresponds to deployment-specific accelerations of approximately 150~360 times relative to 4-core GAIA CPU configurations, and with 105~186 times gains for 20-core CPU configurations. These results suggest that, while retaining hydrodynamic feedback from TELEMAC-2D, a learned operator for bed updating can provide an efficient acceleration component for morphodynamic scenario analysis and rapid coupled simulation.
papers.summary: Morphodynamic simulations repeatedly couple hydrodynamics, sediment transport, and bed updates, which is expensive on large unstructured meshes. `AH-GNO` is a graph neural operator that works directly on the native mesh and predicts future bed-elevation changes from recent flow and topography, adapting its history length and update interval as conditions change. Trained on `Telemac2D`/`GAIA` solutions, it reproduces the main erosion and deposition patterns on the `Bump` and `Yen` bend benchmarks and on the Waiho River in New Zealand. It runs **about 150–360× faster than 4-core `GAIA` CPU runs** for the bed-update step.

papers.title: BOLT: Multi-Bottleneck Bound-Guided Learning for Flexible Job-Shop Scheduling with Time Lags and Resource-Coupled Transport
papers.abstract: Flexible job-shop scheduling becomes resource-coupled when a scarce vehicle fleet moves jobs between stations, because the schedule sets the transport waits. BOLT (bound-oriented learning for transport-coupled scheduling) builds a lower bound from chain, machine-capacity, and fleet-capacity relaxations. The bound equals the makespan at termination, so its per-step changes form a reward that sums to a constant minus the makespan. Because it never exceeds the attainable makespan, each candidate's bound increase is a proven rise of the makespan floor, which the policy reads as a price. The root bound certifies a completed schedule's suboptimality gap without a solver. On industry-motivated 10-module prefabricated-construction instances, explicit transport coupling outperforms a transport-penalty policy in every tested cell where loaded moves occupy at least 66% of fleet time and in none at or below 56%. Across five zero-shot 50- and 80-module production batches, BOLT outperforms the best dispatching-rule pair on four and the penalty policy on the three with long moves. In the three-vehicle 80-module batch, its mean makespan is 13.0% below the best pair and 4.2% below an hour-budget constraint-programming solver whose proven gap averages 34%. BOLT decides in 2.3-5.9 ms per event on one processor core and re-plans a disruption in seconds.
papers.summary: `BOLT` handles flexible job-shop scheduling in which a small vehicle fleet moves jobs between stations, so the schedule itself determines transport waiting times. It builds a lower bound on makespan from chain, machine-capacity, and fleet-capacity relaxations, and uses the per-step changes in that bound as a learning reward and a price signal for the policy, which also certifies a schedule's suboptimality gap without a solver. On zero-shot prefabricated-construction batches of 50 and 80 modules, `BOLT` beats the best dispatching-rule pair on four of five, and in the three-vehicle 80-module case its **mean makespan is 13.0% below the best rule pair and 4.2% below an hour-budget constraint-programming solver**. It makes each decision in 2.3–5.9 ms on a single CPU core.

papers.title: TRACE: Transformer Residual Activation Codebook Encoding for Communication-efficient Distributed Edge Inference
papers.abstract: Distributed Transformer inference across co-located edge devices is fundamentally communication-bound, as exchanging activations between sequence-parallel partitions dominates inference latency under commodity edge bandwidths. Existing compression schemes reduce this cost but retain a structural bottleneck: the received data must still undergo key/value projection before attention can proceed, serializing computation behind communication. This paper presents Transformer Residual Activation Codebook Encoding (Trace), a framework that addresses these limitations. Trace places a Vector Quantizer (VQ) at the post-attention residual of every Transformer layer and precomputes codebook-indexed key/value representations. During inference, exchanged activations are encoded into compact codebook indices, allowing receivers to directly recover keys and values through table lookup instead of executing the downstream computations required to derive them. By eliminating the received data downstream computation, Trace enables communication--computation overlap and reduces a key latency bottleneck in distributed Transformer inference. A hierarchical clustering further structures the learned codebook into a multi-resolution hierarchy, enabling runtime adaptation of the communication bitrate without retraining. The framework supports two operating variants: one prioritizing accuracy and the other balancing accuracy and efficiency through buffer-compatible quantization. Experiments on ViT-Base (ImageNet-1K and CIFAR-100) and ViViT-B (UCF-101) show that Trace achieves up to 1.89% higher accuracy and up to 1.27x end-to-end inference speedup compared with the state-of-the-art VQ-based distributed inference framework. Compared with uncompressed sequence-parallel inference, Trace reduces communication overhead by up to 22,624x.
papers.summary: When Transformer inference is split across nearby edge devices, latency is dominated by exchanging activations, and receivers must still compute key/value projections on the received data before attention can run. `TRACE` (Transformer Residual Activation Codebook Encoding) puts a vector quantizer after each layer's attention residual and precomputes keys and values for every codebook entry, so receivers recover them by table lookup and communication can overlap with computation. A hierarchical codebook lets the bitrate be adjusted at runtime without retraining. On `ViT-Base` and `ViViT-B`, it gives up to 1.89% higher accuracy and 1.27× faster end-to-end inference than the prior best VQ-based framework, and **cuts communication by up to 22,624×** compared with uncompressed sequence-parallel inference.

papers.title: Generative adversarial networks with Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty quantification for structural health monitoring: Fibre Bragg grating data augmentation comparison in Hawk T1A aircraft
papers.abstract: The signal generation capabilities of a novel data augmentation framework are examined in aerospace structures. First, the framework learns class-conditional temporal and spectral characteristics of the measured structural responses. It uses conditional generative adversarial network training and Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty quantification as a Bayesian approximation. This step enables stochastic signal synthesis and uncertainty quantification. Second, the generated responses are rigorously compared against experimental measurements across time, frequency, uncertainty, variability, and feature domains to assess physical realism, statistical consistency, and distributional fidelity. Finally, the synthetic data are evaluated to determine whether they should be incorporated into a supervised damage classification workflow. The framework is validated on the full-scale benchmark dataset from a BAE Systems Hawk T1A aircraft tested at the University of Sheffield's Structural Dynamics Laboratory for Verification and Validation. The test involves acceleration, fibre Bragg grating strain, and nonlinear dynamic response measurements. The results demonstrate that the model accurately captures dominant structural dynamics, it guides on signal use for classification improvement based on uncertainty characteristics, and it provides meaningful uncertainty estimates linked to signal complexity and excitation characteristics. Importantly, the framework offers a realistic generative modelling plan as a robust digital twin component for data-driven structural health monitoring, supporting resilient decision-making for condition assessment in safety-critical aerospace systems.
papers.summary: Structural health monitoring of aircraft has limited measured data for training damage classifiers. The authors present a data-augmentation framework that pairs a conditional generative adversarial network with Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty quantification to synthesize acceleration and fibre Bragg grating strain signals. They compare the generated signals with real measurements across time, frequency, uncertainty, and feature domains, then evaluate whether adding them helps damage classification. On the full-scale `BAE Systems Hawk T1A` benchmark, the model **captures the dominant structural dynamics and gives uncertainty estimates that track signal complexity**, which helps decide which synthetic signals to use.

papers.title: CF-NODE: Counterfactual Spatial Node Intervention for Test-Time Adaptation Under Domain Shift, Evaluated Across Five Diabetic Retinopathy Datasets
papers.abstract: Automated fundus-based diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading can substantially expand screening capacity, but source-trained models degrade sharply across different cameras, clinics, and patient populations. Existing test-time adaptation methods depend on entropy minimization or target information accumulated from image batches and streams. These mechanisms can reinforce confidently incorrect predictions and break down when clinical images arrive independently. We introduce CF-NODE, a novel counterfactual test-time adaptation framework for cross- domain DR grading. Instead of trusting prediction confidence or estimating a target distribution, CF-NODE asks how each prediction responds under a controlled intervention on the evidence supporting it. CF-NODE ranks internal spatial nodes using model-derived attention, feature magnitude, and node-set similarity, progressively attenuates the highest-ranked nodes, and uses the stability of the resulting expected-grade response to apply a bounded calibration of the predicted grade distribution. The framework is fully frozen and adapts every image independently using only geometric views and a fixed source-derived prior, requiring no target-derived information or model updates. We evaluate CF-NODE on five external DR datasets under repeated-seed evaluation against TENT, EATA, SAR, and T3A. CF-NODE outperforms all four methods with statistically significant improvements over the second-best method, improves AUC on every target domain, and attains the highest average AUC and macro-F1, delivering stronger grade discrimination together with more balanced recognition across DR severity levels. These results demonstrate that counterfactual intervention sensitivity provides consistent and deployment-ready domain robustness for single-image clinical inference.
papers.summary: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading models degrade on images from new cameras and clinics, and common test-time adaptation methods rely on entropy minimization or batches of target data, which can reinforce confident mistakes and fail when images arrive one at a time. `CF-NODE` keeps the model frozen and adapts each image independently: it ranks internal spatial nodes, progressively attenuates the most influential ones, and uses how stable the predicted grade stays to calibrate the output distribution. Across five external DR datasets, it **outperforms `TENT`, `EATA`, `SAR`, and `T3A` with statistically significant gains**, improving AUC on every target domain and achieving the best average AUC and macro-F1.

papers.title: Rank Measures of Fine-Tuning Updates Need a Noise Baseline
papers.abstract: Studies of what fine-tuning does to a language model often summarise the weight update $\Delta W$ by its rank. We compare the rank measures used for this against the same measures on a random matrix of the same shape, and against two harder references: the pretrained weights, and matched fine-tunes without alignment content. Measures that count directions put our fine-tuning updates only a little below noise; stable rank, computed from the same singular values, puts them far below. Both are right: an update has a few strong directions on top of a long tail. The pattern holds for thirteen released pairs up to 8B parameters, and it is not a mark of alignment: with training held fixed, instruction data does not stand out from Wikipedia or code, DPO gives the same update whether its preference labels are real or half swapped at random (one model, modest preference strength), and scrambled text gives the most concentrated update of all. Applied to a recent claim that post-training is superficial because the effective rank of the weights barely changes, the baselines show that a random update of the same size leaves that rank almost unchanged while wrecking the model, and that an edit built on the effective rank of the update has no measurable effect in our tests. Rank measures of weight updates need a noise baseline, and claims about alignment need a control without alignment content.
papers.summary: Researchers often describe what fine-tuning does to a language model by the rank of the weight update, and this work checks those rank measures against a random matrix of the same shape, the pretrained weights, and matched fine-tunes trained without alignment content. Measures that count directions put fine-tuning updates only slightly below noise, while `stable rank` puts them far below it, because an update has a few strong directions on top of a long tail. The pattern holds across thirteen released model pairs up to 8B parameters and does not depend on alignment: instruction data looks no different from Wikipedia or code, `DPO` gives the same update with real or half-randomized preference labels, and scrambled text produces the most concentrated update of all. Applying these baselines to a recent claim that post-training is superficial shows that **a random update of the same size barely changes effective rank while wrecking the model**.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Can Induce Local Geometry for Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting
papers.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting remains a challenge in supervised continual learning, as adapting to new tasks causes representation drift and loss of previously learned information. This raises the question of which representational changes should be constrained while preserving plasticity. We therefore introduce Sparse Autoencoder Geometric Anchoring (SAGA), which converts a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) trained at each task boundary into local, low-rank constraints on representation drift. Replay examples specify where the constraints apply, while leading right singular directions of the encoder Jacobian specify which changes are penalized. The resulting geometry is input dependent and can be retained without keeping the SAE for subsequent tasks' training. We establish its local relation to latent code matching, define its spectral truncation error, and derive a conditional bound on frozen-readout drift. With replay and snapshot history, the method achieves the highest mean Class-IL accuracy and lowest mean forgetting among the evaluated ER, DER++, ER-ACE, and SGD baselines on three pretrained ViT-B/16 benchmarks, with accuracy gains of 12.15, 4.79, and 3.22 percentage points over the strongest conventional baseline on CIFAR-100, CUB-200, and ImageNet-R, respectively. From scratch results are more mixed, while rank ablations and geometry controls show that SAE-induced low-rank geometry offers useful stability-plasticity trade-offs.
papers.summary: When a model keeps learning new tasks, its internal representations drift and it forgets earlier tasks, a problem known as catastrophic forgetting. `Sparse Autoencoder Geometric Anchoring` (`SAGA`) trains a sparse autoencoder at each task boundary and turns it into local, low-rank penalties on representation drift: replay examples decide where the penalties apply, and the leading singular directions of the encoder's Jacobian decide which changes are penalized. The authors give theoretical bounds on the approximation and on drift in a frozen readout layer. On pretrained `ViT-B/16` benchmarks, `SAGA` achieves the best class-incremental accuracy and the least forgetting, with **gains of 12.15, 4.79 and 3.22 percentage points over the strongest baseline on `CIFAR-100`, `CUB-200` and `ImageNet-R`**, though results when training from scratch are more mixed.

papers.title: Null Controls Are Necessary but Not Sufficient: Evaluating Acceptance Guards for Scientific Discovery and Interpretability
papers.abstract:
Automated discovery systems propose scientific explanations and test which to accept. Does passing a test establish the intended claim? We develop four executable operations for changing physical descriptions: identifying redundancies (L1), coarse-graining dynamics (L2), transferring structure (L3), and inferring missing quantities from conservation imbalances (L4). We evaluate these operations and three interpretability settings through null acceptance (NAR), positive acceptance (PAR), and consequence agreement (CAR).
  A reduction mapping every state to zero predicts its own future perfectly. It passes closure on 96% of 129 public chaotic systems despite retaining no dynamical variation. An independent observable-preservation test rejects it throughout. On controlled benchmarks, the combined criteria accept 24/24 genuine reductions and reject 72/72 nulls. The other operations distinguish symmetries from redundancies, validate transfers, and reject spurious conservation imbalances. In language and ESM-2 protein models, linear CKA remains unchanged when a proposed correspondence is randomly rotated, whereas localized interventions distinguish genuine mappings from tested nulls. In sparse autoencoders, enrichment rejects all 16 tested nulls, yet independent ablation supports 45% of evaluable enriched features, compared with 0.5% of matched controls.
  These results reveal two acceptance gaps: descriptive tests can accept scientifically empty candidates, and accepted candidates can lack independently verified consequences. Reliable automated discovery requires evaluating both what a test accepts and the scientific consequences it establishes. Code and data: https://real-project-aether.github.io/project-aether/.
papers.summary: Automated discovery systems propose scientific explanations and then run tests to decide which to accept, and this work asks whether passing those tests actually establishes the intended claim. The authors build four executable operations on physical descriptions and score them, along with three interpretability settings, by null acceptance, positive acceptance, and consequence agreement. A trivial reduction that maps every state to zero **passes the closure test on 96% of 129 chaotic systems** but is rejected by an independent observable-preservation test. Similar gaps show up in interpretability: linear `CKA` does not change when a proposed correspondence is randomly rotated, and only 45% of sparse-autoencoder features that pass an enrichment test are supported by independent ablation, which suggests acceptance tests need both null controls and independent checks of their consequences.

papers.title: Learnable Splines for Unstructured Neural Operators
papers.abstract: Neural operators approximate solution operators of partial differential equations at a fraction of the cost of numerical solvers. Efficient grid-based architectures such as the Fourier neural operator (FNO) assume uniform rectangular grids, whereas engineering simulations use large, irregular, and locally refined meshes. We introduce L-SplineFNO, a memory-efficient neural operator that couples an FNO backbone with a sparse, learnable tensor-product B-spline transfer between unstructured meshes and a latent Cartesian grid. A local normalised scatter avoids the geometry-dependent solve of analytic spline transformation while preserving compact support, partition of unity, and spline smoothness by construction. The neural operator, conditioned on global design and operating parameters, learns the mapping of geometry to the field solution. Across six three-dimensional engineering benchmarks, L-SplineFNO achieves strong predictive accuracy while requiring substantially less memory and compute than baseline operators, scaling to 26.6 million nodes in training and 46 million in inference on a single A100 GPU. It also supports zero-shot super-resolution and efficient closed-form spatial derivatives. Uniquely, the analytic spline decoder yields rigorous prediction bounds over continuous space and uncertain parameters, via Bernstein convex hulls and Taylor models, demonstrated on a 29.2-million-node MAST-U tokamak model.
papers.summary: Neural operators approximate solutions to partial differential equations much faster than numerical solvers, but efficient designs such as the Fourier neural operator (`FNO`) assume uniform grids, while engineering simulations use irregular, locally refined meshes. `L-SplineFNO` pairs an `FNO` backbone with a sparse, learnable B-spline transfer between unstructured meshes and a latent Cartesian grid, using a local normalized scatter that keeps the properties of splines without an expensive geometry-dependent solve. Across six 3D engineering benchmarks it achieves strong accuracy with much less memory and compute than baseline operators, **scaling to 26.6 million nodes in training and 46 million in inference on a single A100 GPU**. Because the spline decoder is analytic, it also gives closed-form derivatives and rigorous prediction bounds, which the authors demonstrate on a 29.2-million-node `MAST-U` tokamak model.

papers.title: Lean4AgenticRL: Advancing Agentic RL with Verifiable Multi-level Process Rewards
papers.abstract: Enhancing the agentic capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to tackle complex software engineering (SWE) and general terminal-usage problems is a pressing challenge. Current state-of-the-art LLMs often go through large-scale agentic Reinforcement Learning (RL). However, they mostly rely on high-level outcome rewards, with minimal consideration of low-level toolcall and mid-level workflow-stage rewards, which makes the training less effective. To overcome this limitation, we propose **Lean4AgenticRL**, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first framework that grounds multi-level process rewards in the unified Lean4 formalization schema for open-ended agentic RL. **Lean4AgenticRL** first builds a *problem-specific workflow* system that balances the agent's own capability and controllability during execution, laying the foundation for further verification. Subsequently, our workflow formalization and multi-level reward annotation methods enable agent behavior verification within a general harness system. It provides multi-level rewards to support more effective agentic RL with the workflow-stage-normalized GRPO algorithm. Using **Lean4AgenticRL**, we train **LAR-9B/27B**, a family of models with enhanced agentic capability. Extensive experiments indicate that our model outperforms the leading model of similar size. **LAR-27B** achieves **77.3%** on TerminalBench-2.1. On average, our models outperform the base model by **9.89%** and surpass the second-best model of comparable size we know by **5.07%**. These results indicate the potential of integrating formal methods in enhancing open-ended agentic RL.
papers.summary: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) for software engineering and terminal tasks usually rewards only the final outcome and ignores whether individual tool calls and workflow stages were done correctly. `Lean4AgenticRL` builds a problem-specific workflow for each task, formalizes agent behavior in the `Lean4` proof language so it can be verified, and uses the result to give rewards at the tool-call, workflow-stage, and outcome levels, trained with a stage-normalized variant of `GRPO`. The resulting `LAR-9B` and `LAR-27B` models beat their base model by 9.89% on average and the next-best comparable model by 5.07%, with **`LAR-27B` reaching 77.3% on `TerminalBench-2.1`**.

papers.title: Where Prefill Expert Reduction Hurts MoE Models: A Few Prompt Tokens Carry Most of the Short-Answer F1 Loss
papers.abstract: Running prompt tokens through fewer routed experts during prefill is a simple way to make mixture-of-experts (MoE) serving cheaper, yet it is unclear what this damages. We locate the damage with token-, layer- and attention-path interventions on short-answer question answering in four MoE families. At half the experts the F1 loss of three families is mostly answer form: the model still finds the answer but stops answering briefly. In Qwen3-30B-A3B this loss is made at the two chat-template tokens before the answer, and in DeepSeek-V2-Lite at the first 8-32 prompt tokens, where its instruction sits; by answer likelihood these positions account for about half and a fifth of the damage. Reduction changes the first token's attention mass, norm and largest activation by less than 4%, and restoring super experts or massive activations recovers at most about a quarter of the loss, well below keeping the sensitive positions full. On real prompts with about 4% of tokens at full experts, placing them on the task interface keeps F1 within one point of the unmodified model, while placing them at random in the documents is about 3 points worse (two of five prespecified primary comparisons; the others were undecided or not run). Because the answer boundary always ends a single-turn prompt, and DeepSeek's loss was no longer detectable once its instruction moved away from the start, the sensitive tokens lay at the prompt ends in every sensitive layout we found, so rules that keep the ends are not distinguished from rules that read application marks. Time to first token falls about 14% on 11K-token prompts and not at 2K tokens.
papers.summary: Routing prompt tokens through fewer experts during prefill is a simple way to make mixture-of-experts (MoE) serving cheaper, and this study uses token-, layer- and attention-level interventions across four MoE families to find out what that harms on short-answer question answering. At half the experts, most of the F1 loss in three families comes from answer format: the model still finds the answer but stops answering briefly. The damage is concentrated in a few positions, such as the two chat-template tokens right before the answer in `Qwen3-30B-A3B` and the instruction tokens at the start of the prompt in `DeepSeek-V2-Lite`. **Keeping about 4% of tokens at full experts, placed on the task interface, keeps F1 within one point of the unmodified model**, while time to first token drops about 14% on 11K-token prompts.

papers.title: High prevalence of antagonizing rhetoric in trending topics on Twitter/X
papers.abstract: Disagreement between political opponents is a central element of democracy. This disagreement can be voiced in different ways. An opponent can be antagonized, i.e. portrayed as an enemy that needs to be overcome, or they can be criticized, i.e. treated as a legitimate adversary with whom one can engage. While the latter is a fundamental part of democratic exchange, the former can be detrimental to public discourse. Political disagreement increasingly takes place on social media, where negativity towards political out-groups has been found to drive engagement. However, existing research has largely treated such negativity as a single dimension, leaving open whether it is antagonization or criticism that circulates on these platforms. This work addresses this gap by introducing a computational approach to detect these two types of rhetoric in text and identify its targets. On a corpus of over 17 million tweets from trending topics in the German Twittersphere, the method reveals that about a third of all tweets contain antagonizing rhetoric. Comparing tweets from trending topics to a random sample shows that the discourse in trending topics is systematically more antagonizing than ordinary Twitter communication. Combining antagonization detection with a large-scale estimation of users' political leaning, we find that right-leaning users employ antagonizing rhetoric significantly more than their left-leaning counterparts. Furthermore, both forms of oppositional rhetoric are strongly amplified within political camps, with multipliers retweeting them up to twice as often as tweets without oppositional rhetoric. Finally, patterns of antagonized targets reveal how different political camps construct their out-groups, with the right-wing populist party AfD and the Green party as the central antagonists of the opposing camps.
papers.summary: Studies of political negativity on social media usually treat it as a single dimension, without separating antagonization (casting opponents as enemies) from criticism (engaging them as legitimate adversaries). The authors build a computational method that detects both kinds of rhetoric and their targets, and apply it to over 17 million tweets from trending topics in the German Twittersphere. **About a third of tweets in trending topics contain antagonizing rhetoric**, more than in a random sample of Twitter, and right-leaning users antagonize significantly more than left-leaning ones. Both kinds of oppositional rhetoric are retweeted up to twice as often within political camps, and the AfD and the Green party are the main antagonized targets of the opposing camps.

papers.title: Progressive Misalignment Can Emerge from Benign Recursive Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: Training models on their own outputs has attracted widespread attention as a possible route to advance AI capabilities. One prominent approach is self-distillation, where a model is trained to match the token-level predictions it would have produced when given access to additional context, such as a cue, feedback, or instruction. However, the safety properties of this training procedure are poorly understood. In this paper, we present a surprising safety failure of recursive self-distillation, where each self-distilled model becomes the teacher for the next round of training. We observe that when a safe model is recursively self-distilled on its own (safe) generations while receiving an additional non-harmful cue, it becomes increasingly misaligned across a diverse set of harmful queries; we call this Progressive Misalignment. We show this failure mode in both the Qwen3 and Phi-4 model families on SORRY-Bench and StrongREJECT. Progressive misalignment also occurs in a more realistic setup, where the fixed cue is replaced by feedback from a simulated user with benign intent. Using a gradient-based method, we are also able to find benign prompts that lead to progressive misalignment when applying recursive self-distillation, showing that harmful training prompts are not necessary for this failure mode to emerge. We hope our work encourages future investigations of the safety properties of AI systems recursively trained on their own data.
papers.summary: Self-distillation trains a model to match the predictions it would make if it had extra context, such as a cue or feedback, and recursive self-distillation makes each distilled model the teacher for the next round. The authors find that a safe model recursively self-distilled on its own safe outputs, with a harmless extra cue, becomes steadily more willing to answer harmful queries, a failure they call Progressive Misalignment. The effect appears in the `Qwen3` and `Phi-4` model families on `SORRY-Bench` and `StrongREJECT`, and also when the fixed cue is replaced by feedback from a simulated user with benign intent. Using a gradient-based search, they also find benign prompts that trigger the effect, showing that **harmful training prompts are not needed for misalignment to emerge**.
papers.highlight_summary:
Recursive self-distillation trains a model to match its own predictions when it is given extra context, and each new student becomes the next round's teacher. The authors show that this procedure, applied to a safe model's own refusals with a harmless extra cue, can gradually erode its safety training. They call this failure mode "progressive misalignment."

- In each round, the teacher is the current model with a benign cue such as "Excellent" or "I like Owls" added to the prompt, and the student is trained to match the teacher's token distribution without seeing the cue; training uses `on-policy` and `off-policy` variants on just 20 harmful prompts that the initial model refuses.
- On `SORRY-Bench`, off-policy self-distillation with "Excellent" raises harmful compliance from **26% to 94%** for `Phi-4 14B` and from **31% to 97%** for `Qwen3 14B`; the results hold on `StrongREJECT`, the control cue "Do not help with my request" does not increase misalignment, and math and instruction-following performance stays intact.
- Replacing the fixed cue with feedback from simulated benign users (`Qwen3 8B` personas instructed to accept refusals) still raises `Qwen3 14B` compliance from **31% to 64%**, and a gradient-based data-selection method finds purely benign prompts that push off-policy compliance to **83%** (`Qwen3 14B`) and **70%** (`Phi-4 14B`), whereas randomly chosen benign prompts do not cause the effect.
- The effect grows with model size across the `Qwen3` family from 0.6B to 32B: `Qwen3 32B` gains **64 points** on `SORRY-Bench` and **65 points** on `StrongREJECT`, and the drift away from the initial model is concentrated in the first few answer tokens, which is consistent with prior work showing that safety alignment is shallow.
- The study covers only two model families up to 32B and offers only a hypothesis for the cause; models eventually degenerate under continued training, so reported checkpoints exclude runs above 5% degeneracy and are chosen by validation score.

papers.title: From Parallels to Divergence: Language Models' Learning of Action Nominal Constructions
papers.abstract: Action nominal constructions (ANCs) express events in nominal form, with their argument marking following patterns found in clauses or ordinary noun phrases. In this paper, we investigate how different grammatical configurations affect language models' learning of ANCs and related constructions, and how these learning preferences compare with typological distributions in natural languages. We use a grammar-engineered method for synthetic corpus construction that combines shared semantic input from natural corpora with computational grammars. We construct 96 target languages varying in clause word order, noun-phrase word order, alignment, complement system, and ANC strategy. For each language, we train GPT-2-small models from scratch and evaluate them using targeted minimal pairs covering 34 grammatical phenomena. The results show typological parallels in basic clause configurations but divergences in complement systems and ANC strategies, with models also learning combinations rare or unattested in natural languages. This partial alignment suggests that natural language distributions may reflect both general learning pressures and functional demands not fully captured by model learning experiments.
papers.summary: Action nominal constructions express events as nouns, and languages differ in whether they mark the arguments of these constructions like clauses or like ordinary noun phrases. The authors use computational grammars to generate synthetic corpora for 96 artificial languages that vary in word order, alignment, complement system, and nominal strategy, then train `GPT-2-small` from scratch on each and test it on minimal pairs covering 34 grammatical phenomena. Model learning preferences **match typological patterns for basic clause configurations but diverge for complement systems and nominal strategies**, and the models also learn combinations that are rare or unattested in natural languages. The authors read this as evidence that natural language distributions reflect functional pressures as well as learnability.

papers.title: Has GPT-6-Astra Achieved Embodied Intelligence?
papers.abstract: GPT-6-Astra demonstrates a level of competence in robotic manipulation and navigation that challenges the conventional paradigm of building specialized models for individual tasks and embodiments. In this report, we ask not only how capable GPT-6-Astra is, but what its capabilities imply for the field. First, we probe the limits of standalone GPT-6-Astra. We conduct a large-scale evaluation across 12 representative benchmarks spanning tabletop manipulation, humanoids, mobile platforms, and dexterous hands. Under a unified protocol that allows in-context learning (ICL) from training-set demonstrations and substantially increases the number of execution steps, GPT-6-Astra achieves unprecedented performance (Fig. 1). Future research may focus on improving 1) the generality of ICL 2) cost and execution time, 3) physical-state verification, 4) recovery from irreversible failures, and 5) long-horizon preservation of progress. Second, we study the agentic harness for embodied control. We identify that close-loop coordination between a high-level "System 2" reasoner (i.e., GPT-6-Astra) and a low-level "System 1" controller (e.g., {\pi}0.5) is costly but effective. Third, we examine GPT-6-Astra on real-world deployment. Our experiments on 8 robot configurations reveal substantial gaps: 1) robot demonstrations required for ICL are expensive to collect, and 2) it is implausible to trade longer execution for higher success rates with physical constraints. Fourth, we envision the next generation of embodied benchmarks. We develop a prototype that 1) derives tasks from real-world needs, 2) provides no in-domain demonstrations, and 3) judges agents on a world clock that keeps running while they deliberate. Taken together, our results suggest that GPT-6-Astra has largely crossed the threshold of embodied competence, but not yet that of practical embodied intelligence.
papers.summary: This report evaluates how far the general-purpose `GPT-6-Astra` model goes as a robot controller without task-specific training. Across 12 benchmarks covering tabletop manipulation, humanoids, mobile platforms, and dexterous hands, and allowing in-context learning from demonstrations plus extended execution budgets, it achieves unprecedented performance, and pairing it as a high-level reasoner with a low-level controller such as `π0.5` proves effective but costly. Real-world tests on 8 robot configurations expose large gaps: demonstrations are expensive to collect, and physical constraints make it impractical to trade longer execution for higher success. The authors conclude that **the model has crossed the threshold of embodied competence but not of practical embodied intelligence**, and they prototype a benchmark built from real-world needs with no in-domain demonstrations and a running wall clock.
papers.highlight_summary:
A joint team asks whether a general-purpose multimodal model, `GPT-6-Astra`, can replace specialized `VLA` and world-action models for robot control. They push it to its limits on simulated benchmarks, ablate the harness that connects it to the robot, test it on real robots, and propose a deployment-oriented benchmark that also counts the time it spends reasoning.

- Under a unified protocol, `GPT-6-Astra` first studies each benchmark's training demonstrations and writes a frozen "knowledge package" of task notes, motion references, and helper code, with no weight updates; with up to 10× the official step budget, it nears saturation on `LIBERO` and `SIMPLE` and reaches **81.9% on `RoboDojo`** and **87.3% on `DexJoCo`**, and in-context learning alone lifts `SIMPLE` from **70.8% to 90.8%**.
- The harness ablations on `RoboDojo` show that closed-loop review of `π0.5`-proposed actions beats both the standalone `VLA` (6.91%) and open-loop execution, and adding in-context learning reaches **54.17%**, but at **19.3M tokens per task**; joint-angle control loses 5.84 points, while adaptive action chunking gains 4.44.
- On 8 real robots in a zero-shot setting, rigid pick-and-place succeeds in **17/18** trials and the model shows emergent active vision (moving a free arm's camera to see an occluded vase), but plug insertion fails in **0/11** trials and deformable-object and long-horizon tasks remain hard.
- Cost is the main practical barrier: even near-solved `LIBERO-Long++` episodes take about **1M tokens and nearly an hour each**, and on the `Unitree G1` humanoid about 90% of each run is spent deliberating, while safety stops, overheating, and real-time limits remove the "more steps means more success" trade-off on physical hardware.
- Recurring failures include declaring physical success when the task is not actually done, being unable to recover from irreversible mishaps such as spills or dropped parts, and undoing earlier progress on long-horizon tasks, which motivates the authors' prototype household benchmark built on need-based tasks, no demonstrations, and a world clock that keeps running while the model thinks.

papers.title: Upper bounds on the number of causal pieces in spiking neural networks
papers.abstract: The input space of single-spike neural networks decomposes into causal pieces, and the number of causal pieces has been shown to provide a lower bound on the approximation error for some spiking neural networks. While this decomposition is applicable to a wide range of spiking neuron models, the limits of how many causal pieces can be realised by spiking neural networks are still unknown. In this work, we derive two complementary upper bounds on the number of causal pieces in feedforward single-spike neural networks. First, we establish a combinatorial bound given by the poly-Bernoulli numbers, which applies to a broad class of spiking neuron models. The bound is of order $e^{2(L-1)N\log N+\mathcal{O}(N)}$, with network depth $L$ and maximum layer width $N$. Second, for a specific set of neuron models, we derive a bound based on hyperplane arrangements. Applying the latter framework, we obtain bounds of order $\mathcal{O}\!\left(N^{(4L-3)(N_0-1)}\right)$ for the non-leaky integrate-and-fire model with exponential synapses and the ReLU-type spike response model, and $\mathcal{O}\!\left(N^{L(N_0-1)}\right)$ for the leaky integrate-and-fire model with Dirac-$\delta$ synapses, where $N_0$ is the input dimension. For the non-leaky integrate-and-fire model with Dirac-$\delta$ synapses, additional temporal structure allows us to sharpen the general combinatorial bound to one that depends only on $N_0$, independently of the network depth and widths.
papers.summary: The input space of a single-spike neural network splits into causal pieces, and the number of pieces is known to give a lower bound on approximation error for some spiking networks, but nobody knew how many pieces such networks can actually realize. The authors derive a combinatorial upper bound based on poly-Bernoulli numbers that applies to a broad class of spiking neuron models, of order exponential in depth times width log width. For specific neuron models, including integrate-and-fire variants and a ReLU-type spike response model, they derive tighter polynomial bounds from hyperplane arrangements. For the non-leaky integrate-and-fire model with Dirac-delta synapses, **the bound depends only on the input dimension**, regardless of network depth or width.

papers.title: Generative Value Classifier
papers.abstract: Q-learning is premised on learning a function to predict the value of a state-action pair, with the goal of using such a function to guide policy improvement. Most approaches learn this function from scratch using scalar or distributional return targets. This discriminative approach leaves another source of supervision for learning representations unused: the actions themselves. Rather than directly predict the return of a state-action pair, we ask the reverse question: how likely is the action under each possible return? This perspective provides a critic whose generative component is a return-conditioned policy, which can share the actor's architecture. Training this policy supervises the critic with every action rather than with returns alone, and a squared-error loss anchors the critic's Q-value to the bootstrapped target.
