We evaluate our approach on both offline and online RL tasks and show gains over leading discriminative methods, including distributional RL methods.
papers.summary: Q-learning critics are usually trained only to predict returns, which ignores a second source of supervision: the actions themselves. The `Generative Value Classifier` reverses the question and models how likely an action is under each possible return, so the critic's generative component is a return-conditioned policy that can share the actor's architecture. Training this policy supervises the critic with every action, and a squared-error loss ties its Q-value to the bootstrapped target. Across offline and online RL tasks, the method **outperforms leading discriminative critics, including distributional RL methods**.

papers.title: RealCLI: Toward a Unified Evaluation of Human-Agent Collaboration for CLI Agents
papers.abstract: Command-line interface (CLI) agents increasingly execute longer-horizon tasks, yet existing benchmarks either assume that user instructions remain fixed throughout execution or evaluate task outcomes without capturing runtime collaboration quality. In this paper, we present REALCLI, a paired benchmark that unifies the evaluation of task execution and human-agent collaboration quality on realistic CLI tasks. To comprehensively measure collaboration, REALCLI builds a five-dimensional framework, operationalized into 22 sub-dimensions and 51 interaction scenario templates. REALCLI provides two modes for paired comparison: REALCLI-EXEC supplies complete specifications upfront, whereas REALCLI-COLLAB introduces a scripted user that delivers progressive information, corrections, constraint revisions, and authorization decisions. Evaluations reveal profound capability gaps in frontier agents: the best configuration attains an average score of only 49.2%, and when evaluated by the joint collaboration score ($J_{\mathrm{collab}}$), the peak performance reaches merely 37.6%. These results show that task effectiveness diverges sharply from collaboration quality, with models consistently struggling in steerability, trust calibration, and safety boundary management. REALCLI provides a rigorous, reproducible foundation for measuring and advancing collaborative CLI agents.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for command-line interface (CLI) agents usually assume the user's instructions stay fixed, or they score only the final result without measuring how well the agent collaborates while it runs. `RealCLI` pairs two modes on realistic CLI tasks: `RealCLI-Exec` gives the full specification upfront, while `RealCLI-Collab` uses a scripted user who reveals information gradually, issues corrections, revises constraints, and makes authorization decisions, scored on a five-dimension framework with 22 sub-dimensions. The best frontier configuration averages only 49.2%, and **the peak joint collaboration score is just 37.6%**. Models struggle most with steerability, trust calibration, and respecting safety boundaries, and task success turns out to be a poor predictor of collaboration quality.

papers.title: AuditKIT: A Unified Evaluation Spine for Benchmarking, Judging, and Comparing Large Language Models and Agentic Systems
papers.abstract: Evaluating language models and agents requires combining benchmark accuracy, judge-based assessment, runtime performance, tool-use behavior, and retrieval quality. Differences in interfaces, metric semantics, and trace formats complicate these comparisons and can hide failures in agentic workflows. We present AuditKIT, a source-available evaluation library that records these measurements in one result representation, with direction-aware metric contracts, configuration fingerprints, and extensible metrics and backends. For agents, it provides turn-aware tool-call matching, separates parallel from sequential execution, and distinguishes verified task outcomes from trajectory-level diagnostics. Missing or unobservable evidence is marked unscored rather than counted as failure. For retrieval-augmented generation, it combines ranked retrieval metrics, judged grounding, and deterministic evidence checks. Seven case studies spanning model comparison, serving runtimes, retrieval, tool calling, and interoperability show how answer extraction, runtime behavior, and metric selection change evaluation outcomes.
papers.summary: Evaluating language models and agents means combining benchmark accuracy, judge scores, runtime performance, tool-use behavior, and retrieval quality, and differences in interfaces and trace formats across these can hide failures. `AuditKIT` is a source-available library that records all these measurements in one result format, with direction-aware metric contracts and configuration fingerprints. For agents it matches tool calls turn by turn, separates parallel from sequential execution, and **marks missing evidence as unscored rather than as a failure**. For retrieval-augmented generation it combines ranking metrics, judged grounding, and deterministic evidence checks, and seven case studies show how answer extraction, runtime behavior, and metric choice can change evaluation outcomes.

papers.title: Predicting Privileged Information Effectiveness for On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) enables large language models (LLMs) to learn from privileged information (PI) without a separate teacher model. However, prior work largely treats PI as a fixed design choice, leaving the effects of its content and construction poorly understood. This challenge is particularly important in multi-turn agentic settings, where trajectories contain actions, observations, and reasoning that can be transformed into PI in many ways. We systematically evaluate 16 PI configurations across three multi-turn agentic benchmarks and three student models that vary in scale and reasoning mode. We find that PI effectiveness depends on its content, generation source, and the student model. Information-dense trajectories and PI produced by more capable generators generally yield larger gains, whereas thinking models benefit less consistently. To assess PI before training, we compare PI utility with two KL-based metrics: sampled-token reverse KL ($D$) and error-step KL contrast ($\Delta d^{-}_{\mathrm{err}}$). The KL-based metrics track post-training performance more consistently than PI utility, which can be distorted by information leakage. Empirically, selecting each task's PI by $\Delta d^{-}_{\mathrm{err}}$ also improves post-training performance over random selection, most when the PI candidates differ widely. Finally, effective PI remains beneficial when combined with GRPO, allowing the combined objective to outperform a strong GRPO baseline. Overall, our results provide practical guidance for constructing and evaluating PI in OPSD training.
papers.summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) lets a large language model learn from privileged information (PI), such as hints or reference trajectories, without a separate teacher, but how to build that information has mostly been treated as a fixed design choice. The authors test 16 PI configurations on three multi-turn agentic benchmarks and three student models, and find that information-dense trajectories and PI from stronger generators usually help more, while thinking models benefit less consistently. Two KL-divergence metrics computed before training predict post-training performance better than raw PI utility, which information leakage can distort, and **choosing PI per task with the error-step KL contrast beats random selection**. Effective PI also improves results when combined with `GRPO`, beating a strong `GRPO`-only baseline.

papers.title: Towards Reconstructing Geographically Diverse Architecture with 3D Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Internet-scale photo collections of real-world landmarks have driven progress in 3D computer vision yet remain highly challenging for modern 3D foundation models (3DFMs) that estimate scene structure in a single feed-forward pass. In this work, we introduce ArchWorld, a benchmark of 3D architectural landmarks with high geographic coverage and rich metadata. We use this benchmark to conduct a thorough error analysis of current 3DFMs to understand where they fall short and how they can be improved. We examine socially relevant disparities in model error and find that model performance varies by geographic region; however, unlike typical fairness regimes, the trends only partially match training data representation. Our investigation reveals that the observed geographic disparities reflect not only differences in data representation and scene size but also differences in region-specific architectural features and background distractors that make scenes from different regions inherently vary in difficulty. Leveraging insights from these model failings, we introduce an intervention scheme that improves 3DFM performance while simultaneously reducing geographic disparities.
papers.summary: 3D foundation models, which estimate scene structure in a single feed-forward pass, still struggle with internet photo collections of real-world landmarks. The authors introduce `ArchWorld`, a benchmark of architectural landmarks with wide geographic coverage and rich metadata, and use it for a detailed error analysis. Model accuracy varies by region, but **the disparities only partly track training-data representation** and also reflect scene size, region-specific architectural features, and background distractors. Based on these failure modes, the authors propose an intervention that improves accuracy while reducing geographic disparities.

papers.title: alkhder at ImageEval 2026 Shared Tasks: Constrained Selection and Rotation-Averaged Logit Scoring for Multimodal Hallucination Detection
papers.abstract: We describe our submission to Subtask~1b of ImageEval 2026. The task consists of selecting the single visually valid statement from three candidates paired with an image, and is in both English and Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). Our system uses a pre-trained 7B vision--language model in a zero-shot setting, without task-specific training or fine-tuning. We formulate the task as a constrained selection problem and choose the answer using next-token log-probabilities. To reduce answer-position bias, we apply a Latin-square rotation to the candidate statements. Our system achieves CI scores of 0.0510 on the English test set and 0.0960 on the MSA test set, reducing CI relative to the official 3B baselines reported on devtest by 83.7\% and 80.4\%, respectively.
papers.summary: This shared-task submission tackles multimodal hallucination detection: picking the single visually valid statement out of three candidates paired with an image, in both English and Modern Standard Arabic. The system uses a pretrained 7B vision-language model zero-shot, frames the task as constrained selection over next-token log-probabilities, and rotates candidate order with a Latin square to reduce position bias. It **reduces the task's CI metric by 83.7% (English) and 80.4% (Arabic) relative to the official 3B baselines**.

papers.title: Source-Aware Dynamic Pricing with Strategic Buyers
papers.abstract: In modern commerce, firms and platforms typically use customer features from different sources to personalize prices: some features are verified using seller records or third-party data, while others are self-reported and may be strategically manipulated by buyers seeking lower prices. We therefore introduce a novel source-aware framework for contextual dynamic pricing with strategic buyers in a high-dimensional semiparametric setting, where buyer valuations follow a sparse linear model with an unknown noise distribution. To account for differences in manipulability across feature sources while enabling effective valuation learning, we develop the Source-Aware Localized exploration and calibrated Exploitation (SALE) pricing policy, which draws on verified features to localize price exploration and combines verified and reported features to correct for strategic manipulation during exploitation. Our localized exploration design allows converting binary purchase feedback into unbiased signals of conditional mean valuations, yielding a new population equation that supports consistent sparse estimation despite non-i.i.d. buyer arrivals. Building on this estimate, we develop a localized empirical-process analysis that exploits intrinsic sparse geometry to establish uniform guarantees for nonparametric estimation of the noise distribution in the high-dimensional setting. With these estimation guarantees, we establish SALE's self-recovery property, which keeps localized exploration valid with high probability and leads to a sublinear expected regret bound. Both simulation studies and real-data experiments demonstrate the appealing performance of SALE. To the best of our knowledge, our study is the first to provide a theoretical and practical framework for incorporating information provenance into dynamic pricing with strategic buyers.
papers.summary: Platforms that personalize prices use customer features from different sources: some are verified, while others are self-reported, and buyers may misreport those to get lower prices. The `SALE` pricing policy uses verified features to localize price exploration and combines verified and reported features to correct for manipulation when exploiting, in a high-dimensional setting where valuations follow a sparse linear model with unknown noise. The analysis turns binary purchase feedback into unbiased valuation signals, estimates the noise distribution nonparametrically, and proves a **sublinear expected regret bound**. Simulations and real-data experiments support the theory.

papers.title: Learning User Representations to Improve Simulation Fidelity
papers.abstract: User simulators enable interactive training and evaluation of AI assistants at scale. Yet current simulators struggle to reproduce the diverse behaviors of real users, leading to assistants that generalize poorly to underrepresented users. We identify user representations as an underexplored bottleneck in user simulation. User representations are natural-language descriptions that condition simulators to reproduce a particular user's behavior. A representation's quality becomes apparent in hindsight, through the behavior it induces in a simulator. To evaluate and optimize user representations, we formulate a conversation reconstruction task: given an original conversation, we generate a representation, condition a simulator on it, simulate a conversation, and then measure fidelity by comparing user behavior in the original and simulated conversations. This comparison also yields hindsight feedback, which identifies where the representation falls short and how it can be improved. We introduce hindsight distillation, an online training procedure that distills feedback-conditioned improvements into the representation generator, enabling it to generate improved representations directly from the original conversation. We present UserRepGen-4B, a representation generator trained with hindsight distillation. Across 700 conversations spanning seven datasets, hindsight feedback helps improve user representations at test time, and UserRepGen-4B generates representations that enable more faithful simulation than those generated by GPT-5.5. Beyond conversation reconstruction, learned representations improve simulation fidelity for unseen tasks, better preserve the population-level diversity of real users, and better distinguish users across conversations.
papers.summary: User simulators let AI assistants be trained and evaluated interactively at scale, but they struggle to reproduce how diverse real users behave. The authors point to the natural-language user description that conditions the simulator as a key bottleneck, and they measure its quality through conversation reconstruction: generate a description from a real conversation, simulate a new conversation from it, and compare user behavior. Their hindsight distillation method trains the description generator on feedback about where its descriptions fell short, producing `UserRepGen-4B`. Across 700 conversations from seven datasets, **`UserRepGen-4B` yields more faithful simulations than descriptions written by `GPT-5.5`**, and the learned descriptions also transfer to unseen tasks and better preserve population-level diversity.

papers.title: Learning smooth dynamics via Kinematic Interpolants
papers.abstract: Inferring dynamics from real-world experimental data is inherently ambiguous, as many plausible dynamical systems can explain the same positional observations at measurement times. For higher fidelity modeling of applications ranging from single-cell RNA to vortex dynamics and even flocking of birds, scientific observables increasingly also include velocity estimates that serve to resolve this issue. However, incorporating this rich information in a scalable manner, free of simulation or unnecessary approximations, has remained a difficult challenge. In this paper, we introduce Kinematic Interpolants (KI), a novel framework that extends the seminal methodology of stochastic interpolants to infer nonlinear dynamics across multiple snapshots in phase space, i.e., observables with position and velocity measurements. Empirically, we demonstrate that across several scientific datasets, KI achieves superior reconstruction of the underlying dynamics compared to existing baselines while requiring only a fraction of the training time.
papers.summary: Inferring dynamics from experimental snapshots is ambiguous when only positions are observed, and many scientific datasets, from single-cell RNA to bird flocking, now also include velocity estimates that could resolve that ambiguity. `Kinematic Interpolants` extend the stochastic interpolants framework to learn nonlinear dynamics across multiple snapshots in phase space, using both position and velocity, without simulation or unnecessary approximations. Across several scientific datasets the method **reconstructs the underlying dynamics better than existing baselines while needing only a fraction of their training time**.

papers.title: Learning the Shared Latent Structure of Cryo-EM Inverse Problems
papers.abstract: Understanding biomolecular function requires characterizing three-dimensional structure and conformational variability, for which cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) is a powerful tool. Cryo-EM produces noisy two-dimensional particle images in which molecular structure, particle pose, and imaging conditions are jointly encoded. Recovering biological information from these observations spans inverse problems including pose estimation, heterogeneity analysis, and reconstruction. These tasks are usually addressed independently despite shared protein structure and image formation, motivating a common representation across inverse problems. Since biologically meaningful differences may be spatially localized, we study self-distillation with complementary global and masked patch objectives. Because experimental dataset discrimination can reflect acquisition-specific cues, we develop controlled synthetic and experimental evaluations and find that structural discrimination benefits from dense spatial features. We introduce the EMber family of vision transformers, pre-trained on >50 million experimental particle images from 214 EMPIAR datasets together with simulated projections from 268,000 molecular assemblies. EMber improves upon existing methods at conformational and compositional discrimination by 14.85 and 14.26 percentage points, estimates conformational populations to within 1.59pp error with a linear probe, and produces particle assignments yielding reference-quality reconstructions in fewer epochs. We demonstrate how to learn representations that capture biological information for use across multiple cryo-EM inverse problems.
papers.summary: Cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) produces noisy 2D particle images that mix molecular structure, particle pose and imaging conditions. Tasks such as pose estimation, heterogeneity analysis and reconstruction are usually solved separately, even though they share the same underlying structure. The authors introduce `EMber`, a family of vision transformers pre-trained by self-distillation with global and masked-patch objectives. Training used over 50 million experimental particle images from 214 `EMPIAR` datasets plus simulated projections of 268,000 molecular assemblies. `EMber` beats existing methods at conformational and compositional discrimination by **14.85 and 14.26 percentage points**, estimates conformational populations within 1.59pp error using a linear probe, and produces particle assignments that reach reference-quality reconstructions in fewer epochs.

papers.title: alkhder at AlexandriaX-2026: Context-Aware English-to-Dialectal Arabic Dialogue Translation with QLoRA-Fine-Tuned NileChat-3B
papers.abstract: This paper describes team Alkhder's submission to Subtask 1 of the AlexandriaX-2026 shared task, which asks systems to translate English dialogue turns into thirteen Arabic dialects. We fine-tune NileChat-3B-Base with QLoRA on the Alexandria parallel dialogue corpus, training one set of adapter weights for all dialects. Each turn is translated conditioned on the target country and dialect, the domain, the participant roles, the speaker-addressee gender direction, and the preceding dialogue context. At inference, conversations are translated autoregressively and the model is fed its own previous outputs back as context without using any gold target-side test information. Under the constrained track, using only Alexandria data, it trains in about one hour and translates the private test set in under two hours. The system reaches a country-macro-averaged spBLEU of 20.36 and chrF++ of 36.64 on both tracks.
papers.summary: This is a shared-task system for the AlexandriaX-2026 challenge, which asks for English dialogue turns to be translated into thirteen Arabic dialects. The team fine-tuned `NileChat-3B-Base` with `QLoRA` on the `Alexandria` parallel dialogue corpus, using one set of adapter weights for all dialects. Each turn is conditioned on the target dialect, domain, participant roles, speaker-addressee gender and preceding context, and at inference the model's own earlier outputs are fed back as context. Training takes about an hour, and the system reaches a country-macro-averaged **spBLEU of 20.36** and chrF++ of 36.64.

papers.title: Literal Lock-In: How Test Language Shifts Literal Attraction in Typed Decision Models on Bengali Idioms
papers.abstract: Decision models, non-generative scorers that report a probability over caller-supplied options and emit no text, are increasingly deployed as routers, classifiers and guardrails. Because they generate nothing, rationales and chain-of-thought do not apply. We audit three: an encoder scorer, a decoder scorer and a closed API, entirely through interventions on their input, using expert-annotated Bengali idioms carrying a gold figurative and a gold literal gloss. Dropping an idiom's own literal gloss into the option list draws every arm toward it, taking 65% to 96% of each arm's remaining Bengali errors. A model-by-language matrix over one shared item set shows how far this depends on the test language: every arm is 1.9 to 6.4 times more captured in Bengali than in English on the same paired entries, the commercial model's apparent resistance is a property of its test language, and capability does not order the failure. Calibration degrades in all three arms, and on the open arms confidence inverts, so gating on it is worse than gating at random. On a semantics-free option list, where accuracy is at chance, the best-calibrated arm still reports mean confidence 0.82. Code and data: https://github.com/sakhadib/literal-lock-in.
papers.summary: Decision models are non-generative scorers that output probabilities over options supplied by the caller and are often used as routers, classifiers and guardrails. Because they produce no text, chain-of-thought inspection does not apply, so the authors audit three of them (an encoder scorer, a decoder scorer and a closed API) purely by intervening on inputs, using expert-annotated Bengali idioms with gold figurative and literal glosses. Adding an idiom's literal gloss to the option list pulls every model toward it, accounting for 65% to 96% of each model's remaining Bengali errors, and models are **1.9 to 6.4 times more captured in Bengali than in English** on the same items. Calibration also degrades: on the open models, confidence inverts so that gating on it is worse than gating at random.

papers.title: Pearl-Chat: Engineering a native Luganda language model from first principles in JAX and Flax NNX
papers.abstract: Autoregressive foundation language models predominantly target high-resource Indo-European languages, imposing computational and morphological penalties on under-represented African languages. Generic multilingual tokenizers routinely exceed fertility rates of 3.2 tokens per word on agglutinative Bantu languages, degrading context efficiency and inflating latency. We present Pearl-Chat, an 8,473,122-parameter ($\sim$8.5M) causal decoder-only transformer engineered for Luganda (Oluganda, ISO 639-2: lg), a low-resource Niger-Congo Bantu language spoken by over 10 million people in East Africa. Built from first mathematical principles in JAX and Flax NNX, Pearl-Chat uses explicit functional state decomposition (nnx.split and nnx.merge), deterministic resumable data streaming via Google Grain, and SPMD tensor parallelism using jax.sharding.Mesh. We introduce a byte-level byte-pair encoding (BPE) subword tokenizer trained from scratch on curated Luganda corpora ($V = 8,192$), achieving 4.88 characters per token compression and 1.60 tokens per word fertility, a two-fold compression improvement over LLaMA-3 (128K) and Gemma (256K). The model is trained with a two-stage curriculum: Stage 1 pre-training on 59,501 sequences across parallel, biblical, encyclopedic, and journalistic corpora, and Stage 2 instruction fine-tuning on 510 dialogues with assistant-only loss masking. Across 4,000 optimization steps, validation cross-entropy loss drops monotonically from 9.4695 (perplexity: 12,958.98) to 0.1818 (perplexity: 1.20), a decrease of 9.2877 nats. On a three-tier held-out diagnostic benchmark, Pearl-Chat achieves 0.9792 ROUGE-L and 0.9405 BLEU while maintaining concordial agreement across Bantu noun classes. We provide a Python Server-Sent Events (SSE) streaming runtime and open-source all weights, tokenizers, and code.
papers.summary: Generic multilingual tokenizers split agglutinative Bantu languages into many tokens per word, which wastes context and inflates latency. `Pearl-Chat` is an 8.5M-parameter decoder-only transformer for Luganda, built from scratch in `JAX` and `Flax NNX` with deterministic data streaming via `Google Grain` and tensor parallelism. Its custom byte-level BPE tokenizer reaches **1.60 tokens per word**, roughly twice the compression of the `LLaMA-3` and `Gemma` tokenizers on Luganda. The model is pre-trained and then instruction-tuned on 510 dialogues; on a held-out diagnostic benchmark it reports 0.9792 ROUGE-L and 0.9405 BLEU, and all weights, tokenizers and code are released.

papers.title: Are Large Reasoning Models Good Everyday Reasoners? A Comparison with Non-Reasoning Models on Logical Reasoning Tasks
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) that leverage test-time computation achieve strong performance on mathematical and scientific benchmarks and are increasingly deployed in real-world applications. However, their ability to perform \textit{everyday logical reasoning}, which often departs from textbook formal logic, remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically evaluate how well reasoning models align with everyday reasoning patterns by introducing a benchmark based on linguistic and pragmatic reasoning phenomena. We also compare reasoning models with non-reasoning models under controlled prompting conditions. We find that, in many cases, (1) reasoning models show degraded performance in everyday reasoning when such reasoning deviates from formal logical rules, (2) some non-reasoning models with chain-of-thought prompting outperform comparable reasoning models in everyday reasoning, and (3) prompting with additional instructions provides limited control over reasoning behavior. These findings suggest that current reasoning models do not reliably capture everyday reasoning and point to limitations in post-training, motivating improved training objectives and evaluation across diverse forms of reasoning.
papers.summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs), which spend extra computation at inference time, do well on math and science benchmarks, but little is known about how they handle everyday logical reasoning that departs from formal logic. The authors build a benchmark from linguistic and pragmatic reasoning phenomena and compare reasoning models with non-reasoning models under controlled prompting. They find that **reasoning models often get worse when everyday reasoning deviates from formal logical rules**, that some non-reasoning models with chain-of-thought prompting beat comparable reasoning models, and that extra prompt instructions give little control over reasoning behavior. The authors attribute these gaps to limitations in post-training.

papers.title: Don't Retrain, Remix: Adaptation of Web Agents using Mixture Hypernetworks
papers.abstract: The web is not static or uniform. Websites that serve the same purpose can look and navigate very differently. Even within a single site, successive redesigns can change how familiar features are presented and accessed. Humans adapt to this by recognizing familiar interaction patterns and reusing what they already know. We give web agents a similar ability with WebMix, a mixture hypernetwork that adapts them to unseen interfaces by composing previously trained low-rank adapters. WebMix begins with a bank of adapters trained on source interfaces. At deployment, a scout agent explores the target interface and summarizes its observations into a compact manual. A lightweight router uses this manual to predict mixing coefficients over the adapter bank, which combine the existing adapters into a new one for inference. Adapting to a new interface takes only a scouting run and a forward pass, without gradient updates on the target. With Qwen and Llama models, we evaluate domain transfer on TimeWarp and WebArena-Lite-v2, and version transfer on TimeWarp. In all three settings, WebMix matches or outperforms in-context learning and LoRA baselines, often matching the average success of specialists trained directly on those interfaces. On TimeWarp domain transfer, it gains about 8 percentage points on average over the best baseline with both models. These gains do not come at the cost of seen interfaces, where WebMix keeps its lead, and extend to version transfer. Adapting to a new interface can therefore rely on exploration and composition instead of retraining.
papers.summary: Web agents struggle when they meet unfamiliar website layouts or redesigned versions of sites they already know. `WebMix` is a mixture hypernetwork that adapts an agent by combining low-rank adapters (LoRA) already trained on other interfaces. A scout agent explores the new interface and writes a compact manual, and a lightweight router uses that manual to predict mixing weights over the adapter bank, so no gradient updates on the target are needed. With `Qwen` and `Llama` models on `TimeWarp` and `WebArena-Lite-v2`, `WebMix` matches or beats in-context learning and LoRA baselines and often matches specialists trained on the target, with an average **gain of about 8 percentage points** over the best baseline on `TimeWarp` domain transfer.

papers.title: HeRE: A Novel Benchmark for Hebrew Relation Extraction via LLM-Guided Denoising of Knowledge Graph Alignments
papers.abstract: While LLMs demonstrate strong capabilities in English Relation Extraction (RE) tasks, a significant gap remains in assessing their RE performance in low-resource languages, due to a lack of standardized benchmarks. Creating native, language-specific annotated RE benchmarks is expensive and requires human expertise, while relying on translation yields suboptimal, inaccurate datasets that introduce English-centric biases. To tackle this, we propose a scalable, language-agnostic methodology to create RE data by denoising naturally occurring yet noisy alignments of knowledge bases and corresponding texts. We define a proper alignment via a Natural Language Inference (NLI) task, where a relation triplet is entailed by an input text. We empirically assess five denoising strategies, and demonstrate that multilingual models outperform language-specific models in the few-shot LLM setting, while Hebrew-specific encoders remain competitive under NLI fine-tuning and are strongest in the label-free cross-training setting. We further find that prompting in the native language achieves performance on par with or slightly exceeding English prompts, confirming that the pipeline operates naturally in the target language. The best open-weights model, Gemma-4-31B-it (F1\,=\,0.915), matches the best API model, GPT-5.4 (0.921), and reaches F1\,=\,0.844 on a fully held-out, dual-annotated test set. Applying the optimized pipeline, we release HeRE: a novel, massive, 1.5-million-instance silver dataset for Hebrew RE, designed to support data-intensive experimentation and model fine-tuning. HeRE bridges a critical gap in standard Hebrew RE evaluation, while providing the NLP community with a reproducible, language-agnostic pipeline for RE dataset construction in other low-resource settings.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for relation extraction (RE) in low-resource languages are scarce: native annotation is expensive, and translated data carries English-centric bias. The authors propose a language-agnostic pipeline that denoises naturally occurring alignments between knowledge bases and text, framing a valid alignment as a natural language inference (NLI) task in which the text entails the relation triplet. Among five denoising strategies, multilingual models lead in few-shot LLM settings, while Hebrew-specific encoders stay competitive under NLI fine-tuning. The best open-weights model, `Gemma-4-31B-it`, reaches F1 = 0.915, close to `GPT-5.4` at 0.921, and the pipeline yields `HeRE`, a **1.5-million-instance silver dataset** for Hebrew RE.

papers.title: On the SPOT: Enhancing Speculative Decoding for Diffusion Language Models via Commit-Order Prediction
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) promise parallel text generation, but in practice face an unresolved speed-quality trade-off. Exact decoding fills in only one masked position per model pass, while faster multi-token decoding schemes are lossy. Speculative decoding is the standard lossless acceleration for autoregressive models. However, it does not transfer directly to DLMs, which must choose both what to generate and where. We show that this order is the missing piece: the model's own predictions from the previous pass already give the right token at 92-100% of positions, but not which position comes next. Based on this observation, we introduce Speculating Positions Order Trajectory (SPOT), which learns to predict this order. A 0.62M-parameter model reads only the target's output distributions and proposes a tree of candidate continuations, and the target verifies all of them in a single pass by checking whether each equals its own next state. On the verification side, our analysis shows that prior block-diffusion verification approaches either assume $T=0$ or a sequential proposal interface. To support tree-based speculation at any temperature, we propose using coupled-noise match verification for diffusion blocks, following shared-Gumbel-noise coupling approaches. Our comprehensive experiments show that SPOT cuts target passes by up to 6.8x and reaches up to 3.2x the throughput of standard decoding, beating the calibrated and training-free drafting baselines in every task and budget at $T=0$ and $T=1$. In addition, we show that the learned drafter transfers across models, demonstrating successful transfer across six different DLMs. Project page: https://eliezer318.github.io/SPOT-dLLM/
papers.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) can in principle generate text in parallel, but exact decoding fills only one masked position per pass, and faster multi-token schemes lose quality. Standard speculative decoding does not carry over directly because a DLM has to choose where to generate as well as what. The authors observe that the previous pass already predicts the right token at 92-100% of positions; what is missing is the order in which positions get filled. `SPOT` (Speculating Positions Order Trajectory) trains a 0.62M-parameter drafter to predict that order and propose a tree of candidates, which the target verifies in a single pass using coupled-noise matching so that it works at any temperature. It cuts target passes by up to 6.8x and reaches **up to 3.2x the throughput** of standard decoding, and the drafter transfers across six different DLMs.

papers.title: Cultural (In)Competence: Investigating Culture-Specific Stereotype Detection Capabilities of LLMs
papers.abstract: Stereotypes are subjective constructs that are mediated by the cultural context in which they are viewed. Successfully modeling them thus also requires cultural competence. When using large language models (LLMs) for stereotype-related tasks, such as their detection, it is therefore crucial that models can access relevant cultural knowledge and adjust responses accordingly. Since LLMs have shown disparities in what cultural knowledge is available to them, their capacity regarding stereotypes may also be disparate across languages and cultural contexts (e.g., for non-English languages or for non-US contexts). In this paper, we systematically investigate the effectiveness of LLMs for culture-specific stereotype detection across three factors: (1) the prompting language, (2) the instruction tuning language, and (3) the fine-tuning dataset size. We conduct experiments for US, Dutch, and Chinese cultural contexts. Our results suggest that LLMs do not reliably account for cultural contexts and overpredict the presence of stereotypes. Non-English prompts seem to improve consideration of cultural context and thus lead to more effective predictions. Moreover, we find that additional instruction tuning reduces false-positive rates and that training data size moderates detection effectiveness non-monotonically.
papers.summary: Whether a statement is a stereotype depends on cultural context, so using LLMs to detect stereotypes requires cultural knowledge that may be uneven across languages and regions. The authors test culture-specific stereotype detection in US, Dutch and Chinese contexts while varying three factors: the prompting language, the instruction-tuning language and the fine-tuning dataset size. They find that **LLMs do not reliably account for cultural context and over-predict stereotypes**. Non-English prompts improve attention to cultural context, extra instruction tuning lowers false positives, and training data size affects detection non-monotonically.

papers.title: When Plans Change, Remember: Replanning-Guided Visual Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Long-horizon, multi-stage Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies often require visual information that is no longer present in the current observation. Retaining the complete observation history is computationally expensive and highly redundant, motivating selective visual memory. We introduce RePlanMem-VLA (Replanning-Guided Keyframe Memory for VLA), which turns a policy's own plan revisions into an online memory-write signal. Under receding-horizon execution, consecutive action chunks predict some of the same future actions. RePlanMem-VLA treats unusually large disagreement between these temporally aligned predictions as evidence of a task-relevant event. We first compare 35 disagreement measures across single-task autoregressive decoder-only and Flow-Matching Transformers trained from scratch, then validate the selected signals on pretrained OpenVLA-OFT and $\pi_{0.5}$ policies over MIKASA-Robo-VLA tasks. The resulting detectors achieve ROC-AUC of 0.981-0.997. We then use the selected signals in RePlanMem-VLA to trigger updates to a bounded visual memory, with a robot-masked write filter suppressing redundant frames. In the evaluated memory-retention experiments, RePlanMem-VLA preserves task-relevant observations until the later decision point in 100% of episodes. Real-robot replay data further show that event selection and redundancy suppression extend beyond simulation. These results establish plan revision as a policy-internal signal for controlling what a VLA remembers. Website: https://vika787.github.io/RePlanMem/.
papers.summary: Long-horizon Vision-Language-Action (VLA) robot policies often need visual information that has dropped out of the current view, but storing the full observation history is expensive and redundant. `RePlanMem-VLA` uses the policy's own plan revisions as a signal for what to remember: when overlapping action chunks disagree sharply about the same future actions, it treats that as a task-relevant event and writes the frame to a bounded memory. After comparing 35 disagreement measures, the selected signals detect events with ROC-AUC of 0.981-0.997 on pretrained `OpenVLA-OFT` and `π0.5` policies on `MIKASA-Robo-VLA` tasks. In memory-retention experiments, the system **keeps task-relevant observations until the later decision point in 100% of episodes**, and real-robot replay data show the approach holds up outside simulation.

papers.title: Deterministic Bounds on Accuracy and Stability of Metric-Space Regression and Classification
papers.abstract: Data-driven approaches often face ambiguity in datasets due to sensor or target noise, insufficient information, and noise in the input data. While best-fit machine learning methods can accommodate such noise through uncertainty estimates, they are prone to overfitting and it is challenging to quantify ambiguity of the relation between inputs and targets. We introduce a geometric framework that quantifies this ambiguity through the average kernel size, computed with data-dependent, i.e. model-independent, feasible sets derived from worst-case input and target noise. The framework provides computable, deterministic, non-asymptotic bounds on the best achievable empirical error and accuracy for a finite, constructed dataset, independent of the predictive model class, and applies to regression and classification with pseudo-metric input spaces and metric target spaces. The ambiguity of the input-target relation implies three consequences: an empirical error floor, an accuracy-stability trade-off, and, under standard probabilistic assumptions, a strictly positive distribution-training error gap when training below the accuracy bounds. Under standard Borel assumptions for Euclidean norms, the distributional analogue of the average kernel size is related to Bayes risk as it reduces to the optimal distribution root-mean-squared error times the square root of two. Experiments spanning tabular regression, image regression and classification datasets yield nontrivial bounds on the best achievable empirical error and accuracy on a constructed dataset, alongside descriptive comparisons with model performance on the original datasets. The bounds provide a computable, model-independent reference scale on the constructed dataset and comparisons with model performance on the original dataset are descriptive.
papers.summary: Noisy inputs and targets make the relationship between them ambiguous, and best-fit machine learning methods make that ambiguity hard to measure. The authors propose a geometric framework that measures ambiguity through an average kernel size computed from data-dependent feasible sets, derived from worst-case input and target noise. The framework gives **computable, deterministic, non-asymptotic bounds on the best achievable empirical error and accuracy** on a constructed dataset, regardless of model class, for regression and classification over pseudo-metric input spaces. Consequences include an empirical error floor and an accuracy-stability trade-off, and experiments on tabular and image datasets yield nontrivial bounds.

papers.title: Coverage Cliffs in Off-Policy Quantile Certification
papers.abstract: We study when logged contextual-bandit data can certify an upper tail quantile for a policy selected from the same sample. We construct a PAC-Bayes Bernstein lower-confidence envelope for the target cumulative distribution function (CDF), simultaneous over a predeclared threshold grid and all data-dependent posteriors. The resulting procedure, TailCert, uses the envelope's first crossing of level p to return an atom-safe upper confidence bound on the selected posterior's pooled p-quantile (or inconclusive). It can also be used to select a policy under a certified tail constraint. The concentration ingredients are standard; the main theoretical contribution is a matched finite-class certification boundary comparing full logs with their joint weighted CDF indicators at a fixed threshold. On an explicit rare-action class, the required sample size grows linearly with the overlap factor W, logarithmically with policy-search and confidence complexity, and quadratically with the inverse CDF safety margin; the upper and lower bounds agree up to constants in the stated regime. On this class, the CDF reduction hides which actions exceeded the budget; retaining action counts restores the full-log rate. Simulations verify the predicted search-complexity shift, winner's-curse failure of naive reuse, and the power cost of splitting.
papers.summary: The question studied is when logged contextual-bandit data can certify an upper tail quantile for a policy chosen from that same data. The proposed method, `TailCert`, builds a PAC-Bayes Bernstein lower-confidence envelope for the target cumulative distribution function (CDF) and uses it to return an upper confidence bound on the selected policy's quantile, or to report the result as inconclusive. The main theoretical result is a matched certification boundary: on a rare-action class, **required sample size grows linearly with the overlap factor**, logarithmically with search complexity, and quadratically with the inverse CDF safety margin, with upper and lower bounds that agree up to constants. Simulations confirm the predicted effects, including the winner's-curse failure of naively reusing the data.

papers.title: Who Do Perspectivist Models Predict Well? Annotator Agreement, Sparsity, and Performance
papers.abstract: Successful completion of perspectivist natural language processing (NLP) annotation tasks requires algorithms to be aligned across diverse perspectives in order to predict how different humans will rate text. This work studies how the performance of such algorithms varies for annotators who behave differently than others, either by providing annotations that diverge from others' responses or by providing fewer annotations altogether. To aid with characterizing model performance, we curate the largest collection to date of perspectivist NLP datasets with ordinal annotations. After evaluating multiple classes of perspectivist algorithms across each of the datasets, we model the relationship between individual annotator idiosyncrasy and algorithm performance. In general, we find that algorithms perform better on annotators who tend to agree with others, but that annotator response rate does not have a statistically significant positive correlation with algorithm performance.
papers.summary: Perspectivist NLP models try to predict how each individual annotator would rate a text, rather than a single consensus label. The authors assemble the largest collection to date of perspectivist datasets with ordinal annotations and evaluate several classes of perspectivist algorithms on them. They then model how performance relates to annotator idiosyncrasy. They find that **algorithms predict annotators who agree with others better**, while an annotator's response rate has no statistically significant positive correlation with performance.

papers.title: Repairing LLM-Generated Specifications with Deterministic Diagnosis
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as formalizers: given a reasoning problem expressed in natural language, they produce a formal specification that a symbolic solver can then solve, with guarantees relative to that specification. Many specifications are runnable yet semantically wrong, encoding incorrect constraints, domains, objectives, predicates, or goals, and solver-error feedback dries up once execution succeeds. Purely LLM-based diagnosis, lacking a formal ground truth, often fails to spot these errors, and its ungrounded critiques cause regressions in 11.8% of initially correct specifications in our experiments. We propose DRAGO, a repair framework that replaces this ungrounded critique with deterministic, formalism-specific diagnosis, and retains a rewrite only when the diagnosed error weight strictly decreases under a reference-free acceptance predicate. Across five benchmarks spanning logical reasoning (SMT-LIB2), constraint programming (MiniZinc), and planning (PDDL), DRAGO cuts regressions by nearly an order of magnitude, to 1.3%, while improving answer accuracy by 12.9 percentage points over zero-shot formalization and 8.7 percentage points over LLM-diagnostic repair, averaged across benchmarks. We also uncover two rendering defects in Planetarium that cause 50% (3,086 instances) of its floor-tile split to be inconsistent with the reference formalizations, and release a corrected split.
papers.summary: LLMs are increasingly used to turn natural-language problems into formal specifications for symbolic solvers, but many of these specifications run fine yet encode the wrong constraints or goals, and purely LLM-based critique can break specifications that were already correct. `DRAGO` replaces LLM critique with deterministic, formalism-specific diagnosis and keeps a rewrite only when the diagnosed error weight strictly decreases. Across five benchmarks in `SMT-LIB2`, `MiniZinc` and `PDDL`, it **cuts regressions from 11.8% to 1.3%** and improves answer accuracy by 12.9 points over zero-shot formalization and 8.7 points over LLM-diagnostic repair. The authors also find rendering defects that make half of `Planetarium`'s floor-tile split inconsistent, and release a corrected split.

papers.title: Structure-Aware Spatial Kernels for Gaussian Process Distributed Port-Hamiltonian Systems
papers.abstract: Gaussian process distributed port-Hamiltonian systems (GP-dPHS) enable data-driven modeling of distributed dynamical systems while preserving their physical structure. However, standard stationary kernels can be inefficient for spatially heterogeneous systems because they neither exploit known input invariances nor reflect structured spatial dependencies. We address this limitation with a structure-aware kernel design that removes irrelevant state coordinates and decouples state and spatial dependencies through a tensor-product covariance. This modular construction allows qualitative knowledge of spatial heterogeneity to be incorporated by selecting an appropriate spatial kernel without requiring an analytical description of the underlying profile. Numerical experiments on a nonlinear string with periodic, smoothly varying, and semi-piecewise stiffness profiles demonstrate that structural decoupling consistently improves reconstruction accuracy, while profile-matched spatial kernels yield substantially larger gains in force-field and trajectory reconstruction.
papers.summary: Gaussian process distributed port-Hamiltonian systems (`GP-dPHS`) learn models of distributed dynamical systems from data while preserving their physical structure, but standard stationary kernels handle spatially varying systems poorly. The authors propose a structure-aware kernel that drops irrelevant state coordinates and separates state and spatial dependence through a tensor-product covariance, so qualitative knowledge of spatial variation can be encoded by choosing a spatial kernel. On a nonlinear string with several stiffness profiles, decoupling consistently improves reconstruction accuracy, and **spatial kernels matched to the profile give substantially larger gains** in force-field and trajectory reconstruction.

papers.title: Embodiment-Classifier Guidance: Transferring Frozen VLAs Across Robot Dynamics without Demonstrations
papers.abstract: Flow-based policies such as $\pi_0$ are trained on a fixed set of embodiments, and transferring them to new ones is an open problem. To adapt a frozen $\pi_0$ to a new embodiment without additional demonstrations or parameter updates, we train a lightweight embodiment classifier to distinguish successful action chunks on the source body from those on the target body, using a few calibration tasks. On transfer tasks that $\pi_0$ saw on its source body but the classifier was never trained on, we nudge each denoising step of $\pi_0$ with the classifier's gradient, which estimates the direction from the distribution of successful actions on the source body toward that on the target body. On the LIBERO simulation benchmark with four modified controllers, embodiment-classifier guidance raises $\pi_0$'s average success on the target bodies from 72% to 80% across 12 suite-controller pairs, with a 31% relative reduction in failures (11 of 12 gain; 5 significant after Holm correction). In simulation, guidance is data-efficient, needing few target-body rollouts per task, which makes it promising for sim-to-real transfer, where rollouts are costly. Guidance is mixed on weak wrists and harmful on a locked wrist, when the classifier lacks data or favors infeasible motions. Collecting more target-body data with guided $\pi_0$ can fill such gaps: on one weak-wrist arm, guided $\pi_0$ solved a task on which unguided $\pi_0$ had zero successes in the original data, and retraining the classifier on the guided successes raised success from 52.5% to 70.7%.
papers.summary: Flow-based robot policies such as `π0` are trained on a fixed set of embodiments, and moving them to a new body is an open problem. The authors keep `π0` frozen and train a lightweight classifier that separates successful action chunks on the source body from those on the target body, then steer each denoising step with the classifier's gradient, with no new demonstrations or parameter updates. On `LIBERO` with four modified controllers, this **raises average success from 72% to 80%** across 12 suite-controller pairs, improving 11 of the 12. It helps less on weak wrists and hurts on a locked wrist, but retraining the classifier on guided successes raised one weak-wrist task from 52.5% to 70.7%.

papers.title: Noise-Robust Forced Alignment for Spontaneous Speech
papers.abstract: We show that forced aligners degrade on spontaneous, noisy real-world speech, and that fillers, laughter, and disfluencies corrupt word boundaries, impacting many downstream applications. We revisit the classical GMM-HMM aligner with upsampled WavLM features instead of MFCCs, explicit phone units for fillers and non-lexical vocal events trained on verbatim-annotated spontaneous speech, and a discriminative projection fitted on clean and noise-corrupted feature pairs to improve robustness. The pipeline is self-bootstrapped from 149h of curated audio without manual or external boundary targets. On conversational (Buckeye) and disfluent (FluencyBank) speech it reaches word-boundary MAEs of 20.6 and 76.9ms, 19% and 17% lower than the strongest of ten baselines. Catastrophic misalignments (>200ms) are 2.7 times rarer than Montreal Forced Aligners (MFA) best model even after widening MFA's search beam, which we show removes a large pruning artifact from its conversational error; event units halve the error next to laughter, while being meaningfully more robust than existing aligners.
papers.summary: Forced aligners, which find word boundaries in transcribed speech, degrade on noisy spontaneous speech, where fillers, laughter and disfluencies throw boundaries off. The authors revisit the classic GMM-HMM aligner, replacing MFCC features with upsampled `WavLM` features, adding explicit units for fillers and non-lexical vocal events, and fitting a discriminative projection on clean and noise-corrupted feature pairs. The pipeline bootstraps itself from 149 hours of audio with no manual boundary labels. On `Buckeye` and `FluencyBank` it reaches word-boundary errors of 20.6 and 76.9 ms, **19% and 17% lower than the strongest of ten baselines**, and large misalignments are 2.7 times rarer than with the `Montreal Forced Aligner`.

papers.title: Initiating Removal from Operational Symptoms in Federated Vehicular Networks
papers.abstract: Connected vehicles train a driving model through federated learning (FL) and drive with it, so a faulty contribution often surfaces only as a delayed symptom on the road. Federated unlearning (FU) assumes that a removal request names what to forget. A symptom names no vehicle or round, and aggregation has already spread its cause across the fleet. We propose \underline{A}ggregation-\underline{T}ime \underline{O}perational-evidence \underline{N}eutralization of \underline{E}ffects (\method{}), which makes unlearning a term of the FL aggregation rule. \method{} projects everyday driving errors and reported symptoms onto a subspace spanned by recent global increments. It propagates the surviving effect of every contribution with curvature estimated from these increments and scores all contributions in one backward pass. A two-tier correction suppresses suspected effects in every round and eliminates confirmed ones after a one-round probe. We prove that backward scoring matches forward scoring and that the elimination is exact when training is flat outside the subspace. On three driving datasets, \method{} leaves 43\% to 61\% less residual harm than the strongest baseline in eight of nine settings while staying within 0.36 points of full retraining in utility.
papers.summary: When connected vehicles train a driving model with federated learning (FL), a faulty contribution may only show up later as a symptom on the road, and existing federated unlearning methods assume the removal request already names what to forget. `ATONE` builds unlearning into the aggregation rule: it projects driving errors and reported symptoms onto a subspace spanned by recent global updates, estimates every contribution's lingering effect in one backward pass, and uses a two-tier correction that suppresses suspected effects and removes confirmed ones. The authors prove the removal is exact when training is flat outside that subspace. On three driving datasets, it **leaves 43% to 61% less residual harm** than the strongest baseline in eight of nine settings, while staying within 0.36 points of full retraining in utility.

papers.title: Mitigating Demographic Disparities in Explanation-Human Alignment via Rationale Regularization
papers.abstract: We study explanation fairness in hate speech detection. High classification performance does not always mean that a model produces equally plausible explanations for different demographic groups. Using the HateXplain dataset, we introduce Plausibility-EFG, a metric that measures the largest difference in explanation plausibility across demographic groups by comparing model-generated token attributions with human-annotated rationales. We evaluate BERT, RoBERTa, and ADV-RoBERTa, an adversarially trained model, using Integrated Gradients and SHAP. Our results show that ADV-RoBERTa improves classification performance and alignment between explanations and human rationales while reducing explanation disparities across demographic groups. These improvements are observed with both attribution methods and remain consistent across training, validation, and test splits. We also show that reducing prediction-level bias alone does not eliminate disparities in explanations, suggesting that predictive fairness and explanation fairness are related but distinct objectives. Finally, our fairness-performance analysis shows that stronger adversarial regularization can further reduce Plausibility-EFG, although it may cause a small decrease in macro-F1. Overall, this work presents explanation fairness as an important objective in hate speech moderation and introduces Fair-REF, a framework designed to reduce disparities in model explanations across demographic groups.
papers.summary: A hate speech classifier can be accurate overall yet give less plausible explanations for some demographic groups than for others. Using `HateXplain`, the authors define `Plausibility-EFG`, which measures the largest gap across groups in how well token attributions match human rationales. They evaluate `BERT`, `RoBERTa` and the adversarially trained `ADV-RoBERTa` with `Integrated Gradients` and `SHAP`. Adversarial training improves both accuracy and explanation alignment while narrowing the gaps between groups, and **reducing prediction-level bias alone does not remove explanation disparities**. The work is packaged as the `Fair-REF` framework.

papers.title: SAG2: Embedding-Free Multi-Hop Retrieval with BM25 and JEV
papers.abstract: Strong multi-hop retrieval should be practical to deploy without expensive corpus preparation or complex database infrastructure. We present SAG2, an embedding-free retrieval architecture built around a single SQLite database, BM25, and contextual evidence decisions from JEV. SAG2 follows the query-time association principle of SAG (SQL-Retrieval Augmented Generation), while replacing its event-entity and dense indexes with a lexical index over original passages. Selected passages supply terms for further retrieval, and newly retrieved evidence guides subsequent decisions. This moves semantic evidence selection to query time, eliminating offline embedding computation, LLM-based event-entity extraction, and dedicated database servers. The resulting system combines lightweight preparation with strong retrieval accuracy: on 1,000-question subsets of MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and HotpotQA, SAG2 achieves the highest Recall@5 and Recall@10 among the compared methods, with Recall@10 of 86.62%, 97.43%, and 99.00%. It also reaches 81.10% document Recall@10 over the 511,962-document EnterpriseRAG-Bench corpus. Indexing all 11,656 MuSiQue passages takes 2.36 seconds, produces a 25.87 MiB database, and requires no model calls. SAG2 demonstrates that accurate multi-hop evidence retrieval can be supported by compact, rapidly prepared infrastructure, making it a practical foundation for knowledge retrieval applications.
papers.summary: Multi-hop retrieval systems usually need precomputed embeddings, LLM-based extraction and dedicated database servers. `SAG2` instead runs on a single `SQLite` database with `BM25` lexical search, using `JEV` at query time to decide which passages count as evidence; terms from the selected passages drive further retrieval rounds. On 1,000-question subsets of `MuSiQue`, `2WikiMultiHopQA` and `HotpotQA`, it achieves the highest Recall@5 and Recall@10 among the compared methods, with Recall@10 of 86.62%, 97.43% and 99.00%. Indexing all of `MuSiQue` takes **2.36 seconds, produces a 25.87 MiB database, and requires no model calls**.

papers.title: Flat Loss, Evolving Features: Grokking in Modular Addition
papers.abstract: Can a network keep learning while its training cross-entropy stays nearly flat at a positive level? We show that it can. On modular addition, a standard testbed for grokking, ReLU networks trained with supported-Polar hidden updates, normalized output-layer updates and weight decay can keep 100% training accuracy while their hidden features change and held-out accuracy rises from zero to above 90%, at relatively flat training cross-entropy. Correct classification need not minimize cross-entropy, which still depends on prediction confidence. We prove this coexistence for one-hidden-layer networks in two finite-window theorems from constructed initializations: one gives a constant gain in the Fourier fraction of the hidden features, and the other holds at arbitrarily low positive loss, where a readout refitted on the training data generalizes before the network. Experiments from random initialization show the same coexistence on a window fixed in advance, and in deeper networks held-out accuracy also rises over post-hoc windows with a net increase in training cross-entropy. With a last-layer rate set per training fraction and head decay scaled with the prime, deeper networks at p=47 and 61 meet a criterion on post-hoc windows, fixed in advance, in nearly all fresh runs. A one-block transformer trained with the same updates and a slowly decaying output gain keeps every training pair correct at every logged checkpoint while its training cross-entropy rises and its held-out accuracy approaches one; with two blocks this holds through the held-out rise, after which training pairs begin to flip. A plateau in training loss need not be a plateau in learning. Code: https://github.com/akashkumar-d/flat-loss-evolving-features.
papers.summary: Studies whether a network can keep learning while its training cross-entropy stays nearly flat at a positive level, using modular addition as a testbed for grokking (delayed generalization long after the training data is fit). ReLU networks trained with supported-Polar hidden updates, normalized output-layer updates and weight decay keep 100% training accuracy while their hidden features change and **held-out accuracy rises from zero to above 90% at relatively flat training loss**. Two finite-window theorems prove this coexistence for one-hidden-layer networks, and experiments extend it to deeper networks and to one- and two-block transformers, where training loss can even rise while held-out accuracy approaches one.

papers.title: The Model Knows Better: Defending Medical Multi-Agent Systems Against Prompt Injection
papers.abstract: Medical multi-agent systems, in which LLM agents discuss a case, are increasingly studied for clinical decision support. Prompt injection, text that an attacker adds to a model's input, can manipulate LLMs into wrong decisions. How it affects these systems, and how to protect them, remains unclear. Across two systems, two model families and three benchmarks, a single injected passage succeeds in up to 61% of cases, and collaboration does not consistently protect against it. Existing defenses help only partly: they miss injections that look like ordinary clinical text. Yet when asked to check the injected text against the patient's findings, a model that followed the injection usually rejects it. We therefore propose a training-free defense that verifies the clinical judgments behind the system's decision. Following clinical practice, it separates the patient's findings from clinical judgments, such as diagnoses, recommendations and instructions, and checks each judgment against the findings alone, so the decision rests only on supported judgments. Our defense outperforms all baselines on every benchmark, lowering attack success on MedQA to 4-7% while maintaining accuracy on cases without an attack, and remains effective with a medical model and against defense-aware and adaptive attacks.
papers.summary: Examines prompt injection in medical multi-agent systems, where several LLM agents discuss a clinical case, and finds that a single injected passage succeeds in up to 61% of cases and that collaboration between agents does not reliably protect against it. Existing defenses miss injections that read like ordinary clinical text, but a model that followed an injection usually rejects it when asked to check it against the patient's findings. The proposed training-free defense separates patient findings from clinical judgments such as diagnoses and instructions, then verifies each judgment against the findings alone. It **lowers attack success on `MedQA` to 4-7%** without hurting accuracy on clean cases and holds up against defense-aware and adaptive attacks.

papers.title: Diagnosing GNN Failure Modes with Layer-Wise Probe Entropy
papers.abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are typically evaluated only at their final layer, obscuring how task-relevant information evolves during message passing. We introduce a post-hoc diagnostic that freezes a trained GNN, fits an independent linear probe to each layer, and tracks probe accuracy alongside normalized predictive entropy. Across real and synthetic graph settings, layer-wise probe entropy distinguishes beneficial, neutral, and harmful smoothing, a capability not demonstrated by existing geometric measures. Moreover, by comparing shallow and deep models, we show that the onset of entropy degradation separates the two main GNN failure modes: structural mismatch under heterophily, which appears from the earliest layers even in shallow models, and excessive-depth oversmoothing, which emerges only as propagation depth increases. These results establish probe-entropy trajectories as a tool for analyzing information flow in GNNs and motivate future work on adaptive depth selection and early-exit mechanisms.
papers.summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are usually evaluated only at their final layer, which hides how task-relevant information changes during message passing. The proposed diagnostic freezes a trained GNN, fits a linear probe to each layer, and tracks probe accuracy together with normalized predictive entropy. These **probe-entropy trajectories distinguish beneficial, neutral and harmful smoothing**, and the layer at which entropy starts to degrade separates heterophily-driven structural mismatch, which appears from the earliest layers, from depth-driven oversmoothing.

papers.title: Broad and Efficient PII Detection with Unified Labels
papers.abstract: Personally Identifiable Information (PII) detection models must efficiently find identifiers across diverse contexts while maintaining a low false-positive rate (FPR) on high-volume traffic. Recent detectors increasingly rely on complex architectures that raise deployment cost, yet many are fine-tuned on only a few synthetic datasets that limit their coverage. Combining public datasets is challenging because their taxonomies differ, and even after categories are mapped to a common schema, labels can disagree on what counts as a detection, producing inconsistent training and evaluation signals. To address these problems, we present a practical 141M-parameter encoder-based detector trained on 1.12 million examples from 77 public datasets, relabeled under a detailed definition of broad contextual detection for 12 structured PII categories. Evaluated on the AI4Privacy and Nemotron-PII benchmarks at a low-FPR operating point, our model achieves the highest recall against larger baselines in 11 of 14 comparisons under our labels and 9 of 14 under the original labels. Its largest recall gains include useful additional coverage, such as multilingual disclosures and IP addresses embedded in URLs. It achieves this with 2-10x higher throughput and 94-97% less peak GPU memory than the baselines, delivering leading detection performance at substantially lower cost.
papers.summary: Builds a practical detector for personally identifiable information (PII) that needs broad coverage and a low false-positive rate on high-volume traffic. The authors train a 141M-parameter encoder on 1.12 million examples from 77 public datasets, relabeled under one consistent definition of contextual detection across 12 structured PII categories. On the `AI4Privacy` and `Nemotron-PII` benchmarks at a low false-positive operating point, it achieves the highest recall against larger baselines in 11 of 14 comparisons, with **2-10x higher throughput and 94-97% less peak GPU memory**.

papers.title: Can LLMs predict the outcomes of machine learning experiments?
papers.abstract: Recent advances in AI make Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) increasingly plausible. Large Language Models (LLMs) can already propose, select, and run Machine Learning (ML) experiments. However, the space of possible design choices in ML is vast. An LLM that proposes an experiment needs a reliable intuition of whether it is worth running given the timing constraints of long training runs. In this work, we measure such intuition in current frontier LLMs by evaluating how accurately they predict the impact of self-generated ML experiment ideas before these are put into training runs. To this end, we construct a dataset of 288 LLM-proposed ideas on eight MLE-bench tasks. We then prompt five frontier LLMs (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.3) to predict the impact of each idea and compare their predictions with the actual outcomes after training. We report four main findings. First, LLM predictions are substantially better than random chance but far from accurate: even the best model, Claude Opus 5.5, explains only half of the variance in outcomes (R^2 = 0.49). Second, we notice that all tested models systematically underestimate the magnitude of the changes. Third, prediction quality varies widely across tasks. Finally, the choice of the coding harness that actually implements the ideas has little effect on outcomes, and we find no evidence of self-preference. Higher reasoning settings and additional context lead to modest gains. Overall, our results show that current LLMs have useful but limited intuition about which ML ideas will work. We release our dataset to support further study.
papers.summary: Tests whether frontier LLMs have reliable intuition about which machine learning experiments are worth running, a capability relevant to recursive self-improvement (RSI) and automated ML research. The authors collect 288 LLM-proposed ideas on eight `MLE-bench` tasks, run them, and compare the real outcomes with predictions from five frontier models. Predictions beat chance but remain far from accurate: **the best model, `Claude Opus 5.5`, explains only about half the variance (R^2 = 0.49)**, all models systematically underestimate effect sizes, and quality varies widely across tasks. The coding harness that implements the ideas has little effect on outcomes, the authors find no evidence of self-preference, and more reasoning or context gives only modest gains.

papers.title: Rarity of Singletons Matters & Supplementary Materials
papers.abstract: Estimating missing-mass and unseen-species counts from finite samples relies heavily on rare-event occupancy statistics, particularly singletons. In small-sample regimes, these statistics can be highly variable, making classical estimators sensitive to sampling fluctuations and potentially unreliable. We propose a fragility-aware (FA) framework that explicitly quantifies this sensitivity and adaptively regularizes conventional missing-mass and unseen-species estimators. Using singleton-based fragility measures derived from probability mass and occupancy counts, we formulate an entropy--Kullback--Leibler (KL) optimization that adjusts the reliance on base estimates according to their fragility. The resulting objectives are strictly concave, admit unique closed-form solutions, and require no Poissonization or asymptotic approximations. The framework provides a lightweight correction to classical estimators, including Good--Turing and Good--Toulmin, while reducing reliance on potentially unstable rare-event statistics. Across 360 experimental configurations spanning synthetic distributions and real-world language corpora, our method remains competitive in stable regimes while improving estimation accuracy and stability in fragmented, long-tailed, and small-sample settings. The findings demonstrate that accounting for the fragility of rare observations can improve the reliability of inference about unobserved species and their associated probability mass.
papers.summary: Estimators of missing mass and unseen-species counts rely heavily on singletons, which fluctuate strongly in small samples and make classical estimators unreliable. The proposed fragility-aware (FA) framework measures this sensitivity from singleton statistics and solves an entropy-Kullback-Leibler (KL) optimization that adjusts how much to trust base estimators such as `Good-Turing` and `Good-Toulmin`. The objectives are strictly concave with closed-form solutions, and across 360 configurations on synthetic distributions and language corpora the method **improves accuracy and stability in fragmented, long-tailed and small-sample settings** while staying competitive elsewhere.

papers.title: Shift-Reliance Alignment: Ranking Vision-Language Models by the Cues They Trust
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are usually chosen from leaderboards, which give one ranking for every application. On questions about objects that a scene suggests but does not contain, however, the model with the lowest error on the POPE hallucination benchmark is not the one with the lowest error on such questions. For yes/no questions about object presence, we show that the best model for a target domain can be predicted without running any candidate on that domain, given 650 to 1,200 labeled target items that calibrate a detector. We measure each model's reliance on a cue, a feature such as scene context or text in the image, by editing 100 labeled source images so that the cue suggests the wrong answer, and comparing with a matched control edit. Reliance predicts which VLMs are misled by physical sticker attacks (Spearman .93 on nine models not used to design the score) and which hallucinate on unedited COCO photographs, beyond what their tendency to answer yes explains. Shift-Reliance Alignment (SRA) scores a model by its source error on the labeled source questions plus its reliance multiplied by the shift. The shift is the proportion of target questions on which the cue misleads, and a detector estimates it on the unlabeled target images. SRA selects the model with the lowest score. In pre-registered tests on new images where most questions mislead, it lowered the error of the selected model from 30.4% under selection by source error to 18.8% on Objects365 and OpenImages but, against its prediction, not on COCO. On CueDial, a benchmark we release that varies how often a cue misleads, selection by model confidence falls more than 40 percentage points behind the best model when overlaid text denies a visible object, and SRA stays within 3 points.
papers.summary: Argues that leaderboards pick the wrong vision-language model (VLM) for domains where visual cues such as scene context or overlaid text mislead object-presence questions. The method measures each model's reliance on a cue by editing 100 labeled images so the cue suggests the wrong answer, then predicts target-domain error as source error plus reliance times an estimated shift, the share of target questions where the cue misleads.
