This `Shift-Reliance Alignment` (`SRA`) score predicts susceptibility to physical sticker attacks (Spearman .93), and in pre-registered tests it **cut the selected model's error from 30.4% to 18.8% on `Objects365` and `OpenImages`**, though not on `COCO`. The authors also release `CueDial`, a benchmark that varies how often a cue misleads.

papers.title: When Does Uncertainty Measure RAG Hallucination Risk?
papers.abstract: Uncertainty can measure hallucination risk in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), but only when retrieved evidence constrains the answer. When evidence is present, unsupported factual claims become less likely; when retrieval coverage is poor, the model can answer from internal knowledge and assign high probability to unsupported claims. We test this across four instruction-tuned models on HotpotQA and SQuAD. After matching faithful and hallucinated answers within word-count bins, length-only classifiers fall near chance, while perplexity reaches 0.81--0.91 AUROC on targeted unsupported edits. Varying retrieval depth shows why the score changes meaning: detection can weaken with only the top-ranked passage, then recover after adding a second passage. A combined uncertainty and semantic-drift score improves calibration, and measurements remain above chance on RAGTruth QA. Results support a conditional view of uncertainty as a useful measure of RAG hallucination risk.
papers.summary: Asks when a model's own uncertainty is a reliable signal of hallucination in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and argues it works only when the retrieved evidence actually constrains the answer. Across four instruction-tuned models on `HotpotQA` and `SQuAD`, length-matched controls bring length-only classifiers near chance, while **perplexity reaches 0.81-0.91 AUROC on targeted unsupported edits**. Varying retrieval depth shows detection can weaken with only the top passage and recover once a second passage is added. Combining uncertainty with a semantic-drift score improves calibration, and the signal stays above chance on `RAGTruth`.

papers.title: Trajectory-Guided Steering: Mitigating Spurious Feature Bias in Clinical Classification
papers.abstract: Large language models rely on spurious features in clinical classification: swapping a single gender token in clinical notes alters gender-irrelevant diagnoses in up to 53.5% of cases. Existing inference-time corrections either need counterfactual data built around the specific spurious feature or behave unpredictably. We observe that how a model's preference between answers evolves across layers, its prediction trajectory, indicates for each document whether a correction is likely to help. We propose Trajectory-Guided Steering (TGS), which decides from the trajectory alone whether to correct each prediction and in which direction, with no counterfactual data and no knowledge of the spurious feature. On 16 clinical classification tasks from i2b2, TGS fixes 17.7% of errors while breaking only 1.3% of correct predictions and stays net-positive across all tested hyperparameter settings; all baselines are net-negative or near zero. The same corrections reduce reliance on the spurious feature: on the most affected diseases, gender-swap inconsistency falls sharply (hypertension 53.5% -> 38.0%, diabetes 35.1% -> 21.5%). Applying the correction to every document instead raises breaks on correct positive predictions from 0.1% to 6.4%, so per-document selection is essential. TGS also transfers to three model families and three other clinical and biomedical datasets.
papers.summary: LLMs rely on spurious features in clinical classification: swapping one gender token in a clinical note changes gender-irrelevant diagnoses in up to 53.5% of cases. `Trajectory-Guided Steering` (`TGS`) looks at how the model's preference between answers evolves across layers and uses that alone to decide, per document, whether to correct a prediction and in which direction, without counterfactual data or knowledge of the spurious feature. On 16 `i2b2` tasks it **fixes 17.7% of errors while breaking only 1.3% of correct predictions**, reduces gender-swap inconsistency (for example hypertension from 53.5% to 38.0%), and transfers to other model families and datasets.

papers.title: Noise-shaped Sampling and Annealing for Scalable On-the-edge Training of Binary and Ternary AI Models
papers.abstract: The training loss of binary and ternary neural networks, expanded as a multilinear polynomial over the discrete weights, is structurally equivalent to the energy of a hierarchical high-order Ising model. We exploit this equivalence to apply Ising solvers to discrete-weight network training, while accounting for a fundamental difference in objectives: an Ising solver seeks the ground state of a fixed energy function, whereas training seeks solutions that generalize to unseen data. Our key contribution is $\Sigma\Delta$-Sampler, an optimizer that reconciles these objectives by embedding a stochastic sampling-and-annealing step as a noisy quantizer inside a first-order $\Sigma\Delta$ noise-shaping loop. The loop pushes noise from weight quantization, high-order frustration, and mini-batch sampling out of the low-frequency adaptation band, so that discrete weight updates follow the smooth descent trajectories embedded in the rugged loss landscape. We validate the framework on a planted quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) benchmark with a known minimizer; on CIFAR-10, where a $13$M-parameter ternary model comes within $1\%$ of full-precision accuracy; on ImageNet-1k, where a ternary ResNet-18 comes within $0.4\%$ Top-5 accuracy of a ternary baseline; on class-incremental continual learning, where prior-task accuracy is preserved; and on MatMul-free language models up to $2.7$B parameters, where it outperforms a straight-through-estimator baseline under matched continued pre-training. Compared with standard quantization-aware training, $\Sigma\Delta$-Sampler reduces the training memory footprint by over $50\%$, delivers an order-of-magnitude speed-up, and reduces weight-update memory traffic by four orders of magnitude, making it attractive for on-device training and fine-tuning of large binary and ternary models.
papers.summary: Observes that the training loss of binary and ternary neural networks is equivalent to the energy of a high-order Ising model, and adapts Ising-style solvers to train them while still aiming for generalization rather than a ground state. The resulting optimizer, `ΣΔ-Sampler`, places stochastic sampling and annealing inside a sigma-delta noise-shaping loop so that discrete weight updates follow smooth descent paths. A 13M-parameter ternary model comes within 1% of full precision on `CIFAR-10`, and on `MatMul-free` language models up to 2.7B parameters it beats a straight-through-estimator baseline. Compared with quantization-aware training it **cuts training memory by over 50% and gives an order-of-magnitude speed-up**, targeting on-device training and fine-tuning.

papers.title: Understanding Stability of Outer Nesterov Momentum on Stochastic Pseudo-Gradients
papers.abstract: Large neural networks are commonly trained across many workers, and communication between them is a major cost. Workers therefore take several local optimization steps before sending their net parameter displacements, or pseudo-gradients, to an outer optimizer, which often applies Nesterov momentum. We study how the outer momentum, the number of local steps and the averaging over workers control the training dynamics, and in particular their stability. For random quadratics, we derive an exact mean-square stability criterion in any dimension, which reveals that the inner batch size determines whether increasing the number of local steps eventually stabilizes or destabilizes the outer iteration. Moreover, while averaging the pseudo-gradients of independent workers can make larger outer momentum values admissible, the number of workers required for stability can grow exponentially with the number of local steps. Finally, we show that the mean-square dynamics governing stability can be probed directly at intermediate neural-network checkpoints using shared-minibatch perturbations. We test our theoretical findings across networks, and measure their consequences for training loss.
papers.summary: In communication-efficient distributed training, workers take several local steps and send their parameter changes, called pseudo-gradients, to an outer optimizer that often uses Nesterov momentum. For random quadratics the authors derive an exact mean-square stability criterion and show that the inner batch size determines whether adding local steps eventually stabilizes or destabilizes training. Averaging over more workers allows larger outer momentum, but **the number of workers needed for stability can grow exponentially with the number of local steps**. They also show how to probe these dynamics at intermediate neural-network checkpoints and test the predictions on real networks.

papers.title: Network-Wide Freeway Speed Nowcasting and Forecasting from Sparse Fixed Sensors with a Probe-Supervised Graph Convolutional Recurrent Network
papers.abstract: Traffic agencies need current and near-future speeds on every link of their network, but their fixed sensors cover only part of it. We study joint nowcasting and next-hour forecasting of hourly speeds on all 4{,}127 directional freeway links of the Dallas--Fort Worth region from sensors on 643 links (15.6%). Historical probe-vehicle data supervise every link in training; only sensor readings are used at inference. We call this setting probe-supervised sparse sensing. We propose GCRN+, a graph convolutional recurrent network that predicts deviations from a historical speed profile. It combines a parameter-free, direction-aware kernel interpolation of sensor anomalies, used as input features and as an output baseline, with a diffusion-convolutional GRU on the directed road graph, a low-rank adaptive graph and learnable link embeddings. It scales linearly with network size and trains on a CPU. Sensor readings are emulated from probe speeds, which isolates spatio-temporal inference from detector calibration. On four held-out test days, GCRN+ attains an RMSE of 2.21~mph for the current hour and 2.39~mph for the next hour on unsensored links, against 3.23~mph for the historical average. The best baselines that use the same interpolation features reach 2.53 and 2.75~mph. Adapted recent models without these features (STID, STAEformer, ImputeFormer, MoGERNN) reach at best 2.54 and 2.53~mph; this comparison is between complete pipelines rather than architectures. GCRN+ is best in every distance band except links not connected to any sensor through the road graph. Ablations within one recurrent backbone attribute most of the gain to the link embeddings and the adaptive graph, which can be trained because probe labels exist for every link. For congestion detection on unsensored links, recall rises from 77\% (historical average) and 86% (best competitor) to 89% at aprecision of 0.94.
papers.summary: Estimates current and next-hour speeds on all 4,127 directional freeway links in the Dallas-Fort Worth region using fixed sensors on only 15.6% of them, with historical probe-vehicle data supervising every link during training. The proposed `GCRN+` combines direction-aware interpolation of sensor anomalies with a diffusion-convolutional recurrent network, an adaptive graph and learnable link embeddings, and it trains on a CPU. On unsensored links it reaches **2.21 mph RMSE for the current hour and 2.39 mph for the next**, against 3.23 mph for the historical average and at best 2.53 mph for adapted recent models, and it raises congestion-detection recall to 89%.

papers.title: A Plausible Explanation Is Enough to Mislead Multimodal Judges
papers.abstract:
Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) increasingly serve as judges in training and evaluation pipelines, often assessing answers together with explanations. Although AI judges are sensitive to textual factors, it remains unclear whether ordinary plausible explanations can sway judgments requiring visual verification. We introduce JUPE, a visual-question-answering (VQA)-style benchmark that fixes answers while varying explanations.
  Across 14 MLLM judges, ordinary explanations that sound plausible mislead judges, with effects comparable on average to deliberately persuasive arguments. Plain justifications and chain-of-thought rationales reduce rejection of incorrect answers by 12.7 and 13.8 percentage points, respectively. We call this failure plausibility capture. Using signal detection theory, we find a significant mean shift in decision criterion toward acceptance, without a clear change in mean discriminability. Explanations sway judgments across domains, explanation generators, and judging protocols, while tested mitigations offer limited, model-dependent protection. Such shifts can inflate performance estimates when judges evaluate answers with explanations.
papers.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used as judges, often scoring answers that come with explanations. The `JUPE` benchmark holds visual-question-answering (VQA) answers fixed while varying their explanations, and across 14 MLLM judges, ordinary plausible explanations mislead about as much as deliberately persuasive arguments. **Plain justifications and chain-of-thought rationales reduce rejection of incorrect answers by 12.7 and 13.8 percentage points**. A signal-detection analysis attributes this "plausibility capture" to a shift toward acceptance rather than lost discrimination, and the tested mitigations give only limited, model-dependent protection.

papers.title: ToMStories: Interpreting Theory-of-Mind in Synthetic Narratives
papers.abstract: Understanding people often requires inferring what they feel or want from how they behave rather than from what they state outright. We ask whether language models can make these inferences, and how they do so. We introduce Theory-of-Mind Stories (ToMStories), an evaluation dataset of ~6,000 short synthetically generated narrative vignettes, each paired with a multiple-choice or open-ended question about a character's emotion, fear, motivation, or emotional wound. These psychological states are conveyed implicitly (showing), explicitly (telling), or with conflict between dialogue and description. Evaluating thirteen open-weight models (1B-72B parameters), we find that the largest models match humans on multiple choice but not open-ended questions. Our analyses point to simplifications models make in both interpretation and generation of implicit psychological states, indicating that synthetic data can help us understand how models perform interpretation, but likely overestimates how well models interpret humans.
papers.summary: Introduces `ToMStories`, about 6,000 synthetic narrative vignettes that probe theory of mind by asking about a character's emotion, fear, motivation or emotional wound, conveyed implicitly, explicitly, or with dialogue and description in conflict. Across thirteen open-weight models from 1B to 72B parameters, **the largest models match humans on multiple-choice questions but not on open-ended ones**. Further analysis shows that models simplify implicit psychological states both when interpreting and when generating them, suggesting synthetic data likely overestimates how well models understand real people.

papers.title: Alert-List Concordance for Evaluating Imputation Strategies in ICU Sepsis Prediction
papers.abstract: Preprocessing is an under-measured reliability risk in clinical prediction: a model can keep a similar AUROC and still change who receives an alert. Imputation quality is commonly evaluated using reconstruction error or aggregate discrimination, neither of which directly measures agreement on which patients are flagged. At a matched alert rate, pipelines with similar aggregate performance can produce different patient lists. This question is especially relevant under the frequent, structured missingness of real ICU records. We therefore introduce alert-list concordance, which asks whether two pipelines identify the same high-risk patients, measured by the Jaccard similarity of their top-k% alert sets with patient-level bootstrap confidence intervals. On PhysioNet/CinC 2019 (40,336 patients, 71.9% missingness), we compare nine imputation strategies and a native-missingness baseline using a fixed XGBoost configuration, fitted and Platt-calibrated separately for each strategy. After Bonferroni correction, 22 of the 28 reconstruction-method pairs showed no statistically significant difference in patient-level AUROC, yet their alert lists overlap at Jaccard 0.518 to 0.750. Similar aggregate discrimination can therefore accompany different patient selections. ForwardFill is a separate outlier, pairing higher discrimination with the lowest overlap in the matrix, 0.40 to 0.45. The broad pattern holds within each hospital system and under six patient-level aggregation rules. At the row level, eight of ten methods fall within an AUROC range of 0.011. In this row-level pipeline, deep imputers did not outperform mean imputation on discrimination, and the sequential implementations cost 5 to 12 times mean imputation in total pipeline wall-clock time on our hardware.
papers.summary: Argues that imputation choices in clinical prediction can change which patients get flagged even when aggregate AUROC barely moves. The authors propose alert-list concordance, the Jaccard overlap of two pipelines' top-k% alert sets, and compare nine imputation strategies on `PhysioNet/CinC 2019` sepsis data (40,336 patients, 71.9% missingness) with a fixed `XGBoost` model. Most method pairs show no significant AUROC difference, yet **their alert lists overlap at only 0.518 to 0.750 Jaccard**, and forward-fill pairs higher discrimination with the lowest overlap. Deep imputers did not beat mean imputation and cost 5 to 12 times more pipeline time.

papers.title: Measuring Mechanistic Uncertainty in Large Language Models via Causal Robustness
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in critical domains, where their susceptibility to hallucinations makes reliable and interpretable uncertainty quantification essential. We introduce the concept of mechanistic uncertainty, which characterizes uncertainty through the stability of the internal mechanisms supporting a model's response. We propose the causal robustness margin, defined as the minimum internal intervention required to deviate the model's output, and operationalize it using Jacobian Lens (Jlens) concept steering vectors. Across three open-source models and five question-answering datasets, we show incorrect and uncertain responses exhibit smaller margins, indicating greater sensitivity to internal interventions, and the causal robustness margin complements conventional output-based uncertainty methods. Finally, in a controlled knowledge injection experiment, correctly learned facts show increased margins after training, suggesting that causal robustness provides a mechanistically grounded signal of uncertainty.
papers.summary: Proposes mechanistic uncertainty, which measures an LLM's uncertainty through how stable the internal mechanisms behind its answer are. The causal robustness margin is defined as the smallest internal intervention, using `Jacobian Lens` (`Jlens`) concept steering vectors, needed to change the output. Across three open models and five question-answering datasets, **incorrect and uncertain answers have smaller margins**, and the signal complements output-based uncertainty methods. In a controlled knowledge-injection experiment, margins grow for facts the model has learned correctly.

papers.title: Inductive Learning of Concept Embeddings from Cross-Linguistic Colexification Patterns with Textual Attributes
papers.abstract: The advent of distributional semantics as a framework for computational semantics marked a paradigm shift in the nature of representations, by which meanings are represented as dense vectors commonly known as word embeddings. Computational approaches to historical or typological language comparison, on the other hand, still mostly rely on discrete representations, while the potential of embedding-based methods remains largely untapped in this context. Recent studies have proposed concept embeddings as a language-independent, onomasiological counterpart to word embeddings, based on networks of cross-linguistic colexification patterns. While the resulting concept embeddings reflect meaningful semantic properties and relations, they suffer from a lack of scalability, since they rely on transductive embedding approaches which only learn embeddings for nodes present in the training data. In this study, we present an inductive framework for learning concept embeddings, combining the structural properties of full and partial colexification networks with semantic information from short concept descriptions. This framework allows the embedding of unseen concepts based on a short definition. We show that the resulting concept embeddings correlate with various cross-linguistic measures of similarity or relatedness, while generalizing well to new concepts that were absent from the training data.
papers.summary: Concept embeddings built from cross-linguistic colexification networks, which record cases where one word covers several concepts, capture meaningful semantics but can only embed concepts present in training. The authors propose an inductive framework that combines the structure of full and partial colexification networks with short textual concept descriptions, so **unseen concepts can be embedded from a definition alone**. The resulting embeddings correlate with several cross-linguistic similarity and relatedness measures and generalize well to held-out concepts.

papers.title: SAFETYEDIT: Sparse Internal Targets with Prompt-Wide Control for LLM Jailbreak Backdoors
papers.abstract: Model-editing backdoors aim to induce harmful responses under a trigger while preserving ordinary behavior on untriggered input. Recent model-editing approaches target affirmative response prefixes through rank-one updates to a small subset of model weights. Yet when this prefix-level target is satisfied, the model may still revert to refusal or produce a coherent, apparently compliant response that does not address the request. To overcome this limitation, existing internal-representation approaches shift focus from output tokens to dense, high-dimensional compliance directions in latent space. Existing representation-level approaches rely on preservation constraints to maintain conditionality, motivating us to ask whether a smaller internal target can offer a different effectiveness-preservation trade-off. Motivated by the comparable control capability of single-coordinate interventions, we investigate a sparse refusal-related MLP coordinate as this target. We propose SAFETYEDIT, which optimizes a single refusal-related coordinate and uses KV-cache marking in early attention layers to propagate a prefix-trigger signal across subsequent instruction positions. On some checkpoints a downstream MLP reader converts this signal into control of the coordinate, while on others the propagated signal alone suffices; the method is defined by the sparse target rather than by a fixed writer-reader pair. Across four open-weight LLMs and three dataset groups, SAFETYEDIT achieves the highest triggered Guard ASR in 11 of 12 comparisons and the highest mean StrongREJECT score in all 12, relative to the baselines evaluated for each model. Crucially, comprehensive ablation and behavioral audits confirm generally minimal changes in untriggered behavior and general capabilities in the tested configurations.
papers.summary: Studies model-editing backdoors that make an LLM produce harmful jailbreak responses when a trigger is present while behaving normally otherwise. Instead of targeting affirmative output prefixes or dense compliance directions, `SAFETYEDIT` optimizes a single refusal-related MLP coordinate and marks the KV cache in early attention layers so the trigger signal reaches later instruction positions. Across four open-weight LLMs and three dataset groups it achieves **the highest triggered Guard attack success rate in 11 of 12 comparisons and the highest `StrongREJECT` score in all 12**, with minimal changes to untriggered behavior and general capabilities in the tested configurations.

papers.title: The Ephemeral Cost of Switching Optimizers Across LLM Training Stages
papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that switching optimizers between pretraining and subsequent training stages incurs a performance cost, but systematic investigation of this phenomenon is lacking. We study the mismatch between AdamW and Muon optimizers by pretraining 1.2B Llama-3 models from scratch while varying the proportion of updates taken with each optimizer, and similarly interpolating between the two optimizers during continued pretraining and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Surprisingly, we find little evidence of a meaningful optimizer mismatch penalty: final performance is largely explained by the independent effects of the pretraining and post-training optimizers, with downstream performance generally improving as the proportion of Muon updates during SFT increases. Although matching the pretraining optimizer can reduce forgetting during SFT, this does not translate into improved final benchmark performance. We further evaluate AdamW and Muon for task-general SFT of open-weight models, across the Llama and Qwen families up to 14B parameters, where Muon remains competitive with AdamW, despite these models having been pretrained with AdamW. Together, our results suggest that the choice of optimizer for post-training can be made largely independently of the optimizer used during pretraining.
papers.summary: Tests whether switching optimizers between pretraining and later training stages carries a real penalty, by pretraining 1.2B `Llama-3` models with varying mixes of `AdamW` and `Muon` updates and interpolating between the two during continued pretraining and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). The authors find **little evidence of an optimizer mismatch penalty**: final performance is largely explained by the separate effects of each stage's optimizer, and downstream results generally improve as the share of `Muon` updates during SFT increases. Matching the pretraining optimizer reduces forgetting but does not improve benchmark scores, and `Muon` stays competitive for SFT of `AdamW`-pretrained `Llama` and `Qwen` models up to 14B parameters.

papers.title: Evidence-Gated Bilingual RAG for Reliable Consumer Banking Search
papers.abstract: Consumers often describe what they need rather than use the terminology found on a banking website. For example, a natural-language request ("a card for travel") may not share the keywords of the relevant product page, and the problem is harder in bilingual services, where the same intent may be expressed in Arabic or English. This paper presents an evidence-gated bilingual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework for consumer banking search that operates entirely on local infrastructure. The framework combines structured web-content refinement, hybrid dense-lexical retrieval, intent-aware evidence selection, cross-encoder reranking, and a three-outcome Answer / Related Mismatch / No Answer decision mechanism. On 210 URL-labeled Arabic and English queries, the proposed approach improves Top-1 hit rate from 50.48% to 79.05% and MRR@5 from 0.571 to 0.797 over a hybrid baseline. A separate 26-case end-to-end evaluation achieved 69.2% strict success, with 72.7% of generated answers classified as supported by an automated faithfulness judge. These results are preliminary: the retrieval queries are paraphrases of a small reference set, and the end-to-end test is small and uses an automated rather than human judge, so they do not establish human-verified answer correctness or generalizable performance.
papers.summary: Builds a bilingual Arabic-English retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system for consumer banking search that runs entirely on local infrastructure and handles requests phrased as needs rather than product terms. It combines web-content refinement, hybrid dense-lexical retrieval, intent-aware evidence selection, cross-encoder reranking, and a three-way Answer, Related Mismatch or No Answer decision. On 210 labeled queries it **raises Top-1 hit rate from 50.48% to 79.05%** over a hybrid baseline, and a 26-case end-to-end test reached 69.2% strict success. The authors call the results preliminary because the queries are paraphrases of a small reference set and the end-to-end judge is automated.

papers.title: Is a Linear Probe Evidence of a Linear Representation?
papers.abstract: The linear representation hypothesis holds that pretrained vision models encode generative factors as linearly decodable directions in feature space, and comes with a standard methodology: train a linear probe, declare a factor represented if accuracy is high. We show this test is too permissive. Asymptotically, any sufficiently rich feature map, including a random one, admits a linear readout, so high probe accuracy is consistent with two very different geometries: a true linear world model, where the latent-aligned subspace dominates the representation, or a kernel machine, where the latents lie linearly inside a much larger curved manifold. This distinction matters because the curved structure orthogonal to the probe is relevant for out-of-distribution generalization, robustness, and compositional transfer. We propose three asymmetric diagnostics that distinguish the two cases: reverse predictivity, spectral concentration, and out-of-distribution generalization. We validate them in a fully observed simulation where ground truth is known. Applied to six pretrained vision transformers on SVG-World, our deterministic generative benchmark with paired visual styles, and to two of them on CelebA, they show pretraining produces structure beyond a random kernel but well short of a linear world model. On dSprites, 3D Shapes and MPI3D, forward decodability and latent-aligned variance dissociate. Thus, forward decoding alone does not show that the probed factors align with the dominant geometry of the representation. In summary, our work cautions about the success of linear probes as opposed to truly linear and low dimensional representations.
papers.summary: The standard test for the linear representation hypothesis is to train a linear probe and call a factor represented if accuracy is high. The authors argue this test is too permissive: any sufficiently rich feature map, even a random one, admits a linear readout, so high accuracy cannot tell a true linear world model apart from a kernel machine in which the latents sit inside a much larger curved manifold. They propose three diagnostics to separate the two cases (reverse predictivity, spectral concentration, and out-of-distribution generalization) and validate them in a simulation where ground truth is known. Applied to six pretrained vision transformers on their new `SVG-World` benchmark and on `CelebA`, the diagnostics show that **pretraining yields structure beyond a random kernel but well short of a linear world model**, and on `dSprites`, `3D Shapes`, and `MPI3D` forward decodability and latent-aligned variance come apart.

papers.title: Secondhand Stress: How Stressful Disclosures Affect Psychosocial Wellbeing in Online Graduate Admissions Communities
papers.abstract: Online communities provide spaces for individuals navigating stressful life transitions to disclose difficulties and seek peer support. Yet encountering others' distress may also have psychosocial implications for community members. Drawing on stress crossover theory, we examine how engagement with peer distress during graduate admissions is associated with subsequent psychosocial expression and participation, and whether similar associations extend through downstream interactions. We analyze 171,981 posts and 1,130,413 comments from two Reddit communities across three admissions cycles, using propensity-score stratification and baseline-adjusted comparisons. Users who engaged with distress disclosures during application preparation subsequently exhibited higher classifier-estimated anxiety, depression, and stress expression, alongside greater commenting activity and lexical redundancy. These associations recurred across admissions cycles, while no significant psychosocial associations were detected among downstream respondents interacting with previously exposed users. Our findings highlight how greater distress-related expression can coexist with continued community participation, while distinguishing direct engagement with distress disclosures from subsequent social contact. We discuss implications for designing online communities that preserve opportunities for self-disclosure and peer support while remaining attentive to the experiences of those encountering distress-related content.
papers.summary: Drawing on stress crossover theory, the study asks whether reading and engaging with other people's distress in online graduate-admissions communities affects members' own wellbeing. It analyzes 171,981 posts and 1,130,413 comments from two Reddit communities across three admissions cycles, using propensity-score stratification and baseline-adjusted comparisons. Users who engaged with distress disclosures while preparing applications later showed **higher classifier-estimated anxiety, depression, and stress expression**, along with more commenting and more repetitive language. No significant psychosocial effects were found among downstream users who interacted with those exposed users.

papers.title: Exploring The Empirical Privacy Landscape of Synthetic Data
papers.abstract: Methods for training language models on sensitive data differ in how they balance capability gains against the risk of leaking private information. In this paper, we present a controlled comparison of data-level and training-level interventions for navigating the capability-privacy tradeoff on synthetic medical records with canaries to probe for leakage. Direct finetuning performs best on capability metrics but leads to the most privacy leakage, while DP-SGD reduces leakage at substantial cost to capabilities. Generating synthetic data from these records offers a more favorable balance, particularly when guided by a uniqueness-aware instruction to replace private details. Relative to naive paraphrasing, privacy-aware rewriting improves privacy protection across a variety of different rewriting models. We also find that more capable rewriting models generally reduce the risks of downstream privacy leakage, although held-out fit does not improve monotonically and increased test-time compute yields inconsistent gains. Overall, these results highlight privacy-aware rewriting as a promising direction for achieving a more favorable trade-off between capabilities and empirical privacy compared to other training-level methods, and our evaluation framework supports comparisons of future models and methods.
papers.summary: The work runs a controlled comparison of ways to train language models on sensitive data, using synthetic medical records seeded with canaries to measure leakage. Direct finetuning gives the best capability but leaks the most, while `DP-SGD` (differentially private stochastic gradient descent) cuts leakage at a large cost to capability. Training on synthetic rewrites of the records strikes a better balance, and **privacy-aware rewriting guided by a uniqueness-aware instruction outperforms naive paraphrasing across many rewriting models**. More capable rewriters generally reduce downstream leakage, though held-out fit does not improve monotonically and extra test-time compute gives inconsistent gains.

papers.title: Edit Discovery in Human-AI Interactions
papers.abstract: Human-AI interactions are becoming a rich source of data for improving AI systems: while many model responses are already satisfactory, others expose failures that could become valuable supervision if identified and corrected. We study this setting through the notion of an editor: a more capable evaluation process that can inspect a response and either confirm it or modify it, but whose invocation is costly. The editor may be a human expert, a stronger AI system, or the same model equipped with additional computation, context, tools, or information. The key challenge is to decide which interactions to send to the editor before knowing whether an edit will actually be made, since invoking the editor itself consumes limited resources such as expert time, inference cost, latency, or tool-use overhead. We formulate this problem as Edit Discovery Optimization (EDO), which seeks to minimize edit opportunities missed among skipped interactions while controlling unnecessary confirmations and respecting an editor-cost budget. We characterize the population-optimal policy and show that it takes the form of a cost-adjusted threshold on the posterior probability of an edit. Building on this structure, we develop EDIT (Edit Discovery via Iterative Thresholding), an online algorithm for the partial-feedback setting in which edit labels are revealed only for selected interactions. EDIT combines an adaptive edit score, a confirmation-control threshold, and a cost-aware selection rule; it satisfies the editor budget at every round and controls the average confirmation rate up to a vanishing finite-horizon term, without distributional assumptions on the interaction stream. Across four reasoning and factual question-answering benchmarks, EDIT achieves a better trade-off between editor cost, Type-I error, and Type-II error than direct LLM-based batch selection.
papers.summary: Some logged human-AI interactions contain failures that would make useful supervision if a costly "editor" (a human expert, a stronger model, or the same model with more compute or tools) corrected them, so the problem is deciding which interactions to send for review before knowing whether an edit is needed. The authors formalize this as `Edit Discovery Optimization` (`EDO`) and show that the population-optimal policy is a cost-adjusted threshold on the posterior probability of an edit. They then propose `EDIT` (Edit Discovery via Iterative Thresholding), an online algorithm for the partial-feedback setting that **satisfies the editor budget at every round and controls the confirmation rate without distributional assumptions**. On four reasoning and factual QA benchmarks, `EDIT` trades off cost and Type-I and Type-II errors better than direct LLM-based batch selection.

papers.title: ProPerAgent: Toward Memory-Driven Proactive Assistance
papers.abstract: As assistants move from reactive answering toward proactive intervention, memory changes role: it no longer only supplies the answer to a query, it determines whether and when to speak at all. Prior work in this setting hands the system the relevant fact in context; we study the regime that makes the problem hard, where the evidence justifying an intervention must be mined from a long-horizon personal memory. We introduce ProPerMem, a benchmark for memory-driven proactive assistance (MPA), pairing egocentric video with year-long, distractor-rich user memories (~618K tokens on average), human-verified trigger windows, and a protocol that scores content and timing jointly. Every baseline we evaluate performs poorly (at most 15%), including frontier models given summarized or retrieval-augmented memory. A controlled study explains why: with oracle evidence delivered inside the trigger window GPT-5.3-Chat reaches 96%; letting it choose the timing drops it to 38%, and replacing oracle evidence with retrieval drops it to 15%. Content and timing are separately necessary, and missing either is catastrophic. Guided by this, we build ProPerAgent (Proactive Personalized Agent) with a plug-and-play harness that surfaces memory from a graph-organized store and gates it down to what is worth interrupting for, plus a lightweight RL stage that curbs early and repeated firing. Without any training, ProPerAgent lifts strict accuracy from below 10% to 37.5% on Qwen3.8-27B and 38% on GPT-5.3-Chat; RL post-training reaches 42.4%.
papers.summary: The paper studies memory-driven proactive assistance (MPA), where an assistant must decide whether and when to interrupt based on evidence buried in a long personal memory rather than handed to it in context. The new `ProPerMem` benchmark pairs egocentric video with year-long, distractor-rich user memories averaging about 618K tokens, plus human-verified trigger windows, and scores content and timing together. Every baseline scores at most 15%, and a controlled study shows content and timing are each necessary: `GPT-5.3-Chat` reaches 96% with oracle evidence delivered inside the trigger window, but falls to 38% when it must choose the timing itself and to 15% with retrieval. The proposed `ProPerAgent` uses a graph-organized memory store with gating and lifts strict accuracy **from below 10% to about 38% without training**, reaching 42.4% after a lightweight RL stage.

papers.title: Not All Graphs Are Maps: A Task-Agnostic Exploration Framework for Mobile GUI Navigation
papers.abstract: Modern mobile GUI agents can perceive visible screens and execute local actions, but they still lack persistent app-specific navigation knowledge: where functions live, which pages contain them, and which screens are equivalent across repeated visits. We introduce TAG-Nav, a Task-Agnostic Graph Navigation framework that wraps existing GUI-agent backbones with reusable destination memory. Offline exploration is distilled into compact records of app functions, target pages, and waypoint routes before any evaluated instruction is seen. When a future task's destination is covered, TAG-Nav retrieves the destination and provides route guidance without task-specific demonstrations. This separates mobile GUI destination navigation from full task completion: many tasks share the prefix of reaching the right page, while final actions may enter content, send data, make purchases, delete information, or change sensitive settings. To evaluate route finding without downstream execution confounds, we introduce DestBench, a navigation-only protocol that asks whether an agent reaches the correct pre-action destination screen. DestBench enables a controlled graph-memory study comparing no-memory agents with random, automated BFS, and clean graph memory. Graph-derived memory improves strict navigation success rate of UI-TARS-1.5-7B from 52.4% without graph memory to 58.3% with automated BFS memory, and improves Qwen-VL-Max success rate from 59.5% to 71.4% on the same conditions. Together, TAG-Nav and DestBench show that destination coverage and route cleanliness strongly shape graph-memory value, making graph quality a measured variable rather than an assumed benefit of exploration.
papers.summary: Mobile GUI agents can act on the screen in front of them but lack persistent knowledge of where functions live inside an app. `TAG-Nav` (Task-Agnostic Graph Navigation) wraps existing agent backbones with a destination memory distilled from offline exploration (app functions, target pages, and waypoint routes) and uses it for route guidance without task-specific demonstrations. To measure route finding separately from the final actions, the authors introduce `DestBench`, which checks only whether an agent reaches the correct pre-action screen. Graph memory built by automated BFS raises strict navigation success from 52.4% to 58.3% for `UI-TARS-1.5-7B` and **from 59.5% to 71.4% for `Qwen-VL-Max`**, and the results show that destination coverage and route cleanliness strongly determine how much the memory helps.

papers.title: AlphaBet: Reinforcement Learning for LLM Event Forecasting Agents
papers.abstract: Forecasting an unresolved event requires finding relevant evidence and deciding how strongly it supports each outcome. Yet outcome-based training of Large Language Model (LLM) forecasters often begins with preassembled evidence at a single prediction date, leaving evidence acquisition outside the learning loop. We introduce AlphaBet, an agentic reinforcement learning (RL) framework that trains a single LLM policy to search, reason, and report probabilities across multiple pre-resolution dates. Each dated forecast is scored by a proper scoring rule against the eventual outcome, allowing one resolved event to supervise decisions under different information states. We decompose forecasting regret into an evidence-acquisition gap and a probability-reporting gap, and show that Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)'s standard-deviation normalization can distort the reporting target under multi-class proper scores. On GLM-4.5-Air, AlphaBet reduces the Brier score from 0.731 to 0.626 on Forecast-Dojo and from 0.612 to 0.528 on FutureX. Controlled ablations attribute these gains to multi-date training and show that they come from improvements in both information acquisition and probability reporting. Our empirical results validate that GRPO's std normalization degrades proper-scoring-rule performance while leaving top-outcome accuracy largely unchanged.
papers.summary: Outcome-based training of LLM forecasters usually starts from a fixed set of evidence at a single prediction date, which leaves evidence gathering outside the learning loop. `AlphaBet` is an agentic reinforcement learning framework that trains one policy to search, reason, and report probabilities at several dates before an event resolves, scoring each dated forecast with a proper scoring rule. The authors split forecasting regret into an evidence-acquisition gap and a probability-reporting gap, and show that the standard-deviation normalization in `GRPO` (Group Relative Policy Optimization) distorts the reporting target under multi-class proper scores. On `GLM-4.5-Air`, `AlphaBet` **cuts the Brier score from 0.731 to 0.626 on `Forecast-Dojo`** and from 0.612 to 0.528 on `FutureX`, and ablations credit the gains to multi-date training improving both search and calibration.

papers.title: Multimodal Filesystem Memory For Long-Horizon Embodied Agents
papers.abstract: Agents operating over long horizons need an effective memory that allows them to reuse their experience throughout long interactions. If the entire history of an interaction is retained, it becomes difficult to find the relevant experience, while compressing it into summaries may result in the loss of visual and spatial details that are required later on. We present \textbf{MFM}, a multimodal filesystem memory architecture that keeps complementary types of agent memory. \textbf{Episodic memory} stores the observations, actions, and outcomes, and \textbf{spatial memory} associates experiences with locations. \textbf{Semantic and procedural memory} build up general knowledge and reusable methods of acting, and \textbf{working memory} holds the current plans. MFM makes use of searchable textual records to connect these different representations to the underlying multimodal episodes. The agents are able to find previous experiences by means of contextual cues and to examine the original observations in order to recover details that are missing from their textual descriptions. Through consolidation, the agents convert experience into higher-level knowledge and procedures while still keeping references to the original episodes. In the case of long-horizon Minecraft and computer-use tasks, MFM leads to improved performance with three base models. With GPT-6-Astra, MFM completes \emph{Mine Diamond from Scratch} and reaches 16 out of 24 milestones on the \emph{Ender Dragon} task, as against 12.7 for the best baseline. On CUABench-KiCad it attains a mean reward of 0.440, as compared to 0.400 for the best baseline and 0.267 in the case of no persistent memory.
papers.summary: Long-horizon agents need memory that is easy to search and still keeps the visual and spatial detail that summaries throw away. `MFM` is a multimodal filesystem memory with episodic, spatial, semantic, procedural, and working memory, linked through searchable text records that point back to the raw multimodal episodes, so agents can recall experiences from contextual cues and re-inspect the original observations. A consolidation step turns experience into reusable knowledge and procedures while keeping references to the source episodes. With `GPT-6-Astra`, `MFM` completes `Mine Diamond from Scratch` in Minecraft and **reaches 16 of 24 milestones on the `Ender Dragon` task versus 12.7 for the best baseline**, and it scores 0.440 mean reward on `CUABench-KiCad` against 0.400 for the best baseline and 0.267 without persistent memory.

papers.title: Explore Separately, Adopt Selectively: Execution-Guided Tool Use over Large Tool Libraries
papers.abstract: Large language model agents must discover relevant tools from large libraries, e.g., thousands of tools, as new needs arise during task execution. When several candidates could satisfy the same need, execution may be required to identify the relevant one. Investigating candidates in a shared trajectory can leave alternatives unexplored or allow failed attempts to influence subsequent reasoning. To address this, we present BRIA (BRanch-Inspect-Adopt), a simple yet effective agent that temporarily isolates candidate investigations in separate branches. Each branch retrieves and executes tools to investigate its candidate; a task agent inspects the resulting execution evidence and adopts only useful results into its continuing trajectory. BRIA retrieves additional tools as new capability needs arise during task execution. We evaluate BRIA on PlanBench-XL and MCP-Atlas using a shared pool of 1897 tools, three language models, and static and adaptive retrieval baselines. Across all settings, BRIA matches or exceeds the strongest retrieval baseline. On MCP-Atlas, it achieves an average claim score of 89.77, compared with 75.40 for MCP-Zero, a gain of 14.37 percentage points. BRIA also lies on the Pareto frontier for task performance and input-token cost.
papers.summary: LLM agents working over libraries of thousands of tools often have to execute several candidate tools to find the right one, and doing this inside a single trajectory can leave alternatives untested or let failed attempts derail later reasoning. `BRIA` (Branch-Inspect-Adopt) investigates each candidate in its own temporary branch that retrieves and runs tools, after which the main task agent inspects the execution evidence and adopts only the useful results; it also retrieves new tools as new needs arise. Evaluated on `PlanBench-XL` and `MCP-Atlas` with a shared pool of 1,897 tools and three language models, `BRIA` matches or beats the strongest retrieval baseline in every setting. On `MCP-Atlas` it reaches an average claim score of **89.77 versus 75.40 for `MCP-Zero`**, and it sits on the Pareto frontier of task performance against input-token cost.

papers.title: Quantum-Classical Neural Networks for Solving Lindblad Master Equations
papers.abstract: Variational quantum algorithms have emerged as a promising approach for simulating open quantum systems, yet their expressive power and trainability remain poorly understood. We propose a variational framework for solving Lindblad master equations by minimizing a residual cost function using a compositional ansatz obtained by combining a classical neural network with a parameterized quantum circuit. The density matrix is represented through a purification on an enlarged Hilbert space, ensuring positivity, Hermiticity, and unit trace by construction, while all gradients are evaluated exactly via the parameter-shift rule. Beyond the algorithmic formulation, we derive an upper bound for the covering number of the proposed compositional model and compare it with that of purely quantum neural networks. Our analysis shows that the classical parametrization enlarges the effective hypothesis class while providing finer control over its complexity, thereby establishing a theoretical connection between expressivity, covering numbers, effective dimension, and the barren plateau phenomenon. Numerical experiments validate both the accuracy of the proposed method for representative Lindblad master equations and the theoretical predictions regarding gradient concentration. These results provide a unified variational and theoretical framework for the simulation of dissipative quantum dynamics using compositional quantum machine learning models.
papers.summary: The authors propose a variational method for solving Lindblad master equations, which describe open quantum systems, by minimizing a residual cost with an ansatz that combines a classical neural network and a parameterized quantum circuit. The density matrix is represented as a purification on an enlarged Hilbert space, so positivity, Hermiticity, and unit trace hold by construction, and gradients are computed exactly with the parameter-shift rule. They derive an upper bound on the covering number of this compositional model and show that **the classical part enlarges the hypothesis class while giving finer control over its complexity**, linking expressivity, effective dimension, and barren plateaus. Numerical experiments confirm both the solver's accuracy and the predicted gradient-concentration behavior.

papers.title: Optimal approximation of smooth functions by ReLU neural networks
papers.abstract: We study uniform approximation of the H\"older ball $\mathcal H_1^s([0,1]^D)$ by fully connected ReLU networks. Except in the one-dimensional Lipschitz case, existing constructions remain separated from the information-theoretic efficiency limit. This article closes the gap for every $s>0$ and $D\ge1$: networks with width $O(N)$, depth $O(L)$, and parameter magnitude $O(1)$ attain uniform approximation error of order $(N^2L^2\log N)^{-s/D}$. No relation between width and depth is required. The construction uses new encoding and decoding mechanisms that exploit higher-order finite-difference bounds for local Taylor coefficients of the target function. As a statistical consequence, empirical risk minimizers over the corresponding clipped network classes attain the minimax regression rate $n^{-2s/(2s+D)}$ without additional logarithmic factors. The paper also gives a detailed exposition of the key approximation techniques, covering both established and new mechanisms.
papers.summary: The paper studies uniform approximation of Hölder-smooth functions on the unit cube by fully connected ReLU networks, where existing constructions fell short of the information-theoretic limit except in the one-dimensional Lipschitz case. It closes this gap for all smoothness levels and dimensions: **networks of width O(N), depth O(L), and bounded parameters achieve error of order (N²L²log N)^(−s/D)**, with no required relation between width and depth. The construction relies on new encoding and decoding mechanisms based on higher-order finite-difference bounds for local Taylor coefficients. As a statistical consequence, empirical risk minimizers over these network classes reach the minimax regression rate without extra logarithmic factors.

papers.title: Chance-Constrained Personalized LLM Routing with Online Preference Learning
papers.abstract: We study personalized LLM routing, where a router selects among heterogeneous models with different costs and capabilities. The router must minimize cumulative inference cost while ensuring reliable realized response quality, even though user preferences are unknown and must be learned from feedback during deployment. We formulate this problem as a constrained contextual bandit and develop an algorithm that learns preferences while balancing cost and quality. Under a logistic preference model and a strict-feasibility condition, we establish sublinear expected cost regret relative to an optimal stationary randomized contextual oracle and a high-probability guarantee on realized cumulative satisfaction. The framework extends beyond LLM routing to broader online model-selection problems with reliability requirements.
papers.summary: The paper addresses personalized LLM routing, where a router chooses among models with different costs and capabilities and must keep response quality reliable while learning unknown user preferences from feedback during deployment. It frames the problem as a constrained contextual bandit and gives an algorithm that learns preferences while balancing cost against quality. Under a logistic preference model and a strict-feasibility condition, the authors prove **sublinear expected cost regret against an optimal stationary randomized oracle, together with a high-probability guarantee on cumulative user satisfaction**. The framework also applies to other online model-selection problems with reliability requirements.

papers.title: Data Provenance Aggregation and Structural Descriptors for Query-Template Identification
papers.abstract:
Runtime query similarity identification supports several activities, including workload analysis, identifying recurring behaviour, auditing, debugging, and anomaly detection. Existing methods for evaluating query similarity mostly rely on SQL text, execution plans, or result values but do not account for input data or how results are derived during query execution.
  This paper proposes a novel approach using data provenance for query-template identification. We construct query-level profiles that capture explicit data dependencies, occurrence frequencies, and structural properties by aggregating tuple-level Lineage and Why-provenance across entire query results. We also derive Provenance Structural Descriptors (PSD), which summarise these profiles using a small set of numerical features.
  We evaluate our proposals using these profiles to identify query templates over \(12{,}500\) distinct query instances generated from parametrised TPC-DS query templates. The experimental evaluation shows that query templates can be identified solely from their provenance footprints, and that accuracy improves as more historical data becomes available. It also shows that PSD achieve high classification accuracy with limited training history and low test-processing cost.
papers.summary: Methods for spotting similar database queries at runtime usually rely on SQL text, execution plans, or result values, and ignore which input data a result was derived from. The authors build query-level profiles by aggregating tuple-level Lineage and Why-provenance across whole query results, and summarize them with a small set of numerical features they call `Provenance Structural Descriptors` (`PSD`). On 12,500 query instances generated from parametrized `TPC-DS` templates, **query templates can be identified from provenance footprints alone**, with accuracy improving as more history becomes available. `PSD` reach high accuracy with limited training history and low processing cost at test time.

papers.title: GlobeBench: Evaluating Text-Based World Model Capabilities for Scalable Environment Simulations
papers.abstract: Text-based world models have recently shown potential to simulate complex RL environment state transitions for a diverse set of use cases. However, no standardized benchmark exists to compare, study and improve these models. Through this paper, we attempt to solve this problem by building GlobeBench, a novel benchmark with 1,632 tasks across five separate domains and nineteen simulation skills. The tasks check whether models can predict the environment's response to a specific action given the full agent trajectory by understanding earlier state changes, following environment rules, and predicting the effects of actions on both related and unrelated objects. We compare the predicted environment response with an execution-derived reference, using a hybrid architecture with both deterministic gates and a semantic judge. Among 20 general-purpose LLMs and specialized text world models, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest task success rate at 49.57%. We find that model accuracy decreases as actions affect a larger portion of the environment. Specifically, when the agent's changes must propagate to dependent objects, task success drops to an average of 5.1% across all 20 models. Although model strengths differ across tasks, 631 tasks remain unsolved by any model, suggesting a significant gap in general LLM capabilities as a world model.
papers.summary: Text-based world models that simulate how RL environments respond to actions have had no standard benchmark. `GlobeBench` provides 1,632 tasks across five domains and nineteen simulation skills, asking a model to predict the environment's response to an action given the full agent trajectory, and scoring it against an execution-derived reference using deterministic checks plus a semantic judge. Among 20 general-purpose LLMs and specialized text world models, `GPT-6 Astra` scores highest at 49.57% task success. Accuracy falls as actions affect more of the environment: **when changes must propagate to dependent objects, average success drops to 5.1%**, and 631 tasks are solved by no model.

papers.title: Normalizing Flow Maps
papers.abstract: Scalable approaches to learning neural dynamical systems have placed diffusion, flow matching, and few-step generators in flow maps at the forefront of generative modeling. Such state-of-the-art models have limited access to explicit model densities despite evolving from classical generative modeling approaches that leveraged tractable likelihoods, e.g., Normalizing Flows and Autoregressive models. In this paper, we combine these threads of few-step generation and tractable sample likelihoods and introduce Normalizing Flow Maps (NFM), a class of exactly invertible pushforward maps that generalizes normalizing flows and flow maps. More precisely, NFMs learn the integrator of an underlying dynamical system, but crucially, they provide efficient exact likelihood evaluation by construction. To enable scalable training of NFMs, we derive two complementary axes of consistency inherent to NFMs that yield (self) distillation objectives: (1) pointwise matching, which unlocks $\ell_2$-based flow-map style regression losses, and (2) distributional matching, which matches pushforward distributions to the marginals of a prescribed forward process. On conditional image generation on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-64, NFMs achieve state-of-the-art sample quality among parameter-matched normalizing flows, while supporting likelihood-based RLHF. For equilibrium sampling in Boltzmann Generators, NFMs outperform prior state-of-the-art normalizing flows on both single-system and transferable peptide benchmarks.
papers.summary: Modern few-step generators such as diffusion and flow-map models generally do not offer exact likelihoods, unlike older normalizing flows and autoregressive models. `Normalizing Flow Maps` (`NFM`) are exactly invertible maps that learn the integrator of an underlying dynamical system while giving exact likelihoods by construction, generalizing both normalizing flows and flow maps. Training uses two self-distillation objectives: pointwise matching, which allows ℓ2 flow-map-style regression losses, and distributional matching against the marginals of a forward process. `NFM` achieve **state-of-the-art sample quality among parameter-matched normalizing flows on `CIFAR-10` and `ImageNet-64`**, support likelihood-based RLHF, and outperform prior flows as Boltzmann Generators on single-system and transferable peptide benchmarks.
papers.highlight_summary:
Diffusion, flow-matching and few-step flow-map models sample well but cannot cheaply give the exact likelihood of a sample, and classical normalizing flows only give exact likelihoods for noise-smoothed data. `Normalizing Flow Maps` (`NFM`) close this gap with a family of exactly invertible two-time maps along a stochastic-interpolant path, so the model samples in a few steps like a flow map and gives an exact change-of-variables likelihood for each one-step sample, with no Tweedie denoising needed.

- Two self-distillation objectives train the maps on an `iTARFlow` backbone: `NFM-R` uses MeanFlow-style ℓ2 regression on flow-map consistency (pointwise matching), and `NFM-D` minimizes a conditional KL between each pushforward and the forward-process marginals (distributional matching), with proofs that both control the quality of the generated endpoint distribution.
- On class-conditional `ImageNet-64`, `NFM-R` reaches **FID 3.60 / FLD 3.15 at 127M parameters**, compared with 4.89 / 6.98 for an MLE-trained `iTARFlow`; on `CIFAR-10` it improves FID from 6.55 to **3.87**, and the fully invertible `NFM-D` (6.26) beats `SoftFlow` (6.76).
- Because the endpoint likelihoods are exact, the models can be post-trained with standard RL (KL-regularized REINFORCE or maximum-entropy objectives) against VLM-based rewards such as `ImageReward` and `PickScore`, and they gain more reward than best-of-64 and SMC baselines.
- As Boltzmann generators, `NFM-D` cuts energy-W2 on the 10-residue peptide Chignolin to **3.42**, against 10.82 for the `SBG` baseline; in zero-shot transfer to unseen 4- and 8-residue peptides it beats `Prose` and `Robin` on five of six metrics while using **118M vs 288M** parameters (compared with `Prose`).
- Limitations: `NFM-R` gets the best sample quality but tends to become numerically non-invertible, so staying invertible requires noise annealing and FP64 inference, and its invertible variant scores worse (CIFAR FID 5.17); multi-step `NFM-R` sampling gives up exact likelihoods, and diffusion models such as `EDM` (FID 1.36) still produce better images.

papers.title: Spectral Limits of Polynomial Graph Filters on the Long-Range Ising Model Benchmark
papers.abstract: The Long-Range Ising Model benchmark (LRIM) guarantees long-range dependence by construction: each label is the node's spin times the spin field convolved with a power-law coupling, so any model's distance from the target is measurable. We prove that a readout whose filter is a polynomial in the adjacency, the linear core of isotropic message passing and spectral graph networks, leaves an error floor that no degree lowers, because the target varies along a level set of the spectrum on which every such filter is constant. Computed exactly, the floor and the best filter of each degree predict two spectral networks adapted from published architectures to within a tenth of a decade. A filter escapes the floor only if it weighs separately the offsets the adjacency lumps together, and must still resolve the coupling across the whole lattice. A strided filter of about fifty coefficients does both: fitted to the training labels, its test error is 52 times below the best published network's. A dilated convolutional network beats the best published result at 256 nodes, matches it at 1,024, and gives the first in-domain results at the three larger sizes, while a Fourier neural operator with its standard modes falls further behind as the lattice grows. At its standard budget the dilated network stays two to four orders of magnitude short of a larger strided filter fitted to the labels. The analysis carries over to the benchmark's second coupling.
papers.summary: The Long-Range Ising Model benchmark (`LRIM`) builds long-range dependence into its labels by construction, so how far a model is from the target can be measured exactly. The authors prove that any readout whose filter is a polynomial in the adjacency matrix, the linear core of isotropic message passing and spectral graph networks, has an error floor that no polynomial degree removes, because the target varies along a level set of the spectrum on which all such filters are constant. A strided filter with about fifty coefficients avoids this floor and, fitted to the training labels, reaches **test error 52 times lower than the best published network**. A dilated convolutional network also beats or matches the best published results and gives the first in-domain results at larger lattice sizes, while a standard Fourier neural operator falls further behind as the lattice grows.

papers.title: First Passage Attention
papers.abstract: Augmenting softmax attention with forget gates typically relies on summing decay contributions along the key--query path. Because such accumulation is monotonic, these mechanisms cannot selectively erase intermediate context while preserving older, structurally relevant tokens. We propose First Passage Attention (FPA), which shifts from path summation to path extrema by lowering a key's logit proportionally to the deepest dip of a learned scalar field below that key's level over the intervening span. FPA encompasses the Forgetting Transformer (FoX) as a special case, and when the field and levels follow a shared learned walk, the alive keys with unpenalised logits naturally form a stack. We show that a constant-dimension FPA head realises any subset of keys left alive by subsequent dips, whereas softmax heads with positional biases or token-level forget gates require a head dimension linear in the number of keys. In synthetic experiments, one-layer FPA heads converge to these target sets while comparable softmax and FoX baselines fail on every seed. Scaling to a 110M-parameter language model, FPA matches FoX in perplexity and uniquely achieves perfect passkey retrieval at $8\times$ the training length, even with its key--value cache compressed to about $25\%$.
papers.summary: Forget-gated attention mechanisms sum decay along the path between key and query, and because that sum only grows, they cannot erase intermediate context while keeping older tokens that still matter. `First Passage Attention` (`FPA`) instead penalizes a key's logit by the deepest dip of a learned scalar field below that key's level over the intervening span; it contains the `Forgetting Transformer` (`FoX`) as a special case and can naturally keep a stack of alive keys. The authors prove that a constant-dimension `FPA` head can represent any such set of alive keys, whereas softmax heads with positional biases or token-level forget gates need head dimension linear in the number of keys. In a 110M-parameter language model, `FPA` matches `FoX` in perplexity and is the only model to reach **perfect passkey retrieval at 8× the training length, even with its key-value cache compressed to about 25%**.

papers.title: Risk and Refusal: Mechanisms of LLM Responses to Suicidal Ideation
papers.abstract: Refusal is a common safety mechanism in large language models (LLMs), yet in contexts of suicidal ideation (SI), refusing to engage can itself constitute a safety failure. We evaluate how eight instruction-tuned LLMs respond to SI and self-harm disclosures across three datasets, varying whether models are informed that a disclosure expresses SI and whether they receive a clinician-developed response protocol, and complement this with mechanistic analyses in six open-weight models. Our results reveal a nuanced relationship between refusal and response-level risk. At baseline, elevated risk in model responses is driven primarily by inattention to the disclosure, alongside refusal to engage. Mechanistic analyses suggest that models may refuse SI disclosures through the same direction that mediates their refusals of harmful requests. However, informing models of the SI context, or suppressing refusal directly, increases engagement without reliably lowering response risk, and may raise it. In contrast, the clinician-guided protocol consistently reduces response-level risk while also reducing refusal. Together, these analyses and ablations motivate the need for models that refuse only when warranted and engage in interactionally safe ways when users disclose SI.
papers.summary: Refusal is a standard LLM safety mechanism, but refusing to engage with someone disclosing suicidal ideation (SI) can itself be a safety failure. The authors test eight instruction-tuned LLMs on SI and self-harm disclosures from three datasets, varying whether models are told the message expresses SI and whether they get a clinician-developed response protocol, and run mechanistic analyses on six open-weight models. Risky responses come mainly from inattention to the disclosure plus refusal, and models appear to refuse SI disclosures through the same direction that mediates refusals of harmful requests. Telling models about the SI context or suppressing refusal increases engagement without reliably lowering risk, while **the clinician-guided protocol consistently reduces both response risk and refusal**.

papers.title: ARBOR: Locating Reasoning Failures in Long Chains of Thought through Reasoning State Tracking
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models solve complex problems through long chains of thought, in which prior work has documented failure modes such as overthinking, underthinking, and unsupported deductions. Existing methods detect these failures from local signals: textual similarity to nearby steps, switch tokens, or an LLM's judgment of a step's correctness. However, what a step contributes to the solution depends on the state that earlier steps have established, so identifying failures requires a global view that tracks that state across the trajectory. Therefore, we propose ARBOR, a reasoning-failure attribution framework that represents each trajectory as a tree of reasoning states, built as each step creates, verifies, prunes, or revisits a state, and attributes each failure to a relation between a step and the state preceding it. Using ARBOR, we refine the three failure modes into distinct subtypes that harm reasoning through different mechanisms and at different costs. We find that the tree state ARBOR maintains before a step separates failure steps from the at-risk steps at which the failure did not occur. We discuss how ARBOR integrates with existing mitigations at inference time and in training data. Code, data and interactive examples are available at https://inklab.usc.edu/ARBOR.
papers.summary: Known failure modes in long chains of thought, such as overthinking, underthinking, and unsupported deductions, are usually detected from local signals like similarity to nearby steps, switch tokens, or an LLM judge, even though a step's contribution depends on the state built up by earlier steps. `ARBOR` represents each reasoning trajectory as a tree of reasoning states that steps create, verify, prune, or revisit, and attributes each failure to the relation between a step and the state before it. This lets the authors split the three failure modes into distinct subtypes that cause harm through different mechanisms and at different costs. They find that **the tree state before a step separates actual failure steps from at-risk steps where the failure did not occur**, and they discuss how the framework fits with inference-time and training-data mitigations.

papers.title: CoLU: Confidence-Weighted Layerwise Unlearning for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) unlearning aims to forget certain information while preserving others, without retraining from scratch. SoTA methods such as NPO, SimNPO, and SatImp balance forgetting and retain through whole model fine-tuning, while FOM-UL explores selective layer updates. Prior works show that suppressing target information can damage retained knowledge. This trade-off can vary across layers even under the same unlearning loss. In this work, we propose Confidence-Weighted Layerwise Unlearning (CoLU), which combines a novel confidence-weighted forgetting and retain regularization while updating a single selected transformer layer, rather than the whole model for unlearning. To reduce CoLU compute cost, we further propose Brief Layer Screening (BLS), which uses a newly defined normalized forgetting-retention (NFR) score to first rank layers through a brief unlearning trials using a subset of forgetting dataset and fewer epochs. BLS pre-selects top-k ranked layer candidates, which will then be fully profiled using full data analysis. BLS is proven to reduce the runtime of CoLU by 60.2-79.7% with almost the same performance. On TOFU dataset, CoLU improves both forgetting and retention over NPO, SatImp, and GA-based FOM-UL in all six TOFU settings, and over SimNPO in five of the six settings. On MUSE Books and News datasets, CoLU achieves the highest retained KnowMem and the PrivLeak closest to zero among the compared SOTA unlearning methods. CoLU presents a new record performance in both unlearning and retain in most settings up to date. Moreover, across the measured settings, average CoLU GPU memory usage is 77.4% to 79.5% lower than full-model unlearning.
papers.summary: LLM unlearning tries to remove specific information without retraining, but suppressing the target knowledge often damages knowledge the model should keep, and this trade-off varies from layer to layer. `CoLU` (Confidence-Weighted Layerwise Unlearning) combines confidence-weighted forgetting with retain regularization while updating only one selected transformer layer, and `Brief Layer Screening` (`BLS`) picks candidate layers through short trial runs, cutting `CoLU`'s runtime by 60.2–79.7% with nearly the same results. On `TOFU`, `CoLU` improves both forgetting and retention over `NPO`, `SatImp`, and `FOM-UL` in all six settings and over `SimNPO` in five, and on `MUSE` Books and News it achieves the best retained knowledge with privacy leakage closest to zero. It also uses **77–80% less GPU memory than full-model unlearning**.

papers.title: The LLM-Attacker: A Unified Red-Team Framework for Privacy Evaluation of Split and Distributed LLM Systems
papers.abstract: Split language models keep input text on a client but send intermediate representations to a server. Attacks can reconstruct text from these messages. Comparing privacy evaluations is difficult when attackers see different messages, know different model weights or use different datasets and recovery measures. We present LLM-Attacker, a framework that records these choices and lets researchers check, compare and extend an evaluation. Compatible attacks reuse recorded messages, and their predictions are saved for independent scoring. The scoring rule requires a linked undefended reference before a defence can pass. Reports also identify attacks that remain untested. In a controlled GPT-2 experiment, adding gradients returned during training increased token recovery from 94.20% to 97.38% and exact-document recovery from 13.71% to 37.77%. The 95% interval for the token gain lay above the two-percentage-point threshold fixed before testing. This experiment is shared with a companion study; here, it tests how the evaluation responds to a change in attacker access. Further studies measure how corpus choice and compression defences affect recovery, compare an adapted published attack with its reference implementation, and test the measurement code. The framework reports implementation checks separately from measured attack effectiveness. Each privacy claim should state the attacker, dataset and scoring rule, report its controls and identify untested attacks.
papers.summary: Split language models keep the user's text on a client but send intermediate representations to a server, and attacks can reconstruct the text from those messages.
