Privacy evaluations are hard to compare because they differ in what the attacker sees, which weights the attacker knows, and which datasets and scoring measures are used. `LLM-Attacker` is a framework that records these choices, saves attack predictions so they can be scored independently, requires a linked undefended reference before a defence can pass, and reports which attacks remain untested. In a controlled `GPT-2` experiment, giving the attacker gradients returned during training raised exact-document recovery **from 13.71% to 37.77%**, and token recovery from 94.20% to 97.38%.

papers.title: A misinformation playbook sharpens judgement without breeding cynicism
papers.abstract: Misinformation harms public health and democracy, and generative artificial intelligence now writes falsehoods as persuasive as people's. Defences range from fact-checking individual claims to training people to resist falsehoods. Yet many claims are too new to check, and interventions that teach doubt can reduce belief in truth too. We propose a defence that targets not the facts of each claim but the persuasion strategies that recur across them. Here we show that learning misinformation's persuasion playbook, mapped from 214,646 fact-checked claims in 51 languages, can sharpen human and machine judgement of claims they know little about, without making either more cynical about true claims. The playbook spans social influence, information manipulation and emotional appeals, combined around a core of fear, conspiracy and fabrication. Briefed with it, plus a reminder that persuasion is not proof of falsehood, a language model better distinguished true from machine-generated false claims about events after its training data. In a pre-registered experiment, the same briefing improved people's discernment of claims they reported as unfamiliar and left their belief in true claims unchanged. Averaged over all claims, the gain was not statistically significant. Because it targets what recurs, this defence need not wait for claim-specific fact-checks.
papers.summary: Fact-checking cannot keep up with new claims, and training people to doubt can also make them doubt true claims. The authors propose a defence aimed at recurring persuasion strategies rather than the facts of individual claims, using a playbook mapped from 214,646 fact-checked claims in 51 languages that centres on fear, conspiracy and fabrication. Given the playbook and a reminder that persuasion does not prove falsehood, a language model better separated true claims from machine-generated false claims about events after its training data. In a pre-registered human experiment, the same briefing improved discernment of claims people reported as unfamiliar **without lowering belief in true claims**, but the gain averaged over all claims was not statistically significant.

papers.title: OrderFlowDiT: Transport-Regularized Diffusion Transformer for Probabilistic Limit-Order Supply Forecasting
papers.abstract: We study the conditional distribution of limit-order volume submitted over the next five minutes, given the current order book and recent order flow. The task requires capturing price placement, total volume, and predictive uncertainty jointly. Coordinate-wise diffusion losses do not explicitly account for price displacement, while normalizing fields to unit mass removes information about total volume. Agreement on selected summary statistics also does not establish fidelity to the joint field distribution. We introduce OrderFlowDiT, a conditional Diffusion Transformer for unnormalized bid and ask volume-at-price fields, trained with an unbalanced optimal-transport (UOT) auxiliary loss. We also develop a full-field evaluation framework that combines a transport cost sensitive to price placement and total volume with proper scoring rules and calibration diagnostics. In the primary comparison on 1950 validation conditions across 30 U.S. equities, adding UOT reduces full-field transport cost by 45.8% and the transport energy score by 26.1% relative to training with mean squared error alone. Both measures improve for every stock. These findings support incorporating price geometry and volume into generative modeling, with field accuracy and predictive uncertainty evaluated together.
papers.summary: The task is forecasting the distribution of limit-order volume submitted over the next five minutes, which requires modelling price placement, total volume and uncertainty together. `OrderFlowDiT` is a conditional Diffusion Transformer over unnormalized bid and ask volume-at-price fields, trained with an auxiliary unbalanced optimal-transport (`UOT`) loss. It comes with a full-field evaluation framework that combines transport costs, proper scoring rules and calibration checks. Across 1,950 validation conditions on 30 U.S. equities, adding `UOT` cut full-field transport cost by **45.8%** relative to mean-squared-error training alone, and both evaluation measures improved for every stock.

papers.title: TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Advances in frontier coding agents have sharply increased the token costs of AI-assisted software engineering. Their token efficiency is typically evaluated on isolated tasks, whereas real-world developers use them to continuously build, update, and maintain large-scale projects. This mismatch motivates us to evaluate agents over sequences of realistic coding tasks, where we find that agents exhibit recurring environment-dependent token costs that existing methods struggle to reduce. To minimize these costs, we introduce TokenEconomizer, an external controller that cuts environment-specific token costs over a sequence of tasks. These cuts come from determining (i) which operational micro-skills to inject, (ii) which persistently irrelevant tools to prune, and (iii) when to intervene in unproductive failure loops. Across Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot CLI paired with frontier models, TokenEconomizer reduces the average token cost by 18.4-30.9% with comparable task success. Savings hold in every repository under every tested agent-model setting and generalize to diverse domains such as sequential web development and security auditing, where costs fall by 6.4-21.2% depending on task structure. Our work establishes adaptive black-box cost control as a promising direction for reducing token costs of coding agents in realistic settings.
papers.summary: Coding agents are usually evaluated on token efficiency one task at a time, but developers use them across long sequences of tasks in the same project, where recurring environment-specific costs build up. `TokenEconomizer` is an external black-box controller that learns from experience which operational micro-skills to inject, which persistently irrelevant tools to prune, and when to step in on unproductive failure loops. Across `Claude Code`, `Codex` and `GitHub Copilot CLI` paired with frontier models, it reduces average token cost by **18.4–30.9% with comparable task success**, and the savings hold in every repository tested. The approach also carries over to sequential web development and security auditing, with cost reductions of 6.4–21.2%.

papers.title: Thunder-DeID+: Boundary-Aware Korean De-identification from Court Judgments to Broader Sensitive Documents
papers.abstract: This study examines the transferability of a de-identification model developed for Korean court judgments to a broader range of sensitive documents, focusing on boundary precision, label granularity, and recall. The agglutinative structure of Korean causes Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) tokenizers to frequently merge Personally Identifiable Information (PII) with adjacent particles, which complicates accurate span recovery. Furthermore, current PII taxonomies lack sufficient granularity for legal texts. To address these issues, this study introduces Thunder-DeID+, which integrates a refined three-tier PII taxonomy with a boundary-aware tokenizer. The tokenizer enhances a pretrained BPE vocabulary by incorporating N-gram and boundary-scoring components to better align token and PII span boundaries. The proposed approach is evaluated using a tokenizer-independent word-segment-level protocol. On full-length judgments, the tokenizer consistently improves W. Strict Typed F1-score from 0.76-0.77 to 0.87-0.88 across four model sizes (150M, 395M, 750M, and 1B), mainly by increasing precision rather than model scale. With fine-tuning on 1,000 broader sensitive documents, the judgment-trained model further achieves 0.93 W. Strict Typed F1-score, indicating effective transfer beyond court judgments.
papers.summary: De-identifying Korean legal text is hard because Korean attaches grammatical particles to words, so Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) tokenizers often merge personally identifiable information (PII) with neighbouring particles, and existing PII taxonomies are too coarse for legal documents. `Thunder-DeID+` combines a refined three-tier PII taxonomy with a boundary-aware tokenizer that extends a pretrained BPE vocabulary using N-gram and boundary-scoring components. On full-length court judgments, the tokenizer raises word-segment-level strict typed F1 **from 0.76–0.77 to 0.87–0.88** across four model sizes from 150M to 1B parameters, mostly by improving precision rather than through scale. After fine-tuning on 1,000 broader sensitive documents, the judgment-trained model reaches 0.93 F1.

papers.title: Reading the News Without Hindsight: NoLBERT Topics and the Cross-Section of Stock Returns
papers.abstract: Language models that read financial news are usually trained on text from the same years used to test them, so a backtest can reward hindsight. We build news topics from NoLBERT, an encoder pretrained only on text published between 1976 and 1995, adapted into a sentence encoder by contrastive fine-tuning on passages of the same article, with no labels or returns. We compare it with LDA, MiniLM and FinBERT readers on 1.26 million articles from 2012 to 2024, convert each reader's topics into attention shocks and stock exposures, and forecast the returns of the 1,000 largest US stocks with eight models at three rebalancing frequencies. Models are fitted on 2013-2019, choices are made on 2020-2021, and 2022-2024 is held out. The experiment with the best validation score loses money at every frequency. Measuring attention shocks against the past 63 trading days instead of 5 raises the test rank IC of every reader. NoLBERT gives the most stable topics and forecasts about as well as LDA. An equal-weight combination of all readers and models earns a monthly net Sharpe ratio of 1.12, significant against zero before adjusting for the search but not against a price-only benchmark.
papers.summary: Language models that read financial news are usually trained on text from the same years used to test them, so backtests can reward hindsight. The authors build news topics with `NoLBERT`, an encoder pretrained only on text from 1976–1995 and turned into a sentence encoder through contrastive fine-tuning, and compare it with `LDA`, `MiniLM` and `FinBERT` on 1.26 million articles used to forecast returns of the 1,000 largest US stocks. The configuration with the best validation score loses money at every rebalancing frequency in the 2022–2024 held-out period, while `NoLBERT` produces the most stable topics and forecasts about as well as `LDA`. An equal-weight combination of all readers and models earns a monthly net Sharpe ratio of 1.12, but this is **not significant against a price-only benchmark**.

papers.title: Native Geometry vs. Linear Recoverability: How Alignment Changes Platonic Scaling
papers.abstract: Do larger models learn increasingly similar representations of the same world? The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) predicts that they should, but similar can mean native cosine geometry---nearest-neighbour structure induced by cosine similarity before any learned alignment---or linear recoverability: correspondence revealed by a supervised linear map. Using matched Legacy Survey and Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC) embeddings across five model families, we find that Ridge alignment strengthens the relationship between model size and cross-dataset neighbourhood correspondence relative to native cosine geometry. The effect appears in all five families and persists when both representations are reduced to dimension, so it is not simply that wider embeddings give alignment more dimensions to work with. The learned maps remain far from rotations or uniform scaling, and Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) and Block-Sparse Featuriser (BSF) features give no advantage over the same alignment applied to dense embeddings. Model scale thus improves linear recoverability more clearly than native cosine-neighbourhood correspondence, without establishing convergence toward a shared native metric geometry.
papers.summary: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (`PRH`) predicts that larger models converge on similar representations, but "similar" can mean native cosine-neighbourhood geometry or correspondence that only appears after fitting a supervised linear map. Using matched `Legacy Survey` and Hyper Suprime-Cam (`HSC`) astronomical image embeddings across five model families, the authors find that `Ridge` alignment strengthens the link between model size and cross-dataset neighbourhood correspondence compared with native cosine geometry. The effect holds after matching embedding dimension, the learned maps are far from rotations, and Sparse Autoencoder (`SAE`) features offer no advantage over dense embeddings. Scale therefore improves **linear recoverability more clearly than native geometric convergence**.

papers.title: Refusal Is Not Robustness: Measuring Harmful Reachability in Autoregressive Language Models
papers.abstract: LLM safety evaluations via jailbreaking typically index on attack success rate (ASR): whether a generated response violates safeguards. However, ASR only evaluates sampled outputs and provides little information on the underlying generation process. Autoregressive language models define distributions over possible outputs, and a sampled refusal can coexist with substantial probability mass on harmful generation paths. We study this hidden structure through bounded continuation analysis (BCA), which models autoregressive generation as a stochastic process over token prefixes and computes the finite-horizon probability that generation reaches a harmful continuation. BCA constructs a bounded continuation tree, labels terminal continuations with a semantic harm evaluator, and estimates harmful reachability using exact probabilistic model checking. BCA complements ASR by measuring how much harmful behavior remains accessible beneath a sampled safe response. This makes it useful for distinguishing models that look identical under measured ASR values, and allocating red-team effort toward regions of the generation process with greater hidden risk. Across four instruction-tuned LLMs and 100 JailbreakBench behaviors, we show that BCA effectively quantifies hidden harmful behavior and provides a useful signal to guide red teaming.
papers.summary: Jailbreak evaluations usually report attack success rate (`ASR`), which checks only sampled outputs, even though a model that samples a refusal can still place substantial probability on harmful continuations. Bounded continuation analysis (`BCA`) treats generation as a stochastic process over token prefixes, builds a bounded continuation tree, labels its endpoints with a semantic harm evaluator, and computes the finite-horizon probability of reaching harmful output using exact probabilistic model checking. Across four instruction-tuned LLMs and 100 `JailbreakBench` behaviours, `BCA` measures **hidden harmful reachability beneath sampled safe responses**, separates models that look identical under `ASR`, and helps decide where red-team effort should go.

papers.title: Shape-Aware Neural Time Fields for Rigid-Body Motion and Manipulation Planning
papers.abstract: Rigid-body motion planning is fundamental to robotic transport and manipulation, where both object position and orientation determine whether a body can move through cluttered environments. This coupling makes planning chal- lenging because translation and rotation can be constrained very differently by surrounding geometry. We propose Shape- Aware Neural Time Fields, a physics-informed neural motion planning framework that learns a reusable travel-time, or cost- to-go, representation for rigid-body motion while explicitly accounting for these distinct geometric restrictions. The learned field captures local motion difficulty in translation and rotation and is paired with a sampling-based planner that balances progress toward the goal with the cost of reaching nearby poses. We evaluate the framework across 2D and 3D rigid- body planning tasks and non-prehensile manipulation through object pushing in diverse environments. Results show substantial improvements in planning success and inference efficiency over physics-informed neural planning baselines, while remaining competitive with classical sampling-based planners at significantly lower planning times. Ablation studies further validate the contributions of both the learned representation and the proposed planning strategy. Finally, closed-loop pushing experiments under execution deviations and external disturbances demonstrate that fast replanning enables reactive and adaptive task execution.
papers.summary: Planning rigid-body motion is difficult because surrounding geometry can constrain translation and rotation very differently. `Shape-Aware Neural Time Fields` is a physics-informed neural planner that learns a reusable travel-time (cost-to-go) field capturing local motion difficulty in translation and rotation separately, paired with a sampling-based planner that balances progress toward the goal against the cost of reaching nearby poses. On 2D and 3D rigid-body planning and non-prehensile pushing tasks, it substantially improves planning success and inference efficiency over physics-informed neural baselines and is **competitive with classical sampling-based planners at much lower planning times**. Closed-loop pushing experiments show that the fast replanning handles execution deviations and external disturbances.

papers.title: Acquisition Function-Guided Generation for Bayesian Optimization over Discrete Spaces
papers.abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) over discrete spaces is challenging due to missing gradients and the sparsity of valid solutions. Latent-space BO sidesteps both issues by fitting a surrogate in the latent space of a generative model, which however substantially complicates the direct incorporation of domain knowledge that is naturally expressed in the original discrete space. In this work, we instead combine a pretrained generative model with a surrogate defined directly in data space, where inductive biases such as domain-specific kernels can be readily incorporated. Rather than maximizing the acquisition function over the discrete design space, our method samples candidates from the generative model under a distribution tilted by the acquisition function. To recover useful gradients for sampling, we embed this tilted distribution into a diffusion bridge that yields a smooth, posterior-averaged acquisition function. This leads to \emph{acquisition function guided generation} (AFGG), which we instantiate with a categorical diffusion model and an autoregressive normalizing flow. Across a broad suite of molecular benchmarks, the diffusion model variant performs on par with leading BO methods, while the flow model variant outperforms state-of-the-art methods in most cases and remains highly competitive otherwise. Our implementation is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/afgg.
papers.summary: Bayesian optimization (BO) over discrete spaces such as molecules lacks gradients, and latent-space BO makes it hard to use domain knowledge expressed in the original data space, such as domain-specific kernels. Acquisition function guided generation (`AFGG`) keeps the surrogate model in data space and samples candidates from a pretrained generative model under a distribution tilted by the acquisition function. A diffusion bridge supplies a smooth, posterior-averaged acquisition function that provides gradients for this sampling. Across molecular benchmarks, the categorical diffusion variant matches leading BO methods, and the **autoregressive normalizing flow variant outperforms state-of-the-art methods in most cases**.

papers.title: One Communicator, Three Vendors: Extending the MoA Predictive Theory to a Real NVIDIA+AMD+CPU MPI Ensemble
papers.abstract: The companion MPI-extension paper validated the first communication-bearing machine-shape ensemble: four NVIDIA A100 ranks and four CPU ranks on one NCSA Delta node under one Open MPI job, reassembled by MPI_Gatherv. This paper extends it to a multi-vendor communicator. A Slurm heterogeneous job spanning Delta's A100 and AMD MI100 partitions places A100, MI100 and CPU ranks (nine in all) under one communicator for the first time. We give the theory (a w_i proportional to 1/t_i weight split for three concurrent realizations; a het-job specification as an admissible directive) and report real results, including what the run exposed: the 1/t split assumes time linear in rows, and this fails for the MI100 rank (6 rows took 597 ms against a linear prediction of 1.6 ms). A launch-geometry model, with predictions recorded before measuring, succeeds for the A100 (time flat from 128 to 3456 rows, stepping at exactly 3520 and 6976) and places the MI100 floor in the key loop; changing its launch settings cut about 600 ms to 14.6 ms and the energy per call at 6 rows by 32x, though the MI100 remains about 95x slower than an A100 at 8192 rows. Controlled reruns show that the companion paper's 8.1x A100 result and 22 ms Gatherv were artifacts of four ranks sharing one GPU under Open MPI's default transport. A key/value-split partition whose message sizes are derived from shapes alone is then run: the ring Allreduce of the 8.5 MB message took 11.3, 16.0 and 15.3 ms against a predicted 11-12 ms, the small Allreduce missed its prediction in every run, and compute times reproduce to about 1% while communication times vary up to 4x between runs. Each idea is introduced with a figure and closed with worked examples.
papers.summary: Building on a companion paper, this work places NVIDIA `A100`, AMD `MI100` and CPU ranks under one MPI communicator through a Slurm heterogeneous job, and extends a predictive theory that splits work in proportion to each device's speed. The run showed that the linear-time assumption fails on the `MI100`, where 6 rows took 597 ms; a launch-geometry model correctly predicted `A100` timing steps, and changing the `MI100` launch settings cut that call to 14.6 ms. Controlled reruns showed that the companion paper's **8.1x A100 result and 22 ms gather time were artifacts** of four ranks sharing one GPU. Compute times reproduced to about 1% across runs, while communication times varied up to 4x.

papers.title: Unit-level aggregation breaks coverage in causal foundation models
papers.abstract:
Causal foundation models (CFMs) show promising results for treatment-effect estimation, with unit-level estimates that are competitive on standard benchmarks. Many causal analyses, however, inform decisions through effects averaged over groups of units, such as the full sample, the treated units, or a subgroup, and for such decisions a CFM is useful only if its credible intervals are calibrated. We examine these intervals and find that their coverage degrades, both in simple synthetic settings and on standard benchmarks. On ACIC 2016, for example, temperature-calibrated 95% intervals from CausalPFN fall below nominal coverage beyond groups of 30 out of 4802 units, and intervals for the full-sample average contain the true value in only 20% of datasets.
  We trace this problem to how these models are trained and how their intervals are formed. They output a predictive distribution for one unit at a time and, at inference time, combine the unit-level variances as if the errors on different units were independent. We show formally that posterior uncertainty over the data-generating process makes these errors correlated. As a result, the combined variance is too small by a factor that grows with the size of the group. Empirically, this factor predicts where coverage fails and by how much. We then show that two neural process models, which make joint predictions for a group of units, account for this correlation and substantially improve coverage on synthetic tasks and, as heads on a frozen CausalPFN, on all six benchmarks.
papers.summary: Causal foundation models (`CFMs`) give competitive per-unit treatment-effect estimates, but many decisions depend on effects averaged over groups, which requires calibrated credible intervals. The authors show that coverage degrades as groups grow; on `ACIC 2016`, intervals from `CausalPFN` for the full-sample average contain the true value in **only 20% of datasets**. They prove that the cause is combining per-unit variances as if errors were independent, when uncertainty about the data-generating process makes them correlated, so the combined variance is too small by a factor that grows with group size. Neural process models that predict jointly for a group of units account for this correlation and substantially improve coverage, including as heads on a frozen `CausalPFN` across all six benchmarks.

papers.title: Reusing Calibration Gains across Model Representations
papers.abstract: Scale calibration learns an update for one model representation. We study how much of that update can be reused by another representation of the same pretrained model. Our transfer procedure extracts positive group-wise gains and installs them in the recipient's weights or native quantization scales without recipient-side optimization. On a quantized recipient, it preserves integer codes, zero points and storage layout. For a Qwen3-1.7B floating-point/GPTQ INT3 pair, bidirectional transfer retains 76.9-90.5% of the text-loss improvement from recipient-specific calibration on fresh WikiText and C4 cohorts excluded from project development. Shuffling the same gain values within each projection worsens both recipients, showing that their learned group assignment matters after transfer. A Llama-3.2-3B control keeps the initial native tensors at all four calibrated projections identical and changes nine projections elsewhere. Cross-installation retains 98.6-99.3% of the text-calibration benefit, alongside a small, resolved preference for each recipient's own gain. These results quantify both the adaptation carried by a reusable calibration update and the remaining benefit of recipient-specific training.
papers.summary: Scale calibration learns an update for one representation of a model, such as full precision or a quantized version, and the question is how much of that update another representation of the same model can reuse. The proposed procedure extracts positive group-wise gains and installs them in the recipient's weights or native quantization scales without any further optimization, leaving integer codes and storage layout unchanged. For a `Qwen3-1.7B` pair of floating-point and `GPTQ` INT3 versions, transfer in either direction **retains 76.9–90.5% of the improvement** from recipient-specific calibration on held-out `WikiText` and `C4` data. Shuffling the gains within each projection hurts both recipients, which shows that the learned group assignment carries over.

papers.title: Anytime Contracts for AI Services
papers.abstract: AI services are prone to moral hazard, as model providers can silently route requests to cheaper, lower-quality models, and the inherent stochasticity of model outputs makes this degradation hard to detect. Contract theory addresses moral hazard by designing payment rules that reward high-quality outputs and prevent strategic overcharging. However, existing frameworks assume interactions of fixed duration, whereas AI services are typically consumed through subscriptions and pay-as-you-go APIs that users can terminate at any time based on observed performance. We show that this flexibility can break standard contracts, opening them up to abuse by either the providers or users. To address this, we extend contract theory to account for unknown exit rules. We formalize the problem as a Principal-Agent game, and show that budget-optimal contracts in this setting are proportional to anytime-valid hypothesis tests based on likelihood-ratio e-values. We give an efficient algorithm for computing anytime contracts and show how betting e-processes can be used to approximate them when the models are unknown. Finally, we evaluate our findings on synthetic data and data from deployed LLMs.
papers.summary: AI services are open to moral hazard: providers can quietly route requests to cheaper models, and the randomness of model outputs makes this hard to detect. Standard contract theory assumes fixed-length interactions, but subscriptions and pay-as-you-go APIs let users quit at any time, and the authors show this flexibility can break standard contracts. Modelling the setting as a principal-agent game with unknown exit rules, they prove that **budget-optimal contracts are proportional to anytime-valid likelihood-ratio e-value tests**. They give an efficient algorithm for computing these contracts, use betting e-processes to approximate them when the models are unknown, and evaluate the approach on synthetic data and data from deployed LLMs.

papers.title: Next Token or Vector? Learning How Far to Decode
papers.abstract: Standard autoregressive decoding advances one token at a time, even when several upcoming tokens can be predicted together. We propose CADENCE (Context-Adaptive DEcoding), a generation method that learns both what to draft and how far to draft. Gaussian prediction heads represent future spans as continuous latent vectors, and a shared decoder converts the selected vector into token predictions in parallel. A learned router selects the prediction length from the model's own hidden states and predicted Gaussian parameters, adapting generation granularity to the current context with single-token generation as a fallback. The backbone verifies each proposed continuation and retains the prefix that matches its greedy predictions. Experiments with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on Alpaca, GSM8K, and HumanEval show that router-selected positions yield higher draft acceptance than applying the corresponding prediction length everywhere. CADENCE achieves up to 1.3x higher generation throughput than standard greedy decoding.
papers.summary: Standard autoregressive decoding produces one token at a time even when several upcoming tokens are predictable together. `CADENCE` (Context-Adaptive DEcoding) uses Gaussian prediction heads to represent future spans as continuous latent vectors, which a shared decoder turns into tokens in parallel, and a learned router chooses how far ahead to draft from the model's hidden states. The backbone model verifies each draft and keeps the prefix that matches its greedy predictions, with single-token generation as a fallback. With `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct` on `Alpaca`, `GSM8K` and `HumanEval`, router-chosen draft lengths are accepted more often than a fixed length, giving **up to 1.3x higher throughput** than greedy decoding.

papers.title: Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have shown promising potential in coding tasks, and their performance is jointly determined by the policy model and the harness that mediates their interaction with the environment. Indeed, harness and policy are mutually reinforcing and evolving only one component is suboptimal---a harness tuned for one checkpoint may not target the failure modes of an updated policy, while policy learning remains limited to the trajectories elicited by a fixed harness. In light of this, we propose Self-HPO, a recursive self-improving framework for coding agents that alternates harness and policy optimization, using the evolving policy as its own harness proposer. Specifically, in each round, the current policy first analyzes its own failures and proposes new harness candidates (H-step). The policy is then updated through reinforcement learning (RL) under the selected harness (P-step), and hard tasks identified during training form the next harness search set, keeping harness optimization targeted to the policy's evolving failure modes. Across three coding benchmarks, Self-HPO consistently outperforms harness-only and policy-only baselines, improving Qwen3.5-35B-A3B's average resolve rate from 57.8% to 64.8%, with gains generalizing to out-of-distribution settings. Further analysis shows that both optimized components retain gains even when paired with their base counterparts, while their joint gain exceeds the sum of their individual gains. Self-HPO also improves reliability (Pass@1) and expands the capability frontier (Pass@k) over the base agent. Additionally, we show that with a stronger external model (e.g., Opus 4.8) as the harness proposer, the same framework yields a further performance boost.
papers.summary: A coding agent's performance depends on both the policy model and the harness that mediates its interaction with the environment, and improving only one of them leaves gains on the table. `Self-HPO` alternates between the two: the current policy analyses its own failures and proposes new harness candidates, then is trained with reinforcement learning (RL) under the selected harness, and hard tasks found during training become the next round's harness search set. Across three coding benchmarks, it raises `Qwen3.5-35B-A3B`'s average resolve rate **from 57.8% to 64.8%**, outperforming harness-only and policy-only baselines, with gains that extend to out-of-distribution settings. The joint gain exceeds the sum of the individual gains, and using a stronger external model such as `Opus 4.8` as the harness proposer improves results further.

papers.title: Prune the Leaky Neurons: Mitigating Private Data Leakage in Fine-Tuned LLMs via Joint-Embedding-Guided Pruning
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on proprietary records enables domain adaptation but introduces two challenges: (i) privacy leakage of memorized private data, such as personally identifiable information (PII), and (ii) balancing private data removal with utility preservation. Existing defenses, including data sanitization and differential privacy, often degrade performance, while privacy-neuron editing lacks a PII-free reference to distinguish identity-specific neurons from those supporting useful text. We propose JEPA-Prune, a post-hoc neuron pruning framework guided by a model trained exclusively on PII-free views. Alongside the fine-tuned private model, JEPA-Prune, trains a public model on surrogate and masked views of the same records using a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), capturing domain knowledge without identifiers. A cross-model representation probe quantifies deviations between private representations of leaked records and this PII-free reference. Integrated gradients and a scale-invariant specificity score then identify PII-responsive neurons, which are pruned without retraining. Experiments show that pruning just 1.6% of neurons reduces PII inference accuracy by up to 7.4x and PII extraction recall by up to 13.9x, while keeping unseen-text perplexity within 16% of that of the unpruned model for most LLMs. In contrast, privacy-neuron editing increases perplexity by at least 26x.
papers.summary: LLMs fine-tuned on proprietary records can leak memorized personally identifiable information (PII), and existing defences such as differential privacy or privacy-neuron editing tend to hurt utility. `JEPA-Prune` trains a companion public model on PII-free surrogate and masked views of the same records using a joint-embedding predictive architecture (`JEPA`), and uses it as a reference to find neurons whose representations deviate on leaked records. Integrated gradients and a specificity score identify the PII-responsive neurons, which are pruned without retraining. Pruning **just 1.6% of neurons cuts PII extraction recall by up to 13.9x** and inference accuracy by up to 7.4x, while unseen-text perplexity stays within 16% of the unpruned model for most LLMs; privacy-neuron editing, by comparison, increases perplexity by at least 26x.

papers.title: Ori: Drift-Aware Streaming $k$-PCA for Very Low-Rank LLM Training
papers.abstract: A prominent family of low-rank LLM optimizers, pioneered by GaLore, performs gradient-subspace projection: at each step, they project the gradient into a low-dimensional subspace and map the update back to the full model. Most existing work either recomputes the gradient subspace at certain intervals, or performs post-hoc adaptation to catch up to the moving subspace. In this work, we explicitly identify in practice the slow, stable manner in which LLM gradient subspaces drift across time. To this end, we propose Ori, a novel low-rank optimizer for training LLMs that captures the shifting principal gradient directions over time to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy under stringent low-rank constraints. Ori employs a streaming $k$-PCA algorithm inspired by Oja++, whose low per-step cost enables high-frequency, on-the-fly subspace tracking. In practice, Ori reduces the performance gap of the state-of-the-art low-rank optimizers to full-rank optimizers by up to 69.3\% on a 1B LLaMA pretraining task, and achieves the best performance on 10 out of 16 task scenarios in Roberta-Base fine-tuning. Together, these contributions allow Ori to further push the performance and efficiency frontiers of gradient-projecting optimizers, narrowing the gap to full-rank training for LLMs. Code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Ori-Submission-2132.
papers.summary: Low-rank LLM optimizers in the `GaLore` family project gradients into a low-dimensional subspace, but they usually recompute that subspace only at intervals or adjust to its movement after the fact. The authors observe that LLM gradient subspaces drift slowly and steadily over training, and propose `Ori`, which tracks the shifting principal directions at every step using a cheap streaming k-PCA algorithm inspired by `Oja++`. On 1B-parameter `LLaMA` pretraining, `Ori` **closes up to 69.3% of the gap** between state-of-the-art low-rank optimizers and full-rank training. It also achieves the best result in 10 of 16 `RoBERTa-Base` fine-tuning scenarios.

papers.title: Causal Latent Workspaces for Looped Transformers
papers.abstract: Reusing a Transformer block across depth increases computation without replicating its parameters, but successive passes have no dedicated state through which positions can exchange compact summaries of their causal prefix. We introduce the causal latent workspace Transformer: an anchored, four-round shared-depth architecture in which each position writes gated vectors into prefix-specific latent slots and retrieves a content-addressed summary before the next shared block application. This path complements causal self-attention while the original input embedding remains accessible at every round. Across three byte-level corpora, three seeds, and two matched parameter budgets, the proposed model achieves the best mean held-out perplexity in five of six settings against five Transformer controls. At 101.71M parameters it leads on WikiText-103 raw, enwik8, and TinyStories, reaching perplexities 2.7820, 2.7843, and 1.6823; these improve upon the strongest non-workspace control on each corpus by 1.06%, 0.73%, and 1.01%. All nine seed-labelled comparisons at this budget favor the workspace. At 0.918M parameters it leads on WikiText-103 and TinyStories, whereas a conditioned loop is stronger on enwik8. Architectural ablations show that adding the workspace improves upon the anchored loop in all six settings and support refreshing its causal summaries at each round. Together, these results identify a causal, content-addressable prefix workspace as an effective structural augmentation of looped Transformers.
papers.summary: Looped Transformers reuse one block across depth to add computation without adding parameters, but successive passes have no dedicated state for positions to share compact summaries of their causal prefix. The causal latent workspace Transformer adds such a path: over four shared-depth rounds, each position writes gated vectors into prefix-specific latent slots and retrieves a content-addressed summary before the next block application, while the original input embedding stays available every round. Across three byte-level corpora, three seeds and two parameter budgets, it achieves the best mean held-out perplexity in **five of six settings** against five Transformer controls, improving on the strongest non-workspace control by about 0.7–1.1% at 101.71M parameters. Ablations show the workspace improves on the plain anchored loop in all six settings.

papers.title: Reasoning Reranking with Semantic IDs as the Sole Item Representation
papers.abstract: Reasoning rerankers write a rationale before ranking a candidate slate, and existing systems read item metadata to do so, even though generative recommenders increasingly represent items as compact Semantic IDs (SIDs). Ranking from SIDs alone has two appeals: SID prompts are far shorter than the matched item text, and although item codes are fixed from content, the backbone learns their token embeddings in part from user-item interaction sequences, so the tokens can carry behavioral signal that item text lacks. That training targets next-item generation, and whether it supports ranking a supplied slate from SIDs alone is untested. We build ReRankID, a controlled testbed in which models reason and rank from a history and slate shown only as SIDs, varying item rendering, history length, and slate size one at a time. On this testbed, such models often copy the input order instead of reranking, and readable metadata does not repair the failure. We compare supervised fine-tuning, rejection-sampled self-training, on-policy distillation, and verifier-based reinforcement learning as post-training methods and find that they elicit the missing behavior. The strongest post-trained model, the 8B model trained with a graded ranking reward, gives the best SID-only ranking and matches strong text-reading LLMs whose prompts are about 20x longer. It ranks above random with no history at all, where a caption-reading reference does not, and it keeps its gains at long histories, where text prompts pass 50k tokens and the caption-reading reference stops improving. In a paired rationale audit, this model argues trade-offs better than that reference but describes items less accurately. The common post-training methods we test thus elicit ranking from SIDs but not faithful item descriptions, which calls for post-training that improves the reasoning itself, not only the ranking it produces.
papers.summary: Reasoning rerankers write a rationale before ranking candidate items, and they normally read item metadata, while generative recommenders increasingly represent items as compact Semantic IDs (`SIDs`). Using `ReRankID`, a controlled testbed where models see histories and candidate lists only as `SIDs`, the authors find that models often copy the input order instead of reranking. Supervised fine-tuning, rejection-sampled self-training, on-policy distillation and verifier-based reinforcement learning all elicit real reranking, and the best 8B model trained with a graded ranking reward **matches strong text-reading LLMs whose prompts are about 20x longer**. An audit of its rationales shows it argues trade-offs well but describes items less accurately than a caption-reading reference, so these methods improve ranking without producing faithful item descriptions.

papers.title: Veil-Then-Reveal: Protecting PII Privacy via Reversible Pseudo-Anonymization in Zero-Trust User--LLM Interaction
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly process sensitive documents and personal information, yet sending prompts containing personally identifiable information (PII) to remote providers exposes data subjects and organizations to risks from logging, retention, model training, and unintended disclosure. Existing anonymization methods often mask or remove PII, while conventional encryption eliminates the lexical and structural cues needed for effective LLM processing. We present Veil-then-Reveal (VtR), a user-side PII pseudo-anonymization framework for privacy-preserving LLM interaction under a zero-trust threat model. VtR treats remote LLM providers as untrusted and sends only pseudo-anonymized prompts, keeping plaintext PII on the user. VtR first detects PII and replaces it with realistic, same-type, in-vocabulary surrogates before prompts leave the user's device, preserving their linguistic and structural properties. It combines format-preserving encryption (FPE) for structured PII, such as phone and credit-card numbers, with a keyed-hash dictionary and secure vault for semantic PII, such as names, locations, and organizations. Session-specific mappings provide cross-session unlinkability, while user-side restoration reversibly replaces surrogates with their original values in LLM responses. We further introduce a rank-class FPE strategy for dates that preserves format and ambiguity while reducing cipher evaluations. Evaluation on three datasets containing 11,322 annotated PII instances achieves 97.9% detection recall, 95.2% protection of detected values, and 99.9% round trip; 100% of echoed surrogates end-to-end round-trip restoration.
papers.summary: Sending prompts that contain personally identifiable information (PII) to remote LLM providers exposes that data to logging, retention, and training. Masking or removing it breaks the task, and encrypting it strips the cues the model needs. `Veil-then-Reveal` (`VtR`) runs entirely on the user's side under a zero-trust threat model. It swaps detected PII for realistic surrogates of the same type before the prompt leaves the device. Structured values such as phone and card numbers go through format-preserving encryption (`FPE`), while names, places, and organizations are mapped through a keyed-hash dictionary and a secure vault, and the original values are restored in the model's response. Per-session mappings keep sessions unlinkable. Across three datasets with 11,322 annotated PII instances, it reports 97.9% detection recall, 95.2% protection of detected values, and **100% end-to-end restoration of echoed surrogates**.

papers.title: On the Position Bias of Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Study
papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that position bias remains a critical vulnerability in large language models (LLMs), undermining both the integrity of multiple-choice evaluations and the reliability of retrieval-augmented generation. However, existing understanding of this phenomenon is largely derived from studies with limited model coverage and English-centric benchmarks, leaving the behavior of frontier models and diverse languages underexplored. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive investigation of position bias across model scales ranging from billion-level to trillion-level parameters, covering both multiple-choice and multi-document tasks in five languages. Our experiments reveal that while position bias remains noticeable in small-scale models and Non-English languages, increasing model scale and employing standard Chain-of-Thought prompting significantly mitigate this issue. Moreover, we demonstrate that emerging \emph{thinking models} with extended reasoning capabilities are nearly immune to position bias, suggesting a costly but general approach toward resolving this vulnerability.
papers.summary: Position bias means a model's answer depends on where options or documents appear in the prompt. It undermines multiple-choice evaluation and retrieval-augmented generation, but most studies have tested few models and mostly English. This study measures position bias in models from billions to trillions of parameters, on multiple-choice and multi-document tasks in five languages. The bias is still noticeable in small models and in non-English languages. Larger scale and standard `Chain-of-Thought` prompting reduce it substantially, and **thinking models with extended reasoning are nearly immune to it**, though that fix is expensive.

papers.title: Watermarkability: Measuring and Improving Language-Model Compatibility with Logit-Based Watermarks
papers.abstract: Language-model watermarks can help identify model-generated text, encode provenance information, and detect post-generation edits. A broad class of logit-based watermarks increases the logits of a designated token set at each decoding step. Because a base model's native probability mass on this set varies across contexts, models, and watermark rules, the same logit bias can yield different adherence rates and increases in perplexity (PPL). We introduce watermarkability to characterize the compatibility between a model and the token sets requested by a watermark. At a target mass $\tau$, we quantify this property through a watermarkability cost: the expected minimum KL divergence from the base-model distribution required to assign probability at least $\tau$ to the requested set. A lower cost means that the model is more watermarkable for that request distribution. To reduce this cost, we propose a two-stage method. In the first stage, we train a target-set-conditioned low-rank adapter on unions drawn from a 16-way vocabulary partition to increase the requested set's probability mass. In the second stage, a closed-form controller applies the smallest remaining uniform logit bias needed to reach the target mass. We evaluate the method on six watermark schedules using OPT-125M and Qwen3-8B. Across the 12 model-schedule pairs, the pre-adaptation watermarkability cost correlates with the log-PPL increase under a near-hard fixed-bias baseline (pooled Pearson $r=0.929$). For every schedule, at least 99.80% of sampled tokens fall in the target set requested at their decoding step. At this reliability, the adapter and controller reduce average per-schedule prompt-conditional PPL by 46.3% on OPT-125M and 5.2% on Qwen3-8B relative to the fixed-bias baseline.
papers.summary: Logit-based watermarks boost the logits of a chosen token set at each decoding step. Because a model's natural probability on that set varies by context, the same bias can produce very different adherence rates and perplexity increases. The authors define watermarkability as the minimum KL divergence needed to push the requested set's probability above a target. They reduce it with a two-stage method: a low-rank adapter conditioned on the target set, followed by a closed-form controller that adds only the remaining uniform bias needed. On `OPT-125M` and `Qwen3-8B` across six watermark schedules, the cost strongly predicts perplexity damage (**Pearson r = 0.929**), and the method keeps at least 99.8% of tokens in the target set while cutting perplexity by 46.3% and 5.2% respectively.

papers.title: Replay Pruning and Few-Bit Integer Inference for Hardware-Efficient Speed-Sign Recognition
papers.abstract: Speed-limit sign recognition on an automotive camera system-on-chip (SoC) must fit a detector and a classifier (the reader) into the memory, arithmetic, and energy budgets of the device. In our two-stage recognizer, the detector, a YOLO-family network with ReLU and hard-sigmoid operators, is compressed by channel replay: an iterative pruning cascade identifies the channels to remove, the recorded deletions are replayed on the original task-trained network, the parent, and one continuous knowledge-distillation recovery follows. On a YOLOv5n, replay removes 60.3% of the parameters at the accuracy of the parent and, in validation mAP50-95 over five matched seeds, outperforms iterative pruning and training from scratch, and its per-step variant (per-step replay) is the most accurate pruning method. On a YOLOv8n, replay and per-step replay outperform every other method and the unpruned parent. The reader, a five-layer CNN with 18k parameters, and the post-processing of the YOLOv5n and YOLOv8n heads use integer arithmetic only. With 4-bit weights and 8-bit activations (W4A8), the reader matches FP32 accuracy in 12.1 KB of on-chip memory, and an executable streaming model reproduces the INT8 class predictions of its runtime on all 9,850 test crops. On a Jetson AGX Orin, INT8 is faster than FP16 only in the implicit formulation of TensorRT, and the replay detector runs fastest on the deep-learning accelerator (DLA). Trained on public data only, the combined system of 0.72 M parameters recognizes 95.2% of the signs of a held-out automotive camera at 90% precision and 94 frames per second.
papers.summary: Recognizing speed-limit signs on an automotive camera chip means fitting both a detector and a classifier into tight memory, arithmetic, and energy budgets. The detector is compressed with channel replay: an iterative pruning cascade records which channels to delete, the deletions are replayed on the original trained network, and one knowledge-distillation recovery follows. Replay removes 60.3% of `YOLOv5n` parameters at the original accuracy and outperforms the other pruning methods tested on `YOLOv5n` and `YOLOv8n`. An 18k-parameter integer-only reader at 4-bit weights and 8-bit activations matches FP32 accuracy in 12.1 KB of memory. The combined 0.72M-parameter system recognizes **95.2% of signs at 90% precision and 94 frames per second**.

papers.title: Causal Edit Serialization
papers.abstract: Standard autoregressive language models generate text sequentially, but revision requires referring back to tokens in the input context or those already generated. Causal Edit Serialization (CES) is introduced as a framework for expressing such revisions within the same causal token stream. Special pointer tokens are paired with predicted source addresses, allowing insertion, deletion, replacement, copying and movement to be localized explicitly. A lightweight localization head and dual-index rotary position encoding support both address prediction and conditioning on previously emitted pointers, while retaining a standard causal attention mask. A pretraining procedure combines ordinary language modeling with serialized repairs derived from random corruptions, model-generated edits and repeated text. Across model scales and editing baselines, CES models demonstrate complete applied edits with modestly higher clean-text bits per byte than clean autoregressive models. Supervised and reinforcement-learning post-training provide a grammatical-error-correction proof of concept, producing more beneficial than harmful changes under reference-blind model judging. Correct repair programs also improve subsequent text prediction while the original context and its cached states are retained. CES provides a common interface for generation and localized revision, with potential extensions to iterative refinement and additional pointer-addressed transformations.
papers.summary: Autoregressive language models can only append text, so revising earlier tokens has no native representation. `Causal Edit Serialization` (`CES`) expresses edits inside the same causal token stream using special pointer tokens paired with predicted source addresses. These support insertion, deletion, replacement, copying, and moving text, and rely on a lightweight localization head and dual-index rotary position encoding. Pretraining mixes ordinary language modeling with serialized repairs derived from corruptions and model-generated edits. **CES models complete applied edits at only modestly higher clean-text bits per byte than standard models**, and a grammatical-error-correction proof of concept with supervised and RL post-training makes more beneficial than harmful changes.

papers.title: Partial-Revelation Panel Forecasting: Predictive Information Gain, Allocation, and Coarsening-Consistent Operators
papers.abstract: We study partial-revelation panel forecasting: given $k$ of $n$ annotator votes on the previous dialogue turn, predict the full count distribution of the next turn's panel. This cross-turn predictive information differs from same-item annotation value. Under any nested revelation mechanism, the population decrement satisfies $V(k)-V(k+1)=I(Y;R_{k+1}\mid X_k)$; a fitted model also contributes adjacent excess-risk differences. Coarsened-completely-at-random (CCAR) masking supplies the exchangeable random-rater interpretation used in our operators. We define coarsening-consistent panel operators with a closed-form Dirichlet-multinomial realization, learned completion, and rater-count transfer. Against per-level lookup, cold-start count negative log-likelihood differences are -0.422/-0.166/-0.014 nats on IEMOCAP/M3ED/EmoWOZ. A held-out rater experiment measures same-item value: first and second additional votes reduce NLL by 0.583/0.221, 0.578/0.184, and 0.180/0.069 nats, respectively. Cross-turn and same-item gains are not interchangeable, and CCAR masks are controlled interventions rather than observed arrival processes. Consistency is auditable but does not guarantee predictive improvement; per-level marginalization can outperform a shared table. Target-free allocation beats uniform only where row-level signal is predictable: at budget one it recovers 83--93% of retrospective feature class headroom on IEMOCAP/M3ED but does not improve EmoWOZ. Gains are modest and corpus-dependent, with several small or null partial-revelation differences. Code and aggregate result artifacts accompany the preprint.
papers.summary: Given k of n annotator votes on the previous dialogue turn, the task is to predict the full vote distribution for the next turn. The authors formalize this cross-turn predictive information and define coarsening-consistent panel operators, including a closed-form `Dirichlet-multinomial` version, learned completion, and transfer across rater counts. On the emotion corpora `IEMOCAP`, `M3ED`, and `EmoWOZ`, cold-start operators beat per-level lookup tables, and additional same-item votes reduce negative log-likelihood. Budget-aware vote allocation recovers 83–93% of the available headroom on two corpora but does not help on `EmoWOZ`. The authors stress that **gains are modest and depend on the corpus**.

papers.title: Too Emotional to Be Fake? Intra-Utterance Emotion Shifts Expose Failure Modes in Speech Deepfake Detectors
papers.abstract: Expressive speech synthesis can now change emotion within a single utterance, yet its impact on deepfake detection remains unclear. We introduce EmoShift, a benchmark comparing emotion-stable (AA) and emotion-changing (AB) speech to examine these effects while accounting for static emotion identity and acoustic confounds. It comprises 7,240 bona fide utterances from four source datasets and 9,720 synthetic utterances generated using four expressive TTS systems. Across seven detectors, we find that emotion changes can make synthetic speech appear more genuine, increasing spoof miss rates by up to 25.3 percentage points on OMG-Emotion at fixed thresholds. Conversely, emotion-changing bona fide speech increases false-alarm rates by up to 24.4 percentage points on IEMOCAP. Further analyses reveal detector-specific sensitivities to emotion trajectories, not fully explained by static emotion identity or splicing artifacts. These findings underscore the importance of emotion dynamics in deepfake detection.
papers.summary: Expressive speech synthesis can now shift emotion within a single utterance, and `EmoShift` tests how this affects speech deepfake detectors. The benchmark pairs emotion-stable and emotion-changing speech: 7,240 genuine utterances and 9,720 synthetic ones from four expressive text-to-speech systems, with controls for static emotion and acoustic confounds. Across seven detectors, emotion shifts make synthetic speech look more genuine, **raising spoof miss rates by up to 25.3 percentage points** on `OMG-Emotion`. They also make genuine emotion-changing speech look fake, raising false alarms by up to 24.4 points on `IEMOCAP`. These sensitivities are not fully explained by static emotion identity or splicing artifacts.

papers.title: The Reliance Hypothesis: Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness Rises as Language Resource Level Falls
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) faithfulness matters for monitoring, explaining and safely deploying large language models, yet it has been studied mostly in English. Languages differ in level, the amount of text available to learn from, so models know less in lower-resource languages, which may change how much they rely on their reasoning. To our knowledge, we are the first to relate CoT faithfulness to both resource level and task type (knowledge- or reasoning-intensive). On parallel multiple-choice questions from Multilingual Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMMLU) in eight languages, faithfulness rises as resource level falls on knowledge-intensive tasks but not on reasoning-intensive ones, a gap that points the same way across four models and several faithfulness measures. We propose, and find support for, the Reliance Hypothesis: models rely more on their reasoning when they cannot recall the answer, as in lower-resource languages on knowledge-intensive tasks. Model confidence partly explains the effect of resource level, but not the knowledge-reasoning gap. Languages in which models are less confident rely more on reasoning, yet less confident answers within a language do not, a Simpson's paradox. In lower-resource languages, models rely on their reasoning for more answers, not more strongly for each. CoT monitoring may therefore be most informative in lower-resource languages, where it is least often validated.
papers.summary: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) faithfulness, meaning how much a model's answer actually depends on its stated reasoning, has mostly been studied in English. Using parallel `MMMLU` questions in eight languages across four models and several faithfulness measures, the authors find that **faithfulness rises as a language's resource level falls on knowledge-intensive tasks but not on reasoning-intensive ones**. They propose the Reliance Hypothesis: models lean on their reasoning when they cannot simply recall the answer. Model confidence partly explains the resource-level effect, with a Simpson's-paradox pattern across and within languages. CoT monitoring may therefore be most informative in lower-resource languages, which is where it is least often validated.

papers.title: Benchmarking and Enhancing Agentic Causal Discovery
papers.abstract: LLM agents can now run causal discovery algorithms on a dataset and report what comes out. Whether they do more than that, such as noticing where an algorithm went wrong and fixing it with further tests, is hard to tell from current benchmarks. Most of them give the variables meaningful names, and an LLM shown only the names of the T\"ubingen cause-effect pairs already gets 99% of the directions right. With the names removed, the data are usually clean enough that picking a better algorithm than PC closes most of the gap. We introduce Heuresis, a benchmark of anonymous simulated datasets whose mechanisms range from linear Gaussian to heavy-tailed. For each family of datasets it separates what a better existing algorithm can gain from what only a closer look at the data can gain, and it traces every edge an agent changes. Every family leaves a gap that none of the algorithms, the router and the two causal-discovery foundation models we ran can close, so a score above the best chosen algorithm has to come from using the data. We instantiate the benchmark with an agent harness and three LLMs, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5 and Qwen 3.8 Flash. GPT-6.1 Sol surpasses the best chosen algorithm on all six families, by 14% adjacency F1 on the most difficult one, and Claude Opus 5.5 does so by 7.4% there. A third of the true edges the two agents restore on the two hardest families appear in no algorithm's output. The code and data will be publicly released to facilitate future work.
papers.summary: Existing causal-discovery benchmarks give variables meaningful names, which an LLM can exploit without reading the data. Names alone get 99% of `Tübingen` cause-effect directions right, and with names removed, choosing a better algorithm than `PC` closes most of the remaining gap. `Heuresis` uses anonymous simulated datasets ranging from linear Gaussian to heavy-tailed mechanisms. For each family it separates what a better off-the-shelf algorithm can gain from what only closer analysis of the data can gain, and it traces every edge an agent changes. In an agent harness, `GPT-6.1 Sol` beats the best chosen algorithm on all six families, by **14% adjacency F1 on the hardest**, and `Claude Opus 5.5` beats it there by 7.4%. A third of the true edges these agents restore on the hardest families appear in no algorithm's output.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Budget Allocation for Efficient LLM Tree Search
papers.abstract: Tree search enhances multi-step reasoning in large language models (LLMs), yet prevailing methods expand every step with a fixed budget, irrespective of the marginal utility of expansion. We first show, across existing search algorithms, that continuations sampled from a shared intermediate state are largely duplicates and collapse to a few distinct answers. Critically, we find that the semantic dispersion of sibling actions predicts the redundancy of their downstream continuations, permitting a subtree's budget to be fixed before expansion. An information-theoretic analysis motivates this: treating the per-step budget as the Monte Carlo sample size for estimating a step's residual answer entropy, we derive a sufficient budget that shrinks with sibling dispersion. We accordingly propose $\textbf{Uncertainty-Aware Allocation}$ (UAA), a training-free framework that decouples value from uncertainty: values determine which candidates are promising, while uncertainty, estimated from sibling dispersion at no additional model cost, determines how many merit expansion, via uncertainty-aware pruning and uncertainty-aware budgeting. Across mathematical reasoning, logical reasoning, and planning benchmarks, UAA reduces token usage by up to $90\%$ and latency by up to $9\times$ at comparable accuracy, generalizing across four tree search algorithms and both open- and closed-source LLMs.
papers.summary: LLM tree search usually expands every step with a fixed budget, even though continuations sampled from the same intermediate state often collapse to a few distinct answers. The authors show that how semantically spread out sibling actions are predicts how redundant their downstream continuations will be. An information-theoretic argument then gives a sufficient per-step budget that shrinks as that spread decreases. `Uncertainty-Aware Allocation` (`UAA`) is a training-free method: value estimates decide which candidates to pursue, and sibling dispersion decides how many to expand, at no extra model cost. Across math, logic, and planning benchmarks, four tree search algorithms, and open and closed models, it **cuts token usage by up to 90% and latency by up to 9x at comparable accuracy**.

papers.title: Identify, Classify, Act: Per-Instruction Controlled Compliance for LLMs over External Data
papers.abstract: LLMs over external data face a per-instruction tension: a single document or tool return often interleaves legitimate directives with adversarial prompt injections, and the model must follow the former while rejecting the latter. Existing defenses suppress or trust all external instructions, collapsing the safety-utility frontier and forcing a choice between over-refusal and over-compliance. We argue the missing capability is \textbf{per-instruction credit attribution} and formalize it as External-Data Instruction Classification, an identify-classify-act decision over each embedded directive. We propose \textbf{EDIC}, a decomposed reward framework for per-instruction compliance. A scene-grounded pipeline injects mixed beneficial and harmful instructions with counterfactual filtering, while a generative judge is initialized by SFT and refined with GRPO to attribute compliance at the instruction level. The judge then produces a reward that separately encourages beneficial compliance and penalizes harmful compliance for RL training. Across two backbones and five benchmarks, EDIC improves both safety and utility over the strongest prior defense, lifting harmful-rejection by up to 7.7\% and Arena-Hard-Auto utility by 12.5\% on Qwen3-4B. The code repository is hosted at https://github.com/yingyingxia666/EDIC.
papers.summary: A single document or tool output can mix legitimate instructions with prompt injections, and current defenses either distrust or trust all embedded instructions. That forces a trade-off between over-refusal and over-compliance. The authors frame the problem as classifying each embedded instruction and propose `EDIC`, a decomposed reward framework. It generates training data by injecting mixed beneficial and harmful instructions with counterfactual filtering, and trains a generative judge with SFT and then `GRPO` to attribute compliance at the instruction level. The judge's reward then trains the policy with RL, rewarding beneficial compliance and penalizing harmful compliance separately. On `Qwen3-4B`, it improves harmful-instruction rejection by up to 7.7% and **`Arena-Hard-Auto` utility by 12.5%** over the strongest prior defense.

papers.title: Cooperation Without Adaptation: LLM Agents in a Collective-Risk Dilemma
papers.abstract: Language-model agents are increasingly deployed to act on behalf of people in settings where individual decisions shape shared outcomes. We examine whether five production models adapt their contributions to changing risks and partner behaviour, or instead follow a relatively fixed strategy. In a collective-risk dilemma game (CRG), six players contribute to a shared pool over ten rounds; if the pool falls short of its target, a catastrophe may destroy their remaining resources. Four models contributed approximately an equal share at every positive risk level, and four of the five also contributed when risk was zero, even though contributing could not improve their payoff. Explicitly stating that only the agent's own payoff mattered reduced zero-risk contributions for most models, while a more neutral prompt did not. Several models correctly identified which action offered the higher expected payoff at different risk levels, yet their contributions changed little. Against fixed partners, no model consistently chose the payoff-maximising response, and in mixed-model groups, a single agent's shortfall in the final round could cause an otherwise successful group to fail. Payoff-based selection also depended on population composition: in a single six-agent group, it favoured the model that contributed least and reduced group success, whereas in larger, randomly mixed populations, it favoured an exact fair-share model at moderate and high risk. These findings show that cooperative self-play alone is not evidence of strategic adaptability. Consistent with a machine-behaviour approach, evaluations of agents in multi-agent systems should test how they respond to incentives, partner actions, and population composition.
papers.summary: Five production LLMs played a collective-risk dilemma: six players contribute to a shared pool over ten rounds, and a shortfall risks a catastrophe that destroys their remaining resources. Most models contributed roughly an equal share at every risk level, and four of five kept contributing even when risk was zero and contributing could not help them. Several models correctly identified the payoff-maximizing action, yet their behavior barely changed. **No model consistently best-responded to fixed partners.** In mixed groups, one agent's final-round shortfall could sink an otherwise successful group, and which model selection favored depended on population composition. The authors conclude that cooperative self-play does not show strategic adaptability, and that multi-agent evaluations should test responses to incentives, partner behavior, and population makeup.

papers.title: ToPA: Block-wise Toeplitz Adaptation for Expressive and Efficient Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) has emerged as a prevalent strategy for adapting large pre-trained models. Among PEFT techniques, reparameterization-based methods, particularly those that employ low-rank or sparsity structures, have attracted significant attention. However, these approaches often underperform full fine-tuning. Specifically, low-rank methods constrain the update rank, which is misaligned with the inherently high-rank nature of full fine-tuning. In contrast, sparsity-based techniques limit the flexibility of the parameter space and compromise connectivity across weights. To overcome these limitations, we explore the use of Toeplitz matrices, whose entries are constant along each diagonal, therefore providing a compact parameterization without imposing explicit rank or sparsity constraints. A straightforward approach is to update weights via a product of Toeplitz matrices. However, similar to RNNs, long multiplicative chains often lead to gradient instability. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{ToPA}, a more refined version of this idea that replaces standard Toeplitz matrices with block-wise Toeplitz, greatly increasing each factor's capacity and shortening the chain, thereby stabilizing training and improving expressiveness. We theoretically show that products of block-wise Toeplitz matrices can approximate arbitrary matrices under shorter chain length, justifying the structural design of ToPA. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ToPA offers greater expressivity than existing low-rank and sparse parameterizations. Empirical evaluations across 21 NLP and CV datasets, spanning 5 model architectures, consistently validate the effectiveness of ToPA.
papers.summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods based on low-rank or sparse updates often underperform full fine-tuning, because they restrict either the rank or the connectivity of the weight update. `ToPA` instead parameterizes updates as products of block-wise Toeplitz matrices, which have constant diagonals, giving a compact form with no explicit rank or sparsity limit. Block-wise structure gives each factor more capacity and shortens the multiplicative chain, which avoids the gradient instability seen with plain Toeplitz products. The authors prove these products can approximate arbitrary matrices with shorter chains and are more expressive than low-rank and sparse parameterizations. Experiments on **21 NLP and computer vision datasets across 5 architectures** support the method.

papers.title: Learning to Be Guided: Shaping Latent Geometry for Classifier-Free Guidance
papers.abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is a standard component of conditional diffusion models, and guided generation performance has become the \textit{de facto} measure of state-of-the-art models. Recent work on latent diffusion models seeks to learn latent spaces that are easier to model with diffusion. However, under CFG, generation additionally depends on how conditions are arranged in the latent space. We study this arrangement under discrete class conditions, termed \emph{class geometry}, and investigate what class geometry allows a latent space to work well with CFG. Under a Gaussian class model, we show that shifting variance from intra- to inter-class at fixed total variance makes classes more distinguishable under noise, and derive a noisy posterior objective whose per-sample descent direction is proportional to the oracle CFG correction. Based on the analysis, we propose Prototype Regularization (PR), a lightweight surrogate for the intractable noisy posterior objective, which applies a cosine prototype classifier to spatially pooled latents. With a controlled training budget (20 epochs for VAE, 80 epochs for DiT), adding PR to an LDM baseline reduces guided gFID on ImageNet from 3.31 to 2.28, surpassing a DINOv3-aligned VA-VAE (2.44) with negligible overhead. We further demonstrate that PR generalizes to pseudo-labels derived from clustering, continuous text-embedding conditions, and video latents. Together, our findings highlight class geometry as a critical factor in guided generation and take a first step toward CFG-compatible representation learning. Our project page is available at: https://maps-research.github.io/cfg-geometry/.
papers.summary: Under classifier-free guidance (CFG), diffusion generation quality depends on how classes are arranged in the latent space, which the authors call class geometry. In a Gaussian model, shifting variance from within-class to between-class makes classes easier to tell apart under noise, and the resulting objective's descent direction matches the ideal CFG correction. `Prototype Regularization` (`PR`) is a cheap surrogate for that objective: it applies a cosine prototype classifier to pooled latents. Adding it to a latent diffusion baseline **lowers guided gFID on `ImageNet` from 3.31 to 2.28**, beating a `DINOv3`-aligned `VA-VAE` at negligible overhead. It also works with clustering-based pseudo-labels, text-embedding conditions, and video latents.

papers.title: Batched Contextual Reinforcement II: Does RLVR Need Long Rollout Windows?
papers.abstract: Long rollout windows make reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) expensive, yet simply shortening them can remove the correctness signal: when every single-problem rollout truncates before an answer, group-relative accuracy advantages vanish. As a technical continuation of Batched Contextual Reinforcement (BCR), we study how concurrent rewards relax this dependence on long windows. Concurrent Constraint Reinforcement (CCR) places three independently verifiable problems in one capped training completion. Correct answers completed before truncation retain credit, while a shared budget encourages shorter useful reasoning without an explicit length penalty. We connect this mechanism to conditional reward- and update-variance analyses and study 4B and 8B mathematical reasoning models. Against single-problem GRPO with a 32k window, CCR with an 8,000-token window reduces tokens per training step from 975,464 to 174,957 on 4B and from 793,832 to 165,788 on 8B, saving 82.1% and 79.1%, respectively. An 8B training trace shows increasing accuracy reward alongside shorter completions. Single-problem evaluations provide supporting evidence of retained reasoning quality. These results identify reward-preserving training structure as a practical route to lower per-step cost in short-window RLVR.
