papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) needs long rollout windows, because when every rollout truncates before an answer, group-relative advantages vanish. `Concurrent Constraint Reinforcement` (`CCR`) puts three independently verifiable problems into one capped completion, so answers completed before truncation still earn credit. The shared budget also encourages shorter useful reasoning without an explicit length penalty. On 4B and 8B math reasoning models, CCR with an 8,000-token window instead of single-problem `GRPO` at 32k **cuts tokens per training step by 82.1% and 79.1%**. Accuracy reward rises as completions shorten, and single-problem evaluations suggest reasoning quality is retained.

papers.title: NLData2Opt: Benchmarking Parameter Derivation and Prediction for Modeling Optimization Problems from Natural Language and Data
papers.abstract: Formulating optimization problems from raw inputs of problem descriptions and data is time-consuming and costly. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising way to automate this process, existing benchmarks overestimate their capabilities by relying on idealized inputs where all data is relevant and complete. This diverges from reality, where data-centric reasoning is required to extract, compute, and predict parameters from noisy sources. To address this, we introduce NLData2Opt, a benchmark to evaluate LLMs on the multi-stage reasoning inherent in practical optimization workflows. NLData2Opt decomposes problems into problem descriptions and data, and requires models to (1) extract relevant parameters from data containing misleading attributes, (2) compute missing parameters derived by transforming existing data attributes, and (3) predict unavailable future values from historical observations. Evaluation results show substantial performance decline relative to existing benchmarks, indicating that benchmark progress does not directly translate to formulation accuracy in practical optimization workflows. NLData2Opt is available at https://github.com/sumarivyn/NLData2Opt.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for LLM-based formulation of optimization problems assume clean, complete, relevant inputs, which overstates real-world capability. `NLData2Opt` separates problem descriptions from data and requires models to do three things: extract relevant parameters from data containing misleading attributes, compute missing parameters by transforming existing ones, and forecast unavailable future values from historical observations. Models show **substantial performance drops relative to existing benchmarks**. Progress on idealized benchmarks therefore does not carry over to practical optimization workflows.

papers.title: What Accuracy Hides In Learned Transformer Programs
papers.abstract: Transformer Programs (TP) (Friedman et al., 2023) constrain a Transformer's architecture so that its learned computation can be extracted as readable Python code. TP expose learned computations, but token accuracy can hide incorrect complete answers. In this work, we examine how program inspection provides insights beyond accuracy scores and helps guide training. We first evaluated TP on nine algorithmic tasks. We compared token accuracy with accuracy on complete output sequences and checked for failures missed by sampled tests. Further, we assessed training data improvements informed by program inspection and failure analysis, finding gains in sequence accuracy on several tasks. We examined a counting task where a program achieved 100% accuracy on sampled test sequences but failed on another input using the symbols and lengths allowed during training. The program counted correctly, but the required answer was missing from its output labels. After adding training examples with larger counts, the retrained models passed exhaustive evaluation over the bounded domain. In the frequency ranking task, inspection showed how correct counts contributed to incorrect answers in programs trained before and after changes to the training data. Finally, we studied constraints imposed by TP training and operations. The TP training process can lead to accuracy losses late in training. Our reference constructions also show how composing the restricted TP operations can use many layers or large lookup tables.
papers.summary: `Transformer Programs` constrain a Transformer so its learned computation can be extracted as readable Python. The authors test them on nine algorithmic tasks to see what inspecting the extracted program reveals beyond accuracy scores. Token-level accuracy can hide wrong complete answers. In one counting task, a program scored **100% on sampled tests but failed on valid inputs** because the needed count was missing from its output labels, and adding examples with larger counts fixed it under exhaustive evaluation. Training data changes guided by inspection improved sequence accuracy on several tasks. The study also documents late-training accuracy losses and the many layers or large lookup tables that the restricted operations can require.

papers.title: Bengali Hallucination Detection with Retrieval and Programs: A System Study
papers.abstract: Bengali hallucination detection must distinguish unsupported factual claims from incorrect reasoning, often without a supplied reference passage. We present and characterize an inference-only system that combines response-conditioned query rewriting, hybrid retrieval, and task-specific language-model judging. Six retrieval routes search question-answer and passage collections; a router directs each example to a 27B textual judge or a 14B agent that can compare retrieved answers, reason directly, or generate and execute Python. We characterize the system using version-specific code, saved predictions, execution traces, and corpus metadata from the Olikbochon challenge. Kaggle associates a displayed private macro-F1 of 0.956 with Version 2; its saved run processes 2,516 examples in 220.99 minutes on two T4 GPUs. Of 253 math-routed examples, 88 terminate through candidate matching, while execution traces expose 49 stderr-bearing run events across 35 examples. A later run changes six predictions despite identical core worker code. A bounded audit of 1,090 benchmark-related corpus records finds exact question or context overlap for 38 processed evaluation inputs, precluding an unqualified claim of corpus-independent generalization. The contribution is a concrete retrieval-and-computation judging architecture with an auditable operational characterization, not a controlled estimate of component gains. We distinguish the reported leaderboard result from independently recomputed diagnostics and identify the evidence needed for stronger effectiveness and reproducibility claims.
papers.summary: This is a system study of an inference-only Bengali hallucination detector built for the `Olikbochon` challenge. It must flag both unsupported factual claims and incorrect reasoning without a reference passage. It rewrites queries based on the response, searches six hybrid retrieval routes, and routes each example either to a 27B text judge or to a 14B agent that can compare retrieved answers or write and run Python. The submission has a **displayed private macro-F1 of 0.956** and processes 2,516 examples in about 221 minutes on two T4 GPUs. An audit finds that 38 evaluation inputs overlap exactly with corpus records, so the authors do not claim corpus-independent generalization.

papers.title: Competence-Based Evaluation of Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have brought impressive performance across diverse tasks; however, shortcomings remain in logical reasoning, including inconsistencies under linguistic variation. To improve the reasoning capacity of LLMs, we must be able to accurately measure their reasoning capacity. Current benchmarks primarily report single accuracy numbers on selected reasoning tasks. Such a performance-based evaluation methodology says little about a model's generalization capacity in reasoning. To address this limitation, we argue for a different evaluation paradigm, called competence-based evaluation (CBE), which tests whether models reliably apply the same competence across a family of problems. A parameterized generator scales complexity while keeping the required competence fixed, and matched answer-preserving presentations test correctness beyond one formulation. We instantiate CBE on elementary ordering tasks, scaling input size while varying presentations of the same ordering rule. Across six GPT and Qwen models, performance is reasonably good over bounded complexity ranges, but even strong models fail the competence condition across the tested family. Chain-of-thought and GRPO extend strong performance without resolving all tested failures; supervised LoRA shows little held-out transfer. CBE provides diagnostic profiles and an evaluation protocol that can grow with future models.
papers.summary: Single accuracy numbers on reasoning benchmarks say little about whether an LLM applies a reasoning skill reliably. Competence-based evaluation (`CBE`) uses a parameterized generator that scales problem complexity while the required competence stays fixed, and presents each problem in several answer-preserving formulations. Applied to elementary ordering tasks across six `GPT` and `Qwen` models, performance is reasonably good over bounded complexity ranges, but **even strong models fail the competence condition across the tested family**. Chain-of-thought and `GRPO` extend the range of strong performance without fixing every failure, and supervised `LoRA` transfers little to held-out cases.

papers.title: When to Forget: Risk-Controlled Context Adaptation for Long-Horizon Agents
papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents learn from failure, but the value of a failure record can change as execution progresses. We study when retaining, compressing, or removing the same history block improves subsequent execution relative to full-history KEEP. We introduce RECAP, a framework that combines matched context interventions, execution-relational prediction, and independent policy certification. Matched environment states and rollout seeds measure success and continuation prompt-cost differences; prefix-only relations between a failure block and the current execution propose promising edits. Independent task bundles then select a policy subject to harmful-intervention and non-positive-benefit risk constraints under a fixed measurement protocol. A five-seed longitudinal case holds both the failure block and its summary fixed: compression fails at an early state and becomes a cost-saving intervention at a later state. Across five backbones, RECAP produces positive paired-success saving estimates with backbone-specific reliability-efficiency tradeoffs. On Hunyuan-A13B, it edits 43.24% of retained checkpoints while matching KEEP's observed 91.89% continuation success and reducing unconditional mean continuation prompt cost by 4,619.8 tokens (2.13%). The framework provides an execution-level reference for deciding when to forget: retain history by its value to what comes next.
papers.summary: For long-horizon agents, the value of keeping a past failure in context can change as execution goes on. `RECAP` studies when keeping, compressing, or removing a history block helps compared with keeping the full history. It measures effects with matched environment states and rollout seeds, predicts promising edits from how a failure block relates to the current execution, and certifies a policy on independent task bundles under explicit risk constraints. In one case study, compressing the same failure block hurts at an early state but saves cost at a later one. On `Hunyuan-A13B`, RECAP edits 43.24% of retained checkpoints while **matching full history's 91.89% continuation success** and reducing mean prompt cost by 2.13%.

papers.title: A Feature Selection Layer Approach for Multi-Class Classification on Neural Networks
papers.abstract: In the age of data-driven decision-making, deep learning models have become powerful tools for uncovering patterns and making predictions that influence many aspects of society. However, their broader adoption in scientific and business applications is often limited by a lack of interpretability. Feature weighting methods, which assess the relevance of individual features, are among the most widely studied approaches for improving interpretability. While post hoc techniques have advanced significantly, especially in modeling nuanced relationships between features and labels in multiclass problems, embedded methods typically fall short in this regard. Embedded techniques integrate feature relevance learning directly into the model training process, but they are often unable to capture label-specific relationships. To address the limitation, we propose multiple extensions to the Feature Selection Layer, an embedded feature weighting mechanism for neural networks. Through extensive experimentation, we identify the most effective extension and benchmark it against established feature weighting methods. Our results show that the proposed method matches existing techniques in identifying globally relevant features and outperforms them in capturing label-specific relevance. By leveraging the internal dynamics of the trained neural network, it reveals how individual features contribute to the prediction of specific labels, requiring no post-processing beyond the training process.
papers.summary: Embedded feature-weighting methods, which learn feature relevance during training, usually give one global relevance score and miss which features matter for each class in multi-class problems. The authors propose several extensions to the `Feature Selection Layer`, an embedded weighting mechanism for neural networks, and select the best one through extensive experiments. It **matches established feature-weighting methods at identifying globally relevant features and outperforms them at capturing label-specific relevance**. It also needs no post-processing beyond training.

papers.title: FederatedBytes: Tokenizer-Free, Byte-Level Small Language Models for Efficient Multimodal Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a powerful machine learning framework that allows building a global model from the contributions of multiple, distributed clients, while ensuring the privacy of their local data. However, its heavy computational and communication overheads challenge its use for contemporary AI workloads such as natural language processing (NLP) and multimodal analysis. For this reason, this paper presents a novel small language model that leverages byte-level text and multimodal data processing, enhanced by a linear attention mechanism, to enable manageable Federated Learning of NLP and multimodal analysis tasks. The proposed model, nicknamed FederatedBytes, manages to process text and any other data types, including images, by treating its input as a mere sequence of bytes, while its lean linear attention mechanism allows abating the overall memory and computational footprint. To prove the effectiveness of the proposed model we have carried out an extensive performance evaluation on sentiment analysis tasks in multilingual and multimodal settings over the Multilingual Amazon Reviews and ScienceQA datasets. The experimental results show that FederatedBytes has been able to outperform comparable models such as ByT5 and LSTM, achieving higher accuracy while significantly reducing memory and communication overheads.
papers.summary: Federated learning, where many clients train a shared model without sharing their private data, is costly in computation and communication for language and multimodal workloads. `FederatedBytes` is a small language model that needs no tokenizer: it treats any input, whether text or images, as a plain sequence of bytes and uses linear attention to reduce memory and compute. On sentiment tasks from `Multilingual Amazon Reviews` and `ScienceQA`, it **outperforms `ByT5` and `LSTM` baselines in accuracy while substantially cutting memory and communication overhead**.

papers.title: Where's the Indirect Evidence? Investigating Grammatical Generalization with Influence Functions
papers.abstract: Language models generalize beyond their training corpus to learn linguistic phenomena (Patil et al., 2024; Misra and Mahowald, 2024), showing that there exists indirect evidence driving learning. Prior work has inferred that indirect evidence exists without identifying its character or considered specific hypotheses about what it might be. We explore an alternative bottom-up method for identifying indirect evidence. We use influence functions (Koh and Liang, 2017) to measure how individual training sentences affect model predictions in 15 grammatical phenomena from BLiMP (Warstadt et al., 2020). We filter out a phenomenon's direct evidence using hand-constructed rules and take the 60,000 most influential remaining sentences as indirect evidence. This indirect evidence substantially affects learning: retraining without it lowers held-out accuracy more than removing a matched random group for every phenomenon across five models (by a median of 12 points). We characterize the indirect evidence by its similarity to our direct evidence filters: it (partially) meets the filters' structural conditions at a median of 4.7 times the rate of a matched random group. Finally, clustering phenomena by indirect-evidence overlap recovers three of the five BLiMP categories that include multiple phenomena, suggesting that this method can reveal linguistic relationships.
papers.summary: Language models learn grammatical rules that their training data never shows directly, so the work searches bottom-up for the indirect evidence that drives this learning. The authors use influence functions to score how much each training sentence affects predictions on 15 grammatical phenomena from the `BLiMP` benchmark. They filter out direct evidence with hand-written rules and treat the 60,000 most influential remaining sentences as indirect evidence. Retraining without these sentences **lowers held-out accuracy by a median of 12 points more than removing a matched random set**, across five models. These sentences partially match the structure of direct evidence far more often than chance, and grouping phenomena by shared indirect evidence recovers several of `BLiMP`'s linguistic categories.

papers.title: Sep-Latent: Separator Tokens as Natural Compression Anchors for Implicit Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable success in complex reasoning through explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT), but the associated computational overhead and token verbosity remain significant barriers to efficiency. While implicit reasoning in continuous latent spaces offers a promising alternative, existing methods like Coconut and CODI often rely on fixed-length latent sequences and suffer from representational collapse. In this paper, we propose Sep-Latent, an adaptive implicit reasoning framework that utilizes separator tokens as structural semantic anchors. By introducing an Attention-Decay mechanism, we force the model to aggregate and compress reasoning logic into these anchors during training. We then align explicit and implicit pathways through multi-level distillation across all layers to ensure logical consistency. Crucially, Sep-Latent enables dynamic reasoning depth by adaptively terminating the latent thinking phase based on query complexity. Experimental results on the GSM8k-Aug benchmark show that Sep-Latent achieves an accuracy of 56.8\% with an average of only 5.4 tokens, significantly outperforming prior fixed-length implicit models in efficiency while narrowing the performance gap with explicit CoT. Further analysis via PCA and symbolic variant testing confirms that our method ensures semantic grounding and exhibits superior robustness to perturbations.
papers.summary: Explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is accurate but long, while existing latent-reasoning methods such as `Coconut` and `CODI` use fixed-length latent sequences and suffer from representational collapse. `Sep-Latent` uses separator tokens as anchors that compress reasoning: an Attention-Decay mechanism pushes reasoning information into them during training, and distillation across all layers keeps the latent path consistent with explicit reasoning. The model also decides when to stop thinking based on how hard the query is. On `GSM8k-Aug` it reaches **56.8% accuracy using an average of only 5.4 tokens**, beating fixed-length implicit methods and narrowing the gap to explicit CoT.

papers.title: Scalable Levenberg-Marquardt Training Framework for Deep Learning
papers.abstract: The Levenberg-Marquardt (LMA) algorithm is a widely used nonlinear least-squares solver known for its rapid convergence. For small-scale neural networks, LMA provides better convergence and architectural robustness than first-order optimizers like Adam. However, LMA imposes prohibitive memory and computational costs. These costs are primarily from the Jacobian matrix, whose dimensions scale with both the number of samples and parameters. This bottleneck prevents its use in large-scale neural networks. Recent efforts scale LMA using preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) solvers to avoid materializing the Jacobian. However, PCG only approximates the solution, requiring many network propagations and a task-specific preconditioner. Other studies optimize LMA to reduce costs, but they restrict their methods to specific tasks or network architectures. As a result, LMA remains impractical for training general large-scale neural networks. In this paper, we propose LeMA, a distributed LMA algorithm for large-scale neural network training on multi-GPU platforms. Our contributions are twofold: First, an exact dual formulation of LMA removes the memory dependence on the parameter dimension. Second, a Jacobian sharding strategy computes Jacobian shards on the fly and in parallel to avoid materializing the full Jacobian. For large-scale neural networks, LeMA reduces the memory footprint of LMA from quadratic in the number of parameters to quadratic in the batch size. This makes exact LMA steps feasible for billion-parameter models without approximate PCG solves. Furthermore, for a convolutional neural network with 1,000,022,632 parameters on an 8-GPU node, LeMA achieves a 7.97x speedup over a single GPU, corresponding to a 99.7% strong scaling efficiency.
papers.summary: The Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm (LMA) converges quickly for small neural networks, but its Jacobian matrix makes memory costs prohibitive at scale. `LeMA` is a distributed, multi-GPU version of LMA built on two ideas: an exact dual formulation that removes memory dependence on parameter count, and Jacobian sharding that computes Jacobian pieces in parallel without ever storing the full matrix. Memory becomes quadratic in batch size rather than in parameter count, which makes exact LMA steps feasible for billion-parameter models. On a 1-billion-parameter CNN it achieves a **7.97x speedup on 8 GPUs, a 99.7% strong-scaling efficiency**.

papers.title: Conformal Policy Selection: When to Deploy AI Decisions for Targeted Intervention
papers.abstract: Artificial-intelligence (AI) policies are increasingly used to make consequential decisions in medicine, finance, education, and public services, yet deploying them responsibly requires knowing not only whether a policy helps on average, but for whom. Existing tools for off-policy evaluation and safe policy learning provide population-level guarantees, but some individuals may experience adverse treatment effects. We recast targeted deployment as a multiple-testing problem: for each candidate unit, test whether the outcome under the AI policy would exceed a user-specified threshold, and control the false discovery rate (FDR) among the selected set. Our method, Conformal Policy Selection, combines weighted conformal $p$-values that account for the distributional shift from behavior to target policy with a two-step selection-and-pruning procedure. We prove finite-sample FDR control and establish a doubly robust asymptotic guarantee, where FDR remains controlled if either the outcome model or the propensity model is correctly specified. Synthetic experiments verify these guarantees across four misspecification regimes, and a semi-synthetic study built on real electronic-health-record covariates illustrates how the same FDR control can act as a deployment safety gate, bounding the harmful treatments that a globally trained policy would otherwise administer to a high-risk subpopulation where it misgeneralizes. The framework offers a principled method for safe AI deployment in high-stakes applications.
papers.summary: AI decision policies can help a population on average while still harming particular individuals, so deploying them safely requires knowing whom they help. `Conformal Policy Selection` treats deployment as a multiple-testing problem: for each individual, it tests whether the outcome under the AI policy would exceed a threshold, while controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) among those selected. It combines weighted conformal p-values, which correct for the shift between the policy that generated the data and the new policy, with a select-then-prune procedure. The authors prove **finite-sample FDR control plus a doubly robust guarantee**, and a semi-synthetic study on electronic health records shows the method blocking harmful treatments for a high-risk subgroup.

papers.title: ASR-Style Transcript Normalization Removes Useful Pragmatic Signal for Dialogue Act Classification
papers.abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) pipelines often normalize transcripts by removing filled pauses and punctuation and expanding colloquial forms, potentially discarding cues useful for dialogue act classification. We evaluate nine transcript conditions across six classifiers (TF-IDF logistic regression, RoBERTa, BERT, ALBERT, GPT-2, and BiLSTM) and three conversational corpora (Switchboard, ICSI MRDA, and SLUE-HVB), supplemented by multi-seed experiments, normalization controls, and real-ASR evaluations. Across five random seeds, heavy normalization reduces Macro-F1 in all 15 neural model-corpus combinations under the original preprocessing protocols. Removal using the original filler and backchannel lexicon consistently degrades performance on MRDA and SLUE-HVB but produces mixed effects on Switchboard. Punctuation-aware TF-IDF experiments show that punctuation removal reduces Macro-F1 by 0.036 on Switchboard and 0.078 on MRDA, demonstrating that the original linear baseline's apparent insensitivity resulted from tokenization. Restricting filler removal to um, uh, and erm preserves degradation on MRDA but largely eliminates the SLUE-HVB effect, where the original lexicon removes class-defining backchannel expressions. These findings demonstrate that normalization effects depend on preprocessing definitions, feature extraction, and conversational context, supporting task-dependent rather than indiscriminate transcript normalization.
papers.summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) pipelines often normalize transcripts by removing filler words and punctuation, which may throw away cues for classifying dialogue acts. The authors test nine transcript conditions across six classifiers, including `RoBERTa`, `BERT`, and `GPT-2`, on the `Switchboard`, `ICSI MRDA`, and `SLUE-HVB` corpora. **Heavy normalization lowers Macro-F1 in all 15 neural model-corpus combinations.** Some effects depend on preprocessing details: for example, a standard filler lexicon removes backchannel expressions that define whole classes in `SLUE-HVB`. The authors argue for normalization chosen per task rather than applied wholesale.

papers.title: Many Biases, One Circuit: Post-Training Tunes a Pretrained Cue-Routing Mechanism
papers.abstract: Language models often abandon a correct answer when the prompt contains a cue, a hint toward a wrong option such as "I think the answer is B." Sycophancy and related biases show this failure. They are often studied separately and blamed on alignment. We test this view causally, tracing the attention heads behind these biases through the stages of two post-training pipelines. In multiple-choice tests on most models, four cue types rely largely on the same few heads, a shared circuit already present in pretrained models. Most base models follow cues in plain text. Fine-tuning a base model on about 200 generic assistant examples without cues activates these heads in chat format, so cue-following can be a side effect of assistant tuning. The final reinforcement learning (RL) stage strengthens the effect of cues in almost every comparison. In Tulu-3-8B and OLMo-2-7B, we swap the attention patterns of six middle layers between the RL checkpoint and its predecessor. For suggested-answer cues, this shifts each checkpoint's cue effect most of the way to the other's level. Post-training thus seems to change when and how strongly models use this circuit. Mitigation for these multiple-choice biases could target this circuit.
papers.summary: Language models often drop a correct answer when the prompt hints at a wrong one, and sycophancy and related biases are usually studied separately and blamed on alignment. Causal tracing of attention heads across two post-training pipelines shows that **four types of cue rely mostly on the same few heads, a circuit already present in pretrained models**. Fine-tuning on about 200 generic assistant examples is enough to activate the circuit in chat format, and the final reinforcement learning (RL) stage strengthens it further. In `Tulu-3-8B` and `OLMo-2-7B`, swapping six middle layers' attention patterns between RL checkpoints moves most of the cue effect with them, which points to this circuit as a target for mitigation.
papers.highlight_summary:
Sycophancy, hints and fake prior answers are usually studied as separate biases that alignment introduces. They all make language models drop correct multiple-choice answers when the prompt contains a cue such as "I think the answer is B." Causal tracing through the stages of public post-training pipelines instead finds that four cue types share one small attention-head circuit, which already exists after pretraining; post-training changes when and how strongly models use it.

- Using activation patching on the `BCT` benchmark, the top eight heads reverse **69–92% of held-out flips** pooled over four cue types in `Llama-3.1-8B`, `Qwen-2.5-7B` and `Gemma-2-9B`, while random head sets reverse at most 8%; copying the base model's query and output weights for these heads into the aligned model barely changes its caving.
- Most base models already follow cues in plain text, and LoRA fine-tuning of the `Llama-3.1-8B` base on just **~200 generic assistant examples with no cues** raises its chat-format caving to the level of the full `Tulu-3` SFT model, which was trained on 939k examples; even 200 code examples have this effect, so cue-following can be a side effect of assistant tuning.
- From the DPO checkpoint to the final RL stage, cue susceptibility rises in **12 of 13 paired tests** (11 significant after Bonferroni correction), and swapping attention patterns in six middle layers between the DPO and RL checkpoints of `Tulu-3-8B` and `OLMo-2-7B` moves each checkpoint **61–73% of the way** to the other's cue effect for suggested-answer cues; in a second, pre-specified wave of controls, every random six-layer swap moved less than 30%.
- The query states carry much of this stage difference, and in base models, scaling middle-band attention to the cue raises susceptibility almost monotonically, which suggests the circuit's role predates any assistant tuning.
- The authors list several limitations: the evidence is mostly from English multiple choice with answers read from letter logits, the causal stage tests use one 7–8B pair per pipeline, and several pre-registered criteria were not met; the attention-scaling mitigation also cannot tell correct cues from wrong ones, since in `Gemma-2-2b` it removes **75% of the added caving but also 76% of the accuracy gain** from correct cues.

papers.title: Beyond Surface Cues: Robust LLM-Generated Korean Text Detection
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) generate increasingly fluent text, the need for reliable detection of LLM-generated content has grown substantially. However, existing research remains heavily English-centric, leaving Korean largely underexplored. Moreover, current evaluations of Korean text detection often rely on superficial cues, leading to overly optimistic estimates of detection performance. To address these limitations, we introduce \textsc{KoLing}, a bias-controlled adversarial benchmark comprising 50.9k instances that suppresses superficial shortcuts while preserving semantic content and separately evaluates LLM-generated and LLM-modified text detection. We further propose KoLingProbe, an interpretable detector grounded in theoretical linguistics that models Korean-specific properties across multiple linguistic levels. Experiments show that KoLingProbe substantially outperforms strong baselines on all detection tasks while remaining robust to adversarial attacks. Our analyses further reveal that integrating complementary linguistic features across multiple levels yields both improved performance and interpretability.
papers.summary: Research on detecting LLM-generated text focuses mostly on English, and existing Korean evaluations rely on superficial cues that overstate detector performance. The authors introduce `KoLing`, a 50.9k-instance adversarial benchmark that suppresses these shortcuts and evaluates fully generated and LLM-modified text separately. They also propose `KoLingProbe`, an interpretable detector that models Korean-specific linguistic properties at several levels. `KoLingProbe` **substantially outperforms strong baselines on all detection tasks and remains robust to adversarial attacks**.

papers.title: Aligning Language Models Towards Counterfactual Invariance
papers.abstract: Small variations in prompt characteristics can meaningfully alter the semantics, tone, and contextual assumptions of large language model outputs. Such characteristics can involve group variables such as demographics or other sensitive latent attributes. Sensitivity to such input variables is undesirable when demographic information is causally irrelevant to the task, but might still be relevant for generation of semantically coherent responses. This makes the task of enforcing counterfactual invariance while preserving model utility difficult. To study this problem, we first show that standard model alignment recipes (such as reinforcement learning) increase differences in response quality across demographics, while improving overall response quality, ultimately amplifying what is known as counterfactual bias. To address this, we develop a policy gradient technique involving a group-level reward function that operates on matched pairs of counterfactual prompts. For completeness, we build a dataset of controlled counterfactual prompt pairs and design an evaluation that separately measures cases where demographic information is causally relevant to the answer. Finally, we validate our findings on several fairness benchmarks. We demonstrate that our methods reduce counterfactual differences while preserving overall response quality and that the models continue to adapt appropriately when such sensitive information is relevant.
papers.summary: Demographic details in a prompt can change the quality of a language model's response even when they are irrelevant to the task. The authors show that **standard alignment recipes such as reinforcement learning improve overall quality while widening quality gaps across demographics**, which amplifies counterfactual bias. To counter this, they develop a policy-gradient method with a group-level reward computed on matched pairs of counterfactual prompts, along with a dataset and an evaluation that separates cases where demographics actually matter. The method reduces counterfactual differences without hurting overall quality, and models still adapt when sensitive information is relevant.

papers.title: Large Diffusion Models Need More Than EMA
papers.abstract: Large-scale diffusion models are commonly trained with a constant learning rate (LR) and exponential moving average (EMA), despite the strong performance of LR decay and Schedule-Free optimization in training large language models. We study whether EMA is uniquely suited to diffusion training, or whether stronger alternatives have been underexplored. Our theory shows that averaging a constant-step trajectory has an inherent optimization limitation, whereas LR decay and Schedule-Free optimization admit vanishing stationarity guarantees under standard nonconvex assumptions. Empirically, LR decay and EMA provide complementary benefits: combining decay with EMA further improves the standard baseline at most tested starting points, although the gain remains sensitive to when decay begins. Schedule-Free avoids this timing requirement and consistently outperforms EMA with a constant LR across training stages, achieving both lower fixed-evaluation objectives and better generation quality. Our analysis further shows that all three strategies substantially reduce parameter variability, yet stronger stabilization is not always better: EMA with a constant LR retains comparatively higher parameter variability, while aggressive decay combined with EMA achieves the lowest checkpoint variability but also weakens continued optimization. Schedule-Free substantially reduces parameter variability while preserving more late-stage progress, providing a better balance between parameter stability and continued optimization. Finally, the benefits of Schedule-Free extend beyond pretraining to ReFL and generator-side DMD, demonstrating its transferability across distinct diffusion optimization settings. Overall, our results suggest that large diffusion models need more than parameter averaging alone: effective optimization requires balancing variance reduction with continued optimization.
papers.summary: Large diffusion models are usually trained with a constant learning rate and an exponential moving average (EMA) of weights, while LLM training has moved to learning-rate decay and `Schedule-Free` optimization. Theory shows that averaging a constant-step trajectory has an inherent optimization limit that decay and `Schedule-Free` avoid. In experiments, decay combined with EMA helps but is sensitive to when decay starts, whereas **`Schedule-Free` consistently beats constant-rate EMA at every training stage** in both loss and generation quality. The gains carry over to `ReFL` and `DMD` fine-tuning settings, and the authors argue that good training balances variance reduction against continued optimization.

papers.title: Recognizing Atari and Assessing Sente: Controlled Evaluation Tasks for Language-Based Go Agents
papers.abstract: Domain terminology provides concise descriptions of game states and strategic relationships, but whether game-playing language models can accurately recognize these concepts and relate them to move evaluation remains unclear. We construct a controlled evaluation set centered on atari and its relationship to sente in Go, examining terminology recognition under local board changes and move evaluation under different strategic conditions. We conduct our tests on LoGos, a Go language model, after fine-tuning it with terminology and commentary supervision. The model struggles to recognize changes in the atari relationship and assess its strategic implications. Its terminology predictions are associated with move preferences even when those preferences contradict the reference evaluation. Our controlled tests provide a framework for examining whether language-based Go agents connect domain terminology with precise board relationships and strategic move values.
papers.summary: A controlled evaluation set tests whether language-based Go agents understand domain terms, focusing on atari (a stone that can be captured on the next move) and its link to sente (keeping the initiative). Tests on `LoGos`, a Go language model fine-tuned with terminology and commentary, show that it **struggles to notice when local board changes alter atari relationships** and to judge their strategic consequences. Its terminology predictions also drive its move preferences even when those preferences contradict the reference evaluation. The tests offer a framework for checking whether game-playing language models tie their vocabulary to precise board facts.

papers.title: On the tradeoff between robustness and geometric accuracy in adversarial training
papers.abstract: For non-parametric binary classification in the presence of an adversary, we prove an optimal quantitative estimate for adversarial classifiers controlling geometric accuracy, as measured by the Hausdorff distance to the Bayes classifier, in terms or their robustness, as encoded by the adversarial budget $\varepsilon$. This rigorously shows that robust classifiers sacrifice at most $O(\sqrt{\varepsilon})$ or $O(\varepsilon)$ in accuracy, depending on the regularity of the underlying Bayes classifier. In contrast to prior work on the incompatibility of robustness and accuracy over low-complexity hypothesis classes, our work shows that high-complexity hypothesis classes allow for robust classifiers with precisely quantified accuracy. Our results apply for adversaries determined by any norm on Euclidean space and in both the infinite and finite data settings.
papers.summary: For non-parametric binary classification against an adversary, the paper proves optimal bounds on how far a robust classifier can drift from the Bayes classifier, measured by Hausdorff distance, as a function of the adversarial budget epsilon. Robust classifiers **give up at most O(sqrt(epsilon)) or O(epsilon) in geometric accuracy**, depending on how regular the Bayes classifier is. Prior work found robustness and accuracy incompatible for low-complexity hypothesis classes; this result shows that high-complexity classes allow robust classifiers with precisely quantified accuracy. The bounds hold for any norm and in both finite- and infinite-data settings.

papers.title: SAFE-Mem: Secure Agentic Memory with Fine-Grained Authority and Governance-Aware Retrieval
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on persistent memory to support long-term reasoning and personalized interactions. However, information collected from external sources can introduce security risks when untrusted claims (i.e., atomic statements) are later treated as authorized preferences, policies, or permissions. Existing defenses typically rely on content-based filtering or coarse-grained provenance tracking, which either fail to prevent unauthorized memory use or block legitimate information, sacrificing memory utility. To address these limitations, we propose SAFE-Mem, a fine-grained memory governance framework that improves security while preserving legitimate memory use. First, SAFE-Mem annotates each claim with three governance labels (i.e., kind, authority, and scope) to capture its provenance and permitted use. Second, governance-aware retrieval matches query requirements with claim permissions to block unauthorized influence while retaining legitimate information. Third, a governance-enabled memory graph connects source sentences, claims, and entities to support provenance tracking and efficient retrieval. Across four LLM backbones on MPBench and LoCoMo, SAFE-Mem attains the lowest attack success among defenses that retain legitimate memory, at least 77% below the strongest of them, and the highest answer accuracy of all evaluated defenses, improving it by up to 15%. The code is available at https://github.com/LVenum/SAFE-Mem.
papers.summary: LLM agents with persistent memory can be manipulated when untrusted claims from external sources are later treated as authorized preferences, policies, or permissions. `SAFE-Mem` labels each stored claim with a kind, an authority, and a scope, then uses governance-aware retrieval to admit a claim only when its permissions fit the query's requirements. A memory graph links source sentences, claims, and entities to support provenance tracking. Across four LLM backbones on `MPBench` and `LoCoMo`, it has the lowest attack success among defenses that keep legitimate memory, **at least 77% below the strongest of them**, and the best answer accuracy, up to 15% higher.

papers.title: What Shapes Brain Alignment of Large Language Models during Dialogue? Insights from Language Production and Comprehension
papers.abstract: Brain alignment of large language models (LLMs) offers a way to investigate representational similarities between LLMs and the human brain during language processing. While previous studies have mainly focused on passive language comprehension, little is known about such alignment during dialogue, in which speakers engage in both language production and comprehension. In this study, using fMRI data collected during dialogue, we examine brain alignment during language production and comprehension across LLM layers and brain regions. We assess its association with the intrinsic dimension (ID) of LLM representations and the contributions of several interpretable linguistic and communicative features. Our results reveal distinct patterns of brain alignment between production and comprehension, as well as strong associations with ID in brain regions associated with each processing mode. Furthermore, we show that the contributions of linguistic and communicative features also vary across processing modes, LLM layers, and brain regions.
papers.summary: Studies comparing LLM representations with human brain activity have mostly looked at passive listening or reading, not dialogue, where people both produce and comprehend language. Using fMRI recordings from dialogue, the authors measure brain alignment across LLM layers and brain regions separately for production and comprehension. They find **distinct alignment patterns for the two modes**, each strongly tied to the intrinsic dimension of the LLM's representations in the brain regions associated with that mode. The contributions of interpretable linguistic and communicative features also vary by mode, layer, and region.

papers.title: Towards Hyperparameter Transfer for Differentially Private Optimization
papers.abstract: Scaling laws and hyperparameter tuning remain central challenges in training large-scale models, particularly under differential privacy (DP), where optimization is further complicated by noise injection and per-sample gradient clipping. While Maximal Update Parametrization ($\mu$P) allows for zero-shot hyperparameter transfer in standard training, we show that it fails under DP constraints due to the distinct spectral properties of high-dimensional noise versus low-rank gradients. In this work, we introduce DP-$\mu$P, a theoretically grounded framework that extends $\mu$P to the privacy-preserving setting. By analyzing the interaction between gradient clipping, noise injection, and feature learning, we derive a Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) condition that governs layer-wise learning rate scaling. Combining this with our proposed spectral scaling formulation, we provide specific scaling rules for DP-SGD, DP-Adam, and DP-Muon optimizers. Empirically, we demonstrate that DP-$\mu$P enables effective zero-shot transfer of learning rates across model widths on diverse architectures (MLP, ViT, GPT-2), matching or exceeding the performance of individually tuned baselines while significantly reducing computational costs.
papers.summary: Maximal Update Parametrization (`μP`) lets learning rates tuned on small models transfer directly to larger ones, but it breaks under differential privacy (DP), where gradient clipping and high-dimensional noise change the optimization dynamics. `DP-μP` analyzes how clipping, noise, and feature learning interact, derives a signal-to-noise condition that sets per-layer learning-rate scaling, and gives concrete scaling rules for `DP-SGD`, `DP-Adam`, and `DP-Muon`. On MLPs, `ViT`, and `GPT-2`, it **transfers learning rates across model widths without further tuning, matching or beating individually tuned baselines** at much lower compute cost.

papers.title: KiranaBench: Can a Language Model Run a Neighbourhood Shop?
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly evaluated on long-horizon tasks, including autonomously running a business. Existing benchmarks for this setting are almost exclusively English-language, Western in retail context, and single-agent, with the agent observing the business directly. We study how these results transfer to a multi-agent Indic setting. We introduce KiranaBench, a simulated Indian general store in which four roles (manager, cashier, helper, and bookkeeper) are each played by a separate LLM agent. Interactions with customers and suppliers occur in English, Hindi, or Hinglish, and product demand is calibrated to India's national Household Consumption Expenditure Survey. Evaluating four open-weight LLMs, we find that all fall far short of a fixed-rule shopkeeper baseline: the best model earns only one-eighth of the baseline's profit, and two models finish below an unmanaged shop. Performance is also consistently lower for Hindi and Hinglish than for English supplier communication. KiranaBench offers evidence that current LLM agents are not yet reliable for autonomously operating small businesses in India, and provides a testbed for developing agents suited to settings that are long-horizon, collaborative, and multilingual.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for LLM agents that run businesses are almost all English-language, Western, and single-agent. `KiranaBench` simulates an Indian general store run by four separate LLM agents (manager, cashier, helper, and bookkeeper), which deal with customers and suppliers in English, Hindi, or Hinglish, with demand calibrated to India's national household consumption survey. All four open-weight models tested fall far short of a fixed-rule shopkeeper: **the best earns only one-eighth of the baseline's profit, and two do worse than an unmanaged shop**. Performance is also consistently lower when suppliers communicate in Hindi or Hinglish than in English.

papers.title: How Murky Before a VLM Knows It Cannot See? Accuracy, Confidence and Abstention on a Physical Visibility Axis
papers.abstract: Robustness studies of vision-language models (VLMs) grade degradation on nominal severity scales ("level 1-5") that carry no physical units, and they rarely ask whether a model's confidence follows the loss of visibility. We measure accuracy, internal (token-probability) confidence, verbalized confidence and an explicit abstain option on a visibility axis in metres: fog follows the Koschmieder model, an underwater arm scales the absorption spectrum of pure water, both are applied with a monocular metric depth map, and the visibility range V is swept over eight log-spaced levels from 250 m to 1.95 m. On 1000 COCO scenes and five small open VLMs (2-5 B parameters), accuracy on a boxed-object identification task falls from near its clean value to chance within a narrow band (half-way visibility V_acc of 12.1-15.9 m in fog and 20.5-38.6 m under water) while, for the four models that are confident on clean images, the confidence stays high: at V=1.95 m in fog their accuracy is at chance but their mean internal confidence is 0.68-0.84 and their verbalized confidence 0.61-1.00, a blind-spot width W=log10(V_acc/V_aware) of at least 0.79 decades, i.e. a factor of 6.2 in visibility. The remaining model is under-confident throughout and its internal confidence follows accuracy. An explicit abstain option follows accuracy when it names the reason (W from -0.21 to -0.06 in fog) but, for one model, lags with a generic "I don't know" (W up to 0.18). ImageNet-C fog severities 1-5 correspond to only 55-110 m of physical visibility, outside the failure band, and leave the accuracy of the models within 5 percentage points of its clean value. Blank-image and shuffled-image controls, a prior-matched answer set and a 200-image pilot that preceded the study are reported. Findings are descriptive: one draw of 1000 images, depth of assumed scale, and models of 2-5 B parameters.
papers.summary: Robustness tests for vision-language models (VLMs) usually rate image degradation on unitless 1-5 severity scales and rarely ask whether confidence drops along with accuracy. The authors apply physically modeled fog and underwater haze to 1000 `COCO` scenes, sweeping visibility from 250 m down to 1.95 m, and test five small open VLMs (2-5B parameters). Accuracy collapses to chance within a narrow visibility band, yet for four of the models **confidence stays high (internal 0.68-0.84) even when accuracy is at chance**. An explicit abstain option tracks accuracy better, especially when it names the reason, and standard `ImageNet-C` fog levels turn out to be too mild to reach the failure band.

papers.title: Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them
papers.abstract: Experience-driven self-evolution offers a promising path for large language model (LLM) agents to continually improve through interaction. Yet existing approaches often rely on successful trajectories or external evaluation signals, leaving unclear whether agents can evolve when such positive anchors are unavailable. We study this question through Cold-Start Failure-Only Evolution (CFOE), where agents start without accumulated experience and learn only from failed interactions without privileged guidance. Across three self-evolving paradigms, multiple LLM backbones, and four interactive environments, we uncover a consistent repair-generalization gap: failure-derived experience can help repair previously failed tasks, but rarely yields sustained improvements on unseen tasks. Further analysis shows that agents often misinterpret failures, while even verified-correct experience remains difficult to transfer. Relaxing CFOE reveals that verifier feedback and additional interaction provide limited gains, whereas successful trajectories substantially improve transfer. These findings suggest that current self-evolving agents are better at repairing observed failures than building generalizable capabilities from failure.
papers.summary: Self-evolving LLM agents usually improve by learning from successful trajectories or external feedback; this study asks whether they can improve from failures alone. In a setting called Cold-Start Failure-Only Evolution (CFOE), tested with three self-evolution approaches, several LLM backbones, and four interactive environments, the authors find a consistent **repair-generalization gap: lessons from failures help fix previously failed tasks but rarely improve performance on unseen ones**. Agents often misread why they failed, and even verified-correct lessons transfer poorly. Verifier feedback and extra interaction help little, while access to successful trajectories substantially improves transfer.

papers.title: Prism Attention: Proposal-Refined Index Sharing Mechanism for Efficient LLMs Inference
papers.abstract: Long-context decoding in large language models (LLMs) is increasingly bottlenecked by the memory and computation required to attend over an ever-growing Key-Value (KV) cache at each autoregressive step. Although token-level sparse attention reduces this burden by restricting computation to a small subset of relevant past tokens, its practical gains are often offset by repeatedly recomputing layer-wise sparse indices as the context grows. A common remedy is to share sparse indices across layers by computing them only at designated anchor layers, but such static reuse ignores the layer-wise evolution of attention patterns, causing the reused indices to progressively deviate from the layer-specific optima and incur substantial attention loss. By revisiting cross-layer sparsity from the perspective of attention dynamics, we find that inter-layer salient token shift is highly localized: although the exact top-$\kappa$ indices differ across layers, the core high-attention tokens remain stable, with changes concentrated near the expanded boundary of previously selected regions. Motivated by this, we propose Prism Attention, a proposal-refined sparse attention framework. It replaces rigid cross-layer index reuse with a coarse-to-fine strategy, preserving layer-wise adaptability while retaining the efficiency benefits of cross-layer sharing. Extensive experiments show that Prism Attention achieves state-of-the-art performance among mainstream sparse attention methods on both reasoning and long-context benchmarks, while attaining a $3.4\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup over FlashAttention at 128K context length.
papers.summary: Sparse attention speeds up long-context decoding by attending only to the most relevant cached tokens, but recomputing which tokens to select at every layer erodes the savings, and reusing one selection across layers loses accuracy. The authors observe that the most-attended tokens stay largely stable from layer to layer, with changes concentrated near the edges of previously selected regions. `Prism Attention` therefore reuses a coarse token selection across layers as a proposal and refines it per layer. It achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among mainstream sparse attention methods on reasoning and long-context benchmarks, with a **3.4x end-to-end decoding speedup over `FlashAttention` at 128K context**.

papers.title: PersonaCUABench: Benchmarking Computer-Use Agents Serving Diverse Personas
papers.abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) are commonly evaluated against fixed task specifications, but users may omit requirements, add constraints, or require approval before consequential actions. Completing the benchmark instruction does not guarantee serving the person who asked. We introduce PersonaCUABench, which holds 74 tasks across 11 domains fixed and varies only who asks. A persona agent, playing one of 44 personas in four groups, rewrites each instruction in that user's own words and answers the CUA's questions, while the CUA sees only the dialogue, never the profile or the original instruction. Across nine backbones (3,330 runs), mean task completion falls by 36% relative to the original requests. The losses have two sources: in 59.9% of cells that lose points, the agent engages with what the user asked for and still gets it wrong, and 11.2% are stops the user requested that the checker scores as failures. Even when a persona request is fully completed, the user gives the top satisfaction rating in only 62.7% of cells, against 84.1% for the original requests. CUAs should therefore be evaluated not only on task completion but also on whether they meet the requirements and constraints users express. Code: https://github.com/MatrAIx-ai/PersonaCUABench. Project page: https://matraix.ai/research/persona-cua.html
papers.summary: Computer-use agents (CUAs) are usually scored against fixed task specifications, but real users leave out requirements, add constraints, or want to approve consequential actions first. `PersonaCUABench` keeps 74 tasks across 11 domains fixed and varies only who is asking: a persona agent playing one of 44 personas rewrites each instruction in that user's own words and answers the CUA's questions, while the CUA never sees the profile or the original instruction. Across nine backbones and 3,330 runs, **mean task completion falls by 36% relative to the original requests**, mostly because agents engage with what the user asked for and still get it wrong. Even when a persona request is fully completed, users give the top satisfaction rating in only 62.7% of cases, compared with 84.1% for the original requests.

papers.title: TALLOP: Joint Optimization of Local Training and Communication Compression for Time-Constrained Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Minimizing the wall-clock time required to reach a target accuracy is crucial in federated learning (FL), where many applications require frequent model updates as data distributions evolve over time. Nevertheless, in heterogeneous environments, slow clients with limited computational and communication capabilities can delay global synchronization, forcing faster clients to wait and increasing the overall training time. To mitigate this straggler effect, recent studies have introduced per-round time constraints and adapted client workloads within the available time. However, these approaches primarily focus on local computation, whereas communication can become a major bottleneck in communication-limited environments, motivating the joint optimization of training workload and communication compression. Although previous studies have explored such joint optimization, determining an effective training--communication balance under a fixed per-round time budget remains challenging, as the resulting model performance depends on both training progress and compression-induced degradation. We therefore propose TALLOP, which jointly optimizes the local training workload and communication compression under per-round time constraints. TALLOP predicts the training loss achievable under different computation budgets from the early-stage mini-batch loss trajectory (LENS), and estimates the degradation caused by communication compression using a compression-error model (CLEN). TALLOP combines these predictions to select the training-communication allocation that minimizes the post-compression loss under the given round time constraint. Experiments in heterogeneous FL environments show that TALLOP generally achieves competitive or improved time-to-accuracy compared with approaches that optimize only local training or neither, although the benefit over training-only adaptation depends on the setting.
papers.summary: In heterogeneous federated learning (FL), slow clients hold up each synchronization round, and past fixes that cap round time mostly adapt local computation while ignoring communication bottlenecks. `TALLOP` jointly chooses each client's local training workload and communication compression level under a per-round time budget. It predicts achievable training loss from the early mini-batch loss trajectory (`LENS`) and estimates compression-induced degradation with a compression-error model (`CLEN`), then picks the allocation that minimizes post-compression loss. Experiments show **competitive or improved time-to-accuracy** against training-only or non-adaptive baselines, though the gain over training-only adaptation depends on the setting.

papers.title: A Label Noise Robust Algorithm for Graph Data using Neighborhood Label Distribution
papers.abstract: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have demonstrated exceptional performance on graph-structured data. However, their success heavily relies on the availability of clean labels, an assumption that often fails in real-world scenarios. The learnability of GCNs is intrinsically linked to the neighborhood structure of nodes, making it critical to understand how this structure changes in the presence of label noise. In this work, we investigate how the neighborhood label distribution of a node changes under label noise. We mathematically derive that label noise smooths this distribution, which inherently increases its entropy and severely decreases interclass distinguishability. To address this challenge, we propose Leave-one-out Entropy Node Screening (LENS), an end-to-end framework that identifies noisy nodes by measuring the reduction in neighborhood entropy when a specific node is removed. LENS further incorporates a relabeling mechanism to recover and preserve valuable feature information instead of entirely discarding the identified noisy nodes. Crucially, the end-to-end computational overhead of LENS is remarkably low. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our algorithm achieves state-of-the-art node classification accuracy while executing an order of magnitude faster than existing noise-robust approaches.
papers.summary: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) depend on clean labels, and the authors analyze how label noise changes the distribution of labels in a node's neighborhood. They prove that noise smooths this distribution, raising its entropy and making classes harder to tell apart. Their method, Leave-one-out Entropy Node Screening (`LENS`), flags noisy nodes by measuring how much neighborhood entropy drops when a node is removed, then relabels them instead of discarding them. It reports state-of-the-art node classification accuracy while running **an order of magnitude faster** than existing noise-robust methods.

papers.title: Controlling the Diversity-Quality Trade-Off of LLMs by Merging Models Before and After Alignment
papers.abstract: Alignment is known to change the output characteristics of large language models (LLMs). Base models tend to generate more diverse outputs, whereas aligned models tend to produce higher-quality outputs. The appropriate balance between the two depends on the task. Existing methods either require costly fine-tuning or, like temperature sampling, mainly improve lexical diversity rather than semantic diversity. We introduce a depth-aware FrankenMerging approach for controlling the diversity--quality trade-off between an aligned model and its base model without additional training. This approach combines the lower layers of an aligned model with the higher layers of its base model based on the hypothesis that lexical diversity is more closely associated with lower layers and semantic diversity with higher layers. Experiments showed that varying the number of layers taken from each model adjusts both diversity and quality. In most cases, the merged models exhibited higher semantic diversity than the aligned model, and at some split positions, they showed higher lexical diversity than both original models. They also demonstrated a better diversity--quality trade-off than temperature sampling in most settings. A supporting ablation, in which we reversed the merging order, yielded results largely consistent with the hypothesis.
papers.summary: Base large language models (LLMs) produce more diverse outputs while aligned models produce higher-quality ones, and existing fixes either require fine-tuning or, like temperature sampling, mainly increase surface-level lexical diversity. The authors propose a training-free, depth-aware `FrankenMerging` approach that stacks the lower layers of an aligned model under the higher layers of its base model, on the hypothesis that lower layers govern lexical diversity and higher layers govern semantic diversity. Changing the split point tunes the trade-off, and the merged models usually show higher semantic diversity than the aligned model and **a better diversity-quality trade-off than temperature sampling** in most settings. An ablation that reverses the merge order gave results largely consistent with the hypothesis.

papers.title: A Minimal ReLU Classifier on Non-Linearly Separable Data: Convergence and Implicit Bias at and beyond the Edge of Stability
papers.abstract: Gradient descent (GD) with large learning rates can successfully optimize neural networks even though classical smoothness-based learning rate conditions are violated. Yet theory for this regime largely covers linear models or linearly separable data. We analyze a minimal setting outside both regimes. Specifically, a two-neuron ReLU network trained with logistic loss on 1D non-linearly separable data. The objective is nonconvex and nonsmooth, and GD exhibits edge-of-stability (EoS) behavior. We identify an active cone in parameter space that contains every perfect classifier, where the problem becomes piecewise logistic regression with a varying effective dataset. Within this cone, we prove a finite-time loss bound for constant learning rates and show that GD converges in direction to an explicit max-margin vector, while the orthogonal component converges to the unique minimizer of a non-strongly convex potential. We further establish catapult results where exponentially small loss is reached after a single loss spike. Furthermore, we propose an adaptive schedule that lets learning rates grow to infinity without leaving the active cone. We prove that this schedule achieves a loss rate of $O(1/(T\log{T})$, which is faster than the standard $O(1/T)$ rate. Our theoretical results extend to local convergence on more general network and are validated on MNIST dataset. Overall, we show that this setup provides a tractable neural-network model for studying large and adaptive step sizes beyond linear predictors and separable data.
papers.summary: Theory for gradient descent (GD) with large learning rates, where training shows edge-of-stability (EoS) behavior, mostly covers linear models or linearly separable data. The authors study a two-neuron ReLU network trained with logistic loss on 1D data that is not linearly separable, and identify an "active cone" in parameter space where the problem reduces to piecewise logistic regression. Inside this cone they prove finite-time loss bounds, directional convergence to an explicit max-margin vector, and catapult behavior in which a single loss spike leads to exponentially small loss. An adaptive schedule that lets learning rates grow without bound achieves **an O(1/(T log T)) loss rate, faster than the standard O(1/T)**, and the results are checked on `MNIST`.

papers.title: "Deep lifts": Neural networks can generalize even with the dumbest optimizer
papers.abstract: Given a labeled dataset $\{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i = 1}^n$, consider drawing a parameter vector $\hat{\theta}$ uniformly at random from those that interpolate the data within a width-$W$ depth-$D$ ReLU architecture with continuous weights bounded within $[-M, M]$. We study the generalization properties of $\hat{\theta}$ in the case where the dataset can, in fact, be explained by a smaller $w$-by-$d$ ReLU network. Despite the obliviousness of the selection rule for $\hat{\theta}$, it adaptively generalizes at the rate $\tilde O\left(\frac{wdWD}{n}\right)$, rather than being governed by the VC dimension of the full $W$-by-$D$ hypothesis class. The reason is due to a particular inductive bias in ReLU networks: the $w$-by-$d$ parameter *witnesses* an exponential volume of $W$-by-$D$ interpolating parameters, which dwarfs the volume of poorly generalizing parameters (conditioned on interpolation). We explicitly construct this set of near-equivalent $W$-by-$D$ parameters by a proof technique called *deep lifting*, and then tie the achievable volume to stability properties of the $w$-by-$d$ witness. Examples show that these techniques allow us to convert approximation-theoretic results into generalization guarantees for nonparametric classes. We further show that generalization of uniform-random interpolators can survive label corruptions.
papers.summary: The authors ask how well a network generalizes when its parameters are picked uniformly at random from all weight settings of a large width-W, depth-D ReLU architecture that fit the training data, in the case where a much smaller w-by-d network could explain that data. They show that this oblivious selection rule still generalizes **at a rate of roughly wdWD/n rather than being governed by the VC dimension of the full architecture**. The explanation is an inductive bias of ReLU networks: a small witness network corresponds to an exponentially large volume of equivalent large-network parameters, constructed explicitly with a proof technique the authors call `deep lifting`. The framework turns approximation-theory results into generalization guarantees and still holds under some label corruption.

papers.title: ECHO: Replacing the Compliance Proxy with Response Harmfulness in Optimization-Based Jailbreak Attack
papers.abstract: Despite extensive safety alignment, large language models remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Existing optimization-based attacks share a single objective: maximize a token-level proxy of victim compliance---such as the likelihood of an affirmative prefix---computed on the prompt rather than the decoded reply. This proxy cannot distinguish a cautious hedge from a fully actionable harmful answer, leaving the search blind to what the model actually says. We propose ECHO (Evaluation-Conditioned Harmfulness Optimization), which replaces the compliance proxy with response-level, continuous harmfulness scores from HarmSig, a 1.7B regressor grounded in actual harmful capability. ECHO couples HarmSig with five word-level perturbation operators and Keyword-Anchored Beam Search with global top-m memory, under a strict black-box threat model. Across five open-weight victims on AdvBench, ECHO achieves up to 0.898 StrongREJECT mean score and 89.23% HarmBench success. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/STANWYW/echo.
papers.summary: Optimization-based jailbreak attacks typically maximize a token-level proxy for compliance, such as the likelihood of an affirmative prefix, which cannot tell a cautious hedge from a genuinely harmful answer. `ECHO` (Evaluation-Conditioned Harmfulness Optimization) instead scores the decoded reply with `HarmSig`, a 1.7B-parameter regressor that outputs continuous harmfulness scores, and searches with five word-level perturbation operators and Keyword-Anchored Beam Search under a strict black-box threat model. Against five open-weight models on `AdvBench`, it reaches up to a 0.898 `StrongREJECT` mean score and **an 89.23% `HarmBench` attack success rate**.

papers.title: Distinguishability and Recovery for a Doubly Sparse Spiked Wigner Model
papers.abstract: We study distinguishability and recovery of a sparse rank-one signal in a spiked Wigner model with independently sparse noise through a variety of algorithms and parameter regimes. The signal and noise have separate sparsity parameters, while the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) remains of constant order as the matrix size grows. For sub-Gaussian noise and spikes whose nonzero coordinates are bounded away from zero, a leave-one-out quadratic thresholding procedure (a generalization of Ding et al., 2024) identifies the support. Sign synchronization yields exact recovery for a Rademacher spike, and spectral refinement yields strong recovery. The quadratic thresholding search parameter gives an explicit tradeoff between signal sparsity, noise sparsity, and computational cost. We also study extensions to sub-Gaussian spike priors through diagonal and quadratic thresholding. For Rademacher spikes with continuous nonzero noise, we develop an identical search algorithm that exploits unblurred signal entries, the existence of which permits distinguishability; connectivity of the graph they reveal provides a sufficient condition for exact recovery. These guarantees do not require moment assumptions on the continuous noise distribution. Together with our previous PCA results (Dumitriu et al., 2026), our analysis covers almost the entire space of parameters and regimes for distinguishing and recovering in our doubly sparse spiked Wigner model.
papers.summary: The authors study when a sparse rank-one signal can be detected and recovered in a spiked Wigner matrix model whose noise is also sparse, with separate sparsity levels for signal and noise and a constant signal-to-noise ratio. A leave-one-out quadratic thresholding procedure identifies the signal's support, after which sign synchronization or spectral refinement gives exact or strong recovery, and its search parameter trades off signal sparsity, noise sparsity, and computational cost. For Rademacher spikes with continuous noise, a related search uses signal entries left uncorrupted by noise, with **guarantees that need no moment assumptions on the noise distribution**. Combined with the authors' earlier PCA results, the analysis covers almost the entire parameter space of the model.

papers.title: Towards Looped Models Done Right, Part I: Topology, Input Injection, Recurrent-State Design
papers.abstract: Looped language models reuse physical Transformer blocks across logical depth, but established architectures entangle recurrence placement, input injection, and recurrent state organization. We isolate these axes in models trained from scratch at matched parameter scale, logical depth, and token budgets, and then test whether the resulting design principles transfer to resident- and active-parameter-matched Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. The prelude-recurrent block-coda sandwich architecture consistently improves performance on context extraction and reasoning-intensive tasks. Input injection primarily enhances knowledge retrieval and context utilization, whereas random initialization and separate H/L recurrent states provide mixed or negative returns. Taken together, these results favor the Huginn-style design: at the 730M-parameter and 336B-token scale, the complete Huginn architecture outperforms Ouro across all ten benchmarks. The advantages of Huginn over Ouro transfer to MoE models. At the 8BA0.8B (32BA3B when unrolled) scale trained on 500B tokens, Huginn outperforms Ouro on nearly all benchmarks spanning knowledge, reasoning, and coding, while also exhibiting more balanced expert routing. Under matched training and inference FLOPs, the Huginn-style model uses 75% fewer resident parameters than a 112-layer feedforward MoE baseline. Despite its smaller physical parameters, it outperforms the feedforward baseline on DROP and GSM8K, matches it on MATH500, and remains competitive on the other benchmarks.
papers.summary: Looped language models reuse the same Transformer blocks across multiple passes, but existing designs bundle several choices together: where the recurrence sits, how the input is re-injected, and how the recurrent state is organized. Training models from scratch at matched parameters, depth, and token budgets, the authors find that a prelude-recurrent-coda "sandwich" helps context extraction and reasoning, input injection mainly helps knowledge retrieval, and separate recurrent states give mixed or negative returns. Together these favor the `Huginn`-style design, which beats `Ouro` on all ten benchmarks at 730M parameters and on nearly all benchmarks in an 8B-total, 0.8B-active Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) setting. At matched training and inference FLOPs, the `Huginn`-style model uses **75% fewer resident parameters than a 112-layer feedforward MoE baseline** while matching or beating it on `DROP`, `GSM8K`, and `MATH500`.
papers.highlight_summary:
Looped language models reuse the same Transformer blocks across logical depth to trade compute for memory, but the two dominant designs, `Ouro` and `Huginn`, differ in several choices at once. The authors separate these into three axes (where recurrence sits, how the input is re-injected, and how the recurrent state is organized), then ablate each one in models trained from scratch at matched parameters, logical depth and token budgets.
