- The controlled path goes from `Ouro`'s full-stack loop (28 blocks × 4) to `Huginn`'s sandwich (an 8-layer prelude, a 12-block core looped 8 times, and an 8-layer coda); every variant has 112 logical layers from 28 stored blocks (730M parameters) and is trained on 336B tokens of `TxT360`.
- Moving recurrence into the prelude–loop–coda sandwich gives the clearest gains, **+12.00 on `MATH500`** and +7.05 on `GSM8K`; re-injecting the prelude representation at each loop step adds **+6.63 on `BBH-CoT`** and +5.49 on `HumanEval+`, but costs 3.60 points on `MATH500`.
- Random state initialization gives two gains and four losses larger than one point, and a shared-module high/low (H/L) state hierarchy brings no consistent benefit while cutting `MATH500` by **7.20**; with all choices combined, the full `Huginn` design beats `Ouro` on all ten dense benchmarks.
- In MoE models with 8B resident and 0.8B active parameters trained on 500B tokens, `Huginn` beats `Ouro` on 8 of 10 benchmarks (**+4.70 `GSM8K`**, +3.60 `MATH500`) and balances expert load better (load-balancing loss 1.571 vs 1.899), and fixing each loop iteration to the experts chosen in the first iteration lowers accuracy on all six probe tasks.
- Against a 112-layer feedforward MoE with matched FLOPs and **4× the resident parameters**, `Huginn` wins on `DROP` and `GSM8K`, ties on `MATH500` and narrows the mean gap from 4.96 to **1.71** points, though results come from a single scale and seed and the MoE study compares only complete configurations, not individual components.

papers.title: GR-OPD: Group-Relative Sequence Credit for On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides token-level teacher feedback, yet common sampled-token updates assign credit locally and omit the effects of earlier actions on subsequent feedback. We introduce \method{} (Group-Relative On-Policy Distillation), which decouples feedback computation from credit assignment by aggregating token feedback into calibrated sequence-level credit. We establish a theoretical basis for this approach by showing that, under ideal on-policy assumptions, broadcasting raw summed feedback to every response token yields an unbiased estimate of the negative gradient of the sequence-level reverse-KL objective. To support effective learning in practice, \method{} discounts later feedback that may become less reliable under distribution shift and uses same-prompt rollout groups to calibrate teacher guidance. It preserves relative response preferences while retaining a controlled fraction of the group mean, which we term collective teacher pressure. Across five Qwen3 teacher--student settings and six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, \method{} outperforms vanilla OPD in macro Avg@K in every setting, including gains of 10.9 and 11.5 percentage points in two settings with matched thinking patterns. It also maintains stable training under mismatched thinking patterns, where vanilla OPD collapses. Ablations show that retaining an appropriate amount of collective teacher pressure can improve learning, while excessive collective teacher pressure or an unrestricted feedback horizon can destabilize training.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) gives token-level teacher feedback, but standard updates credit each sampled token in isolation and ignore how earlier tokens affect later feedback. `GR-OPD` (Group-Relative On-Policy Distillation) aggregates token feedback into sequence-level credit, which the authors show is an unbiased gradient estimate of the sequence-level reverse-KL objective under ideal on-policy assumptions. In practice it discounts later, less reliable feedback and calibrates against groups of rollouts from the same prompt, keeping a controlled fraction of the group mean that the authors call "collective teacher pressure." Across five `Qwen3` teacher-student pairs and six math benchmarks it beats vanilla OPD in every setting, **by up to 11.5 percentage points**, and stays stable when teacher and student think in different patterns, a case where vanilla OPD collapses.

papers.title: DIFFLET: A Fast Inference Engine for Diffusion Transformer Models on AWS Trainium
papers.abstract: On AWS Trainium2, every component of a diffusion model runs as a program compiled ahead of time for fixed shapes, while pipelines differ across models, prompt lengths across requests, and caching decisions across denoising steps. We present Difflet, a serving engine in which five model pipelines share one compilation backend, joint attention is split across cores by attention head, and a host controller decides at each denoising step whether to run the denoiser or reuse its earlier output. A small probe program computes the caching signal on the device and returns one number per step, and a resident model process keeps every program loaded across requests. Across five image and video model families, fused attention accelerates denoiser steps by 1.2-4.3x over the same framework using PyTorch/XLA attention, and at 32.8k visual tokens it is the only attention that compiles. On four of the five models, resident serving is 1.5-3.4x faster than standalone runs that reload weights from a warm file cache for each generation.
papers.summary: On AWS Trainium2, every part of a diffusion model must be compiled ahead of time for fixed shapes, which clashes with varying pipelines, prompt lengths, and per-step caching decisions. `Difflet` is a serving engine in which five model pipelines share one compilation backend, joint attention is split across cores by attention head, and a host controller decides at each denoising step whether to rerun the denoiser or reuse its earlier output, based on a small on-device probe. Across five image and video model families, its fused attention speeds up denoiser steps by 1.2-4.3x over `PyTorch/XLA` attention and is the only attention that compiles at 32.8k visual tokens. Keeping models resident makes serving **1.5-3.4x faster than reloading weights for each generation** on four of the five models.

papers.title: Unifying Embodied Foundation Models via a Model-to-Policy Formulation
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models and world-action models (WAMs) have emerged as promising approaches to robot learning and control. These models integrate multimodal perception and action generation, but differ in their architectures, output representations, and learning objectives. In this paper, we present a unified, architecture-agnostic probabilistic formulation for embodied foundation models based on stochastic kernels. Our formulation has two key components: (i) we characterize embodied foundation models through conditional output distributions and action-realization kernels, which together induce task-conditioned robot policies; and (ii) we connect pretraining and post-training to policy deployment, accommodating model-specific pretraining objectives and offline or online post-training strategies. We instantiate the formulation for OpenVLA and DreamZero, covering autoregressive action-token prediction and joint video-action generation.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models and world-action models (WAMs) both combine perception with action generation for robots, but they differ in architecture, output representation, and training objective. The authors propose an architecture-agnostic probabilistic formulation based on stochastic kernels, describing each model by its conditional output distribution plus an action-realization kernel that together induce a task-conditioned robot policy. The framework also links pretraining and offline or online post-training to deployment, and is **instantiated for both `OpenVLA` and `DreamZero`**, covering autoregressive action-token prediction and joint video-action generation.

papers.title: Same Person, Different Advice: Auditing LLM Financial Advice with Repeated Risk-Tolerance Responses
papers.abstract: AI financial advisers set a client's stock allocation largely from one stated-risk question, yet people do not answer it the same way twice: in a national US panel, 41% of households chose a different answer two years later, and in a laboratory retest a third of people moved two or more points on a 0-10 scale after six months. Seven large language models from five providers gave one-turn allocation advice for 800 real household profiles in which only the risk answer changed. The recommended stock share moved by 10 to 16 percentage points on average, and by 24 to 35 when the answer changed, against 0.6 to 4.2 points for the same prompt asked twice; in the laboratory retest the rating alone moved advice by 11 to 18 points. Without any note, the models respond to the answer about as strongly as when told that it is very reliable (less so for the two Claude models). If that instructed response is how each model maps attitude to advice, discounting the answer for its measured reliability, as classical test theory prescribes, would cut the swings by a factor of 2.4 to 3.3. The swing is largest for clients under 40. A note that the answer is noisy steadies some models, but shifts their weight to the client's age and pulls cautious clients towards a generic middle allocation: clients unwilling to take any risk are advised 22% stocks instead of 4%. Three extra money questions reduce the swing for some models, with no statistically detectable change relative to how much advice differs across people. In a scripted test, one clarifying question removes nearly all of the swing from an answer the client then corrects (33.5 points to 1.9 on average) while keeping the response to a change the client confirms. We argue that same-person retest audits should be a standard check for AI advisers, and that what to do with an unreliable answer is a question of client autonomy as well as of statistics.
papers.summary: AI financial advisers often set a client's stock allocation from a single risk-tolerance question, even though people frequently answer it differently when asked again. Seven large language models from five providers gave allocation advice for 800 real household profiles in which only the risk answer changed. Recommended stock share shifted by 10-16 percentage points on average, against 0.6-4.2 points for repeating the same prompt, and discounting the answer for its measured reliability would cut these swings by a factor of 2.4-3.3. In a scripted test, **one clarifying question cut the swing from 33.5 points to 1.9** while keeping the response to changes the client confirmed, and the authors argue that same-person retest audits should be a standard check for AI advisers.

papers.title: ParetoChat: An LLM-Based Interface for Interactive Multi-Objective Optimization
papers.abstract: Multi-objective optimization models are often deployed in settings where decision makers (DMs) must balance some conflicting criteria. In practice, however, stakeholders must translate their qualitative preferences between different criteria into numerical weights, priorities, or reference points required by optimization methods, which can be difficult to specify and interpret. This paper proposes \emph{ParetoChat}, an LLM (large language model)-based expert-agent interface for interactive multi-objective optimization. The agent translates natural-language user input into structured scalarization parameters, invokes an optimization system, presents candidate solutions, and iteratively elicits feedback. We describe a multi-agent architecture that separates input processing, multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) expertise, solution presentation, and feedback processing. We then present a simulation study using an LLM-based DM agent and benchmark ParetoChat against interactive methods implemented in DESDEO, including reference-point and NIMBUS methods. The computational experiments on multi-objective binary knapsack and set-partitioning instances show that ParetoChat can guide the search efficiently toward solutions that match the DM's preferences. An application to historical courier-order assignment instances illustrates how users can explore objective extremes and intermediate trade-offs through natural-language requests. The results indicate that LLM agents may provide a practical interaction layer between business stakeholders and optimization tools.
papers.summary: Multi-objective optimization requires decision makers to turn qualitative preferences into numerical weights or reference points, which is hard to specify and interpret. `ParetoChat` is a multi-agent large language model (LLM) interface with separate agents for input processing, multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) expertise, solution presentation, and feedback handling. It translates natural-language requests into scalarization parameters, calls an optimizer, and iterates on user feedback. In simulations with an LLM-based decision maker on binary knapsack and set-partitioning problems, it **efficiently guided search toward preferred solutions** compared with reference-point and `NIMBUS` methods in `DESDEO`, and a courier-order assignment case study shows the natural-language interaction in practice.

papers.title: Before Retrieval Begins: Safety and Tool-Use Decisions in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly act as agents that call external tools, yet most tool-safety research examines only what follows a tool call. The prior decision of whether to call the tool remains largely unexamined and can influence downstream safety. Across the seven open-weight models, the unweighted model-average harm rate after admitted harmful requests is 74.5%. To identify what governs this decision, we apply a factorial intervention to the input request. Within our generated construction, neutralizing the requested-operation component produces the largest admission contrast (19 pp). A linear direction estimated from this contrast influences held-out admission in four of seven models; effects on operation-neutralized requests in some models show that it is not an operation-specific mechanism. We then test whether written refusal is behaviorally and representationally coupled to the same decision. Written refusal accompanies 33.6% of admitted harmful calls. Plain-text refusal training reduces unsafe admission in models that retain benign tool use, showing that response-level safety training can transfer to the call decision. Together, these results establish a partial, model-dependent relation between written refusal and tool admission. They motivate direct evaluation and supervision of tool admission rather than treating text refusal as its proxy.
papers.summary: Most tool-safety research looks at what happens after a large language model (LLM) agent calls a tool, not at the earlier decision of whether to call it at all. Across seven open-weight models, **74.5% of outputs are harmful once a harmful request is admitted to a tool call**, and factorial interventions on the request show that neutralizing the requested operation shifts admission the most (19 percentage points). Written refusals accompany 33.6% of admitted harmful calls, so text refusal and tool admission are only partly coupled. Plain-text refusal training does reduce unsafe admission in some models, but the authors argue that tool admission should be evaluated and supervised directly rather than inferred from text refusal.

papers.title: Path to Prior-Data Fitted Relational Models via Learned Latent Multi-table Representations
papers.abstract: Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) show that pretraining on large populations of synthetic tasks can enable generalization to unseen datasets with little or no downstream fine-tuning. This paradigm is effective for transformer-based tabular and relational foundation models such as RDB-PFN, but remains largely unexplored for graph-based relational models built on message passing. We pretrain the graph-based relational foundation model Griffin on large collections of synthetic relational databases and ask whether curriculum learning, which benefits transformer-based relational learners, also improves message-passing representations. Rather than fine-tune on downstream tasks, we use the pretrained encoder as a general-purpose relational representation learner and pass its latent representations to a frozen in-context predictor (\ticl{}); no component is trained on the target task. On 16 real-world relational classification tasks, evaluated over five seeds against raw-feature and untrained-encoder baselines, a purely synthetic curriculum that begins with schema-guided data and continues with schema-agnostic data gives the strongest frozen in-context performance\rev{, outperforming real-data-only pretraining and every unordered single-stage mixture of the corpora; when appended after real-data pretraining, it yields the best encoders overall}. These results provide initial evidence that PFN-style synthetic pretraining transfers to graph-based relational foundation models.
papers.summary: Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) pretrained on synthetic tasks generalize well for transformer-based tabular and relational models, but the approach has not been tested on graph-based relational models built on message passing. The authors pretrain the graph-based relational model `Griffin` on synthetic relational databases and feed its frozen latent representations to a frozen in-context predictor, so nothing is trained on the target task. On 16 real-world relational classification tasks, **a purely synthetic curriculum, starting with schema-guided data and then schema-agnostic data, gives the best frozen in-context performance**, beating real-data-only pretraining and every unordered mixture. Appending this curriculum after real-data pretraining yields the best encoders overall.

papers.title: Where Latents Belong and How They Flow: Joint Identification of Structural Roles
papers.abstract: Latent factors in dynamical systems can play different roles across observations and time. For example, an idea in a group meeting may be expressed by only some participants, inherit information from earlier discussions, and shape what is said next. We formalize this notion as the structural role of a latent factor, describing where it is expressed, whether it receives influence from the past, and whether it transmits influence to the future. The main challenge is correspondence, since the three structures may be identified under different permutations, while a structural role is defined only when they are aligned to the same latent coordinate. We show that, under suitable structural and variability conditions, all three roles are jointly identifiable under a common permutation at each time point. Guided by this theory, we develop RoleTrace, a framework that traces structural roles in a shared latent coordinate system. Synthetic experiments validate structural recovery, while experiments on multiparty meetings examine the identified roles in real sequential interactions.
papers.summary: Latent factors in dynamical systems can play different structural roles: where they are expressed in the observations, whether the past influences them, and whether they influence the future. The difficulty is correspondence, because each of these three structures may be identifiable only up to a different permutation of the latent coordinates. The authors prove that, under suitable structural and variability conditions, **all three roles are jointly identifiable under a common permutation** at each time point. Their framework, `RoleTrace`, recovers these roles in a shared latent coordinate system, validated on synthetic data and applied to multiparty meeting conversations.

papers.title: Disentangling Language Effects on Tool Admission and Post-Retrieval Safety
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly use retrieval tools across languages, yet their safety evaluation remains English-centric. It remains unclear whether language affects tool admission, post-retrieval generation, or both. We independently vary request, retrieved-page, and required response languages in a controlled URL-retrieval setting across ten models and seven languages. We identify Safety Loss through Interlingual Processing (SLIP). Non-English harmful requests increase mean tool admission from 46.9% to 67.4%, with a positive mean change in every model. This pattern also persists in an autonomous retrieval setup across all four models tested in this setting. Requiring answers in the page language increases pooled harmfulness on matched tool calls from 50.3% to 57.4% across four closed-weight models, mainly in Chinese and Hindi. Translating pages alone produces no consistent harm increase in eight models with comparable inference settings. Automated audits show that a non-harmful response may be a genuine safety refusal, a deflection citing language difficulties, or an unusable answer. Harmfulness labels alone cannot distinguish these outcomes. Multilingual safety evaluations should therefore measure tool admission and response harmfulness separately and distinguish refusal from capability failure.
papers.summary: Safety evaluation for retrieval-using large language model (LLM) agents is largely English-centric, leaving unclear whether language affects the decision to call a tool, the generation after retrieval, or both. Independently varying request, retrieved-page, and response languages across ten models and seven languages, the authors identify Safety Loss through Interlingual Processing (`SLIP`): **non-English harmful requests raise mean tool admission from 46.9% to 67.4%**, with an increase in every model. Requiring answers in the page's language raises harmfulness from 50.3% to 57.4% in four closed-weight models, mainly in Chinese and Hindi, while translating the pages alone has no consistent effect. Audits show that non-harmful responses mix genuine refusals, deflections citing language difficulty, and unusable answers, so the authors recommend measuring admission and harmfulness separately and distinguishing refusal from capability failure.

papers.title: Towards a GraphNARX model for structural dynamics
papers.abstract: The current paper introduces the GraphNARX model, a graph-based nonlinear autoregressive exogenous model for structural dynamics. The model is built to account for the geometry of structures and to model dynamic behaviour as the interaction between elements of the structure. Similar to other types of NARX models, GraphNARX is used for system identification. Nodal attributes of the graph encode past displacements and nodal forces, and the output of the model is the next-timestep displacement. The graph formulation of the model allows it to generalise to structures of different dimensions and degrees of freedom. Moreover, because graph-learning is performed locally between the nodes, the GraphNARX model can also learn to infer displacements of nodes for which data are not available, i.e.\ to perform virtual sensing. The proposed model's performance is evaluated in a system-identification framework and a virtual-sensing framework, and achieves good accuracy and exhibits generalisation capabilities to structures of different sizes.
papers.summary: `GraphNARX` is a graph-based nonlinear autoregressive exogenous (NARX) model for system identification in structural dynamics, representing a structure's geometry as a graph whose elements interact. Node attributes encode past displacements and nodal forces, and the model predicts next-timestep displacements. Because learning happens locally between nodes, the model generalizes to structures of different sizes and degrees of freedom and can **infer displacements at nodes with no sensor data (virtual sensing)**, with good accuracy reported in both settings.

papers.title: Domain-specific language alignment of multimodal embeddings towards explainable predictions
papers.abstract: Multimodal data are commonly fused into latent representations that improve downstream task performance but are not interpretable, limiting their application in domains that require explainable model decisions. Vision-language alignment has made image embeddings interpretable through language, but requires vast image-caption training data. However, captioned data are typically not available for multimodal embeddings, as relevant features cannot directly be observed and annotated from embeddings alone. Here, we propose a framework to language-align any embedding space that can be linked to interpretable auxiliary data. Captioning functions convert auxiliary data into partial captions; a soft contrastive loss weights pairs by the similarity of their properties that each caption describes; and a rank-based concept retrieval task evaluates alignment against the auxiliary data rather than the captions. We apply this framework to multimodal Earth embeddings to facilitate explainable predictions for two species distribution modelling tasks: S2BMS and SatBird. AlphaEarth embeddings beat previous state-of-the-art models on 6/7 metrics, while our framework language-aligns domain-specific concepts of the embedding space, outperforming previous Earth observation vision-language models on average concept retrieval for both datasets. Finally, aligned concepts recover species-habitat associations ($\rho$=0.44) and relate habitat descriptions to species predictions, showing that abstract embeddings can be interrogated in the language of domain experts.
papers.summary: Multimodal embeddings improve predictions but are not interpretable, and the usual way to make embeddings readable through language requires large image-caption datasets that do not exist for abstract embedding spaces. The proposed framework language-aligns any embedding space that can be linked to interpretable auxiliary data, using captioning functions that turn that data into partial captions, a soft contrastive loss weighted by property similarity, and a rank-based concept retrieval evaluation. Applied to Earth-observation embeddings for species distribution modelling on `S2BMS` and `SatBird`, `AlphaEarth` embeddings beat prior state of the art on 6 of 7 metrics, and the aligned concepts outperform earlier Earth-observation vision-language models on concept retrieval and **recover species-habitat associations (ρ=0.44)**.

papers.title: LED: Improving Masked Diffusion Language Models by Lookahead Editing
papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive language models, enabling non-autoregressive text generation through parallel decoding. Existing dLLMs can be broadly categorized into two families: masked diffusion models (MDMs) and uniform diffusion models (UDMs) In this work, we theoretically show that MDMs are easier to optimize due to their mask-based transition schedule but have lower computational expressivity, whereas UDMs enable iterative state revision and greater expressivity but are substantially harder to train. This trade-off raises a natural question: can we obtain the expressivity of iterative revision without giving up the simple, easy-to-optimize transition schedule of MDMs? Motivated by this analysis, we propose Lookahead Editing (\ours{}), which augments masked diffusion decoding with a rewritable proposal state. At each decoding step, the model performs several lookahead updates to iteratively refine future predictions in this proposal state before committing tokens to the masked sequence. This design introduces a rewritable proposal that uses additional compute to improve expressivity while keeping the simple mask-based transition schedule of MDMs. We fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen3-8B to obtain LED-\texttt{7B} and LED-\texttt{8B}, respectively. Across eight benchmarks, LED SFT yields average gains of $+11.4$ and $+7.7$ points over standard MDM SFT. Moreover, using SFT alone, LED-\texttt{8B} outperforms LLaDA2.1-16B Q-mode, which is trained with continued pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning.
papers.summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate text in parallel, but they come in two families with a trade-off. Masked diffusion models (MDMs) are easy to optimize but less expressive, while uniform diffusion models (UDMs) can revise earlier choices but are much harder to train. `Lookahead Editing` (`LED`) keeps the simple MDM mask schedule but adds a rewritable proposal state, which the model refines through several lookahead updates before committing tokens. Fine-tuning `Qwen2.5-7B` and `Qwen3-8B` with this method gives average gains of **+11.4 and +7.7 points over standard MDM fine-tuning** across eight benchmarks, and `LED-8B` beats `LLaDA2.1-16B`, which was trained with continued pre-training and reinforcement learning, using supervised fine-tuning alone.

papers.title: Information-Geometric Blind Spots of Conformal Test Martingales
papers.abstract: Conformal test martingales (CTMs) are e-processes for sequentially testing exchangeability via p-values produced by a conformity function $A$. However, any distribution shift that preserves the push-forward $P\circ A^{-1}$ leaves the p-value distribution invariant, rendering it invisible to every CTM based on $A$. We formalise this blind spot through the \emph{$A$-equivalence class} $[P]_A$ and show that, for any target distribution $T$, there is a unique closest element $Q^\ast\in[P]_A$ in KL divergence---the \emph{$A$-cryptic I-projection}---with explicit density $q^\ast(z) = t(z)\,p_S(A(z))/t_S(A(z))$ and a Pythagorean decomposition into detectable and cryptic components. When $A$ is the Neyman-Pearson likelihood ratio, the cryptic component vanishes, connecting our result to optimal e-value design. We demonstrate the theory on high-dimensional image data by empirically constructing this I-projection. By conditionally resampling EMNIST letters to identically match the conformity scores of MNIST digits, we demonstrate that a distribution can be shifted to a disjoint support while leaving the test martingale mathematically blinded.
papers.summary: Conformal test martingales (CTMs) test sequentially whether data are exchangeable, using p-values from a conformity function. Any distribution shift that leaves the distribution of conformity scores unchanged is invisible to them. The authors formalize this blind spot and prove that for any target distribution there is a **unique closest undetectable distribution in KL divergence**, which they call the cryptic I-projection. It has an explicit density and splits the shift into detectable and cryptic parts, and the cryptic part vanishes when the conformity function is the Neyman-Pearson likelihood ratio. In an empirical demonstration, `EMNIST` letters are resampled to match the conformity scores of `MNIST` digits, producing a shift to entirely disjoint data that the martingale cannot detect.

papers.title: MetaCurate: Evolving Curation Filters for High-Quality Agentic Coding Data
papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning on agent trajectories is an effective way to improve coding agents, but selecting useful training examples requires more than identifying successful runs. A resolved patch may follow inefficient reasoning or unnecessary tool use, while a failed run may still contain useful intermediate steps. Training pipelines therefore rely on rules and qualitative assessments to filter trajectories, yet designing these filters typically requires substantial human expertise, and validating improvements through repeated training and evaluation is expensive. We introduce MetaCurate, a training-free framework that evolves executable trajectory curation filters using pairwise LLM judgments. Disagreements between the filter's rankings and the judge's preferences provide targeted feedback for jointly revising its rules, rubric, and aggregation policy. The resulting filter scores trajectories independently, so pairwise comparisons are required only during search. Starting from a blank filter, MetaCurate autonomously discovers a curation strategy that achieves competitive downstream performance without task-specific handwritten criteria. We validate downstream utility through controlled SFT experiments on our uncurated trajectory pool and the Nemotron v3 SWE dataset, with random selection and hand-authored filtering as baselines. In our experiments, MetaCurate achieves the highest mean SWE-Verified score among the compared methods, including hand-authored rule-based filtering and a training-loop baseline whose search costs 3.5x as much.
papers.summary: Choosing which coding-agent trajectories to use for supervised fine-tuning is hard: a successful run may contain wasteful tool use, and a failed run may still hold useful steps. `MetaCurate` is a training-free framework that evolves executable curation filters from a blank start. It uses disagreements between the filter's rankings and pairwise LLM-judge preferences to revise the filter's rules, rubric, and aggregation policy together. Once the search is done, the filter scores trajectories on its own, with no further pairwise comparisons. In controlled fine-tuning experiments on an uncurated trajectory pool and the `Nemotron v3 SWE` dataset, `MetaCurate` achieves the **highest mean `SWE-Verified` score**, beating hand-authored rule-based filtering and a training-loop baseline whose search costs 3.5 times as much.

papers.title: Local proxies for memory-efficient training
papers.abstract: Local learning algorithms can reshape resource requirements of artificial intelligence. The memory bottleneck of standard end-to-end backpropagation lies in the need to store all network activations until the loss gradient has been propagated back through. Local learning avoids this, but typically at a cost in accuracy. We study how to achieve accurate and memory efficient local learning in transformers. For each transformer block, we train a local proxy network to predict the global network output via distillation. Gradients can be independently propagated through this local proxy while estimating well the backpropagation gradients. In theory, this approach is exact for deep linear networks; in non-linear residual models, the gradient error can be bounded when using the appropriate residual proxy. We verify this numerically and demonstrate that optimizing the distillation loss improves gradient estimation. Evaluating the performance of proxy propagation on CIFAR-100 in vision transformers, we find that it achieves a better accuracy/memory trade-off compared to other local algorithms. Finally, we show that the method is further relevant for fine-tuning large language models on a small memory budget. Our method trains faster and achieves higher performance than memory-efficient zeroth-order learning algorithms with comparable memory cost.
papers.summary: Standard backpropagation needs a lot of memory because it stores every activation until gradients flow back, and local learning methods that avoid this usually lose accuracy. In `proxy propagation`, each transformer block gets a small local proxy network that is distilled to predict the global network output, so gradients can pass through the proxy instead of the full network. The method is exact for deep linear networks, and its gradient error is bounded for residual models with a suitable residual proxy. It achieves a **better accuracy/memory trade-off than other local algorithms** on vision transformers trained on `CIFAR-100`, and when fine-tuning LLMs on a small memory budget it trains faster and scores higher than zeroth-order methods with comparable memory use.

papers.title: Grounded Credit Assignment in Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Search Agents
papers.abstract: Outcome-reward reinforcement learning such as GRPO gives every token of a search-agent rollout the same advantage, although the rollout exercises two capabilities: finding evidence and using it. We show that accuracy improves without grounding: Search-R1 raises accuracy on all seven QA benchmarks, yet on Bamboogle the evidence-supported share of correct answers falls from 84.0% to 42.9%. We attribute this to GRPO's credit assignment: rollouts that retrieve answer-bearing evidence are favoured in aggregate only in proportion to their accuracy gain over the rest, a grounding gap that answering from memory or misusing evidence shrinks or reverses. To address this, we propose Grounded Credit Assignment (GCA), which uses verifiable sub-outcomes (evidence retrieval and answer correctness) to correct search and answer credit separately: a wrong answer is blamed more than the search that found the evidence, and a correct answer that bypasses retrievable evidence is credited less. Never negative on evidence-finding search, the correction does not shrink with the grounding gap; capped at 10% of each token's advantage, it never overrides the outcome signal. Without extra models, rollouts, or training stages, GCA improves average EM over Search-R1 by 5.7 (Qwen2.5-3B) and 6.3 points (Qwen3-30B-A3B) and raises this share from 76.9% to 93.4%.
papers.summary: Outcome-reward reinforcement learning such as `GRPO` gives every token in a search-agent rollout the same advantage, even though the rollout involves two separate skills: finding evidence and using it. The authors show that `Search-R1` improves accuracy while weakening grounding: on `Bamboogle`, the share of correct answers supported by retrieved evidence falls from 84.0% to 42.9%. `Grounded Credit Assignment` (`GCA`) uses verifiable sub-outcomes, namely whether evidence was retrieved and whether the answer was correct, to adjust search and answer credit separately, with the correction capped at 10% of each token's advantage. Without extra models or rollouts, `GCA` improves average exact match by 5.7 points with `Qwen2.5-3B` and 6.3 points with `Qwen3-30B-A3B`, and raises the **evidence-supported share of correct answers from 76.9% to 93.4%**.

papers.title: Can AI interview? Comparing AI-led to Human-led Chat Interviews
papers.abstract: Large language model chatbots have been proposed as AI-interviewers for collecting qualitative interview data at scale, potentially bridging social science's longstanding divide between the breadth of surveys and the depth of qualitative interviews. This paper provides the first direct empirical comparison of data quality in AI-led and human-led interviews. In a randomized experiment (N = 41), university students were interviewed via synchronous text chat by either trained non-expert interviewers or a locally hosted AI system; we evaluate exposure, specificity, and relevance. Median interview duration was similar across conditions, but AI-interviewers asked more than twice as many questions per interview and elicited roughly 65 percent more respondent text per interview. Per-question responses were longer with human interviewers, though not after multiple-testing correction; only AI-condition participants skipped questions. Responses were almost uniformly on-topic in both conditions; for specificity we detect no difference, but the design cannot exclude one of up to three quarters of a point. These results were obtained with a small, locally hosted open-weight model (7B parameters), which addresses concerns about data security, GDPR compliance, and scientific reproducibility. Our findings support the viability of AI-interviewing for large-N qualitative data collection.
papers.summary: Social scientists have proposed LLM chatbots as interviewers that could collect qualitative data at scale. A randomized experiment with 41 university students compares text-chat interviews run by trained non-expert humans with interviews run by a locally hosted 7-billion-parameter open-weight model. Interviews lasted about the same time, but the AI asked more than twice as many questions and drew out **roughly 65% more respondent text per interview**. Answers were on-topic in both conditions, and no difference in specificity was detected, although only participants interviewed by the AI skipped questions. The authors argue that small local models can address data-security, GDPR, and reproducibility concerns in large-scale qualitative research.

papers.title: CIIR - Class-Indexed Interface Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Multimodal learning commonly assumes paired or synchronized observations, yet independently collected datasets rarely provide such correspondence. We introduce CIIR, a modular encoder--decoder framework that connects heterogeneous datasets through a class-indexed address space while preserving each dataset's native input format and output module. A known local index selects address $k$, and an input-dependent 128-dimensional address representation Z_k(x) is written to that address. To demonstrate CIIR, we learn this address space from handwritten digits, clothing images, spoken-digit spectrograms, and hand signs without synchronized or instance-matched samples. Newly trained label-free receivers recover the requested addresses with 94.7% macro-average Address Realization Accuracy. We then attach the unseen SVHN dataset after freezing the base address space and train only lightweight adapters, achieving 90.2% MNIST>SVHN and 82.3% SVHN>MNIST end-to-end Address Transfer Accuracy without target-side decoder labels. To demonstrate generalizability of CIIR, we reuse the ten addresses as code elements in collision-free arithmetic and hierarchical address codes for all 100 CIFAR-100 classes and evaluate direct arithmetic-code realization through the existing receivers. These results establish CIIR as a compact interface for modular cross-dataset communication and post-hoc dataset attachment without exhaustive paired multimodal supervision.
papers.summary: Multimodal learning usually needs paired or synchronized data, which independently collected datasets rarely provide. `CIIR` connects such datasets through a shared class-indexed address space while each dataset keeps its own input format and output module. Each class address holds a 128-dimensional, input-dependent representation. The address space is learned from handwritten digits, clothing images, spoken-digit spectrograms, and hand signs without any matched samples, and newly trained label-free receivers recover the requested addresses with **94.7% macro-average accuracy**. After the base space is frozen, the unseen `SVHN` dataset is attached using only lightweight adapters, reaching 90.2% `MNIST`-to-`SVHN` and 82.3% `SVHN`-to-`MNIST` transfer accuracy, and the ten addresses are reused as code elements to encode all 100 `CIFAR-100` classes.

papers.title: Cross-Centaur: Modeling Individual Decision-Making Across Psychological Tasks with Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as computational models of human behavior. Recent models such as Centaur have advanced this goal by fine-tuning LLMs on trial-by-trial decisions from psychological experiments. However, existing large-scale behavioral datasets do not link the same participants across different tasks, so these models learn population-level regularities but are not trained to model individual-level regularities across tasks. We introduce Cross-Psych-101, a dataset of 591 participants and 261{,}551 valid decisions across 12 Bandit, Tradeoff, Structure, and Social tasks. We train Cross-Centaur to predict a participant's target-task actions from a target-task description and the source-task description paired with the same participant's source-task behavior. Cross-Centaur outperforms off-the-shelf LLMs and Centaur on held-out participants, both within and across tasks. Probing analyses suggest that its hidden states encode participant-level behavioral tendencies that transfer across tasks. These results highlight the potential of cross-task individual-level data for predicting human decision-making with language models. Cross-Pysch-101 is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/HikaruAsano/cross-psych-101.
papers.summary: LLMs fine-tuned on psychology experiments, such as `Centaur`, learn population-level patterns because existing behavioral datasets do not track the same participants across tasks. The authors release `Cross-Psych-101`, which links 591 participants and 261,551 decisions across 12 bandit, tradeoff, structure, and social tasks. They train `Cross-Centaur` to predict a participant's choices on one task from that same person's behavior on another. It **outperforms off-the-shelf LLMs and `Centaur` on held-out participants**, both within and across tasks. Probing analyses suggest its hidden states encode individual behavioral tendencies that carry over from one task to another.

papers.title: Nearly Linear Private Learning of Littlestone Classes
papers.abstract:
Differentially private learning aims to learn from data while protecting individual training examples. For binary classification, finite Littlestone dimension characterizes approximate private PAC learnability (Alon et al., JACM 2022). Understanding how this dimension controls private sample complexity remains a central question. For classes of Littlestone dimension $d$, the first general upper bound was doubly exponential in $d$ (Bun, Livni, and Moran, FOCS 2020). Subsequent work improved this to $\widetilde O(d^6)$ (Ghazi et al., STOC 2021) and then to $\widetilde O(d^5)$ (Lyu, STOC 2026). We prove a nearly linear upper bound of $O(d\log d)$.
  Our main algorithmic contribution is a structural exponential mechanism for data-dependent candidate sets equipped with a rank satisfying suitable stability conditions. For natural Littlestone classes such as subspace indicators, this rank has a simple geometric interpretation: it is the codimension. This yields a private PAC learner for subspaces of dimension at most $d$ over any field, with tight linear dependence on $d$ and no dependence on the ambient dimension, improving the quadratic dependence of Kaplan et al. (STOC 2025). Our second contribution is combinatorial: drawing on model-theoretic ideas, we construct a suitable rank for general Littlestone classes and establish the counting bounds required by the mechanism.
papers.summary: In differentially private learning, Littlestone dimension determines whether a binary classification class can be learned privately, but how sample complexity grows with that dimension has been an open question. Previous upper bounds improved from doubly exponential to roughly d^6 and then d^5, and this work proves a **nearly linear bound of O(d log d)**. The main tool is a structural exponential mechanism over data-dependent candidate sets equipped with a stable rank. For subspace indicators, this rank is simply the codimension, which gives a private learner for subspaces with linear dependence on dimension and no dependence on the ambient space. For general Littlestone classes, the authors build a suitable rank using ideas from model theory.

papers.title: Explaining Chess and Go in Natural Language
papers.abstract: Modern chess engines play far beyond human ability, often choosing moves whose underlying ideas are difficult for humans to understand. We propose an automatic metric for evaluating chess explanations, grounded in chess-engine evaluations. Evaluating state-of-the-art language models using this metric, we find that they perform surprisingly poorly, often relying on surface-level board observations rather than robust, transferable chess concepts. We then introduce BinProp, a training-free method that enables these same models to discover reusable chess concepts and use them to explain moves in natural language. BinProp improves explainability for every model tested, nearly tripling the average score compared with direct prompting. Beyond chess, the same method discovers useful concepts in Go, draughts, and shogi without additional tuning.
papers.summary: Chess engines play far beyond human level, but the ideas behind their moves are often hard for people to understand. The authors propose an automatic metric for chess explanations based on engine evaluations and find that state-of-the-art language models score poorly, mostly relying on surface-level board observations. `BinProp`, a training-free method, lets the same models discover reusable chess concepts and use them to explain moves in natural language, **nearly tripling the average score compared with direct prompting** and improving every model tested. Without additional tuning, the method also discovers useful concepts in Go, draughts, and shogi.

papers.title: Chinese Decision: A Family of Language Models for Single-Pass Probabilistic Decision-Making
papers.abstract: Many language-based applications require probabilities over a finite set of decisions rather than open-ended responses. We present Chinese Decision, a family of Chinese-language models for single-pass probabilistic decision-making. Given context, an instruction, and candidate descriptions, the model extracts final-position candidate-letter logits in one forward pass and normalizes them over valid options, without autoregressive answer generation. A shared interface supports Boolean judgments, categorical choices, and ordinal scores. We report a completed 0.8B model trained with distribution cross-entropy on 13.048 million decisions and preliminary 2B checkpoints trained with an additional RLCD objective. On the full CJ-Bench of 307,900 decisions, the uncalibrated 0.8B model achieves 72.24% general-domain accuracy and 76.98% average accuracy across medicine, law, and finance using a single checkpoint, with 1.07% overall expected calibration error. The 2B model reaches 72.56% general-domain accuracy after 40.13% of one epoch but has not surpassed the completed 0.8B model on the professional-domain average. We further evaluate a validation-temperature-scaled deployment model and its Q8 quantization, finding close aggregate performance while documenting individual prediction changes. We release the training, evaluation, and deployment pipeline. The current results establish a reproducible approach to Chinese probabilistic decisions but do not isolate the effect of model scale.
papers.summary: Many applications need probabilities over a fixed set of options rather than open-ended text. `Chinese Decision` is a family of Chinese-language models that read the logits for each candidate's letter in a single forward pass and normalize them over the valid options, covering yes/no judgments, categorical choices, and ordinal scores. A 0.8-billion-parameter model trained on 13 million decisions reaches 72.24% general-domain accuracy and 76.98% average accuracy across medicine, law, and finance on the 307,900-decision `CJ-Bench`, with **1.07% expected calibration error** and no extra calibration. Preliminary 2-billion-parameter checkpoints do not yet beat it on professional domains, and a temperature-scaled `Q8`-quantized deployment model performs close to the full-precision version.

papers.title: Structural Affinity: An Algorithm for Coherent Cage-Based Shape Design
papers.abstract: Cage-based deformation (CBD) parametrises 3D geometry through a small set of control handles, effectively enabling a variety of tasks from animation and interactive modelling to tool-based co-design, neural deformation transfer, and aerodynamic shape optimization. Many optimization approaches relying on CBD employ regularisation strategies to reduce the distortion of the deformed mesh by encouraging smooth, regular cage deformations. These techniques offer soft guidance to an optimization algorithm towards desirable deformations, but compete with the task objective rather than changing the deformation parameterization itself. In this work we introduce Structural Affinity for CBD, an explicit regularisation method which enables smooth deformations through control cages by exploiting a two-cage structure to couple cage-handle motion directly. Structural Affinity precomputes an affinity matrix using mean-value coordinates, binding the inner control-cage to a coarser outer-cage. This matrix defines how much a cage handle displacement propagates to neighbouring handles which substantially decreases and often eliminates cage self-intersections, reduces mesh distortion, and adds linear overhead at deformation time. Across robotic control--morphology co-design, source-to-target neural deformation transfer, and aerodynamic wing shape optimization, Structural Affinity produces more regular deformations and substantially reduces reliance on hand-designed structural loss terms. We report consistent gains on three complementary diagnostics: the cotangent Laplacian, a proxy for surface smoothness; cage distortion, capturing whether control handles move coherently; and surface roughness, which measures undesirable oscillation in wing geometry.
papers.summary: Cage-based deformation (CBD) controls 3D shapes through a small set of handles, but optimization methods that use it rely on soft regularization terms that compete with the actual task objective. `Structural Affinity` binds an inner control cage to a coarser outer cage through an affinity matrix precomputed from mean-value coordinates, so that moving one handle moves its neighbors in a coordinated way. This **substantially reduces and often eliminates cage self-intersections** and reduces mesh distortion, while adding only linear overhead at deformation time. Across robot control-morphology co-design, neural deformation transfer, and aerodynamic wing optimization, it produces smoother deformations and reduces the need for hand-designed structural loss terms.

papers.title: Do Speech BCIs Need Larger Models? Rethinking Neural Decoding beyond Scaling
papers.abstract: Recent speech brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) increasingly rely on large models and complex multi-stage pipelines for neural decoding. However, in speech BCI, where training data are scarce, noisy, and expensive to collect, the benefits of model scaling remain unclear. This work revisits a fundamental question: are large models truly necessary for accurate neural decoding? We propose BEST (Brain-Encoding-Speech-Text), a two-stage framework for efficient neural-to-text decoding. Instead of relying on large generative models or phoneme-centric pipelines, BEST introduces hierarchical intermediate representations and a compact speech-oriented decoder that directly maps neural activity to text. This design preserves essential structure while significantly reducing computational cost, enabling robust generalization in low-resource settings and practical deployment under constrained resources. On the Brain-to-Text '24 and '25 benchmarks, BEST achieves word error rates (WERs) of 6.19% and 1.62%, respectively, using only 3.85% of the parameters required by comparable methods. Beyond these results, we provide three key insights: (1) decoder scaling yields non-monotonic gains; (2) cross-modal alignment is more critical than model size; and (3) overfitting degards sequence-level performance. Representation analysis further reveals a consistent neural-audio-text alignment pathway.
papers.summary: Speech brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) increasingly use large models and multi-stage pipelines, even though neural training data are scarce and noisy. `BEST` (Brain-Encoding-Speech-Text) is a two-stage framework that maps neural activity directly to text using hierarchical intermediate representations and a compact speech-oriented decoder. It achieves word error rates of 6.19% on `Brain-to-Text '24` and 1.62% on `Brain-to-Text '25` while using **only 3.85% of the parameters of comparable methods**. The analysis finds that scaling the decoder gives non-monotonic gains and that cross-modal alignment matters more than model size.

papers.title: Tree-Aware Posterior Distillation for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has become a scalable post-training paradigm for large language models. However, training agents over long-horizon interactions presents two challenges: using only terminal rewards makes turn-level credit assignment sparse and high-variance, while sequential mini-batch updates on a fixed rollout batch introduce policy staleness as the current policy drifts from the behavior policy. Existing approaches obtain denser credit via learned critics, process reward models, or on-policy distillation, but they rely on a value network, step-level annotations, or a stronger external teacher that increase training complexity. Meanwhile, importance sampling and clipping mitigate policy drift, but they do not specify a finite target that stops sequential updates from overshooting. In this work, we introduce TreeOPSD, a critic-free, tree-aware posterior self-distillation framework for long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning. Treating each interaction turn as a tree node, TreeOPSD branches alternative continuations from shared prefixes and recursively backs up terminal rewards into implicit turn-level credit. It then maps each credit to a closed-form, bounded teacher distribution parameterized by the likelihood ratio relative to the frozen behavior policy. Minimizing the divergence between this teacher and the student policy recovers the policy-gradient direction as the tangent at the behavior policy while bounding updates toward a finite target across sequential mini-batches. Empirically, TreeOPSD improves agentic capabilities across several competitive benchmarks and model scales, especially for long-horizon tasks, e.g., raising the average accuracy of Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 by 4.97 points over GRPO on the Deep Research setting.
papers.summary: Training LLM agents on long interactions with only terminal rewards makes turn-level credit sparse and noisy. Repeated mini-batch updates on a fixed batch of rollouts also let the policy drift away from the policy that collected them. `TreeOPSD` treats each turn as a tree node, branches alternative continuations from shared prefixes, and backs up terminal rewards into implicit turn-level credit without a learned critic. Each credit is mapped to a closed-form, bounded teacher distribution, and distilling toward it recovers the policy-gradient direction while limiting how far sequential updates can overshoot. The method improves agent benchmarks across model scales, especially on long-horizon tasks, raising `Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507` by **4.97 points over `GRPO` on the Deep Research setting**.
papers.highlight_summary:
Long-horizon agentic RL has two problems. A single terminal reward gives every turn the same noisy credit, and later mini-batch updates drift away from the policy that collected the rollouts. `TreeOPSD` handles both without a critic, process labels, or an external teacher: it branches rollouts from shared prefixes to estimate per-turn credit, then turns that credit into a fixed, bounded target distribution that the policy is distilled toward.

- Each turn is a tree node, and terminal rewards are standardized and propagated up the tree, weighted by likelihood, to give turn-level credit `V_i`. Each `V_i` maps to a Bernoulli teacher `q_i = 1/2 + V_i/τ`, defined relative to the frozen behavior policy through a length-normalized likelihood ratio, and `τ` is calibrated from group size so every target stays within a fixed radius `ρ` without clipping.
- A forward-KL distillation loss toward this teacher has exactly the tree policy-gradient direction at the behavior policy. On later mini-batches the update weight shrinks with the remaining student–teacher gap, reaches zero at the target, and flips sign on overshoot, unlike fixed-credit updates such as `TreePO`.
- On Deep Research (trained on `OpenResearcher`, evaluated on `BrowseComp-Plus`, `BrowseComp`, `GAIA` and `xbench-DeepSearch`), `Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507` averages **21.20**, compared with 16.23 for `GRPO` (**+4.97**) and 17.59 for `TreePO`, and `BrowseComp-Plus` rises from 12.29 to **17.47** over `TreePO`. `Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507` goes from 12.18 (`GRPO`) to **15.45**.
- Gains on Multi-Hop QA are much smaller, about +0.8 to +1.1 average points over `GRPO`. `TreeOPSD` also trails baselines on some individual sets, such as `2WikiMultiHopQA` at 30B and `Bamboogle` at 4B, and absolute `BrowseComp` accuracy stays low at 3.5–6.4%.
- In ablations, a rollout split of 4 initial trajectories with 2 branches each is the best allocation, beating both 8 independent rollouts (11.28 vs 15.45 on Deep Research) and a split heavier on continuations. Results hold up across radius values `ρ` from 0.1 to 0.4, though experiments cover only two `Qwen3` models.

papers.title: What LLMs Do in the Shadows: Reading Context Reliance from the Unembedding Dark Space
papers.abstract: Detecting faithfulness hallucinations in large language models (LLMs) is crucial for their safe deployment in high-stakes domains. Recent approaches address this by contrasting contextual against parametric knowledge utilization, yet measuring context reliance typically demands noticeable overhead, such as materializing attention maps, running additional forward passes, or training auxiliary probes. In this work, we show that context reliance can be estimated by projecting hidden states onto the dark space - directions that compose weakly with the unembedding matrix. Beyond its recognized function as an initial-token attention sink, we show that this subspace actively mediates context processing, and that its share of hidden-state norm - termed the Dark Matter Ratio (DMR) - provides a direct score of context utilization. Pairing DMR with a parametric knowledge score yields DarkLens, a lightweight faithfulness detector operating strictly within a single forward pass. Evaluated across three QA and summarization benchmarks on six open-weight LLMs (4B-13B parameters), DarkLens matches or outperforms a wide range of baselines without requiring extra forward passes or probe training.
papers.summary: Detecting when an LLM ignores or contradicts its provided context usually requires attention maps, extra forward passes, or trained probes. The authors show that the "dark space" (hidden-state directions that interact only weakly with the unembedding matrix) actively mediates how the model processes context, beyond its known role as an attention sink. The share of hidden-state norm in this subspace, called the `Dark Matter Ratio` (`DMR`), directly scores how much the model relies on context. Combined with a parametric-knowledge score, it forms `DarkLens`, a detector that **matches or beats a wide range of baselines within a single forward pass**, tested on three QA and summarization benchmarks with six open-weight LLMs of 4B to 13B parameters.

papers.title: AMEND: Constraint-Guided Multi-Agent Text Detoxification with Isolated Critics
papers.abstract: Text detoxification requires balancing toxicity removal, semantic preservation, and fluency. Existing methods typically optimize an unconstrained scalar objective---enabling safety scores to mask semantic loss---or rely on open-ended iterative debate prone to semantic drift and high computational cost. We propose AMEND, an inference-time framework that decouples detoxification into role-conditioned proposal generation, isolated multidimensional criticism, and constraint-first selection. AMEND evaluates diverse candidates with role-blind critics and enforces strict semantic and fluency feasibility before ranking by utility. To maximize efficiency, AMEND Lite restricts subsequent search to at most one targeted repair round only when residual toxic spans remain. On ParaDetox, one-round selection over diverse roles improves the joint evaluation metric by $+0.0508$ over the best single role. On a frozen confirmation test set, AMEND Lite achieves a joint score of $0.6597 \pm 0.0062$, outperforming unconstrained multi-round loops by $+0.0489$ ($p < 0.05$) while reducing inference requests by 28.4%.
papers.summary: Text detoxification must remove toxicity while preserving meaning and fluency. Existing methods either collapse these goals into a single score that can hide meaning loss, or rely on costly open-ended debate loops that drift semantically. `AMEND` generates candidates from several role-conditioned agents, scores them with isolated critics that do not know which role produced each candidate, discards any that fail semantic or fluency thresholds, and only then ranks the rest by utility. A lighter variant, `AMEND Lite`, adds at most one targeted repair round when toxic spans remain. On a held-out `ParaDetox` test set it reaches a joint score of 0.6597, **beating unconstrained multi-round loops by 0.0489 while using 28.4% fewer inference requests**.

papers.title: A Stronger Teacher Within: Strengthening MoE Models via On-Policy Bidirectional Distillation
papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs, but its outcome-level rewards provide only sparse supervision. On-Policy Distillation offers dense token-level feedback, yet requires a stronger compatible teacher, while on-policy self-distillation relies on hand-designed privileged information. We observe that the MoE architecture itself offers a way to resolve this dilemma, as increasing the activation budget per token exposes latent expert capacity and yields a potentially stronger teacher within the model. However, naive expansion degrades performance because newly co-activated experts are not optimized to work together. We therefore propose MoEvolve, a bidirectional distillation framework following a recovery-then-improvement strategy: we first restore the activation-expanded high-$k$ model and further strengthen it by exploiting its additional active capacity, then reverse the direction of distillation to transfer the enhanced capabilities back into the original low-$k$ configuration, retaining its inference-time activation budget. Across diverse MoE models and benchmarks, MoEvolve improves the initial models by up to $22.2$ domain-average points and outperforms same-budget RLVR baselines by up to $6.5$ points. Notably, the final low-$k$ models often surpass their activation-expanded teachers.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) gives mixture-of-experts (MoE) LLMs only sparse feedback, while on-policy distillation gives dense feedback but needs a stronger teacher model. `MoEvolve` builds that teacher from the model itself by activating more experts per token, first recovering and strengthening this expanded configuration and then distilling it back into the original, cheaper configuration. Across several MoE models and benchmarks, it improves the starting models by up to **22.2 domain-average points** and beats RLVR baselines with the same compute budget by up to 6.5 points. The final models often surpass the expanded teachers they were distilled from.

papers.title: LangNCO: Compiling Natural-Language Constraints into Inference-Time Interventions for Neural Combinatorial Optimization
papers.abstract: Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) rapidly produces high-quality solutions for problem structures encountered during training, but operational requirements may change after deployment and be communicated in natural language. We propose LangNCO, a framework that compiles instance-specific requirements into structured inference-time interventions for a frozen NCO solver, without changing the pretrained policy's architecture, learned input representation, or parameters. A pretrained LLM serves as a replaceable semantic front end, translating each requirement into a schema-validated domain-specific language (DSL) rule set. A deterministic Rule Executor applies the rules as nonexpansive hard action masks. Because local masking prevents immediate violations but does not ensure that a complete feasible continuation remains reachable, Critical-Offset Decoding extracts rule-referenced critical nodes and reallocates part of a fixed rollout budget to multi-strength biased rollouts. Using controlled task-specific language to isolate solver adaptation from open-ended language robustness, we evaluate a CVRP policy on road closures, time windows, vehicle assignments, visit-order requirements, all pairwise combinations, and twelve additional constraint types. LangNCO achieves 100% feasibility on the four primary datasets with mean reference gaps of 1.63--3.26%, 97.33--100% feasibility when separately generated rules are composed for pairwise constraints, and 98.67% feasibility across the additional constraints. These results demonstrate modular post-training adaptation of a frozen NCO solver through inspectable language-derived rules, without retraining.
papers.summary: Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) solvers quickly solve the kinds of problems they were trained on, but they cannot easily handle new requirements stated in natural language after deployment. `LangNCO` uses an LLM to translate each requirement into schema-validated rules in a domain-specific language. A deterministic executor then applies those rules as hard action masks on a frozen solver, with no retraining. Because masking alone can lead the solver into dead ends, `Critical-Offset Decoding` spends part of the rollout budget on rollouts biased toward nodes the rules depend on. On a capacitated vehicle routing (`CVRP`) policy, it achieves **100% feasibility on the four primary constraint datasets** with mean reference gaps of 1.63–3.26%, plus 97.33–100% feasibility on pairwise constraint combinations and 98.67% on twelve additional constraint types.

papers.title: Proportionality in Ranking Compression
papers.abstract: Motivated by applications in reinforcement learning from human feedback, we consider a setting where a given collection of rankings needs to be compressed into a smaller collection of rankings. This can also be seen as a combination of two fundamental social choice frameworks: ranking aggregation and multiwinner voting. We propose three proportionality notions that capture different types of representation in this setting: positional proportionality, pairwise proportionality, and proportionality for solid coalitions (PSC). On the one hand, we show that positional proportionality and PSC are always satisfiable for any input rankings and target compression size, and a desired output can be found in polynomial time. On the other hand, we prove that pairwise proportionality cannot be satisfied in general, but can nevertheless be attained when the input rankings are single-peaked or single-crossing.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning from human feedback raises the problem of compressing many rankings into a smaller, representative set, which combines ranking aggregation with multiwinner voting. The authors define three proportionality notions for this setting: positional proportionality, pairwise proportionality, and proportionality for solid coalitions (PSC). They prove that **positional proportionality and PSC can always be satisfied in polynomial time** for any input and target size. Pairwise proportionality cannot be guaranteed in general, but it can be achieved when the input rankings are single-peaked or single-crossing.

papers.title: Non-Parametric Optimization for Scalable Learning in Stochastic Decision Problems
papers.abstract: Stochastic optimization (SO) plays a central role in decision-making under uncertainty. Among SO problems, time-varying stochastic optimization (TV-SO) is particularly important due to its applications in adaptive control and machine learning. Non-parametric approaches have been proposed for time-varying deterministic optimization; however, they have not been developed for their stochastic counterparts. This work addresses that gap by developing a stochastic variational framework based on Malliavin calculus. This framework yields non-parametric optimality conditions for SO problems with stochastic decisions and supports the design of a scalable deep-learning algorithm that is insensitive to the parameterization dimension. This algorithm, called the Stochastic Path Follower (SPF), is applied to two important problems under distribution drift, namely least-squares recovery and logistic regression. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art learning-based and gradient-based methods in both performance and scalability.
papers.summary: Non-parametric methods exist for time-varying deterministic optimization but not for its stochastic counterpart, which matters for adaptive control and machine learning under distribution drift. The authors build a stochastic variational framework based on Malliavin calculus that gives non-parametric optimality conditions for problems with stochastic decisions. From it they derive the `Stochastic Path Follower` (`SPF`), a deep-learning algorithm whose performance does not depend on the size of the parameterization. On least-squares recovery and logistic regression under distribution drift, `SPF` **outperforms state-of-the-art learning-based and gradient-based methods** in both accuracy and scalability.

papers.title: MAS-Bai: Linguistically Informed Adaptive Multi-Agent Translation for Bowen-Script Bai
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) remain unreliable for extremely low-resource languages whose writing systems conflict with high-resource pretraining priors. We study Bai-Chinese translation in the Bowen script, where Chinese characters are frequently borrowed phonetically rather than semantically, causing severe literal-translation hallucinations. We propose MAS-Bai, a linguistically informed adaptive multi-agent framework for Bowen-script Bai-Chinese translation. MAS-Bai routes each input through either a lightweight retrieval-translation path or a deeper philological path with etymological and syntactic agents, and uses cycle-consistency with a lightweight reverse translator as an inference-time reliability signal. We construct a 6,536-sentence Bai-Chinese corpus and evaluate on a 1,536-sentence test set. MAS-Bai achieves 16.23 BLEU and 62.15 COMET, improving over Standard RAG by 8.11 BLEU and 6.85 COMET. Forward LoRA, expert ablations and controlled routing experiments distinguish the roles of supervised adaptation, Bai-specific expertise and conditional routing. The largest gains occur on Bowen phonetic loans and divergent Bai word order, while human evaluation and reverse-verifier analyses support the automatic results.
authors: School of Computer Science and Technology
School of Computer Science and Technology
School of Computer Science and Technology
School of Computer Science and Technology

papers.summary: Large language models tend to translate Bowen-script Bai literally and hallucinate, because the script often borrows Chinese characters for their sound rather than their meaning. `MAS-Bai` is a multi-agent framework that sends each sentence down one of two paths: a lightweight retrieval-and-translation path, or a deeper philological path that adds etymological and syntactic agents. A small reverse translator checks cycle-consistency at inference time as a reliability signal. On a new 6,536-sentence Bai-Chinese corpus, it reaches 16.23 BLEU and 62.15 COMET, **improving on `Standard RAG` by 8.11 BLEU**, with the largest gains on phonetic loans and divergent Bai word order.

papers.title: Process Reward Modeling with Reliability- and Conservatism-Aware Bayesian Belief
papers.abstract: Process Reward Models (PRMs) play a central role in test-time scaling for large language model (LLM) reasoning. However, PRMs may provide inaccurate process rewards for test-time scaling, which we identify as arising from two sources of uncertainty: (1) \textit{PRM uncertainty} that arises from insufficient supervision data and imperfect PRM training; and (2) \textit{policy uncertainty} that results from the mismatch between the policy to collect supervision data and the policy for test-time scaling, leading to systematic reward overestimation. Previous studies fail to jointly consider both uncertainties. To bridge this gap, we propose BayesianPRM, which treats the process reward as a random variable within a reward hypothesis space and maintains a Bayesian belief over it. Since exact Bayesian inference over the continuous hypothesis space is generally intractable, we discretize the reward hypothesis space with a reward ensemble and introduce two complementary belief updates, each targeting one source of uncertainty: (1) to address PRM uncertainty, we introduce \textit{reliability-aware belief updating} that measures how well each ensemble member explains the supervision data and updates the belief with an amortized belief network optimized by the evidence lower bound (ELBO); and (2) to tackle policy uncertainty, we propose \textit{conservatism-aware belief calibration} which further reweights the belief toward lower rewards to suppress overestimation. These two updates yield a reliability- and conservatism-aware Bayesian belief, whose expectation determines the process reward. Experiments on multimodal reasoning benchmarks indicate that BayesianPRM consistently yields more accurate process reward estimates while enhancing test-time scaling performance.
papers.summary: Process Reward Models (PRMs) guide test-time scaling for LLM reasoning, but their step-level rewards can be wrong for two reasons. Limited supervision and imperfect training make the PRM itself uncertain, and a mismatch between the data-collection policy and the inference policy causes systematic overestimation. `BayesianPRM` treats each process reward as a random variable and keeps a Bayesian belief over a reward ensemble. A reliability-aware update, learned by an amortized belief network trained on the evidence lower bound (ELBO), handles the first source, and a conservatism-aware calibration shifts the belief toward lower rewards to handle the second. On multimodal reasoning benchmarks it **produces more accurate process rewards and better test-time scaling performance**.

papers.title: ReLaDrift: Recurrent Language Generation via Drifting for Test-Time Scaling
papers.abstract: Drifting Models generate a sample with a single function evaluation, making them attractive for fast parallel language generation, but their one-step formulation does not support iterative refinement. We propose Recurrent Language Generation via Drifting (ReLaDrift), which uses a shared Drifting Model to generate an initial draft from noise and iteratively refine it in a continuous latent space. We train this recurrence by sampling the number of rounds and applying the drifting loss only at the final round, stopping gradients through preceding rounds so that only one round requires backpropagation. Unlike the one-step Drifting Model, whose accuracy does not improve when iterated, ReLaDrift enables a trade-off between test-time computation and generation quality, as diffusion and flow language models do. On Sudoku Hard and GSM8K, it achieves competitive or superior performance compared with these iterative-generation approaches across a range of inference budgets. Our code is available at https://github.com/Yuki-Ots/ReLaDrift
papers.summary: Drifting Models generate text in a single function evaluation, which makes them fast, but they cannot refine their output iteratively. `ReLaDrift` reuses one shared Drifting Model to draft from noise and then refine the draft in a continuous latent space over several rounds. During training it applies the drifting loss only at the final round and stops gradients through the earlier rounds, so only one round needs backpropagation.
