This lets it **trade test-time compute for quality, as diffusion and flow language models do**, and it matches or beats those approaches on `Sudoku Hard` and `GSM8K` across a range of inference budgets.

papers.title: Characterising and Analysing Retrieval-Augmented Generation Techniques
papers.abstract: The advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) across many application domains has increased the need for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to reduce hallucinations and improve LLM performance. Thus far, several RAG techniques with impressive features and capabilities have been proposed in the literature, making it a herculean task to select the most appropriate RAG techniques for specific problem scenarios. Thus, we propose a conceptual framework comprising main dimensions and sub-dimensions for characterising (defining "what it is") and analysing (defining "how well it does") existing RAG techniques. The conceptual framework was developed through a qualitative analysis of the attributes of RAG techniques reported in the literature. It can serve as a pre-empirical filtering mechanism for researchers and practitioners in selecting the highest-fit RAG candidates that meet specific user and task requirements before empirical benchmarking of RAG techniques, which can be computationally and financially expensive.
papers.summary: Many Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) techniques have been proposed, which makes it hard to pick the right one for a given problem. Drawing on a qualitative analysis of attributes reported in the literature, the authors propose a conceptual framework of dimensions and sub-dimensions for characterising what a RAG technique is and analysing how well it performs. The framework is meant as a **pre-empirical filter that narrows down RAG candidates before expensive benchmarking**.

papers.title: MultiAgent-OPD: End-to-End Training of Hierarchical Multi-Agent Systems with On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: In a hierarchical multi-agent system, a Leader assigns tasks and subagents carry them out. Jointly training the Leader and the subagents is difficult because a final answer gives only indirect feedback to the subagents. An LLM judge can score the performance of the subagents, but these scores depend on the judge's own assessment of the quality of subagents' responses. We present MultiAgent-OPD, which combines on-policy distillation with reinforcement learning to jointly train a shared-parameter Leader-Searcher-Answerer team end to end. We first train a Teacher in a Searcher-Answerer workflow using answer correctness. During team training, the frozen Teacher scores student-generated search and summary tokens to provide local process supervision for the Searchers, while the Leader learns from team success and the Answerer from candidate correctness. Across seven datasets, the trained system reaches 38.68% macro avg@4, exceeding Prompted Critic by 4.06 percentage points and C-MAS + RL, the trained cascaded multiagent system, by 2.61 percentage points. The team also solves more questions within four attempts.
papers.summary: Training a hierarchical multi-agent system end to end is hard, because the final answer gives subagents only indirect feedback and scores from an LLM judge depend on the judge's own biases. `MultiAgent-OPD` combines on-policy distillation with reinforcement learning to jointly train a shared-parameter Leader-Searcher-Answerer team. A frozen Teacher, first trained in a Searcher-Answerer workflow, scores the Searchers' search and summary tokens to give them local process supervision. The Leader learns from team success and the Answerer from candidate correctness. Across seven datasets the team reaches **38.68% macro avg@4, beating `Prompted Critic` by 4.06 points and the trained cascaded system `C-MAS + RL` by 2.61 points**.

papers.title: Response-Informed Value Estimation for Cost-Aware Multi-Turn LLM Routing
papers.abstract: Multi-turn LLM routing selects a model at every turn before its response is available, yet task success is revealed only when the interaction ends, leaving each intermediate choice without a label of its own. Logged trajectories, however, retain the response each call produced, which exposes what each turn required and how well the chosen model served it, evidence that outcomes alone hide. We introduce RIVET (Response-Informed Value Estimation for Turn-Level Routing), which exploits this post-call evidence during training while keeping routing strictly pre-call at deployment. RIVET jointly trains two value estimators over a shared state-model representation: a deployable Routing Value Estimator that scores candidate models from pre-call information, and a training-only Response-Informed Value Estimator that additionally observes the realized response. Conditioning on the response turns response-induced return variation from residual noise into an observed covariate, and we show that this reduces the leading asymptotic estimation error of the shared representation. On the MINT benchmark, RIVET solves more held-out tasks than the strongest multi-turn baseline while using 74.7% less total call cost.
papers.summary: In multi-turn LLM routing, a model must be chosen at every turn before its response is seen, and only the final task outcome provides a label. `RIVET` (Response-Informed Value Estimation for Turn-Level Routing) jointly trains two value estimators over a shared representation. One is a deployable router that scores candidate models from pre-call information only; the other is a training-only estimator that also sees the realized response. Conditioning on the response turns response-driven variation in returns from noise into an observed variable, which the authors prove reduces estimation error for the shared representation. On the `MINT` benchmark, RIVET solves more held-out tasks than the strongest multi-turn baseline while **cutting total call cost by 74.7%**.

papers.title: Anisotropic Representation Dynamics in Transformers
papers.abstract: Small differences between internal representations can shrink or grow as they pass through a Transformer layer, affecting how information is preserved and how sensitive the model is to perturbations. Yet it remains unclear when changes in attention weights can turn a representation difference that would otherwise shrink into one that grows. We develop a \textbf{Mixture-Gated Theory of Anisotropic Representation Dynamics} that separates self-attention into value transport, query gating, and key gating. Our analysis reveals how the geometry of attended representations constrains gating and how interactions between these mechanisms can reverse contraction induced by value transport. We formalize this phenomenon as gating-induced regime switching, where a representation difference contracts under fixed attention routing but expands under full attention. We derive a necessary and sufficient spectral criterion that certifies the existence or absence of switching and identifies switching directions without exhaustive search. Beyond existence, our theory characterizes maximum relative switching strength, certifies the severity of contraction that gating can overcome, and determines the largest dimension of a subspace in which every nonzero direction switches. Experiments across four Transformer architectures validate these predictions through analytical and finite-forward comparisons, revealing distinct and joint query--key gating mechanisms and nontrivial switching subspaces. Our results provide a mechanistic and spectral understanding of how attention routing can alter local representation dynamics.
papers.summary: Small differences between internal representations can shrink or grow as they pass through a Transformer layer, and it is unclear when changes in attention weights flip a shrinking difference into a growing one. The authors develop a mixture-gated theory that splits self-attention into value transport, query gating, and key gating. They formalize gating-induced regime switching, where a difference contracts under fixed attention routing but expands under full attention, and derive a **necessary and sufficient spectral criterion that certifies whether switching occurs and identifies the directions in which it does**. Experiments on four Transformer architectures confirm the predictions and reveal nontrivial switching subspaces.

papers.title: MGE-PO: Entropy-Aware Credit Assignment for Mathematical Reasoning
papers.abstract: GRPO assigns the same group-relative advantage to equally rewarded responses within a question, leaving their generation uncertainty unused. We introduce MGE-PO, centered on four-quadrant (4Q) advantage shaping that combines verified correctness with rollout generation entropy. Correctness determines the sign of an additional correction, while entropy controls its magnitude: lower-entropy successes receive larger bonuses and higher-entropy failures receive larger penalties. An online entropy-based question curriculum supports this credit rule using cached rollout measurements. At the final checkpoint after eight training epochs on Qwen3-8B-Base, adding 4Q across three policy optimization settings yields absolute gains of 3.23-3.69% in six-benchmark macro avg@32 and 4.24-11.06% in macro pass@32. On Qwen2.5-7B-Base, the complete configuration raises four-benchmark macro avg@32 from 41.5% to 45.4%.
papers.summary: Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`) gives every equally rewarded response to a question the same advantage, ignoring how uncertain each generation was. `MGE-PO` adds four-quadrant advantage shaping in which correctness sets the sign of a correction and rollout entropy sets its size: confident successes get larger bonuses and uncertain failures get larger penalties. An online entropy-based question curriculum supports this. On `Qwen3-8B-Base`, adding the shaping across three policy optimization settings yields **gains of 3.23-3.69 points in six-benchmark macro avg@32** and 4.24-11.06 points in pass@32.

papers.title: Think More or Read More? A Token-Budget Theory of Reasoning with Shared Context
papers.abstract: Reasoning systems increasingly improve answers by incorporating additional context into the model's input, from multi-agent debate, where agents read their peers' responses, to self-refinement, where a model revisits its own drafts. In these systems, communication consumes context as one agent's output becomes another's input. We study the regime where token reading and generation draw on one fixed token window, so every token spent reading is a token that cannot be spent reasoning. We develop a \textbf{token-budget theory} that formalizes this trade-off, modeling accuracy as a function of the reasoning budget remaining after reading and aggregating votes with a Condorcet jury model that permits correlated errors. For multi-agent debate, the theory gives a closed-form prediction for the optimal number of agents. This quantity is estimated from single-agent measurements, allowing the optimal group size to be determined without running debate, and the same accounting extends to a heterogeneous set of different models. We empirically verify our theory and show that, at the predicted group size, our method outperforms strong baselines under the tightest calibration spend, where debate-calibrated rules can afford only one or two questions. Self-refinement obeys the same accounting, with its own draft in place of a peer message. The theory further predicts that communication pays only when the gain in the accuracy ceiling exceeds the reasoning room spent on reading, with this condition tightening as the window shrinks. Across five open models and four reasoning tasks, self-consistency matches or beats deployed debate at $93$\% of $980$ matched window-and-group-size settings, with the gap being largest under tight windows and nearly disappearing at a loose one, consistent with the theory. Under a shared window, how much room a model has left to \textit{think matters more than what it reads}.
papers.summary: When multi-agent debate or self-refinement feeds one model's output into another's input, every token spent reading comes out of the same fixed window that could otherwise be spent reasoning. A token-budget theory models accuracy as a function of the reasoning budget left after reading, combined with a Condorcet jury model that allows correlated errors. From single-agent measurements alone it gives a closed-form prediction of the optimal number of debate agents. Across five open models and four reasoning tasks, **plain self-consistency matches or beats debate in 93% of 980 matched settings**, with the largest gap under tight context windows.

papers.title: Can the Parts Fool the Test? Counterfactual Pairing Cycles for Relational OOD
papers.abstract: Relational out-of-distribution errors are easy to describe and hard to evaluate cleanly. An image may be natural, a caption may be fluent, and all mentioned objects may be common, yet the caption may describe the wrong relation in the image. Many evaluations intended to test this behavior can be solved without checking the pairing at all, because negatives differ in caption style, template, length, object frequency, or image statistics. We propose counterfactual pairing cycles, a blocked evaluation primitive that reuses the same two images and the same two captions on both sides of the comparison, changing only which image is paired with which caption. This makes image-only, text-only, and additive component shortcuts cancel exactly in finite samples. The same contrast also gives a training loss for relational outlier exposure and a diagnostic for bilinear vision-language scores. Across synthetic controls, GQA, and COCO, cycles separate coarse image-caption matching from directional role-binding failures, while also identifying geometric size relations that remain strongly visible in global features. In a shortcut-contaminated COCO outlier-exposure stress test, a model selected by a near-perfect shortcut validation AUROC retains substantial relational signal but remains below cycle training on exact cycles; cycle training improves CycleAcc from 0.882 to 0.927. The main lesson is simple: to test whether a model understands a pairing, the benchmark should keep the parts fixed, change the pairing, and ask only about coupling. The official implementation is available online.
papers.summary: Many benchmarks for relational understanding in vision-language models can be solved through shortcuts such as caption style, length, or image statistics, without checking whether the image and caption actually match. Counterfactual pairing cycles reuse the same two images and the same two captions on both sides of each comparison and change only which image goes with which caption. This makes image-only, text-only, and additive shortcuts cancel exactly, and the same contrast doubles as a training loss for relational outlier exposure. Across synthetic controls, `GQA`, and `COCO`, cycles separate coarse matching from directional role-binding failures, and **cycle training improves CycleAcc from 0.882 to 0.927** in a shortcut-contaminated stress test.

papers.title: Who Pays for Efficient Inference? Confidence-Based Small-to-Large LLM Routing Across Tasks and Languages
papers.abstract: Small-to-large language model routing can reduce inference cost by escalating difficult inputs while retaining easier ones on a smaller model. Its success, however, depends on identifying examples that benefit from escalation, and the reliability of confidence across multilingual tasks remains unclear. We present a systematic evaluation of confidence-based routing across three model families, four languages, and three task types, covering 72 model, dataset, language, and scale configurations and 42,288 predictions. We compare global confidence routing with random routing, equal-quota confidence routing, and an oracle upper bound. Confidence identifies beneficial escalations on the Belebele reading comprehension and SIB-200 topic classification datasets, with mean correction-detection AUCs of 0.612 and 0.705. At 50% escalation, it improves over random routing by 1.40--4.67 percentage points on Belebele and 2.54--5.63 points on SIB-200. In contrast, the mean AUC on the MMLU-ProX-Lite knowledge and reasoning dataset is only 0.510, and routing provides no consistent improvement over random selection because small models often remain highly confident while incorrect. Global confidence routing also creates language escalation gaps up to 30.33 percentage points, whereas equal-quota routing removes this disparity with little aggregate accuracy cost. These results show that confidence routing is task-dependent and can allocate computation unevenly across languages. Code is available at https://github.com/sabbir5622r/multilingual-llm-routing
papers.summary: Small-to-large routing saves inference cost by escalating only hard inputs to a larger model, but it is unclear how reliable confidence is as a routing signal across languages and tasks. A systematic study covers 72 configurations spanning three model families, four languages, and three task types, totalling 42,288 predictions. Confidence routing helps on `Belebele` and `SIB-200`, beating random routing by up to 5.63 points at 50% escalation, but **on `MMLU-ProX-Lite` it is no better than random because small models stay confident while wrong**. Global confidence routing also creates language escalation gaps of up to 30.33 points, which equal-quota routing removes at little accuracy cost.

papers.title: FLARE: Physics-Grounded Evaluation of Language-Model Agents for Feeder Restoration with Degraded Observations
papers.abstract: Restoring service after distribution-grid faults requires decisions from incomplete and conflicting information while respecting electrical constraints. Addressing this need, we introduce FLARE (Feeder-Level Agent Restoration Evaluation), a physics-grounded benchmark for post-isolation feeder restoration. FLARE con- tains 800 AC-feasible cases across five observation settings and allows agents to gather evidence, evaluate switches, and perform restoration actions under fixed operational limits. We evaluate five instruction-tuned models over 78,750 episodes, including topology, distributed-generation, and loading shifts. Mean normalized regret ranges from 0.082 to 0.148. Although every model has zero median regret, P95 regret ranges from 0.814 to 1.000, revealing an important failure tail. Shadow replay shows that 96.4% of 15,706 guard-rejected actions would have caused a physical violation. FLARE enables reproducible evaluation of language-model based restoration support while emphasizing the need for external safety checks.
papers.summary: Restoring power after distribution-grid faults means making decisions from incomplete and conflicting information while respecting electrical constraints. `FLARE` (Feeder-Level Agent Restoration Evaluation) is a physics-grounded benchmark of 800 AC-feasible cases across five observation settings, in which language-model agents gather evidence, evaluate switches, and act. Across 78,750 episodes with five instruction-tuned models, median regret is zero, but **95th-percentile regret ranges from 0.814 to 1.000**, exposing a heavy failure tail. Replaying the actions the safety guard rejected shows that 96.4% would have caused a physical violation.

papers.title: Ignored, Not Refused: What Low Prompt-Injection Success Rates Hide in Small Tool-Using Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-using agents read untrusted external content, which exposes them to indirect prompt injection (IPI), where hidden instructions hijack the agent's tool calls. Benchmarks measure IPI security by the attack success rate (ASR), which treats every failed attack as a successful defense. To test this assumption, we audit 33,000 trajectories from eleven open-weight agents (2-14B parameters) on InjecAgent and AgentDojo. A label-blind LLM judge shows that most failed attacks are ignored (76-80%) rather than refused (17-18%). With identical model weights, changing only the system prompt shifts InjecAgent ASR from 0.2% to 43%. Our Attack-Task Outcome Matrix (ATOM) further shows that in 21.7% of AgentDojo episodes, the agent stayed safe but did not complete the user's task. A low ASR therefore mostly reflects agents silently ignoring injections, not refusing them. Evaluations should report how attacks fail and whether the user's task is completed, alongside ASR. We release the labeled corpus, judge prompt, and analysis code.
papers.summary: Indirect prompt injection (IPI) benchmarks score security by attack success rate (ASR), which counts every failed attack as a successful defense. An audit of 33,000 trajectories from eleven open-weight agents (2-14B parameters) on `InjecAgent` and `AgentDojo` finds that **76-80% of failed attacks were simply ignored, and only 17-18% were refused**. Changing only the system prompt moved `InjecAgent` ASR from 0.2% to 43%, and in 21.7% of `AgentDojo` episodes the agent stayed safe but did not complete the user's task. The authors argue that evaluations should report how attacks fail and whether the task gets done, and they release their labeled corpus and judge prompt.

papers.title: Sample, Mix, or Verify? Allocating Test-Time Compute under Imperfect Verifiers
papers.abstract: A common way to make language models and agents more accurate is to spend more compute at inference time: generate many candidate solutions and submit the one a verifier prefers. Success then requires that some candidate is correct and that the verifier picks it. The first grows predictably with the number of samples; the second does not, because real verifiers (unit tests, majority votes, LLM judges, reward models) accept wrong answers, reject right ones, and make correlated mistakes. With a fixed budget, a practitioner must decide how many samples to draw, which models to draw them from, and how much to spend on verification, and today these choices are made by rules of thumb. We introduce SPLIT, which makes them from a small labelled pilot. It rests on an exact formula for the probability of submitting a correct answer under accept/reject and top-score selection that accounts for varying task difficulty, blind spots shared across models, and correlated repeated verifier calls. SPLIT fits the formula by empirical Bayes and uses it to plan budgets on unseen tasks. Across seven benchmarks spanning math, science QA, code and software-engineering agents, 26 models, 175 agent systems and six kinds of real verifiers, all from public releases, SPLIT lands within 0.02-0.8 percentage points of the best allocation in hindsight, while every fixed rule we test loses at least 2.5 points in some setting. Regret depends only on how well SPLIT ranks configurations, and it stays near-optimal under compute, price and latency costs and online. The formula also explains when asking more LLM judges lowers precision. As a forecaster far beyond the pilot, SPLIT beats power-law fitting when the verifier caps success, and we report where it loses.
papers.summary: Best-of-n inference needs both a correct candidate and a verifier that picks it, but real verifiers such as unit tests, majority votes, LLM judges, and reward models make errors that are often correlated. `SPLIT` decides how many samples to draw, from which models, and how much to spend on verification, using a small labelled pilot set. It fits, by empirical Bayes, an exact formula for the probability of submitting a correct answer that accounts for varying task difficulty and shared blind spots. Across seven benchmarks including code and software-engineering agents, 26 models, and six kinds of verifiers, it **lands within 0.02-0.8 points of the best allocation in hindsight, while every fixed rule tested loses at least 2.5 points somewhere**.

papers.title: Reasoning Models Can Control Their Chains of Thought When They Tell Themselves To
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) controllability, the ability of reasoning models to control properties of their CoT, is consequential for both their usefulness and reliable oversight. Recent work evaluates this capability by measuring whether models follow CoT constraints given in the user prompt, and reports very low controllability across models. We argue that this low controllability may not reflect an inherent inability of reasoning models to control their CoT, but instead result from naively specifying constraints in the user prompt. To test this, we introduce Self-Instructed CoT Controllability: a complementary evaluation that places the constraint as a self-instruction inside the model's CoT and measures its ability to follow it. We show that, under self-instruction, models achieve significantly higher controllability than with standard user instructions. Even a generic reminder to follow the user's constraint substantially improves controllability. Moreover, effective self-instructions can be bootstrapped into the reasoning through a simple instruction in the user prompt, enabling improved control even without access to the reasoning channel. Finally, using self-instruction, we demonstrate in a realistic monitoring setup that CoT controllability can be leveraged for monitor evasion, posing a risk to CoT monitorability.
papers.summary: Earlier work found that reasoning models rarely follow user-specified constraints on their chain of thought (CoT). The authors argue that this reflects how the constraints were specified rather than an inability to control the CoT. They introduce Self-Instructed CoT Controllability, which places the constraint as a self-instruction inside the model's own reasoning, and show that **controllability rises substantially, even with a generic reminder**. Such self-instructions can be bootstrapped from the user prompt alone, and in a realistic monitoring setup this controllability can be used to evade CoT monitors.

papers.title: ADT: All-Atom Diffusion Tokenizer for 3D Molecular Structures
papers.abstract: Discrete structural tokenization provides a promising route to autoregressive 3D molecular generation. Yet, existing tokenizers face a trade-off between compact representation and all-atom reconstruction: atom-level tokens preserve atomic details but produce long sequences, while compact residue-level protein tokens typically omit side-chain geometry. To overcome this limitation, we propose All-atom Diffusion Tokenizer (ADT), which decouples token granularity from reconstruction resolution. ADT uses one structural token per atom for small molecules and one token per protein residue that jointly represents backbone and side-chain geometry. To mitigate geometric distortion introduced by quantization, we leverage the generative capacity of diffusion models to recover fine-grained atomic geometry beyond deterministic decoding from discrete tokens. Extensive experiments across small molecules and proteins demonstrate that ADT achieves strong reconstruction from compact discrete representations while enabling high-quality autoregressive generation of both small molecules and all-atom protein structures. These results establish compact structural tokens as an effective discrete interface for all-atom molecular reconstruction and generation.
papers.summary: Discrete tokenizers for autoregressive 3D molecular generation face a trade-off: atom-level tokens are detailed but long, while compact residue-level protein tokens usually drop side-chain geometry. `ADT` (All-atom Diffusion Tokenizer) separates token granularity from reconstruction resolution, using one token per atom for small molecules and one token per protein residue that encodes both backbone and side chain. A diffusion decoder recovers the fine atomic geometry that quantization loses. Experiments show **strong all-atom reconstruction from compact tokens** and high-quality autoregressive generation of both small molecules and proteins.

papers.title: Beyond Marginal Influence: Interaction-Aware Memory Selection for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM-agent memory selection often uses retrieval rankings based on record relevance or individual influence. Such rankings cannot identify sufficient subsets under redundant or jointly necessary evidence. We study per-decision memory sufficiency: selecting a small subset that preserves full-memory behavior. To separate search error from model error, we introduce JointCoreBench, a benchmark with nine interaction families, six workflow domains, natural-language decisions, and exact sufficient-set oracles, and JointCore, a relevance cost-ordered group-deletion baseline that tests blocks before individual records. On 6,912 exact conditions, cost-ordered JointCore recovers a minimum-cost sufficient set in 100.0% of cases, reduces subset evaluations from 30.00 to 11.13 (62.9%), and achieves 87.8% active-memory savings. Across four 12B-70B model families and 432 tasks per model, its unweighted mean is 10.28 versus 16.00 model queries and 50.6% versus 43.1% minimum-cost recovery relative to cost aware singleton deletion. Both methods preserve full-memory behavior under the deterministic primary interface. Tests with physical deletion, UNKNOWN masks, PENDING sentinels, counterfactual values, and alternative labels identify interface dependent behavior. JointCore is an efficient benchmark baseline; the study does not establish deployment-ready memory compression.
papers.summary: Agent memory retrieval usually ranks records by relevance or individual influence, which fails when evidence is redundant or only useful in combination. The authors study how to pick a small memory subset that preserves the agent's full-memory behavior. They introduce `JointCoreBench`, which has exact sufficient-set oracles, and `JointCore`, a baseline that tries deleting groups of records, ordered by relevance cost, before testing single records. On 6,912 exact conditions, JointCore **recovers a minimum-cost sufficient set in 100% of cases** while cutting subset evaluations by 62.9%. The authors stress that this does not establish deployment-ready memory compression.

papers.title: NestedVLA: Learning to Consolidate and Generate Skills for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models promise generalist robotic agents, yet consolidating skills learned across heterogeneous tasks and environments remains difficult: training data is fragmented across platforms, joint multi-task training suffers from interference, and model merging tends to introduce parameter conflicts or require architectural changes. We instead advocate a paradigm in which skills are first learned independently and then consolidated post hoc. To this end, we propose NestedVLA, which replaces parameter aggregation with parameter generation: a nested hypernetwork, conditioned on the target task, synthesizes task-adaptive action-expert parameters that compose with a frozen base VLA. Task-specific compressed VLM residuals are retained separately. This formulation enables flexible task-conditioned skill reuse while mitigating interference. Across three RL benchmarks (MetaWorld, ManiSkill, CALVIN), NestedVLA outperforms the strongest model-merging baseline by 41 pp on average, matches per-task fine-tuning within 1 pp on ManiSkill, and substantially closes the gap on CALVIN, pointing toward a storage-efficient route to skill consolidation. Code is available at https://github.com/WanyuGroup/NeurIPS2026-NestedVLA.
papers.summary: Consolidating skills learned across different tasks and robots into one Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model is hard: joint training suffers from interference, and model merging causes parameter conflicts. `NestedVLA` learns skills independently and then uses a nested hypernetwork, conditioned on the target task, to generate action-expert parameters that plug into a frozen base VLA. Across `MetaWorld`, `ManiSkill`, and `CALVIN`, it **outperforms the strongest model-merging baseline by 41 points on average** and comes within 1 point of per-task fine-tuning on `ManiSkill`.

papers.title: DeDiCa: A Scalable Deconfounding Discrete Causal Generative Model
papers.abstract: We introduce DeDiCa, a practical framework for efficient causal inference with discrete variables and hidden confounding that revisits classical probabilistic modeling through a tensorized parameterization of causal Bayesian networks, enabling tractable inference. Given a causal graph, DeDiCa is trained once on observational data by maximum likelihood, exactly marginalizing over hidden confounders, and can then estimate any (proxy-)identifiable interventional query. Despite this deliberately simple parameterization, DeDiCa matches state-of-the-art neural causal generative models in ATE estimation, while supporting memory-efficient CPU training and exact interventional inference in milliseconds. Compared with causal foundation models, DeDiCa scales more effectively with additional observational samples and achieves competitive accuracy at substantially lower inference time and memory. DeDiCa provides a tractable, accurate, and scalable approach to causal inference in discrete settings with hidden confounding.
papers.summary: `DeDiCa` is a framework for causal inference over discrete variables with hidden confounders, built on a tensorized parameterization of causal Bayesian networks that keeps inference tractable. Given a causal graph, it is trained once by maximum likelihood on observational data, marginalizing exactly over the hidden confounders, and can then answer any identifiable interventional query. It **matches state-of-the-art neural causal generative models at average treatment effect (ATE) estimation** while training on a CPU and answering queries in milliseconds, and it scales better with more data than causal foundation models.

papers.title: Verbalising Model's Computation for Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness Detection
papers.abstract: Current Chain-of-Thought (CoT) verification methods detect reasoning faithfulness from model outputs or static activations, but are limited in explaining how unfaithfulness develops during generation. We introduce VERITAS to verbalise the model's computation: how different reasoning anchors emerge, transfer across layers, and surface in the output. VERITAS adopts the layer-wise Jacobian projection to produce a verbalised account of the model's internal reasoning evolution at each generated CoT token. By training a classifier on the extracted features along the traces, we show that these structured features provide insightful perspectives on how and where reasoning diverges toward unfaithfulness. Experiments on four datasets from FaithCoT-Bench and BonaFide show that VERITAS achieves a significant performance gain over LLM-as-Judge, with a 28.4% gain in balanced accuracy, and an average improvement of 16.0% over activation probing. Further analysis shows VERITAS can be generalised to different datasets and model architectures. Our work shows that verbalising model computation provides a richer and more interpretable lens on CoT faithfulness, moving beyond detection toward a mechanistic understanding of how reasoning fails.
papers.summary: Existing ways of checking whether a chain of thought (CoT) is faithful rely on model outputs or static activations and cannot explain how unfaithfulness develops during generation. `VERITAS` uses layer-wise Jacobian projections to produce, for each generated token, a verbal account of how reasoning anchors emerge and move across layers, and trains a classifier on the resulting features. On four datasets from `FaithCoT-Bench` and `BonaFide`, it **beats LLM-as-Judge by 28.4% in balanced accuracy** and activation probing by 16.0% on average, and it generalizes across datasets and architectures.

papers.title: Annotrace: A Workbench for Step-Level Annotation of Agent Traces
papers.abstract: Every study of why LLM agents fail begins by labelling traces by hand, and every such study builds its own throwaway tool. Observability platforms record agent traces but offer no structured labelling; annotation tools label text but have no notion of a step, a delegation or a tool call, leaving it unclear what the smallest unit of execution to label should be. Annotrace reads six trace formats, including OpenTelemetry GenAI, LangSmith and Langfuse, and turns each run into an ordered, nested list of steps. The annotator writes their own labelling codebook; a frontier model proposes a starting set from a sample of their own traces, answers first, and is asked exactly the questions the human is asked, making annotation a joint human-AI process. Annotrace measures agreement between any two annotators, human or AI. On a multi-agent question-answering corpus it reproduces a previous manual effort's 235 annotation units exactly, and two models labelling the same traces agree 91% of the time at $\kappa = 0.82$.
papers.summary: Studies of why LLM agents fail usually begin with hand-labelling traces, and each study tends to build its own throwaway tool. `Annotrace` is a workbench that reads six trace formats, including `OpenTelemetry GenAI`, `LangSmith` and `Langfuse`, and turns each run into an ordered, nested list of steps, delegations and tool calls. Annotators write their own labelling codebook. A frontier model proposes a starting codebook from sample traces and answers the same questions as the human, which makes annotation a joint human-AI process with built-in agreement measurement. On a multi-agent question-answering corpus, the tool exactly reproduces 235 annotation units from an earlier manual effort, and two models labelling the same traces agree **91% of the time (κ = 0.82)**.

papers.title: Data-Efficient Classifier Pretraining Through Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Machine learning with limited data is susceptible to overfitting, especially with modern deep neural networks. Prior to the introduction of AlexNet, reconstruction-based pretraining with auto-encoder and denoising auto-encoder were found to be beneficial, partially due to the limited size of the training sets at the time. Motivated by these traditional approaches, we propose DiffPT, a simple diffusion modeling approach to pretrain a given classifier backbone for limited domain-specific training data. We experiment on time-series data, standard natural-image benchmarks, and medical imaging datasets, and contrast the diffusion approach to a multitude of modern and traditional un/self-supervised methods. While contrastive pretraining performs better on CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet in low-data regimes, DiffPT is particularly effective on medical imaging and time-series tasks, where it outperforms self-supervised baselines across a range of low-data regimes. Our results suggest that DiffPT is a simple and effective approach for data-efficient classifier pretraining on different modalities.
papers.summary: Deep networks trained on small datasets tend to overfit, and before `AlexNet`, reconstruction-based pretraining with auto-encoders was a common remedy. `DiffPT` brings this idea back by using diffusion modelling to pretrain a classifier backbone on limited domain-specific data. It is compared against many modern and traditional unsupervised and self-supervised methods on time-series, natural-image and medical imaging data. Contrastive pretraining still wins on `CIFAR-10` and `Tiny ImageNet` in low-data settings, but **`DiffPT` outperforms self-supervised baselines on medical imaging and time-series tasks** across a range of low-data regimes.

papers.title: Distributed Performance Boosting through Neural Control for Plug-and-Play Networks
papers.abstract: We address the problem of improving the performance of pre-stabilized networked systems subject to plug-and-play (PnP) operations, namely additions or removals of subsystems. While distributed baseline controllers can preserve stability after a PnP transition, augmenting them with expressive neural policies can invalidate the formal stability guarantees. To overcome this issue, we build on recently proposed Performance Boosting controllers based on the Internal Model Control (IMC) principle, which reduce closed-loop stability to a finite $\ell_2$-gain requirement on an auxiliary operator. In the distributed setting, this operator is formed by interconnecting local neural operators that exchange information only between neighboring subsystems. We then derive free parametrizations of this interconnection, namely explicit maps from unconstrained trainable variables to interconnected neural operators satisfying a prescribed network gain bound for every parameter value. The obtained distributed neural controller can therefore be trained by unconstrained gradient-based optimization without stability constraints or projection steps, while retaining the prescribed gain bound at every training iterate. We develop two complementary parametrizations. A neighbor-based compositional parametrization uses local coupling bounds, so that after a PnP event only subsystems whose bounds change need to update their gain parameters. A network-norm parametrization instead uses a bound on the overall coupling matrix and can reduce conservatism, at the price of requiring network-wide information. A PnP DC-microgrid case study shows that the proposed neural layer improves voltage transients under topology changes and load variations while preserving nominal closed-loop stability.
papers.summary: Adding expressive neural policies to networked control systems can break the formal stability guarantees of their distributed baseline controllers, especially when subsystems are added or removed (plug-and-play operations). The authors build on Performance Boosting controllers based on Internal Model Control, which reduce closed-loop stability to a finite gain bound on an auxiliary operator made of interconnected local neural operators. They derive free parametrizations that satisfy the network gain bound for every parameter value, so the controller can be trained with unconstrained gradient descent while **staying stable at every training iterate**. They offer a neighbor-based variant that needs only local updates after a topology change and a less conservative network-norm variant that needs network-wide information. A DC-microgrid case study shows improved voltage transients under topology and load changes.

papers.title: The Optimal Ranking Tradeoffs Between Two Ranking Scores in Two-Class Classification
papers.abstract: The accuracy, true negative rate (negative class recall), true positive rate (positive class recall), negative predictive value (negative class precision), positive predictive value (positive class precision), class-specific intersections over unions, class-specific F-scores, Cohen's kappa, and balanced accuracy are scores that one intuitively wants to maximize when developing machine learning methods. However, they lead to different rankings of such methods. So, how can we establish a ranking that is an optimal tradeoff between any pair of these scores? It turns out that all these scores are special cases of ranking scores: a continuum of scores parameterized by the relative importance values assigned to the true negative, false positive, false negative, and true positive outcomes. Since all these scores are known to induce meaningful rankings, we seek the optimal tradeoffs among them. We consider the tradeoff between two scores to be optimal when it minimizes the Fr\'echet variance regarding the Kendall distance (also known as the bubble-sort distance) between rankings. For any given set of classifiers to rank, the optimal tradeoff lies at the center of the shortest (geodesic) path on the manifold of all rankings induced by the ranking scores. However, in the parameter space of the ranking scores, it is rarely achieved by averaging the importance values corresponding to the initial scores. In this paper, we present an exact analytical solution for determining a ranking score that is an optimal tradeoff for any given pair of initial scores, in the common case where the class priors are the same for all compared performances. We also experimentally investigate what happens when performance follows some distributions with fixed priors.
papers.summary: Common two-class metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, F-scores, Cohen's kappa and balanced accuracy often rank the same classifiers differently. All of them are special cases of a continuous family of ranking scores, parameterized by the importance assigned to each of the four confusion-matrix outcomes. The paper defines the optimal tradeoff between two such scores as the one that minimizes the Fréchet variance under Kendall (bubble-sort) distance between rankings, and shows that this tradeoff rarely corresponds to averaging the two scores' parameters. It gives **an exact analytical solution for the optimal tradeoff score** when class priors are fixed, and experimentally examines how performances behave under fixed-prior distributions.

papers.title: Learning angles for quantum approximate optimization
papers.abstract: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) and its variants are leading algorithms to help solve challenging combinatorial optimization problems. QAOA maps these problems to Ising Hamiltonians such that their ground state is the desired solution. Candidate solutions are then drawn from a variational quantum circuit. The performance of QAOA hinges on a set of variational angles. However, finding good angles is an instance-specific and computationally expensive non-convex classical optimization task. Here, we learn the mapping from the problem instance to high-quality QAOA angles. Our learned models replace the per-instance optimization, that we call the solver, with a single forward pass that is several orders of magnitude faster than the solver with a near identical quality. Our models further generalize to unseen topologies such as Barab\'asi-Albert and 2D grid graphs. Experiments on quantum hardware confirm that QAOA samples with angles produced by our open-source models are indistinguishable from solver angles. Crucially, models sensitive to the topology of the problem instance increase the quality of the QAOA angles. Our work amortizes a major bottleneck in QAOA by an up-front data generation and training cost. Importantly, this cost can be amortized over time in settings where many similar problems are optimized on a regular basis, as is often the case in applications for industry.
papers.summary: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (`QAOA`) depends on variational angles that normally come from an expensive, instance-specific, non-convex classical optimization. The authors train models that map a problem instance directly to high-quality `QAOA` angles, replacing per-instance optimization with a single forward pass that is **several orders of magnitude faster with near-identical quality**. The models generalize to unseen graph topologies such as Barabási-Albert and 2D grids, and topology-aware models produce better angles. Experiments on real quantum hardware show that samples drawn with the learned angles cannot be distinguished from those drawn with solver angles.

papers.title: How the elastic axis folds the transonic flutter boundary: shock energy transfer and conformally calibrated active learning
papers.abstract: Isogai's case A, a pitch-plunge aerofoil whose elastic axis lies half a chord ahead of the leading edge, has a folded transonic flutter boundary in inviscid flow: near the bottom of the transonic dip several flutter speeds coexist at one Mach number. We map this boundary, and the family obtained by moving the elastic axis, with coupled unsteady Euler simulations, a Gaussian-process surrogate of the damping coefficient trained by batch active learning, and split conformal prediction on independent random simulations, which turns the surrogate into stability calls with a distribution-free error rate. Three failure modes of time-domain damping labels that leave no trace in the residuals are documented, and the half-degree mean incidence left by the common one-degree start is shown to raise the flutter speed at the dip by 2.8%, more than any numerical setting. With 80 simulations the learned case A boundary labels 64 of 65 independent runs correctly, and calibrated calls are wrong in at most 1.6% of cases. Over Mach number, elastic axis and flutter speed index, 193 simulations and 40 calibration runs show that the fold exists only for elastic axes more than about 0.4 chord ahead of the leading edge; it closes between 0.39 and 0.33 chord ahead, on two meshes. Chordwise energy budgets, closed against the solver loads and the growth rate within a few per cent, explain the boundary. The lower branch is crossed through the reduced frequency at unchanged shock phase. On the upper branch the shock is pinned at the trailing edge, and moving the elastic axis aft brings the pivot of the flutter mode towards the section, so that the damping of the supersonic surface falls faster than the residual shock input and the fold closes.
papers.summary: Isogai's case A, a pitch-plunge aerofoil, has a folded transonic flutter boundary in inviscid flow, meaning several flutter speeds coexist at a single Mach number. The authors map this boundary and its variants as the elastic axis moves, combining coupled unsteady Euler simulations, a Gaussian-process surrogate trained by batch active learning, and split conformal prediction for stability calls with distribution-free error rates. With 80 simulations, the learned boundary labels 64 of 65 independent runs correctly. They find that **the fold exists only when the elastic axis lies more than about 0.4 chord ahead of the leading edge**, and they explain this with chordwise energy budgets that track shock behaviour on each branch.

papers.title: Look, Reason, Draw a Region: Recursive Refinement for Spatial Context Prediction
papers.abstract: Spatial context prediction requires visual grounding and spatial reasoning to identify vacant regions relative to objects in a scene. Spatial relationships and physical constraints remain challenging for large vision-language models (VLMs). Recursive reasoning has demonstrated strong performance on discrete and abstract reasoning tasks, motivating its use for improving spatial context prediction in natural images. Weight sharing enables higher accuracy with a small trainable parameter count. We introduce Spatial-TRM, a compact recursive model with frozen vision-language features, a convex region decoder, and just 11.2M trainable parameters. This weight-tied reasoner supports six spatial relationships, three reference frames, and open-vocabulary anchor objects. On the RoboSpatial-Home benchmark, Spatial-TRM achieves 29.51% context accuracy, a gain of 9.02 percentage points (44.0% relative) over a separately trained single-step model with the same parameter count. Including the frozen encoders, the model has 877.8M total parameters, approximately $15\times$ fewer than the reported 13B size of RoboPoint. These results show that repeated refinement improves spatial context prediction from pretrained vision-language features at a fixed trainable parameter count on this benchmark.
papers.summary: Spatial context prediction, which means finding vacant regions defined relative to objects in a scene, remains hard for large vision-language models (VLMs). `Spatial-TRM` is a compact, weight-tied recursive reasoner built on frozen vision-language features. It uses a convex region decoder, has only 11.2M trainable parameters, and supports six spatial relations, three reference frames and open-vocabulary anchor objects. On `RoboSpatial-Home` it reaches 29.51% context accuracy, **9.02 percentage points (44% relative) above a single-step model with the same parameter count**, while using about 15× fewer total parameters than the 13B `RoboPoint`.

papers.title: SimOPD: Relational Knowledge Transfer for On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: A key challenge in on-policy distillation (OPD) is extracting effective supervision from teacher knowledge. Supervision from token probabilities may underutilize internal knowledge, while direct hidden-state matching forces the student to shift to the teacher's feature space and complicates cross-architecture transfer. Inspired by contrastive learning's use of relationships between instances, we propose \textbf{SimOPD} to transfer teacher internal knowledge through response similarities. Specifically, SimOPD uses paired memory banks of student-generated responses to extract supervision from the teacher's internal representations as similarity distributions. The student then matches these distributions within its own representation space, retaining representational freedom and removing the need for cross-model projection. Extensive experiments show that SimOPD improves the overall average over the strongest baselines by up to 2.6 and 3.1 percentage points in same- and cross-architecture settings.
papers.summary: In on-policy distillation, supervising the student only with teacher token probabilities may waste the teacher's internal knowledge. Directly matching hidden states, on the other hand, forces the student into the teacher's feature space and complicates transfer across architectures. `SimOPD`, inspired by contrastive learning, transfers relational knowledge instead: it builds paired memory banks of student-generated responses, extracts similarity distributions from the teacher's internal representations, and has the student match them within its own representation space. This removes the need for any cross-model projection and **improves the overall average over the strongest baselines by up to 2.6 and 3.1 percentage points** in same- and cross-architecture settings.

papers.title: Inferring L1 Backgrounds from L2 English with LLM Token Probabilities
papers.abstract: Native language identification (NLI) infers a non-native speaker's first language (L1) from their second language (L2) production. We investigate a token probability approach that scores each text sample as a continuation of a prompt prefix specifying a candidate L1, then predicts the candidate with the highest score. We evaluate our approach using Llama 3.1 8B and 70B on three datasets: TOEFL9, Write and Improve 2024, and BULATS-L1. We compare its performance with previous prompting-based classification approaches. Token-probability scoring substantially improves on direct classification, particularly with the 8B model, while the 70B model achieves state-of-the-art performance across all datasets. Our results indicate that pretrained LLMs' token probabilities contain information useful for distinguishing L1 backgrounds from L2 English production.
papers.summary: Native language identification (NLI) infers a writer's first language (L1) from text written in a second language (L2), here English. Instead of asking an LLM to classify directly, the method scores each text as a continuation of a prompt that names a candidate L1 and then picks the highest-scoring candidate. Tested with `Llama 3.1` 8B and 70B on `TOEFL9`, `Write and Improve 2024` and `BULATS-L1`, token-probability scoring clearly beats direct classification, especially for the 8B model, and **the 70B model achieves state-of-the-art results on all three datasets**.

papers.title: Self-Reflective Chain-of-Thought (SRCoT): Evidence-Based Text Generation via a Closed-Loop Retrieve--Reflect--Revise Pipeline on Edge LLMs
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent outputs that lack source support or conflict with local operational constraints. We introduce Self-Reflective Chain-of-Thought (SRCoT), a modular architecture that organizes generation as a closed Retrieve--Reflect--Revise loop. SRCoT separates environment state, persistent knowledge, accumulated experience, and short-term memory into provenance-labeled stores. BM25 retrieval supplies local context; subsequent passes expose intermediate drafts, missing-information markers, follow-up queries, and optional claim--evidence mappings. These artifacts inform retrieval, revision, clarification, or abstention decisions. We examine the architecture through qualitative, trace-based case studies in two fully synthetic settings: emergency medical services and Munich-Sim, an emergency-operations simulation. Local prototype runs on an Apple M4-family laptop with 128 GB memory illustrate source-labeled documentation, explicit gap marking, and structured dispatch-style outputs. The traces also reveal provenance-assignment errors, incomplete evidence coverage, and unsafe assumptions that remain possible despite prompting constraints. These cases demonstrate report-level inspectability and local execution, not comparative superiority, hallucination reduction, clinical validity, or operational safety. The architecture separates retrieval and control from the model interface, but behavior across different models remains to be evaluated. SRCoT is a research proof of concept requiring human review, with its principal contribution lying in an inspectable control procedure rather than a new model.
papers.summary: Self-Reflective Chain-of-Thought (`SRCoT`) is a modular architecture that runs LLM generation as a closed Retrieve-Reflect-Revise loop, so that outputs stay tied to sources and local constraints. It keeps environment state, persistent knowledge, accumulated experience and short-term memory in separate provenance-labelled stores, uses `BM25` retrieval, and exposes drafts, missing-information markers and follow-up queries to drive revision, clarification or abstention. Qualitative trace-based case studies in synthetic emergency-medical and emergency-operations settings run locally on an Apple M4-family laptop. The authors explicitly claim **inspectability and local execution, not hallucination reduction or safety**, and the traces still show provenance errors and unsafe assumptions.

papers.title: Untrained CNN and coefficient-space regularization for joint reconstruction in photoacoustic tomography
papers.abstract: The joint reconstruction of the initial pressure and spatially varying sound speed in photoacoustic tomography from boundary measurements is considered. A regularized data-driven framework is proposed in which the unknown fields are represented in finite-dimensional wavelet spaces and fixed nonlinear features generated by an untrained convolutional neural network (CNN) are used to reconstruct the initial-pressure coefficients through Tikhonov-regularized least squares. A learned coefficient-space prior is subsequently used to infer the squared sound-speed coefficients. Numerical experiments demonstrate accurate reconstruction on held-out data and strong generalization to previously unseen phantom geometries. The frozen reconstruction map also remains stable under measurement noise not represented during training, with only minor changes in reconstruction accuracy for noise levels up to $10\%$. In comparison with the supervised trained-CNN approach considered in this work, the untrained representation yields substantially smaller reconstruction errors while requiring approximately one-sixth of the computational time. These results demonstrate that fixed random convolutional features combined with regularized coefficient-space learning provide an efficient and robust approach to joint reconstruction in photoacoustic tomography.
papers.summary: Photoacoustic tomography needs both the initial pressure and the spatially varying sound speed to be reconstructed from boundary measurements. The proposed framework represents both fields in wavelet spaces. It recovers the initial-pressure coefficients by Tikhonov-regularized least squares on fixed random features from an untrained convolutional neural network (CNN), then uses a learned coefficient-space prior to infer sound speed. The approach generalizes to unseen phantom geometries, stays stable under up to 10% measurement noise, and **beats a supervised trained-CNN baseline with substantially smaller errors at about one-sixth the compute time**.

papers.title: The Loss or the Architecture? What Matters in Survival Analysis with Competing Risks
papers.abstract: Often, \emph{eg} in healthcare and predictive maintenance, what matters is which of several competing causes will strike first, and with what probability: survival analysis with competing risks. Corresponding deep learning methods are developed as bundles: a new architecture together with a new training loss, tested on one to five datasets against a handful of baselines. Thus, a state-of-the-art result cannot be attributed to the architecture, the loss, or the evaluation protocol. The coupling is not accidental: with one incidence curve per cause, a network's head is tied to the losses expressible on it. We vary the two axes independently, three losses, two of them strictly proper, on four backbones, across two modalities that tease the axes apart: 20 tabular and 3 pathology-image datasets. One loss wins in both: modelling cumulative incidence directly under censoring weighting. It brings twice as much as benefits a good choice of backbone on competing-risks data, and no more than it on single-event data: the loss is decisive for competing risks. The backbone matters too, and must match the modality: tabular networks lead on tables, pretrained vision encoders on images. The two choices compound rather than substitute. Proper scoring rules reveal these dynamics; the concordance index (C-index), which is not proper, does not separate models: neither axis moves it, not even tuning on the loss built to improve it. This is an avenue of progress: composed, the two give a model nobody has tried, RealMLP or TabM trained with the cumulative-incidence loss, which takes the best Brier score in our benchmark.
papers.summary: Deep learning methods for survival analysis with competing risks are usually introduced as a new architecture bundled with a new loss, so it is unclear which part drives the gains. This study varies the two independently, using three losses on four backbones across 20 tabular and 3 pathology-image datasets. **Directly modelling cumulative incidence under censoring weighting wins in both modalities** and contributes about twice as much as the backbone choice on competing-risks data. Backbones still matter and must match the modality, and the two choices compound. The widely used concordance index fails to distinguish models, and the untried combination of `RealMLP` or `TabM` with the cumulative-incidence loss achieves the best Brier score in the benchmark.

papers.title: Peak-Memory Schedules You Can Trust: Exact Realization, Certified Optimality, and the Limits of Recomputation for Inference
papers.abstract: Real-time inference on small devices needs low activation memory without extra latency, which makes operator order the most valuable memory lever: it is free in time. We show that the usual way of deploying a better order, handing it back to the compiler and regenerating code, is unreliable. In PyTorch Inductor the regenerated program misses its predicted peak in 22 of 54 CPU configurations. It is worse than the stock program in 9 of them and in 19 of 50 on a GPU, and on the GPU it also changes numerical results. We instead profile the generated program, model its memory exactly from its own statements and their read/write effects, and permute those statements. We prove that this realizes the modeled peak whenever allocation does not depend on history. It does so to the byte, with bitwise-identical results, in all our CPU runs. On the GPU we characterize why the caching allocator breaks the condition. To know when to stop, we give forward and reverse "trap" lower bounds, each computable with $O(n^2)$ minimum cuts. They certify the found order optimal for 94% of held-out wrapper graphs and all 16 microcontroller-class models we study, in under a second. So most inference graphs are already scheduled optimally. Branching networks are the exception, where reordering is free and pays, e.g. 10.0% on DeepLabV3. In compiled training we save up to 7.6%. Beyond the certified optimum we study selective recomputation with per-operator caps. It is strongly NP-hard for every fixed cap even at treewidth two, encodes knapsack exactly on series-parallel graphs, and is solvable exactly on bounded treewidth. It is useless on public tiny models whose peak is a single layer, but on architectures that hold a cheap value for a late reuse it pays: on the public ReDimNet speaker networks, whose order is already optimal, it lowers the peak by 5.2-6.1% at under 0.4% extra MACs, with bitwise-identical outputs.
papers.summary: Operator ordering is a free way to cut activation memory for inference on small devices, but feeding a better order back to a compiler proves unreliable. In `PyTorch Inductor`, the regenerated program misses its predicted peak in 22 of 54 CPU configurations and can even change numerical results on a GPU. The authors instead permute the statements of the generated program, using an exact memory model, which reaches the modelled peak to the byte with bitwise-identical outputs. They add min-cut-based lower bounds that **certify the found order optimal for 94% of held-out graphs and all 16 microcontroller-class models in under a second**. Reordering pays off mainly for branching networks (10.0% on `DeepLabV3`). Selective recomputation is strongly NP-hard in general, but it cuts the peak of `ReDimNet` speaker models by 5.2–6.1% at under 0.4% extra compute.

papers.title: HiPredict: Predicting the missing HiRISE RED4 spectral channel with machine learning
papers.abstract: The High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) onboard the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) acquires imagery of Mars at 25--30 cm/pixel, supporting studies of martian geology, climate history, and landing-site characterization. Its 14-detector focal plane assembly includes several overlapping detectors that enable the acquisition of three-channel colour-infrared images, which are important for identifying compositional variations and studying active surface processes. In 2023, a detector in the center of the focal plane assembly (RED4) began failing intermittently, creating a gap in acquired imagery and reducing the instrument's colour-imaging capability by half. The HiRISE processing pipeline provides a synthetic red (SYN4) channel obtained by linearly scaling the co-located infrared (IR10) channel. However, this approach cannot capture observed non-linear relationships between the colour channels, limiting its accuracy and applicability. Here, we present HiPredict, a machine-learning framework that reconstructs RED4 from co-located IR10 and blue-green (BG12) imagery, neighbouring red-channel observations, and acquisition metadata. The model employs a U-Net architecture to learn non-linear spatiotemporal-spectral relationships between these inputs and is trained on 81,717 training samples, representing 13,625 observations. Evaluated on 23,348 test samples, representing 3,892 pre-failure observations, HiPredict reconstructs RED4 with a Normalised Mean Absolute Error of 1.1%, substantially outperforming SYN4 (3.1%). The reconstructed products improve colour image recovery and more closely represent features of interest such as icy craters, stratigraphy exposed along ridge crests and chloride deposits. We release HiPredict as an open software tool. This work demonstrates the potential of machine learning to mitigate data loss as planetary missions age and naturally degrade.
papers.summary: Since 2023, the central RED4 detector of the High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) camera on the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter has been failing intermittently, halving its colour-imaging capability. The existing pipeline substitutes a linearly scaled infrared channel. `HiPredict` instead uses a `U-Net` that reconstructs RED4 from co-located infrared and blue-green imagery, neighbouring red channels and acquisition metadata, trained on about 82,000 samples. On held-out pre-failure observations it reaches **a normalised mean absolute error of 1.1% versus 3.1% for the existing synthetic channel**, better preserving features such as icy craters and chloride deposits.

papers.title: Minimax-optimal Scaling Laws in Ridge Regression via Transfer Learning
papers.abstract: Pretrained models are often reused across downstream tasks, motivating the question of whether this transfer learning procedure can provide a substantial performance improvement, namely, in terms of the scaling law. We address this question in the prototypical setting of high-dimensional regression, where (i) a pretrained \emph{source} model is trained via ridge regression, and (ii) a fine-tuned \emph{target} model is regularized via the $L_2$ distance from the source estimator. First, we establish a deterministic equivalent for the risk of this two-step procedure under both model and covariance shift. Next, by specializing the deterministic equivalent to a shared regression function and commuting power-law covariance spectra, we identify a regime where the resulting scaling law achieves the minimax-optimal exponent. Notably, in this regime, the optimal source regularization depends on source data only, indicating its universality across all targets. Furthermore, we show that the same optimal rate is achieved by performing the fine-tuning step via one-pass stochastic gradient descent. We support our theoretical analysis via experiments on both synthetic settings and language models.
papers.summary: The paper asks whether transfer learning can improve the scaling law itself, not just the constants, using high-dimensional ridge regression. In this setup a source model is pretrained with ridge regression and a target model is fine-tuned with an L2 penalty toward the source estimator. The authors derive a deterministic equivalent for the risk under model and covariance shift and identify a regime with power-law spectra where **the scaling law reaches the minimax-optimal exponent**. In that regime the optimal source regularization depends only on source data, and one-pass stochastic gradient descent fine-tuning achieves the same rate. Synthetic experiments and language-model experiments support the theory.

papers.title: SETAREH Transform: A Sorting-Assisted Haar-Wavelet Sparsification Method for Approximate Inner-Product Computation
papers.abstract: Modern deep learning systems increasingly rely on high-dimensional vector operations, in which large input and parameter vectors are repeatedly stored, transferred, and processed. Although substantial research has focused on reducing neural-network model size through pruning, quantization, knowledge distillation, and efficient architectures, the storage, memory-traffic, and communication costs associated with repeatedly presented high-dimensional input vectors remain important practical considerations, particularly in distributed and edge-computing environments. This paper proposes the SETAREH (Sorting-assisted Energy-concentrating Transform for Approximate Representation using Haar wavelets) transform, a Haar-wavelet-based sparsification approach for approximating the inner product between a fixed high-dimensional coefficient vector and successive input vectors. By applying the same sequence of permutations and Haar transforms to both vectors, SETAREH preserves the exact inner product before truncation. It then retains only a subset of the transformed coefficient-input pairs, reducing their representation cost while introducing a controllable approximation error. To evaluate SETAREH, we consider two complementary experimental settings: a synthetic Gaussian-vector baseline and a real apparent-age estimation task using a convolutional neural network on the APPA-REAL dataset. The results show that SETAREH can approximate the evaluated inner products using substantially fewer transformed coefficient-input pairs than the original vector dimension. The findings support its use as a potential structured data-representation method for repeated inner products with fixed weights, while the practical benefit depends on approximation accuracy and the cost of storing or transmitting permutation metadata.
papers.summary: Repeatedly storing and transmitting high-dimensional input vectors is a cost in distributed and edge deep-learning systems, separate from model size. The `SETAREH` transform applies the same sequence of sorting permutations and Haar wavelet transforms to a fixed weight vector and to each incoming input, preserving their inner product exactly, and then keeps only a subset of transformed coefficient pairs. Experiments on synthetic Gaussian vectors and on a CNN age-estimation task on `APPA-REAL` show that **inner products can be approximated with substantially fewer pairs than the original dimension**. Practical benefit depends on the accuracy target and the overhead of storing permutation metadata.

papers.title: Robust Function Calling for LLM Agents Under Interface Drift
papers.abstract: Tool-augmented language-model agents rely on interface text: tool descriptions, argument schemas, and the candidate tool list shown at inference time. These interfaces often change after deployment even when the underlying tool semantics remain fixed, creating a practical reliability problem for function-calling systems. We study this failure mode as interface drift and evaluate whether a lightweight, training-free repair layer can recover robustness without retraining the base model. Our method, SchemaShield-Lite, combines schema validation, candidate-set retry for missing tool names, and one-shot constrained repair. On Qwen3.5-9B, it raises DICE-300 accuracy from 0.717 to 0.813 and BFCL-200 accuracy from 0.580 to 0.805, recovering 19/22 and 33/45 drift-induced failures with no observed repair harms. Naive retry does not explain the gains. Ablations show that candidate-set drift, especially distractor tools, accounts for most observed damage, while description and schema edits alone are less harmful. The results position validation-and-repair as a practical robustness layer for deployed LLM-agent tool use.
papers.summary: Tool-using LLM agents depend on interface text such as tool descriptions, argument schemas and candidate tool lists, which often change after deployment while the tools themselves do not, a problem the authors call interface drift. `SchemaShield-Lite` is a training-free repair layer that combines schema validation, candidate-set retry for missing tool names, and one-shot constrained repair. On `Qwen3.5-9B` it raises `DICE-300` accuracy from 0.717 to 0.813 and **`BFCL-200` accuracy from 0.580 to 0.805**, with no observed repair harms, and naive retry does not explain the gains. Ablations show that changes to the candidate tool list, especially added distractor tools, cause most of the damage.

papers.title: How Finite-Rank Bottlenecks Shape the Low-Rank Adaptation Landscape
papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pretrained models, yet theoretical explanations for why low-rank updates suffice remain incomplete. Most existing analyses rely on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime, which linearizes the network around the pretrained weights. In this work, we take a different approach that requires no linearization: our key observation is that, once the backbone is frozen, the loss sees each adapted weight matrix only through a finite-rank linear map induced by the frozen activations. Trace-norm regularization then forces the optimizer to pick a low-rank matrix among all matrices that produce the same observed output. This yields global minimizers whose ranks are controlled by the rank of this map, which we call the \emph{bottleneck rank}, rather than the sample size. For multi-head attention, we obtain tighter rank upper bounds by exploiting two additional invariances: row-wise softmax is insensitive to additive row constants in the score matrix, and value updates are observable only after attention weighting and frozen output projection. For the factorized LoRA objective with weight decay, we prove a complementary result on the nonconvex side: after an arbitrarily small generic positive semidefinite perturbation, every first-order stationary point is rank-deficient once the LoRA rank exceeds a threshold determined by the bottleneck rank. Finally, we show that global minimizers of the perturbed objective are near-optimal for the original trace-norm problem, and we provide uniform generalization bounds governed by the spectral structure of the frozen features.
papers.summary: Theory for why low-rank adaptation (`LoRA`) works usually relies on the Neural Tangent Kernel linearization. This paper avoids linearization by observing that, with a frozen backbone, the loss sees each adapted weight matrix only through a finite-rank map induced by the frozen activations. Under trace-norm regularization, **global minimizers have rank bounded by this "bottleneck rank" rather than the sample size**, and attention-specific invariances tighten the bounds further. For the nonconvex factorized `LoRA` objective with weight decay, every stationary point becomes rank-deficient after a small generic perturbation once the `LoRA` rank exceeds a threshold, and the paper also gives generalization bounds tied to the frozen features' spectrum.

papers.title: Language Models Learn to Improve Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to automate AI research, including language-model (LM) development, offering a potential path toward recursive self-improvement. However, turning experimental feedback into a learned ability to propose effective improvements across models faces two challenges. First, training such an ability with real feedback is expensive: reinforcement learning (RL) requires evaluating tens of thousands of proposals, each potentially requiring a full model-training run. Even at ten GPU-hours per run, reward collection alone would consume hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours, motivating a cheaper surrogate. Second, surrogate feedback can become unreliable as policy optimization favors overestimated proposals when the proposal distribution shifts. To address these challenges, we propose LM2LM, which trains LLMs with RL to generate effective LM improvement proposals. To provide scalable feedback, we use a research world model (RWM), a frozen LLM that predicts proposal gains from real experimental records provided in context, as the reward model for RL. To maintain feedback reliability, we periodically execute current-policy proposals ranked highly by the RWM and add their measured outcomes to its context. Across eight autoregressive and diffusion LM development environments, real-execution evaluations on held-out tasks show that LM2LM enables Qwen3.8-27B to outperform GPT-6-sol, even when GPT-6-sol is given 300 real experimental records in context, while requiring 33% lower data-generation cost. LM2LM also generalizes to a model family unseen during training.
papers.summary: Using reinforcement learning (RL) to train LLMs to propose language-model improvements is prohibitively expensive when every proposal needs a real training run, and cheap surrogate rewards drift as the policy exploits overestimated proposals. `LM2LM` uses a research world model, a frozen LLM that predicts a proposal's gain from real experimental records in context, as the RL reward model.
