It periodically executes top-ranked current-policy proposals and adds their measured outcomes to the world model's context to keep the reward reliable. Across eight autoregressive and diffusion LM development environments, **`LM2LM` lets `Qwen3.8-27B` outperform `GPT-6-sol` on held-out tasks with real execution**, even when `GPT-6-sol` gets 300 real records in context, at 33% lower data-generation cost. It also generalizes to an unseen model family.
papers.highlight_summary:
Training an LLM with reinforcement learning to propose language-model improvements would normally need a full training run to score each proposal, which costs hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours. `LM2LM` replaces those runs with a frozen LLM, called a "research world model" (`RWM`), that reads real experimental records in context and predicts each proposal's gain. To keep these predicted rewards honest as the policy drifts, it periodically executes the policy's top-rated proposals and adds their real outcomes to the model's context.

- The proposer (`Qwen3.8-27B`) is trained with `DAPO` against rewards from `GPT-6-sol` acting as the `RWM`, and those rewards are normalized per task, clipped, penalized for invalid or repeated proposals, and given a bonus for diverse mechanisms; starting from 100 real records, three on-policy calibration rounds bring the total to **200 real training runs**.
- On held-out tasks across eight autoregressive and diffusion LM families, with every proposal actually executed, `LM2LM` reaches an Avg@4 gain of **17.06** (in 10⁻³ bits per byte) on autoregressive models versus 6.51 for `GPT-6-sol` and 6.15 for `GPT-6-sol` given 300 in-context records, and **7.10** versus 4.94 on diffusion models (in 10⁻² nats per token).
- It beats in-context learning with 300 records while spending **about 33% less on data generation** ($40.1k vs. $60.0k), and on the fully held-out `Qwen3` family it scores **53.72** Avg@4 versus 21.63 for the strongest baseline.
- Calibration is what keeps the reward signal useful: without it, the world model's pairwise ranking accuracy falls from 0.72 to **0.37** (worse than random) by step 128, while the calibrated version holds at 0.61, and calibrating on randomly chosen proposals instead of top-rated ones lowers Avg@4 from 17.06 to 10.84.
- The method is evaluated only on single-proposal improvements to pretraining recipes, not end-to-end research campaigns; it still needs a few hundred real training runs, and on autoregressive tasks it produces more harmful proposals than `GPT-6-sol` with in-context records (**39.2%** vs. 29.6% negative-gain rate).

papers.title: RTSM: Adapting Recursive Models to Multivariate Time-Series Classification
papers.abstract: Accurate multivariate time-series classification requires extracting temporal features and integrating information across a sequence. Weight-tied refinement offers a way to repeatedly process these features without allocating new parameters at each stage. Applying this principle to time series requires choosing both a temporal representation and a latent-state organization suited to classification. We introduce the Recursive Time-Series Model (RTSM), which combines a learned convolutional temporal tokenizer, single-state weight-tied refinement, and a pooled classification readout. Across all 30 UEA datasets, RTSM achieves 72.81% mean accuracy under validation-based configuration and checkpoint selection, the highest observed mean among the 17 evaluated deep-learning models and 1.60 percentage points above MambaSL. Ablations on eight datasets favor the proposed tokenizer over a simple convolutional embedding and the single-state model over the tested two-state variants. The complete classifier reaches 86.10% mean accuracy versus 84.79% for a separately trained tokenizer-only classifier. These findings identify temporal encoding and state organization as key design choices for adapting recursive architectures to time series. The resulting classifier combines competitive accuracy with a shared refinement module whose parameter count is independent of computational depth.
papers.summary: Weight-tied recursive refinement, which reuses the same parameters across repeated processing steps, has worked well on abstract reasoning. This paper adapts it to multivariate time-series classification. The Recursive Time-Series Model (`RTSM`) combines a learned convolutional temporal tokenizer, single-state weight-tied refinement and a pooled classification readout. Across all 30 `UEA` datasets it reaches **72.81% mean accuracy, the highest among 17 deep-learning models and 1.60 points above `MambaSL`**. Ablations favour the proposed tokenizer and the single-state design, and the parameter count stays independent of computational depth.

papers.title: Beyond Success Rate: Interventional Evaluation of Memory in Vision-Language-Action Systems
papers.abstract: When we say that a robot uses memory, does that memory actually play a role? Success-rate ablations alone cannot establish the use of task-relevant facts: they change information and computation together, while aggregate rates can hide offsetting gains and losses. We propose an Interventional Memory Evaluation Protocol (IMEP) for vision-language-action (VLA) systems to address four questions: (1) Does memory provide a net benefit? (2) Under what conditions does memory help? (3) Do changes to memory alter task outcomes? (4) Are these effects specific to task-relevant facts? At the retrieval interface, we compare target-fact substitutions with fact-preserving replacements, minimal numerical perturbations, and exact replicas, while assessing decision correctness separately from motor execution success. We evaluate within-episode, cross-episode, and agentic memory. In cross-episode learned-bank experiments, a one-unit-in-the-last-place (ULP) intervention, including its installation procedure, changes 11.9% of seed-paired outcomes, while changing key facts produces no clear additional effect over fact-preserving replacements. To examine when memory helps, we introduce ChainBench, where correct decisions require historical information unavailable in current observations. The full memory configuration raises task success from 39.1% to 74.3%, matching the oracle-decision condition under shared recorded executions. These results show that correct history can support robot decisions, but establishing whether a memory system realizes this benefit requires fact-specific evidence beyond aggregate success rates.
papers.summary: Success-rate ablations cannot show whether a robot's memory actually uses task-relevant facts, because they change information and computation at the same time. The authors propose the `Interventional Memory Evaluation Protocol` (`IMEP`) for vision-language-action (VLA) systems. At the retrieval interface, it compares swaps of target facts against fact-preserving replacements, tiny numerical perturbations and exact replicas, and it scores decision correctness separately from motor execution. In cross-episode experiments, a one-unit-in-the-last-place (ULP) change alone flips 11.9% of seed-paired outcomes, while changing key facts adds no clear extra effect. On the new `ChainBench`, where correct decisions require past information, full memory raises success **from 39.1% to 74.3%**, matching an oracle-decision condition.

papers.title: Data-Driven Prediction of Optimal MPI Rank Placement and Node Count for Memory-Bound CFD on AMD EPYC Clusters
papers.abstract: Users who run a memory-bound OpenFOAM case on an AMD EPYC cluster must decide how many nodes to use and how many MPI ranks to place on each core complex. The fastest choice is often not the cheapest one. This paper revisits our earlier analytical model of this performance and energy trade-off with 560 measured configurations of the motorBike case on five Zen 4 and Zen 5 EPYC processors, including socket power from processor telemetry. On up to four nodes, small meshes are both fastest and cheapest on a single node on most processors. For the largest mesh the largest node count is both the fastest and the cheapest option, because its speedup is superlinear. A genuine trade-off arises only for medium meshes, where full speed costs a median of 20 to 97% more node hours than the cheapest option. The L3 miss rate and the halo traffic per cell are consistent with this pattern. For a new mesh of the same case, the configuration that was optimal on the nearest measured mesh is near optimal in 75 to 85% of the decisions. Running the two configurations it recommends for speed and for cost raises this share to 85 to 90% for runtime and node hours and determines the trade-off with median errors of 3 to 5 percentage points. Neither gradient boosted trees trained on the same data nor the earlier polynomial model improves on this simple procedure.
papers.summary: Users running memory-bound `OpenFOAM` simulations on AMD EPYC clusters must choose a node count and how many MPI ranks to place on each core complex, trading speed against cost. Using 560 measured configurations of the `motorBike` case on five Zen 4 and Zen 5 processors, including socket power telemetry, the study finds that small meshes are fastest and cheapest on one node and the largest mesh is fastest and cheapest on the most nodes. A real trade-off appears only for medium meshes. Reusing the optimal configuration from the nearest measured mesh is near-optimal in 75 to 85% of decisions, rising to **85 to 90%** when the two recommended configurations are run, and neither gradient boosted trees nor an earlier polynomial model beats this simple procedure.

papers.title: Sentence-Level Topic Modeling with Lexical and Contextual Evidence
papers.abstract: Topic modeling faces a fundamental granularity dilemma: probabilistic topic models assign topics at the word level, whereas transformer-based methods operate at the document level. The latter overlooks that real-world documents typically cover multiple topics, whereas the former relies on individual words, which rarely provide sufficient context to identify them. We introduce SentenceETM, a neural topic model that assigns a topic to each sentence by jointly using lexical and contextual evidence. Each topic is described both by a distribution over the vocabulary, defined through word embeddings, and by a Gaussian over sentence embeddings concentrated on a topic-specific low-dimensional subspace. The topic of a sentence generates both its words and its embedding and is marginalized exactly, so that its posterior combines the two sources of evidence. Document proportions are inferred with amortized variational inference, while the Gaussian parameters are re-estimated in closed form. Experiments show that SentenceETM consistently improves sentence-level topic assignment over state-of-the-art approaches, and a case study of a presidential debate shows how sentence-level topics reveal how candidates handle the same subjects.
papers.summary: Topic models usually work either at the word level, where single words carry too little context, or at the document level, which misses that documents cover several topics. `SentenceETM` assigns a topic to each sentence by combining lexical and contextual evidence. Each topic has a vocabulary distribution built from word embeddings and a Gaussian over sentence embeddings concentrated on a low-dimensional subspace, and the topic is marginalized exactly so that its posterior uses both sources. The model **consistently improves sentence-level topic assignment** over state-of-the-art methods, and a presidential-debate case study shows how candidates handle the same subjects.

papers.title: Forecasting Voltage Time Series under Anomalies Using a WGAN Model With Lipschitz Control and Progressive Kernel Critic Strategy
papers.abstract: In time-series forecasting tasks, the use of recursive forecasting on high-dimensional data substantially increases the complexity of the prediction process. The main challenge is that long-term dynamics becomes harder to model, since the sequences show greater temporal variability. To counteract this limitation and improve the modeling of long-term dynamics, and more importantly, address high-dimensional recursive forecasting, this paper uses a Wasserstein GAN equipped with a progressive Lipschitz penalty and an adaptive kernel. This model is capable of taking a window of the data stream and forecasting the next values, subsequently reconstructing the time-series stream and dynamically adapting its kernel to each new window. The proopsed model is a deep learning framework based on a Wasserstein GAN (WGAN-CLP) with an adaptive kernel to model alterations in streaming voltage time series. To establish the methodological foundation, we review the WGAN-LP formulation another variant model in this class and extend its framework through an adaptive kernel critic model. We then evaluate this extended model using power ratios, correlation coefficient (CC), and relative root mean squared error (RRMSE). The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms benchmark methods in both accuracy and robustness. The evaluation shows promising performance of the WGAN-CLP with an adaptive kernel framework in forecasting sequence alterations across the voltage and energy time-series datasets.
papers.summary: Recursive forecasting of high-dimensional time series struggles to capture long-term dynamics as variability grows. The authors propose `WGAN-CLP`, a Wasserstein GAN with a progressive Lipschitz penalty and an adaptive kernel critic that adjusts to each new window of streaming voltage data. It extends the earlier `WGAN-LP` formulation and is evaluated using power ratios, correlation coefficient (CC) and relative root mean squared error (RRMSE). The authors report that the model **outperforms benchmark methods in accuracy and robustness** on voltage and energy time-series datasets.

papers.title: On the Tip of the Tongue: First-Token Cueing as a Behavioral Probe of Recall Failures in LLMs
papers.abstract: Large language models often answer factual questions incorrectly in closed-book settings, and such errors are usually attributed to missing knowledge. Yet models often encode answers they fail to produce. We show that many closed-book errors are first-token recall failures: the model commits to a wrong first token, but once given the right one it completes the answer and often recognizes it as correct. We study this with First-Token Cueing, a behavioral probe that prefills the response with the first token of the gold answer. Model uncertainty peaks at the first answer token, where it already predicts correctness, and among gold prefixes of any length the first token alone accounts for the largest share of recovered errors. Across 16 open models, this one token corrects between a fifth and a half of the errors on multi-token answers in English QA and improves accuracy in all seven languages of a multilingual benchmark. Most of the errors it corrects are also solved by the model's own sampled reasoning, a criterion for encoded knowledge, and models recognize correct starts they do not produce: they continue a correct start more confidently than an incorrect start of the same answer type and prior probability, yet rarely find it without the gold answer. These results locate a recoverable class of factual errors at the first decoding step, where inference-time methods may gain the most.
papers.summary: Closed-book factual errors in large language models are usually blamed on missing knowledge, but many turn out to be first-token recall failures, where the model commits to a wrong first token yet can complete and recognize the right answer once it is given that token. The authors probe this with `First-Token Cueing`, which prefills the response with the first token of the gold answer. Across 16 open models, this single token **corrects between a fifth and a half of errors on multi-token answers** in English QA and improves accuracy in all seven languages of a multilingual benchmark. Model uncertainty peaks at the first answer token, and most corrected errors are also solved by the model's own sampled reasoning, which suggests the knowledge is encoded and inference-time methods could recover it.

papers.title: Contracting with an Agent under Model Mismatch
papers.abstract: In the classical principal-agent setting, the principal delegates some task to the agent, who receives a payment conditioned on the outcome of the task, which in turn benefits the principal. To align their objectives, the principal designs a contract that incentivizes the agent to take actions beneficial to the principal. In practice, however, the agent may act under misspecified beliefs about the underlying environment, leading to systematically suboptimal decisions. In this work, we study this problem through a principal-agent Markov Decision Process (PAMDP), in which the principal repeatedly interacts with an agent whose transition model may differ from the true environment dynamics. The principal has access to the true transition model and designs contracts that account for the agent's belief and incentives. We characterize contract design under model mismatch and develop a framework that enables the principal to induce desirable long-term benefits even though the agent has a potentially inaccurate understanding of the environment.
papers.summary: In classical principal-agent problems, a principal designs payment contracts to steer an agent, but real agents may act on misspecified beliefs about how the environment behaves. The authors study this in a principal-agent Markov decision process (`PAMDP`), where the agent's transition model may differ from the true dynamics known to the principal. They **characterize contract design under model mismatch** and give a framework that lets the principal secure good long-term outcomes despite the agent's inaccurate world model.

papers.title: Information Estimation with Discrete Diffusion
papers.abstract: Information-theoretic measures, such as Mutual Information (MI), play a crucial role in understanding non-linear relationships between random variables and are widely used across scientific disciplines. Yet, their use on real-world discrete data remains challenging. Existing methods typically rely on embedding discrete data into a continuous space and apply neural estimators originally designed for continuous distributions. This process requires careful engineering for both the embedding model and estimator architecture, but suffers from issues related to high data dimensionality. In this work, we introduce InfoSEDD, a discrete diffusion-based approach that bridges information-theoretic estimation and generative modeling such that they can be used to compute Kullback-Leibler divergences. Backed by Continuous Time Markov Chains theory principles, the design of InfoSEDD is lightweight and scalable and allows seamless integration with pretrained models. We showcase the versatility of our approach through applications on motif discovery in genetic promoter data, semantic-aware model selection in text summarization, and entropy estimation in Ising models. Finally, we construct consistency tests on real-world textual and genomics data. Our experiments demonstrate that InfoSEDD outperforms alternatives that rely on the "embedding trick". Our results position InfoSEDD as a robust and scalable tool for information-theoretic analysis of discrete data.
papers.summary: Estimating information-theoretic quantities such as mutual information (MI) on discrete data usually means embedding the data in a continuous space and applying neural estimators built for continuous distributions, which requires careful engineering and scales poorly. `InfoSEDD` instead uses discrete diffusion models, grounded in continuous-time Markov chain theory, to compute Kullback-Leibler divergences directly, and it can integrate with pretrained models. Applications include motif discovery in genetic promoter data, model selection for text summarization and entropy estimation in Ising models. On consistency tests with real text and genomics data, it **outperforms methods that rely on the embedding trick**.

papers.title: Flash RNN-T: Memory-Efficient Joint Network and Transducer Loss Computation
papers.abstract: The recurrent neural network transducer (RNN-T) remains a practical choice for streaming speech recognition, but training requires large intermediate tensors. We present Flash RNN-T, a joint and loss implementation combining specialized kernels with optional tiled recomputation over the full alignment space and vocabulary. Tiled and untiled Flash form the entire measured throughput-memory frontier on medium and long workloads. On H100, untiled Flash achieves 24-39% higher throughput with 26-56% less memory than the fastest baseline on these workloads wherever it fits. Tiling reduces memory further through recomputation. On medium, tiled Flash uses ninefold less memory than that baseline at 16% lower throughput when both use one backward call per batch. On long, it fits where all tested alternatives with that backward schedule run out of memory with 80 GB. These comparisons use each implementation's lowest-memory configuration reaching at least 95% of its peak throughput.
papers.summary: Training recurrent neural network transducers (RNN-T) for streaming speech recognition requires very large intermediate tensors in the joint network and loss. `Flash RNN-T` combines specialized kernels with optional tiled recomputation over the alignment space and vocabulary. On an H100, the untiled version achieves **24-39% higher throughput with 26-56% less memory** than the fastest baseline on medium and long workloads. The tiled version cuts memory ninefold at 16% lower throughput and fits long workloads where every tested alternative runs out of 80 GB.

papers.title: Residual Stochastic Concept Bottleneck Models
papers.abstract: Concept-based models (CMs) learn human-interpretable intermediate representations that enable users to understand the model's reasoning and steer its predictions through test-time concept interventions. However, in realistic settings, their performance can be limited by concept incompleteness, where the training concepts fail to capture all task-relevant information. Adding an unconstrained residual pathway to the model's predictive process can overcome the consequences of incompleteness. However, this introduces an inscrutable, leak-prone prediction pathway that may weaken concept interventions, as these often leave residual variables unchanged. To address this limitation, we introduce Residual Stochastic Concept Bottleneck Models (Res-SCBMs), a family of concept-based models that jointly model concept and residual variables through a multivariate Gaussian distribution. Res-SCBMs learn a covariance structure that explicitly captures dependencies between the known concepts and learnt residual variables, allowing interventions to propagate to statistically dependent residual variables through Gaussian conditioning. This extends the intervention capabilities of previous CMs without requiring concept completeness during training. Our results show that, across multiple concept-incomplete benchmarks, Res-SCBMs improve predictive performance over competing baselines while retaining effective test-time concept interventions.
papers.summary: Concept bottleneck models make predictions through human-interpretable concepts that users can edit at test time, but incomplete concept sets limit accuracy. Adding an unconstrained residual pathway restores accuracy but weakens interventions, because edits leave the residual unchanged. Residual Stochastic Concept Bottleneck Models (`Res-SCBMs`) model concepts and residual variables jointly as a multivariate Gaussian with a learned covariance, so that concept interventions propagate to dependent residuals through Gaussian conditioning. On concept-incomplete benchmarks they **improve predictive performance while keeping test-time interventions effective**.

papers.title: Bridging Compressed Communication and Local Steps via Spectral Method in Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative training of complex models across large-scale networks of edge devices while keeping data localized. However, data heterogeneity and high communication overhead remain fundamental bottlenecks. Recently, the spectral optimizer Muon has demonstrated remarkable advantages over Adam-like methods in centralized training. While recent efforts have attempted to transition Muon to FL, naive integrations into traditional architectures fail short. Crucially, existing approaches do not support the the communication compression and local steps --- the two foundational techniques of efficient FL. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel spectral FL method that utilizes both local updates and compression. We establish rigorous convergence guarantees under mild assumptions, notably eliminating the restrictive bounded heterogeneity condition. Empirical evaluation on standard image classification benchmarks validates the efficiency and robustness of our approach.
papers.summary: Federated learning (FL) is held back by heterogeneous client data and high communication costs, and earlier ports of the spectral optimizer `Muon` to FL support neither communication compression nor local steps. The authors propose a spectral FL method that supports both. They prove convergence under mild assumptions **without the usual bounded-heterogeneity condition**, and experiments on standard image classification benchmarks support the method's efficiency and robustness.

papers.title: Generative Policy Improvement from Observational Data
papers.abstract: We study how to improve decision policies from observational data to generate better actions when actions are complex, structured objects, such as text messages or images. This task is subject to two major challenges: (i) action-level overlap is often too weak for reliable off-policy evaluation and improvement, and (ii) generating new structured actions often requires expensive training or fine-tuning (e.g., of an LLM) and can be ill-defined due to information loss in action representations. To address both, we propose PolicyLift, a three-stage framework for generative policy improvement with structured actions from observational data. In Stage 1, PolicyLift learns a small set of discrete action codes that capture high-level strategies in the observed action space and are tailored to support policy improvement under limited overlap. In Stage 2, it learns a context-dependent policy over these action codes. At deployment time, Stage 3 "lifts" the learned code-level policy back to the original action space by generating actions from the historical behavior system in a code-conditioned way. We show theoretically that improving the policy over action codes guarantees improvement of the induced policy in the original action space. We demonstrate PolicyLift across experiments in synthetic and real-world text generation tasks with consistent policy improvements over the behavior policy.
papers.summary: Improving decision policies from logged data is hard when actions are structured objects such as text or images, because overlap between logged and candidate actions is weak and generating new actions can require costly fine-tuning. `PolicyLift` learns a small set of discrete action codes that capture high-level strategies, learns a context-dependent policy over those codes, and at deployment generates actions from the historical behavior system conditioned on the chosen code. The authors prove that **improving the code-level policy guarantees improvement in the original action space**. Experiments on synthetic and real-world text generation tasks show consistent gains over the behavior policy.

papers.title: ScoutRoute: Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Routing Using Internal Language Model Signals
papers.abstract: Efficient expert routing is a fundamental challenge in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) systems, particularly for heterogeneous collections of independently trained Large Language Mod els (LLMs). Existing routing approaches typically rely on jointly trained gating networks, prompt-based predictors, or computationally expensive multi-model inference, limiting their flexibility and efficiency. This paper presents ScoutRoute, a lightweight post-hoc routing framework that predicts expert competence using internal language model signals extracted from a single forward pass through an inexpensive scout model. Hidden-state representations are used to estimate cross-model competence through lightweight logistic probes, while logit-derived confidence measures are incorporated within a domain-aware routing strategy for efficient expert selec tion without modifying the underlying language models. ScoutRoute isevaluatedon fiveopen-weightlanguagemodels across fourbenchmark datasets covering mathematical reasoning, code generation, commonsense reasoning, and multidis ciplinary knowledge. Experimental results show that ScoutRoute consistently outperforms individual routing signals while requiring only a single scout-model inference. The proposed competence probes also achieve superior calibration compared with conventional confidence measures, demonstrating that internal language model representations provide transferable information for accurate and efficient expert routing across heterogeneous language models
papers.summary: Routing queries among independently trained large language models usually relies on jointly trained gates, prompt-based predictors or expensive multi-model inference. `ScoutRoute` runs one forward pass of a cheap scout model, uses lightweight logistic probes on its hidden states to predict which expert model is competent, and adds logit-based confidence in a domain-aware routing strategy, without modifying any of the models. Evaluated with five open-weight models on math, code generation, commonsense and multidisciplinary knowledge benchmarks, it **consistently outperforms individual routing signals while requiring only a single scout inference**, and its probes are better calibrated than conventional confidence measures.

papers.title: RECREG: Recovery-based Shielding for Regular Safety Properties in Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: In many real-world scenarios we need to consider formal requirements, such as safety and constraint compliance, to deploy Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents. In this paper we introduce RecReg, a safe RL framework capable of enforcing non-Markovian regular safety properties via recovery-based shielding. RecReg is a unified approach that supports different levels of a priori knowledge and safety guarantees. The paper primarily focuses on building the theoretical foundations for RecReg in the tabular setting, providing rigorous safety and convergence guarantees that are not present in related work. We provide an extensive set of empirical results using the MASA-Safe-RL library, and we outline an extension of RecReg to deep RL domains using SOTA model-based RL. Our empirical results demonstrate that RecReg achieves efficient learning and matches the theory in this paper.
papers.summary: Deploying reinforcement learning (RL) agents often requires formal safety requirements that depend on history, not just the current state. `RecReg` enforces such non-Markovian regular safety properties through recovery-based shielding and supports different levels of prior knowledge and safety guarantees. The paper provides **rigorous safety and convergence guarantees in the tabular setting** that related work lacks, evaluates the approach with the `MASA-Safe-RL` library, and outlines an extension to deep RL using model-based methods.

papers.title: "You" Is Not Toxic: How LLM Labelers Rewrite the Web's Conversation Laws
papers.abstract: What the Web community believes about toxic conversations, such as that toxicity rises in longer and deeper threads, was measured mostly with Google's Perspective API, which is shutting down; large language models (LLMs) will make the next measurements. We find that LLM labelers mistake second-person address for toxicity, and that this one bias manufactures laws that human labels do not show. On 1.25 million news comments with crowd labels, Claude Haiku flags 12% of the non-toxic comments that contain no "you" and 51% of those with four or more; a single crowd rater flags 6% and 10%. Deeper replies address someone more often, so under Haiku toxicity rises with reply depth (+0.93 percentage points per level), while under the crowd's labels it slightly declines (-0.12). Rewriting "you" in the third person removes two thirds of the false rise; flagging only as many comments as the crowd does not remove it, and showing Haiku the parent comment enlarges it. All seven LLMs we test over-flag "you", and at the crowd's flag rate, without the parent, any false rise of the open ones vanishes at a fixed number of second-person words; Haiku also over-flags "you" on Reddit, Gab and Wikipedia talk pages. Agreement with human labels does not reveal the bias: we prove that a fixed Cohen's kappa leaves a law nearly unconstrained. We therefore certify the law instead of the labeler. Threadsafe uses the labeler's scores to choose which comments human raters label and to predict the others, and corrects the predictions with the human labels; linear laws are estimated without bias whatever the labeler does. In simulated audits its intervals for the laws keep nominal coverage from 250 labels on, where uniform-sample methods such as PPI++ fall short, and at 1,000 to 8,000 labels are 0.75 times as wide as those of design-based supervised learning (DSL); a thousand human labels rule out Haiku's rising law.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are replacing Google's soon-retired `Perspective API` for measuring online toxicity, but they mistake second-person address for toxicity. On 1.25 million news comments with crowd labels, `Claude Haiku` flags 12% of non-toxic comments without 'you' and **51% of those with four or more**, which makes toxicity appear to rise with reply depth while human labels show a slight decline. All seven LLMs tested over-flag 'you', and the authors prove that agreement statistics like Cohen's kappa cannot reveal such bias. Their method `Threadsafe` uses labeler scores to choose which comments humans label and corrects predictions with those labels, giving unbiased estimates of linear laws with tighter intervals than `PPI++` or design-based supervised learning (`DSL`).

papers.title: Regularized free deconvolution for spectral repair of resampling distortion in high-dimensional particle filters
papers.abstract: Resampling is the standard remedy for weight degeneracy in particle filters, but in high dimensions it distorts the spectrum of the ensemble covariance in a way that is computable from the importance weights. This paper studies the inverse problem: recovering the pre-resampling spectrum from the observed weights and the empirical spectrum alone, and using it without biasing the filter. We first show that the forward spectral law extends to random importance weights once one conditions on the weights together with the realized offspring counts, rather than on the weights alone. We then construct a regularized free-deconvolution estimator, prove its consistency with an explicit error budget at a fixed resolution scale, and certify model mismatch through a computable forward residual. The repaired spectrum enters the filter only as the preconditioner of a Metropolis-adjusted rejuvenation move, so that spectral error affects mixing efficiency but not the invariant target. For the full filtering cycle, we derive a geometrically summable error recursion under stable scalar dynamics and an explicit law for the cost of abstaining from repair. Pre-registered simulations show that the inversion reduces the spectral error by an order of magnitude, that the corrected preconditioner recovers about 90% of the oracle's sampling efficiency in an anisotropic regime, and that the cost of abstention depends on when abstentions occur rather than on how many. The repair recovers eigenvalue laws, not eigenvectors, and is certified only within an explicitly stated exogenous-weight regime.
papers.summary: Resampling in high-dimensional particle filters distorts the spectrum of the ensemble covariance in a way that can be computed from the importance weights. The authors invert this distortion with a regularized free-deconvolution estimator, prove its consistency with an explicit error budget, and use the repaired spectrum only to precondition a Metropolis-adjusted rejuvenation move, so that errors affect mixing but do not bias the filter. Pre-registered simulations show the inversion **reduces spectral error by an order of magnitude** and recovers about 90% of an oracle's sampling efficiency in an anisotropic regime.

papers.title: Predictable Scaling: Efficient Model Exploration via Scaling-Law Prediction
papers.abstract: Evaluating candidate changes (hypotheses) to recommendation models requires full-scale training runs consuming thousands of GPU-hours, severely limiting the hypothesis space engineers can feasibly explore. We introduce Predictable Scaling (PS), a systematic framework that exploits empirically verified regularity conditions to predict full-scale model performance from small-scale proxies. PS constructs scaled-down variants via composable scaling functions along distinct resource axes, and projects metrics to the target scale via curve fitting with calibrated uncertainty estimates. We compare three prediction strategies of increasing expressiveness: even the simplest (raw proxy) achieves prediction error within the empirical noise floor of repeated-run variance; the most expressive (Gaussian Process) provides an indicative 15% relative MAE improvement and calibrated uncertainty. Evaluation on two ranking models of increasing complexity---a task-specific model and a foundation model---demonstrates that PS correctly ranks actionable hypotheses across diverse hypothesis types at 79-88% compute reductions.
papers.summary: Testing candidate changes to recommendation models normally requires full-scale training runs that cost thousands of GPU-hours. `Predictable Scaling` builds scaled-down model variants along separate resource axes and projects their metrics to the target scale by curve fitting with calibrated uncertainty. Even raw small-scale proxies predict within the run-to-run noise floor, and a Gaussian Process predictor improves relative mean absolute error by about 15%. On two production-style ranking models, the framework correctly ranks actionable hypotheses with **79-88% compute reductions**.

papers.title: HydraLLM: Adaptive Width Slicing for Elastic Text and Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: LLMs and LVLMs are increasingly deployed across heterogeneous hardware, ranging from data-center GPUs to resource-constrained edge devices. Their fixed-size architectures limit the ability to reuse a single model across deployment settings with different compute, latency, and model-size targets. We introduce HydraLLM, an elastic MQA-based architecture. Its number of active attention heads determines the effective widths of the embeddings, attention projections, feed-forward layers, and the output head, forming a nested family of subnetworks within a single parameter set. We introduce a static-to-elastic conversion pipeline that, starting from a pre-trained model checkpoint, includes importance-driven weight reordering and stochastic subnetwork training with knowledge distillation. We extend this principle to multimodal inference through an elastic projection module whose output width follows the active text width. HydraLLM covers a wider range of active parameter configurations than FFN-only elastic architectures. With 75% of heads active, HydraLLM achieves 2.2 percentage points higher TriviaQA accuracy than a state-of-the-art nested baseline configuration which has 17.25% more parameters. With 50% of heads active, our multimodal model achieves a CLIPScore comparable to that of the 7$\times$ larger Gemma 3 4B model. With only 25% of heads active, HydraLLM increases token-generation throughput by 75.3% over the full-width configuration.
papers.summary: LLMs and large vision-language models (LVLMs) have fixed sizes, so one model cannot easily serve both data-center GPUs and edge devices. `HydraLLM` is an elastic multi-query attention (MQA) architecture in which the number of active attention heads sets the width of embeddings, projections, feed-forward layers and output head, creating nested subnetworks within one set of weights. It is converted from a pretrained checkpoint through importance-based weight reordering and stochastic subnetwork training with distillation, and it extends to multimodal models through an elastic projection module. With 75% of heads active it beats a larger nested baseline by 2.2 points on `TriviaQA`, and with 25% active it **raises token-generation throughput by 75.3%**.

papers.title: A low-dimensional dynamical basis for tongue shape control
papers.abstract: Speech production involves the control of a high-dimensional articulatory system with many degrees-of-freedom, but a widespread hypothesis is that speakers navigate this complexity using a set of lower-dimensional control variables. Common candidates for these control variables include individual articulators (e.g. tongue body) and abstract tract variables (e.g. tongue body constriction location), but identifying the most appropriate coordinate system for articulatory control remains an open question. In this study, we advance a model in which holistic tongue shape modes represent a potential low-dimensional control basis for a simple dynamical law. We first discover empirical tongue shape modes in a cross-speaker coordinate space and then fit the model to ultrasound data on monophthongal vowels from 36 speakers of British English. A three-dimensional linear point attractor fitted to these time-varying modes recovers the dynamics of tongue shape with a high degree of accuracy. This suggests that complex tongue movement can arise from independent modes that linearly combine under simple dynamical laws, thereby relocating some complexity from the control signal to the coordinate system. We show that this framing explains why one-dimensional articulatory measures can exhibit observable nonlinearities, and hypothesize that shape modes are a plausible kinematic expression of underlying muscle synergies.
papers.summary: Speech production controls a high-dimensional articulatory system, and an open question is which low-dimensional coordinates speakers actually use. The authors derive holistic tongue-shape modes from a cross-speaker space and fit a three-dimensional linear point attractor to ultrasound recordings of vowels from 36 British English speakers. The model **recovers tongue-shape dynamics with high accuracy**, which suggests that complex movement can come from simple dynamics over well-chosen modes. The authors argue this explains nonlinearities seen in one-dimensional articulatory measures.

papers.title: Graphlet-based Decentralized Finance Transaction Method Classification
papers.abstract: Decentralized Finance (DeFi) transactions involve complex interactions among accounts, smart contracts, and tokens. We investigate whether network topology can identify transaction methods that describe DeFi operations. We extract directed graphlet features to classify the 30 most frequent methods. Our results show that graphlet features complement event log counts in improving classification performance. Using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), we further derive model explanations that reveal method-specific graphlet structural patterns.
papers.summary: Decentralized Finance (DeFi) transactions involve complex interactions among accounts, smart contracts and tokens. The authors test whether network topology alone can identify which transaction method was called by extracting directed graphlet features to classify the 30 most frequent methods. **Graphlet features complement event-log counts** and improve classification, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (`SHAP`) reveal method-specific structural patterns.

papers.title: QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality-Diversity
papers.abstract: Open-ended search combined with foundation models has produced advances such as faster algorithms, new results on open mathematical problems, and self-improving agents. We extend this paradigm to recommendation for decision-making, focusing on decisions where the set of possible choices is fixed but the reasons for choosing them are not. In high-stakes decisions, e.g., which company to acquire or which customer to target, comparing diverse, well-reasoned options can be more useful than a single ranked list. We formalize open-ended recommendation as building a diverse, high-quality set of recommendations, each an item together with a hypothesis, a natural-language reason why the item fits the needs of a decision maker. We propose QD-Rec, a quality--diversity method that selects items with a contextual bandit and generates hypotheses with a foundation model from earlier ones kept in an archive as stepping stones. A new recommendation enters the archive if it is novel or better than its nearest neighbor. Across M&A, customer targeting, and paper and book recommendation, QD-Rec gives the highest mean quality and builds the largest archive in most settings.
papers.summary: For high-stakes choices such as acquisitions or customer targeting, a diverse set of well-reasoned options can be more useful than a single ranked list. The authors frame open-ended recommendation as building a diverse, high-quality archive of items, each paired with a natural-language hypothesis explaining why it fits the decision maker. `QD-Rec` is a quality-diversity method that picks items with a contextual bandit and generates hypotheses with a foundation model, using earlier archive entries as stepping stones. Across M&A, customer targeting and paper and book recommendation, it **achieves the highest mean quality and the largest archive in most settings**.

papers.title: Towards optimal selection schedules for online active learning
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of online linear classification, where a stream of unlabeled samples is available, and annotation is costly. We investigate the optimal query policy, that prescribes whether and when a sample should be labeled and used for a training step, or instead discarded, so as to minimize a given objective. We focus on the realizable case, under Gaussian design, in the high-dimensional regime where data dimension and number of unlabeled samples grow proportionally. We consider two objectives: 1) the generalization error under a labeling budget, and 2) a cumulative cost function where mistakes have unit cost and queries cost $\Delta$. We first show that the myopic policies that greedily minimize at all times the increment in the objective correspond to either small or intermediate-margin policies, that prescribe the selection of samples whose margins fall within certain intervals that shrink with time. Within this class, we numerically ascertain the optimal schedules for the selection thresholds that minimize the final values of the objectives. Taking inspiration from the myopic policy for the cumulative cost, we design a very simple query policy schedule that we compare to other proposed heuristics, on synthetic data and real medical image datasets. Finally, we discuss myopic policies for two-layer neural networks, and exemplify how naive margin-based policies can cease to be optimal.
papers.summary: In online active learning, a stream of unlabeled samples arrives and labels are expensive, so the learner must decide which samples to label and train on and which to discard. The authors study this for linear classification on Gaussian data in the high-dimensional regime, where the data dimension and the number of samples grow together. They target two objectives: generalization error under a labeling budget, and a cumulative cost that charges for both mistakes and queries. They show that greedy (myopic) policies amount to **selecting samples whose margins fall in intervals that shrink over time**, find the best threshold schedules numerically, and propose a simple schedule that they test against other heuristics on synthetic data and medical image datasets. For two-layer neural networks, they show that naive margin-based selection can stop being optimal.

papers.title: MuninAI: A Self-Hosted Agentic Framework for Independent Research Groups
papers.abstract:
Research groups that want a language model grounded in their own literature face a choice between hosted services that receive their unpublished work and self-hosted deployments that keep the data local but give the model no access to the corpus. Munin is an open-source framework for a self-hosted scientific assistant that indexes a group's corpus and its citation graph, and wraps whichever open-weight model the group can serve in an agent harness with specialised reading, search, and computation tools. We claim that the harness, rather than the specific model, is what makes the system useful on domain literature, and we ship the evaluation suite that tests this claim with the software.
  On 199 paired literature questions, the harness more than doubles the accuracy of the base model, from 0.387 to 0.874 (+0.487, 95% CI [0.407, 0.568]), while naive retrieve-then-answer scores below the unaided model on every backbone tested. Under the harness, roughly twice as many answer claims trace to a passage the model read itself as with fixed top-5 retrieval. When the source paper for a question is removed from the corpus, the system abstains on about nine in ten of the questions it had answered correctly on the Qwen backbones and eight in ten on gpt-oss-20b, and it produces no fabricated local citation across 300 fabricated references.
  The pattern holds on three backbones from two developers, including a 20-billion-parameter model that runs on a single consumer-grade GPU. With all outbound network access disabled, both Qwen backbones still exceed the published PaperQA2 accuracy. The evaluation suite runs as a single command, so an adopting group can re-run it on its own corpus and model.
papers.summary: `Munin` is an open-source, self-hosted scientific assistant that lets a research group ground a language model in its own literature without sending unpublished work to a hosted service. It indexes the group's papers and citation graph, and wraps any open-weight model in an agent harness with dedicated tools for reading, search and computation. On 199 literature questions, the harness **raises base-model accuracy from 0.387 to 0.874**, while naive retrieve-then-answer scores below the unaided model on every backbone tested. The gains hold across three backbones, including `gpt-oss-20b` on a single consumer GPU, and with network access disabled both `Qwen` backbones still beat the published `PaperQA2` accuracy; the system also abstains on most questions once their source paper is removed and produced no fabricated local citations.

papers.title: A Topological Signature of Learning under Noisy Labels
papers.abstract: How does noisy supervision change the representations learned by a neural network? Training accuracy measures agreement with training labels but provides little information about representation geometry. We use persistent homology to track loop structure across distance thresholds in neural activations. Experiments span image classification, text classification, and modular arithmetic. On a fixed CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 training probe, equally sized clean-label and corrupted-label subsets show no detectable persistence difference at epoch 10, whereas corrupted-label subsets have higher persistence at epoch 50. The contrast survives uniform-scale controls, even though predictions match the assigned noisy labels for only 7-11% of corrupted probe examples at that checkpoint. Normalisation preserves the crossover between clean and noisy training trajectories on CIFAR-10/ResNet-18, whereas CIFAR-100/ResNet-18 shows no crossover under any of the five evaluated constructions. In a separate noise-rate calibration comparison across five pipelines, mean activation norm achieves a higher mean in-sample R2 than raw persistence (0.936 versus 0.908). These findings show that noisy supervision leaves a measurable geometric signature even when agreement with corrupted labels is low. Comparing persistence under scale controls with label-fitting measurements offers a way to study how representations respond to label corruption beyond what training accuracy reveals.
papers.summary: The authors use persistent homology, a technique that tracks loop structure in data across distance scales, to ask how noisy labels change a neural network's internal representations beyond what training accuracy shows. On `CIFAR-10` with `ResNet-18`, clean and corrupted subsets look the same early in training, but by epoch 50 the corrupted subsets show **higher persistence even though the model fits only 7-11% of their noisy labels**. The effect survives scale controls on `CIFAR-10` but does not appear on `CIFAR-100`, and for estimating the noise rate, a simple mean activation norm slightly outperforms raw persistence. The experiments also cover text classification and modular arithmetic.

papers.title: Adaptive conformal prediction on the Grassmannian
papers.abstract: We introduce a conformal prediction framework for regression with Grassmann-valued responses. The proposed method constructs prediction regions in the form of metric balls directly on the Grassmann manifold, using basis-invariant geometric distances as non-conformity measures and scaling the corresponding non-conformity scores through a learned prediction difficulty estimator. This yields locally adaptive, input-dependent prediction regions that respect the underlying manifold geometry, while retaining the finite-sample marginal coverage guarantee of split conformal prediction under exchangeability. We evaluate several Grassmannian distance metrics and compare their prediction-region efficiency on synthetic benchmarks and an airfoil inverse shape-design problem. The results highlight the advantages of geometry-aware non-conformity scores, while local adaptation improves empirical coverage uniformity across prediction difficulty levels and, in strongly heteroscedastic settings, can substantially reduce prediction-region size while maintaining the target coverage.
papers.summary: The authors extend conformal prediction to regression problems whose outputs are subspaces, which are points on the Grassmann manifold. Prediction regions are metric balls on the manifold, built from basis-invariant geometric distances and scaled by a learned estimate of how hard each input is to predict. The method **keeps the finite-sample coverage guarantee of split conformal prediction** while giving input-dependent regions that respect the manifold's geometry. Tests on synthetic benchmarks and an airfoil inverse shape-design problem show that geometry-aware scores are more efficient, and that local adaptation gives more even coverage and smaller regions when noise varies strongly across inputs.

papers.title: Uncertainty-aware AI-enabled framework for predicting hydrogen dispersion in confined spaces to enhance operator situational awareness
papers.abstract: We present a two-stage AI-enabled framework for enhancing operator situational awareness during compressed hydrogen bunkering in maritime confined spaces. In the event of a leak, the framework first estimates the unknown leakage rate from early sensor readings and then forecasts how the hydrogen cloud will disperse over the next time steps, providing operators with a predicted concentration map together with confidence bounds. The framework is based on two independent AI models building one AI system. The AI system is designed as a decision-support tool. It augments sensor readings, and thus enhances operator situational awareness and supports decision-making. This enables preventive safety barriers to be deployed before hazardous concentrations are reached, while an independent emergency shutdown system remains the ultimate safety layer. The system design incorporates safeguards to ensure the AI system operates within its competence envelope. Trained and tested on an open dataset of confined-space hydrogen releases, the framework achieves a mean absolute error of $0.052$~g/s in leakage-rate estimation and $\approx0.018$ in hydrogen-concentration prediction, approaching the sensor precision bound of $\pm0.01$. The hydrogen-concentration prediction provides well-calibrated uncertainty estimates that allow operators to judge the reliability of each forecast. These results suggest that the framework may provide early information about hazardous concentration build-up, potentially supporting preventive actions by operators.
papers.summary: The authors build a two-stage decision-support system for leaks of compressed hydrogen during refuelling (bunkering) in confined spaces on ships. One model estimates the leak rate from early sensor readings; a second forecasts how the hydrogen cloud will spread and gives a concentration map with confidence bounds. Safeguards keep the system within its validated operating range, and an independent emergency shutdown remains the final safety layer. On an open dataset of confined-space releases, the system reaches a mean absolute error of 0.052 g/s for leak rate and **about 0.018 for concentration, close to the ±0.01 sensor precision**, with well-calibrated uncertainty estimates.

papers.title: Perceive, Solve, Reason: Progressive Capability Formation in Time Series-LLMs
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can now perceive, describe, and reason about images and audio, yet time series understanding remains underestimated: most work uses LLMs as forecasters and classifiers, reasoning studies are few and narrow, and no suite trains and evaluates the full range of capabilities. In this paper, we build the first such suite, with 337K training and 44K evaluation samples across three progressive capabilities, Perceive, Solve, and Reason, and use it to ask how time series should enter an LLM that must master all three, and in what order. We find that a dedicated encoder is essential: with one, a 4B model surpasses GPT-4o on every perception attribute we test, whereas textualizing the series costs 8--10 points in reasoning accuracy. The capabilities then build on one another: learning them in order beats mixing the same data and rivals reasoning-only training with over three times the reasoning data, but only when an encoder is used. Analyses further reveal that capabilities are transferred through distinct network depths rather than simply stacked, and that a stage converged on its own benchmark is not necessarily ready for the next. Distilled into a simple recipe, these findings yield 4B TS-LLMs that, without any target-domain data, outperform four recent 7B TS-LLMs on seven of eight out-of-domain metrics, by up to 11 points. We therefore advocate treating time series as a first-class modality for LLMs, read through dedicated encoders and taught to perceive before they reason.
papers.summary: The authors build what they describe as the first suite that both trains and evaluates three escalating time-series skills in large language models (LLMs): perceiving a series, solving tasks with it, and reasoning about it. The suite has 337K training and 44K evaluation samples. They find that a dedicated time-series encoder is essential: with one, a 4B model beats `GPT-4o` on every perception attribute tested, while converting the series to text costs 8-10 points of reasoning accuracy. Teaching the skills in order beats mixing the same data, and the capabilities are carried by different network depths rather than simply stacked. The resulting recipe yields 4B models that, with no target-domain data, **outperform four recent 7B time-series LLMs on seven of eight out-of-domain metrics**.

papers.title: Interpreting SSL Representations for Spoof Detection: a WavLM Study
papers.abstract: Self-supervised speech models such as WavLM achieve strong spoofing detection performance, yet which layers encode the most spoof-relevant information and what acoustic properties they capture remain opaque. We present a layer-wise interpretability study of WavLM using the ASVspoof 5 database, combining three complementary analyses: (i) per-layer linear probing with attack-level evaluation across speech synthesis, voice conversion, and adversarial attacks; (ii) a canonical correlation analysis (CCA) linking layer representations to spoofing-relevant acoustic features; (iii) an exhaustive grid search over layer subsets showing that use of five layers outperforms full thirteen-layer pooling. CCA analysis reveals that, while most acoustic features peak in alignment with mid-layers and then decay, voice quality measures jitter, shimmer, and the harmonics-to-noise ratio show the opposite trend, with correlation increasing toward later layers. Embedding visualisations reveal that deeper layers capture a continuous acoustic similarity among attacks rather than discrete categories, suggesting these layers encode fundamental synthesis artifacts rather than attack-specific signatures.
papers.summary: The authors study which layers of the self-supervised speech model `WavLM` carry the information used to detect spoofed audio, and what acoustic properties those layers capture. Using the `ASVspoof 5` database, they probe each layer separately across speech-synthesis, voice-conversion and adversarial attacks. They use canonical correlation analysis (CCA) to link layers to acoustic features and search exhaustively over layer subsets. **A subset of five layers outperforms pooling all thirteen**. Most acoustic features align best with the middle layers, while voice-quality measures such as jitter, shimmer and harmonics-to-noise ratio align more strongly with later layers. The deeper layers appear to encode general synthesis artifacts rather than attack-specific signatures.

papers.title: Truth in Contrast: Calibrated Factual Evidence from Language Model Likelihoods
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode substantial factual knowledge. Yet, estimating confidence in factual claims reliably remains challenging. We study likelihood-based factual confidence from the complementary perspectives of discrimination and calibration across multilingual factual statements. Specifically, we instantiate contrastive generative likelihoods as Contrastive Factual Evidence (CFE), which compares the likelihood of the same claim under competing factual and non-factual conditions, and derive its probabilistic counterpart, the Contrastive Factual Posterior (CFP). We show analytically that CFP calibration depends on the differential error between the two surrogate conditionals, allowing errors shared across them to cancel and yield tighter calibration bounds. Empirically, CFP substantially improves calibration while maintaining factual discrimination comparable to its strongest competitor. Nonetheless, discrimination is uniformly weak across methods in lower-resource languages, which simultaneously undermines the utility of the measured calibration. To this end, we interpret a likelihood geometry, within which an evidence-bearing direction is induced, along with an orthogonal evidence-invariant direction. In our investigation, we selectively align target-language claims with stronger English evidence only along the factual-evidence direction, improving discrimination and open-ended factual generation without target-language labels.
papers.summary: The authors study how to score an LLM's confidence that a factual claim is true, judging scores by both discrimination (separating true from false claims) and calibration, across many languages. Their Contrastive Factual Evidence (`CFE`) compares a claim's likelihood under competing factual and non-factual conditions, and its probabilistic form, the Contrastive Factual Posterior (`CFP`), is shown analytically to cancel errors shared by the two conditions. Empirically, **`CFP` substantially improves calibration while matching the best competitor's discrimination**. Discrimination remains weak in lower-resource languages for every method. To address this, they align target-language claims with English evidence along a single factual direction, which improves discrimination and open-ended factual generation without target-language labels.

papers.title: Out of Support, Not Out of Reach: In-Context Learning with Unsupported Instructions and Composed Tasks
papers.abstract: In-Context Learning (ICL) enables pretrained LLMs to adapt to downstream tasks from a small set of input-output demonstrations, without parameter updates. Yet existing theory primarily explains ICL as identifying a latent task already represented in pretraining, leaving unclear whether ICL can succeed when either the instruction or the target task falls outside the pretraining support. We develop a theoretical framework under mild assumptions that separates these two forms of distribution shift. For target tasks represented in pretraining, we show that demonstrations can identify the task and reduce sensitivity to pretrain-supported prompt templates as their number increases. For an unsupported instruction, we show that under a fixed model-induced reference extension, demonstration evidence can dominate an $N$-independent instruction shift while preserving the exponential identification rate. We then use the same ICL framework as an interpretive lens for long-horizon target tasks that are not represented in pretraining but admit a plan that decomposes them into pretraining-supported subtasks. Applying the supported-task analysis step by step yields a standard accumulated-error bound and clarifies how invoking familiar subtasks along an intermediate-state trajectory can avoid directly selecting the unsupported complete task. Together, our results characterize when demonstrations, instructions, and task decomposition can support ICL beyond the corresponding pretraining supports.
papers.summary: Existing theory explains in-context learning (ICL) as the model picking out a task it already saw during pretraining. That leaves open whether ICL can work when the instruction or the task itself lies outside the pretraining data. The authors build a framework that treats these two kinds of shift separately. They show that **demonstrations can outweigh an unfamiliar instruction while keeping exponential task-identification rates**. For long tasks never seen in pretraining, they analyze plans that break the task into familiar subtasks, giving an accumulated-error bound for this decomposition and a precise account of when demonstrations, instructions and decomposition let ICL succeed.

papers.title: EduWild: How Teacher-Configured Chatbots Fail in Real-World Use and How to Fix Them
papers.abstract: Teachers increasingly configure educational chatbots through natural-language instructions, but how these bots fail in real-world use remains poorly understood. We introduce EduWild, a dataset of 1,726 conversations with 217 teacher-configured chatbots, each paired with the instructions and configuration behind it, including 900 conversations from the intended end users of 35 deployed chatbots. We develop a 29-code taxonomy covering factual, workflow, diagnostic, and pedagogical failures and apply it using a human-calibrated LLM judge. The most frequent failures are lapses in following teacher intent --- bots skip required workflow steps (53.8% of end-user conversations), omit expectation setup (33.4%), and overload learners with information or questions (37.1%). Guided by these findings, we design a prompt-based harness targeting the six most frequent failure modes. In a study with 200 college students across ten bots, the harness reduces the mean number of target failure codes per conversation from 1.406 to 0.489, a 65.2% relative reduction with bots weighted equally. These findings show how real-world failure analysis can guide practical improvements to educational chatbots.
papers.summary: `EduWild` is a dataset of 1,726 conversations with 217 educational chatbots that teachers configured with natural-language instructions. Each conversation comes with the bot's configuration, and 900 come from real students using 35 deployed bots. Using a 29-code failure taxonomy applied by a human-calibrated LLM judge, the authors find the most common failures are lapses in following the teacher's intent: bots skip required workflow steps in 53.8% of student conversations and overload learners in 37.1%. A prompt-based harness aimed at the six most frequent failures, tested with 200 college students across ten bots, **cuts target failures per conversation by 65.2%**.

papers.title: ConvexLLM: Scaling Convex-Hull Speech Interfaces to General-Purpose Audio Intelligence
papers.abstract: Speech and audio language models connect continuous acoustic representations to decoders pretrained primarily on text data. Most such models use MLP or Q-Former interfaces to map acoustic features into the decoder's input space, requiring the decoder to learn how to interpret the resulting representations. We investigate whether grounding these representations in the decoder's existing text embeddings can help it use acoustic information while better preserving its pretrained text capabilities. We present ConvexLLM, a general-purpose speech and audio language model whose C-Gate interface represents audio as continuous convex combinations of frozen text embeddings. ConvexLLM achieves an eleven-task VoiceBench aggregate of 75.36, the highest among the open-weight models we compare, and an MMAU Test-mini accuracy of 62.50%. Its largest margins over the baselines are on spoken knowledge and reasoning tasks, while the strongest baselines are more accurate on audio understanding and transcription. In a comparison with a 2B-parameter decoder, C-Gate achieves higher aggregate spoken-language performance than MLP and Q-Former interfaces, with text-task performance close to MLP and task-dependent tradeoffs in transcription and audio understanding. These results support convex combinations of text embeddings as a viable interface for general-purpose speech and audio language models.
papers.summary: Most speech and audio language models connect audio to a text-pretrained decoder through an MLP or `Q-Former` adapter, and the decoder must learn to interpret that adapter's outputs. `ConvexLLM` instead uses a `C-Gate` interface that represents audio as continuous convex combinations of the decoder's frozen text embeddings. The goal is to help the decoder use audio while preserving its text abilities. It scores **75.36 on the eleven-task `VoiceBench` aggregate, the highest among the open-weight models compared**, and 62.50% on `MMAU` Test-mini. Its largest margins are on spoken knowledge and reasoning, while stronger baselines remain better at transcription and audio understanding.

papers.title: Execution Before Memory: Diagnosing Memory Failures in Video World Models
papers.abstract: A memory test for a video world model should say whether the scene was set, whether the asked change was carried out, and whether the last frame shows the result. Current tests fold these into one number, so a low score is easy to read as forgetting. When the change is not carried out, the hidden state transition cannot appear, so the test is not really a test of memory. We introduce MIST, an evaluation that separates the change from the memory it should leave behind. The model first sets the scene while the change stays hidden, and only later is asked to show it, with leakage before that point kept under control. This separation locates the bottleneck: the model sets the scene but does not carry out the instructed change. The same gap appears in general memory evaluations. On that basis we propose M3-Agent (Make the Missing Move), which recursively revises the details of the input instruction so that the model successfully carries out the requested instruction. Relative to the baseline, it more than triples the MIST reveal score. On the benchmarks, WRBench's score T rises by 26.1% and MBench-T's score U by 52.7%. The method meets the problem from the execution side: it shows what the frozen model can do once the move is stated, and it sets a stricter baseline.
papers.summary: Current memory tests for video world models combine several steps into one score, so a model that never carries out a requested scene change looks as if it forgot. `MIST` separates setting up the scene, carrying out a hidden change, and later revealing it, while controlling for leakage. With this separation, the authors find that **models set the scene but fail to execute the instructed change**, and the same gap appears in general memory benchmarks. Their `M3-Agent` repeatedly revises the instruction until the frozen model carries it out, more than tripling the `MIST` reveal score and raising `WRBench` and `MBench` scores by 26.1% and 52.7%.
papers.highlight_summary:
Memory benchmarks for video world models give a single score, so a low result looks like forgetting even when the model never carried out the requested change at all. `MIST` scores scene setup, hidden-state leakage and the final reveal separately, and finds that the real bottleneck is execution rather than memory. `M3-Agent` builds on this by revising the failed instruction at test time on the same frozen generator.

- `MIST` uses three 5-second shots per case: the first sets the scene, the second hides the change behind an opaque gap, and the third asks for the reveal. On `Wan TI2V-5B` across 43 cases, setup scores **0.852** and gap leakage is **0/43**, yet **41 of 43** baseline clips never open to show the hidden state.
- `M3-Agent` writes a short task record, has a VLM label the failure it sees in the last frame (for example no action, wrong binding or a missing departure), and rewrites only the failed operation, with no trained memory module. With one kept clip per case, it lifts **MIST reveal from 0.147 to 0.492** while setup stays flat.
- In an ablation with five tries per arm, the targeted rewrite (**0.763** best-of-five reveal) beats naming the answer alone (0.684) and a generic "open and hold" prompt (0.268). With the target withheld, however, the rewrite collapses to **0.174** and leaves 28 of 43 lids closed.
- The same diagnosis carries over to official benchmarks with `Wan T2V-A14B`: `WRBench` score T rises **26.1% (0.452 to 0.570)**, mostly because the camera now completes the departure and return rather than because frames look better. `MBench-T` score U rises **52.7% (0.292 to 0.446)**, though selection keeps the baseline clip on 23 of 30 items.
- The authors limit their own claims: keep-best selection is an oracle that uses the same scorer that reports the results, rewrites can break cases that were already correct, the study covers one main generator family, and judges are not validated against human labels. A shown final state therefore does not prove the model actually stored it.

papers.title: Causal Discovery beyond Conditional Independence: Identifiability, Algorithms, and Statistical Inference for Directed Acyclic and Cyclic Graphs
papers.abstract: Learning causal structure from data requires assumptions about mechanisms, noises, observation schemes, and interventions. Historically, causal discovery has relied primarily on conditional independence. This review focuses on modern causal discovery methods that exploit properties of distributions beyond conditional independence. Our organizing principle separates the source of identification from the statistical estimator and its computational implementation. This perspective connects conditional-independence methods with distributional asymmetries, conditional-moment restrictions, and variation across environments or individuals. We examine discovery under latent confounding and feedback, distinguishing causal information about observed variables from reconstruction of latent structure and emphasizing the additional semantics required by cyclic models. We also distinguish population identification, frequentist and Bayesian consistency, uncertainty quantification, and algorithmic guarantees. Throughout, examples show why the same observational distribution can support different conclusions under different model classes. We conclude with guidance for comparing methods at their identifiable targets and a research agenda for uncertainty, heterogeneous populations, non-scalar variables, and the intersection of discrete data, feedback, and hidden confounding.
papers.summary: This review covers modern causal discovery methods that go beyond conditional-independence tests. Such methods exploit distributional asymmetries, conditional-moment restrictions, and variation across environments or individuals. Its organizing principle is to **separate what makes a causal structure identifiable from the statistical estimator and its algorithmic implementation**. It covers latent confounding and feedback loops, including the extra assumptions that cyclic models need. It distinguishes population-level identification, frequentist and Bayesian consistency, uncertainty quantification and algorithmic guarantees, uses examples to show how one observational distribution can support different conclusions under different model classes, and ends with guidance for comparing methods and a research agenda.

papers.title: Beyond Latent Personalization: Integrating HRV-Conditioned Personalization via LLM for Interpretable Stress Detection
papers.abstract: Stress detection based on heart rate variability (HRV) has received increasing attention. However, existing personalized approaches integrate personal attributes with HRV through latent representations, limiting the interpretability of their interactions. In this work, we propose an LLM-enhanced personalized stress detection framework that integrates HRV features and personal attributes through LLM-based semantic interpretation. The proposed framework achieves a 29.9% relative MCC improvement over the strongest baseline on TILES-2018 while providing human-readable descriptions of individual physiological responses. The results highlight the potential of LLM-based semantic interpretation for achieving both effective and interpretable personalized stress detection.
papers.summary: Personalized stress detection from heart rate variability (HRV) usually combines physiological signals with personal attributes inside opaque learned representations. The proposed framework instead has an LLM interpret HRV features and personal attributes in natural language. This produces human-readable descriptions of each person's physiological responses. On `TILES-2018` it achieves **a 29.9% relative improvement in Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) over the strongest baseline**.

papers.title: Beyond Expected Values: Risk-Sensitive Planning with Distributional Monte-Carlo Tree Search
papers.abstract: Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) typically stores only scalar mean estimates, which makes it poorly suited for tail-risk objectives such as conditional value-at-risk (CVaR).
