We introduce Categorical Thompson Sampling with Optimism (CATSO) and Particle Thompson Sampling with Optimism (PATSO), two distributional MCTS algorithms that maintain finite-support empirical backup laws at Q-edges. CATSO represents Q-edge laws with categorical atoms and Dirichlet Thompson sampling, while PATSO represents them with adaptive particles. Both algorithms select actions using the CVaR of a Thompson-sampled Q-edge law plus a polynomial optimism bonus, and propagate scalar continuation values through visit-weighted averages of child Q-edge CVaR scores. For the finite-depth nested CVaR planning target, we prove an $O(n^{-1/2})$ bound on the root value error after $n$ rollouts, which upper-bounds the risk-sensitive simple regret. CATSO adds a fixed-grid discretization bias, while capped PATSO adds a tunable Wasserstein compression bias. Experiments on stochastic planning benchmarks show that distributional Q-edges improve lower-tail return and reduce catastrophic outcomes when mean-optimal and risk-sensitive behavior differ.
papers.summary: Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) normally stores only average values, which makes it a poor fit for objectives about tail risk such as conditional value-at-risk (CVaR). The authors introduce `CATSO` and `PATSO`, two distributional MCTS algorithms that keep a full return distribution on each action edge, using categorical atoms or adaptive particles respectively. Both choose actions by the CVaR of a Thompson-sampled distribution plus an optimism bonus. For finite-depth nested CVaR planning, the authors **prove a root value error bound of O(n^-1/2) after n rollouts**. Experiments on stochastic planning benchmarks show better lower-tail returns and fewer catastrophic outcomes in settings where the average-optimal and risk-sensitive choices differ.

papers.title: A general recipe for data-adaptive anytime-valid envelopes for iterative algorithms
papers.abstract: Most convergence guarantees for iterative stochastic algorithms are stated at a fixed iteration count and do not justify stopping at a data-dependent time. Recent work has constructed anytime-valid envelopes that do, but deterministic envelopes are typically too conservative for practical stopping, and existing data-adaptive ones are derived case-by-case, each coupling a specific algorithm to a specific noise model and boundary construction. This paper provides a general recipe for constructing such anytime-valid data-adaptive boundaries for a large class of iterative algorithms. Performance measures of many of these algorithms satisfy a one-step recursion that reduces the entire error analysis to a single general requirement: time-uniform concentration for predictably weighted sums of noise. We formalize this through a strongly adapted sub-$\psi$ condition, and derive off-the-shelf boundary constructions via continuous and discrete mixtures, stitching, and product betting martingales. We show how these boundaries can be directly coupled with a separate algorithmic analysis that derives the one-step recursion to provide a class of readymade anytime-valid envelopes across diverse settings including stochastic gradient descent (SGD), temporal difference learning, and Bures-Wasserstein SGD. In particular, for SGD, our framework either recovers or significantly sharpens every existing envelope we are aware of. Our constructions come with explicit implementation details and are substantiated by numerical experiments.
papers.summary: Most convergence guarantees for stochastic iterative algorithms hold only at a fixed iteration count, so they do not justify stopping at a time chosen from the data. Earlier anytime-valid bounds that do allow this were either too conservative or derived separately for each algorithm. The authors give a general recipe that **reduces the problem to a single time-uniform concentration condition on weighted noise sums**, with ready-made boundary constructions based on mixtures, stitching and betting martingales. They apply it to stochastic gradient descent (`SGD`), temporal-difference learning and Bures-Wasserstein `SGD`. For `SGD`, the recipe recovers or significantly sharpens every existing bound the authors know of.

papers.title: BMuon: Budgeting Muon's Spectral Geometry for Structured Compressibility
papers.abstract: Muon has emerged as a strong optimizer for neural network training and admits an interpretation as steepest descent under a spectral-norm geometry. Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply when their MLP hidden channels are pruned after training. To reconcile Muon's optimization performance with structured compressibility, we introduce Budget Muon (BMuon), which modifies Muon's spectral geometry so that hidden channels across blocks compete for a shared allocation budget. The resulting oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under a family of norms that interpolate between Muon's geometry and structured sparse geometries. Our principal sparsity control is an interpretable global channel-allocation budget, rather than a setting-dependent sparsity-penalty coefficient. For linear factorization models, we show that Muon admits minimum-cost exact representations with redundant hidden width, whereas under the BMuon oracle geometry and a sufficiently scarce budget, every minimum-cost representation is width-minimal. For practical training, we derive a minorization-maximization surrogate for the exact allocation problem. On ImageNet-1K with ViT-S/16, BMuon improves over Muon under gradual structured MLP pruning, and its learned allocations provide a more effective pruning criterion than weight magnitude. On a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb, BMuon improves over Muon under post-training MLP channel pruning.
papers.summary: Transformers trained with the popular `Muon` optimizer can degrade sharply when hidden MLP channels are pruned after training. `BMuon` changes `Muon`'s spectral geometry so that hidden channels across blocks compete for a shared global allocation budget, which is controlled by one interpretable setting rather than a sparsity penalty coefficient. The authors prove that, in linear factorization models, a scarce budget forces every minimum-cost representation to be width-minimal. **`BMuon` improves on `Muon` under structured MLP pruning** both for `ViT-S/16` on `ImageNet-1K` and for a 1B-parameter `LLaMA`-style model trained on `FineWeb`. Its learned allocations are also a better pruning criterion than weight magnitude.

papers.title: MARS: Memory-Aware Routing for Session-Level LLM Assistants
papers.abstract: Long-term LLM assistants must repeatedly decide what prior context to expose and which model should answer as an interaction evolves. Existing memory systems and model routers usually make these decisions separately, although memory construction changes the evidence, distractors, and difficulty of the resulting input. We introduce MARS, a memory-aware routing framework that uses session state as a shared control interface between memory construction and model selection. A Query and Topic Manager (QTM) estimates compact decision-relevant state that guides a fixed state-conditioned memory policy and an online router, enabling each turn to receive an appropriate memory view and a suitable model under a quality-memory-cost trade-off. We evaluate MARS on RealMem and MultiChallenge with 16 system configurations each, covering long-history memory-driven interaction and bounded sessions with structured context interference. On RealMem, MARS preserves 98.2% of full-context GPT-4o's QA while using only 14.5% of its generation API cost, including both generation and controller calls for MARS, and achieves the strongest measured memory-recall and retrieval scores among compared systems. On MultiChallenge, MARS trails the strongest static system overall but approaches its performance at lower recorded cost on a mechanism-focused subset. Together, these results support a favorable quality-memory-cost trade-off for long-history, memory-dependent interaction.
papers.summary: Long-running LLM assistants must decide, turn by turn, which past context to show and which model should answer. Existing systems make these two choices separately, even though the memory choice changes how hard the question is. `MARS` couples them through a shared session state, estimated by a Query and Topic Manager (`QTM`), which drives both a fixed memory policy and an online model router that trades off quality, memory and cost. On `RealMem`, `MARS` **keeps 98.2% of full-context `GPT-4o` QA quality at 14.5% of its API cost** and achieves the best measured memory-recall and retrieval scores among compared systems. On `MultiChallenge`, it trails the strongest static system overall.

papers.title: Analyzing Occupational Gender Bias across the LLM Training Lifecycle
papers.abstract: Post-training is widely assumed to reduce the social biases language models inherit from pretraining, yet direct evidence for this assumption remains mixed. In this paper, we examine how gender disparities evolve across the language modeling pipeline. In particular, we study occupational gender bias in OLMo 3, a fully open language model family, across its post-training stages by prompting each checkpoint to generate open-ended narratives about synthetic personas given their occupation and education. We consider two settings, a gender-given setting in which the profile states the persona's gender explicitly and a gender-assumed setting in which it must be inferred by the model. We find that when gender is stated, post-training increases semantic diversity for male-coded profiles, whereas for female-coded profiles the increase is smaller after SFT and not significant after DPO and RLVR. When gender is assumed by the model, post-training affects narratives about female and male personas similarly. The model's own gender assumptions, however, show a consistent female-preferential skew relative to United States labor-force demographics, except for heavily male-dominated occupations. Every successive post-training stage monotonically increases the odds of attributing a female label over the base model. A provenance analysis of the supervised fine-tuning corpus finds only a modest 7.7% female-token surplus, too small to explain the size of these downstream effects. The project code is available under: https://github.com/manthangadhia/llm-lifecycle-bias.
papers.summary: Post-training is often assumed to reduce the social biases a model picks up in pretraining. The authors test this by tracking occupational gender bias across the post-training checkpoints of the fully open `OLMo 3` models, prompting each one to write narratives about synthetic personas. When the persona's gender is stated, post-training increases narrative diversity more for male-coded profiles than for female-coded ones. When the model must infer gender, it skews female relative to United States labor statistics, except in heavily male-dominated jobs, and **each successive stage (`SFT`, `DPO`, `RLVR`) monotonically raises the odds of a female label**. Only a 7.7% female-token surplus appears in the fine-tuning data, too small to explain the effect.

papers.title: Enhancing RAG-based Medical VQA with Gated Multimodal Representations
papers.abstract: Medical Vision-Language Models (Med-LVLMs) have shown strong performance in Medical Visual Question Answering (MVQA), yet they may still produce factually inconsistent responses. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can mitigate this issue by incorporating external clinical evidence; however, retrieval is often guided by a single modality, potentially overlooking the joint semantics of medical images and clinical questions. We introduce a multimodal RAG framework that learns a joint query representation through a Gated Multimodal Unit, enabling evidence retrieval to leverage information from both modalities while keeping the underlying Med-LVLM frozen. We evaluate the proposed approach on benchmark datasets. Results show that the multimodal query representation consistently outperforms a reference Med-LVLM and remains competitive with state-of-the-art methods. Our findings demonstrate the potential of multimodal query representations for more effective evidence retrieval in Medical VQA.
papers.summary: Medical vision-language models (`Med-LVLMs`) can give factually inconsistent answers in medical visual question answering, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can help by adding external clinical evidence. Most such retrieval, however, is driven by only the image or only the question. The proposed framework uses a Gated Multimodal Unit to learn a joint image-and-question query for retrieval, while keeping the underlying model frozen. On benchmark datasets, **the multimodal query consistently outperforms the reference `Med-LVLM`** and remains competitive with state-of-the-art methods.

papers.title: Boundary Detection for High-Dimensional Point Clouds
papers.abstract: We introduce two new methods for boundary detection in high-dimensional point cloud data, intended to work in situations with non-uniform density, high ambient dimension, and substantial noise. Our first method fits a separating hyperplane on local neighborhoods after doing local dimension reduction---this method works best when one can reliably estimate the intrinsic dimension of the data. Our second method measures the directional uniformity of local neighborhoods, and has the best overall performance on synthetic data. In addition to pointwise numerical boundary scores, our algorithms yield an estimated normal vector at each boundary point. We validate our methodology on synthetic data as well as two real examples: we analyze spatial transcriptomics data, where we show that we can detect the boundary of a tumor, and we also study LLM activation geometry.
papers.summary: Two new methods find the boundary points of high-dimensional point clouds and are built to cope with uneven density, high ambient dimension and heavy noise. The first reduces dimension locally and then fits a separating hyperplane on each neighborhood, and it works best when the intrinsic dimension of the data can be estimated reliably. The second measures how uniformly a local neighborhood spreads across directions, and it gives **the best overall performance on synthetic data**. Both methods also estimate a normal vector at each boundary point. The authors show them finding a tumor boundary in spatial transcriptomics data and use them to study the geometry of LLM activations.

papers.title: When Magnitude Suffices: Reconstructing Time-Domain-Gated Microwave Signals Without Phase on a Thoracic Phantom
papers.abstract: Time-domain gating separates the arrivals that form a microwave S-parameter measurement. It requires the measurement of complex values, so this application almost always uses a vector network analyzer (VNA). We show that, on one calibrated measurement configuration, the gated magnitude the VNA would give can be reconstructed from a magnitude-only sweep of a spectrum analyzer with a tracking generator (SA). We select the gate center for separability of the measured states, correct each instrument once by a per-bin subtraction of a reference state, and train a fully connected network on sweeps from both instruments. The test object is a torso phantom with lung-shaped compartments whose filling takes eleven dielectric states, each held out in turn. On $S_{11}$ the reconstruction from SA input reaches a shape error of 0.08 dB$^2$ with a state ordering of 0.81. This matches the reconstruction from VNA input. On $S_{21}$ it reaches 0.82 dB$^2$ and keeps the ordered groups of the states. An explicit phase prediction performs much worse, because gating needs the phase to about 0.2 rad RMS. Across eleven measurement configurations the dependence of phase on magnitude is strong for reflection and weak for transmission. This explains the difference between $S_{11}$ and $S_{21}$. Where the magnitude carries enough of the phase, a scalar instrument gives the gated response without any phase measurement after installation. On the open UM-BMID breast data set, with whole phantoms held out, the shape error of the network is 30 percent lower than that of a per-bin linear map.
papers.summary: Time-domain gating normally requires complex-valued S-parameter measurements from a vector network analyzer (VNA). The authors show that, for one calibrated setup, the gated magnitude can be reconstructed from a cheaper magnitude-only spectrum analyzer with a tracking generator (SA). They correct each instrument against a reference state and train a fully connected network on sweeps of a thoracic phantom with eleven lung-filling dielectric states. On reflection (S11), the reconstruction from SA input **matches the reconstruction from VNA input**, while transmission (S21) is harder because there magnitude carries little information about phase. On the open `UM-BMID` breast dataset, the network's shape error is 30% lower than that of a per-bin linear map.

papers.title: Not Every Mention Is a Claim: Rethinking Object Hallucination Detection in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Object hallucination in vision-language models (VLMs) is usually measured by checking each object a caption names against the image. Most benchmarks and detectors alike treat every object mention as a claim that the object is present. This assumption fails when a caption names an object without asserting it, as in "a bench for people to sit on", which mentions people without claiming that any are in the image. We call such mentions non-assertive. Treating them as hallucinations inflates the error rates attributed to models that use such language. To separate them from real hallucinations, we introduce NAME-Bench (Non-Assertive Mention Evaluation Benchmark), 25,497 object mentions from captions that five VLMs generate for COCO images. Each mention is labelled concrete (asserted and present), hallucinated (asserted and absent), or non-assertive, and non-assertive mentions are further divided into four subtypes: depictive, purpose, negation and hedged. All the hallucination detectors that we evaluate flag non-assertive mentions as hallucinations, at rates between 14% and 80%. Adding non-assertive mentions to detector training as negatives largely corrects this on LLaVA-1.5. On the four newer VLMs, a comparable correction takes five to ten times more data, and the detectors then catch fewer real hallucinations. These findings show that current detectors conflate mentioning an object with asserting it, and that this conflation is harder to undo on the four newer VLMs than on LLaVA-1.5. Hallucination evaluation should therefore separate what a caption asserts from what it merely mentions.
papers.summary: Object hallucination benchmarks for vision-language models (VLMs) usually count every object a caption names as a claim that the object is present. That miscounts "non-assertive" mentions, such as the people in "a bench for people to sit on". The authors release `NAME-Bench`, 25,497 object mentions from captions that five VLMs wrote for `COCO` images. Each mention is labelled concrete, hallucinated, or one of four non-assertive subtypes. Every detector they evaluate **flags non-assertive mentions as hallucinations at rates of 14% to 80%**. Training on these mentions as negatives fixes the problem for `LLaVA-1.5`, but newer VLMs need five to ten times more data, and the detectors then catch fewer real hallucinations.

papers.title: How Many, but How Sure? Class Competition as a Confidence Proxy in Multi-Class Density-Based Counting
papers.abstract: Multi-class density estimators can count objects in crowded scenes, but their class-wise outputs offer no indication of how reliably density mass has been allocated. We introduce a training-free confidence proxy based on local competition between the strongest class channels. The resulting prominence measure requires only the predicted density maps, with no retraining or access to model internals. We test whether residual competition is diagnostic of cross-class leakage by attenuating contested density at inference time. On DSACA predictions for the Hicks et al. dataset, this reduces overall MAE from 0.920 to 0.846, suggesting that class competition contains useful information about count reliability.
papers.summary: Multi-class density estimators count objects in crowded scenes but give no signal of how reliably they assigned density to each class. The authors propose a training-free confidence proxy that measures local competition between the strongest class channels, and it needs only the predicted density maps. Down-weighting contested density at inference time on `DSACA` predictions for the Hicks et al. dataset **reduces overall mean absolute error (MAE) from 0.920 to 0.846**. This suggests that class competition carries information about how reliable a count is.

papers.title: SIT-Eval: Situation-Based Interactive Turn-by-Turn Evaluation of Conversational Agents
papers.abstract: The rapid proliferation of conversational AI agents necessitates evaluation methods that assess performance across diverse dialogue scenarios, utilizing multiple situational criteria, as appropriate behavior depends on context and encompasses various aspects. Existing dialogue benchmarks typically use static natural conversations, which underrepresent rare situations---a critical safety gap, as low-probability events become frequent failures at production scale. However, limited sample sizes force a choice: either maintain natural dialogues for realism or turn to adaptive situation sampling for comprehensive yet statistically reliable coverage. We introduce SIT-Eval, an adjustable framework for evaluating situation-based conversational agents. We formalize an agent's desired behavior as situational rules: if situation is P, follow rules Q. At each conversation turn, an LLM-interlocutor enacts a uniformly sampled situation. A context-aware LLM-judge leverages all conditionally applicable rules as criteria to evaluate the agent's reply for that situation. The judge is validated using human-verified synthetic golden dialogues. Benchmarking 8 LLMs on 1292 conversation turns reveals failure modes hidden by aggregate metrics: models with similar overall scores vary widely in their adherence to individual rules. All models struggle most with ambiguity clarification and Socratic questioning.
papers.summary: Static dialogue benchmarks rarely contain the unusual situations that become frequent failures once a conversational agent runs at production scale. `SIT-Eval` writes an agent's desired behavior as situational rules of the form "if situation P, follow rules Q". At each turn, an LLM interlocutor acts out a uniformly sampled situation, and a context-aware LLM judge scores the reply against every rule that applies. The judge is validated on human-verified synthetic dialogues. Across 8 LLMs and 1,292 turns, **models with similar overall scores differ widely on individual rules**, and all of them struggle most with clarifying ambiguity and with Socratic questioning.

papers.title: Trajectory-Triggered Sparse Collaborative Decoding
papers.abstract: Dense assistance methods such as speculative decoding repeatedly verify draft tokens with a target model, keeping target computation coupled to generation. We study sparse collaborative decoding, where a draft model generates most tokens and a target model is invoked only for short corrective segments. The key problem is deciding when to call the target. We show that local uncertainty is a weak trigger: entropy, negative log-likelihood, logit margin, top-$k$ mass, and velocity features give near-chance failure prediction, with AUC 0.50-0.53. In contrast, aggregate trajectory-shape features over the draft confidence path reach AUC 0.86 using a lightweight logistic predictor trained only from draft correctness labels. This induces a trigger-timing tradeoff: early calls have more leverage but weaker evidence, while later calls have stronger evidence but less ability to redirect the trajectory. Used online, learned sparse collaborative decoding improves over the best open-loop schedule by +5.3 to +20.0 accuracy points across five GSM8K draft-target pairs. On MATH-500, it gains 7.0-13.5 points when early prediction and target competence align, but loses when either is weak. On StrategyQA, it improves over open-loop by 5.0-8.3 points, showing transfer beyond arithmetics.
papers.summary: Sparse collaborative decoding lets a small draft model generate most of the tokens and calls a larger target model only for short corrective segments, unlike speculative decoding, which verifies tokens continually. The hard part is deciding when to call the target. Local uncertainty signals such as entropy and logit margin predict draft failures at near chance (AUC 0.50 to 0.53), while **features describing the shape of the draft's confidence trajectory reach an AUC of 0.86** with a simple logistic predictor. Used online, this trigger beats the best fixed schedule by 5.3 to 20.0 accuracy points on `GSM8K` and by 5.0 to 8.3 points on `StrategyQA`. Results on `MATH-500` are mixed and depend on how early failures can be predicted and on how capable the target model is.

papers.title: The Sign Code: The Hidden Binary Nature of Deep Networks
papers.abstract: Every neuron in a trained network outputs a number that can be separated into its sign (positive or negative) and its magnitude (absolute size). We call the set of all neuron signs the \textit{sign code}. This raises a key question: does classification depend more on the sign code or on the magnitudes? For overparameterized vision classifiers with sign-preserving activations, the answer is overwhelmingly the sign code. A $k$-nearest neighbor classifier operating only on this binary sign code achieves accuracy comparable to the full model across different architectures, activation functions, and datasets. Moreover, replacing all magnitudes in every layer with random noise while keeping the original signs barely changes residual network performance. In contrast, flipping just 20\% of the signs reduces accuracy to chance. Models generalize well when same-class inputs share similar sign codes. When this overlap is disrupted by a regularizer, training accuracy remains high, but test performance collapses. A margin decomposition helps explain these results: the sign-only contribution to each logit grows as $\sqrt{d}$ in network width, dominating the magnitude residual. The natural unit of analysis for these networks may not be through their continuous weight space but instead through their discrete sign codes.
papers.summary: The authors ask whether trained vision classifiers rely more on the signs of their neuron outputs, which they call the "sign code", or on the magnitudes. For overparameterized networks with sign-preserving activations, a k-nearest-neighbor classifier that sees only the binary sign code matches the full model's accuracy across architectures and datasets. **Replacing every magnitude in a residual network with random noise barely changes accuracy, while flipping 20% of the signs drops it to chance.** A margin decomposition explains this: the sign-only contribution to each logit grows with the square root of network width and dominates the magnitude term. Generalization also tracks how much same-class inputs share sign codes.

papers.title: ThetreStageAI: Multi-View Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Structured Bengali Theatre Production Planning
papers.abstract: Staging a theatre performance requires coordinating dialogue, actor movement, stage directions, lighting focus, cue timing, and equipment constraints within the same production plan. This work presents ThetreStageAI, a retrieval augmented framework for structured Bengali theatre production planning. Rather than retrieving from one mixed corpus, the system maintains separate scene, actor-blocking, and lighting views. Bengali text is embedded with BGE-M3 and indexed in view-specific Qdrant collections. Retrieved references are combined with a production brief and passed to Gemini, which generates schema-constrained JSON containing characters, scenes, dialogue, stage directions, blocking, lighting, and optional sound cues. Structural and semantic checks are applied before acceptance, with at most one constrained repair attempt. We also construct a human-guided, LLM-assisted synthetic dataset of 500 short Bengali theatre records that expands to 1,500 retrieval documents. Dataset diagnostics confirm consistent identifiers and valid lighting fields while also revealing substantial dialogue repetition. A paired camera-ready evaluation compares single-combined and full multi-view retrieval under matched settings. The source code, dataset, and evaluation materials are publicly available.
papers.summary: `ThetreStageAI` is a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system for planning Bengali theatre productions, covering dialogue, actor blocking, lighting and cues. Instead of one mixed corpus, it keeps separate scene, actor-blocking and lighting indexes, embedded with `BGE-M3` and stored in `Qdrant`. It feeds the retrieved references to `Gemini`, which produces schema-constrained JSON, and the output gets structural and semantic checks plus at most one repair attempt. The authors also build a synthetic dataset of 500 Bengali theatre records, expanded into 1,500 retrieval documents, and **compare single-corpus with multi-view retrieval** under matched settings.

papers.title: GRAFT-EEG: Gauge-Aware Physical Field Transport for Cross-Dataset Motor-Imagery EEG
papers.abstract: Cross-dataset EEG decoding often treats montage, reference, and active-sensor changes as representation shift, although they also alter the observation operator. We study target-statistics-blind transfer: fitting receives no target signal, label, or empirical statistic, and electrode coordinates only instantiate a fixed prediction operator. method removes the active-set common-reference gauge and transports each native mask through a template motor leadfield. A source-fitted spectral classifier anchors the decision; a bounded state-space-model (SSM) residual is secondary. We establish restricted identifiability and an operator-perturbation bound. Across five leave-one-dataset-out targets (253 participants), dynamic method achieved 60.865% equal-target balanced accuracy versus 52.684% for strict-clean 5/5 BIOT (hierarchical difference +8.182 points; 95% CI +6.382 to +10.196; positive in every target). On four EEGPT-clean targets, the descriptive means were 61.520% and 59.057%. In four post-hoc exact same-parent tests, FULL exceeded coordinate-basis, matched-spectrum, row-shuffled, and wrong-anatomy controls by 9.959, 9.698, 11.241, and 3.985 points, respectively (all 95% CIs excluded zero; Holm-adjusted P<0.001). A separate 60-participant same-paradigm evaluation retained a positive physical-operator contrast (+4.029 points; +2.338 to +5.773), whereas dynamic--static was inconclusive; its preregistered status is partial confirmation rather than unrestricted external validation. The SSM added +1.059 points (+0.013 to +1.892). Claims remain bounded to five binary motor-imagery domains and the tested operators.
papers.summary: When EEG decoders move between datasets, differences in electrode montage and reference change the observation operator itself, not only the data's representation. `GRAFT-EEG` removes the common-reference effect and maps each dataset's electrode set through a template motor leadfield, then classifies with a source-space spectral model plus a small state-space-model (SSM) residual, all without using any target-dataset statistics. In leave-one-dataset-out tests on five motor-imagery datasets with 253 participants, it reaches **60.9% balanced accuracy, against 52.7% for `BIOT`**. Control experiments with scrambled or wrong-anatomy operators confirm that the physical model drives the gain.

papers.title: Deconstructing Multi-Task Active Learning: The Paradox of Gradient Conflict and Orthogonal Decomposition
papers.abstract: Existing multi-task active learning (MTL-AL) methods predominantly rely on linear scalarization of heterogeneous objectives such as uncertainty, diversity, and gradient conflict. We argue that this entangled formulation is fundamentally limited, as linear combination fails to capture Pareto-optimal trade-offs under conflicting objectives. We propose a shift from combination to deconstruction and introduce a principled framework that rethinks MTL-AL along three orthogonal dimensions. First, we identify the Conflict Paradox: although the optimization literature treats gradient conflict as interference to be suppressed, penalizing conflict when ranking candidates is measurably worse than not scoring it at all. We therefore decouple the two concerns: the acquisition function does not score conflict, and the resulting interference is resolved by gradient surgery during training. Second, we introduce Orthogonal Decomposition, separating acquisition into Informativeness and Exploration. This two-stage process, informativeness filtering followed by coverage maximization, prevents "diversity dilution" by excluding uninformative outliers before enforcing diversity. Third, we propose Cross-Task Mutual Information (CTMI), a covariance-based statistic of cross-task dependency computed from MC-dropout task entropies. Extensive experiments on COCO, Cityscapes, and NYUv2, including comparisons against recent MTL-AL and data-selection baselines, demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, highlighting that structural rethinking of acquisition yields larger gains than incremental heuristic design. Code is available at https://github.com/Juho-Jung/multitask_active_learning_official.
papers.summary: Multi-task active learning methods usually rank unlabeled samples with a weighted sum of uncertainty, diversity and gradient conflict. The authors report a "Conflict Paradox": **penalizing gradient conflict when choosing samples does worse than ignoring it**, so they leave conflict to gradient surgery during training instead. They split acquisition into an informativeness filter followed by coverage maximization, which keeps uninformative outliers from diluting diversity. They also propose Cross-Task Mutual Information (`CTMI`), a measure of cross-task dependency computed from MC-dropout task entropies. Experiments on `COCO`, `Cityscapes` and `NYUv2` show consistent gains over state-of-the-art baselines.

papers.title: PresenceBench: An Exploratory Evaluation of Large Language Model Adaptation to User State
papers.abstract: Presence-aware intelligence is the capacity of an AI system's intelligence layer to adapt appropriately to the functional state of the person it serves (here readiness, flow, and stability) while preserving task quality and safety. We introduce PresenceBench, an instrument for measuring it. PresenceBench evaluates how the intelligence layer uses a supplied state, not how that state is sensed, and breaks the capability into measurable properties. Two are tested here. Receptivity: does the model take up the state and give a better response than with no signal? Specificity: does any improvement depend on the correct state, rather than on extra structured context? A third, adaptation across states, is a required endpoint not measured in this release. A five-arm causal design answers both questions, against each model's own baseline and an equally structured mismatched-state control, scored by a correctness-gated human paired comparison. The exploratory evaluation covered four models across eighteen single-turn, six fixed three-turn and six simulated natural-conversation scenarios. Supplying a synthetic state, raw or translated into a response policy, gave human-preference point estimates above 0.5 for all four models (Claude Sonnet 5, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Gemini 3.6 Flash, GPT-5.6 Terra), with three of eight 95% intervals excluding chance. Specificity was not resolved: no per-model interval excluded chance, and the design cannot yet separate the state values from a generic instruction to adapt. Policy delivery reduced priced cost and output tokens against each model's baseline; these are resource-use changes, not efficiency gains, because correctness non-inferiority was not established. Safety-floor failures were rare (13 of 360 cases), with a non-significant excess under policy delivery. We report the instrument, the frozen results, and the controls a confirmatory study needs.
papers.summary: `PresenceBench` measures whether an LLM gives better answers when it is told the user's functional state, such as readiness, flow or stability. A five-arm causal design with a mismatched-state control tests two properties: whether the model uses the state at all, and whether any gain depends on the correct state. Human-preference estimates favored state-informed responses for all four models tested (`Claude Sonnet 5`, `DeepSeek V4 Pro`, `Gemini 3.6 Flash`, `GPT-5.6 Terra`), but only three of eight confidence intervals excluded chance. **Whether the gain depends on the correct state remained unresolved**, and the authors frame the release as exploratory.

papers.title: Deep LLM layers expose passage-level context in EEG during silent reading
papers.abstract: In a previous report we showed that a decoder can recover open-vocabulary word-level information from 19-channel EEG recorded during silent reading, by aligning short EEG windows with hidden-state embeddings of the presented word taken from a large language model (LLM). That analysis contrasted two of the model's 33 layers: the context-free input embedding and one mid-depth layer. Here we ask how EEG-decodable structure is distributed over the full depth of the language model. We trained one decoder per layer of Llama-3.1-8B, with and without a causal transformer over the sequence of EEG windows. We distinguish word-level decodability from a context-tracking component. Word-level decodability peaks in early layers and declines steadily towards the last layer. In contrast, the context-tracking component of the retrieval gain rises with depth, both with and without a causal transformer. Unexpectedly, a decoder that sees a single 0.5-s window at a time tracks the text passage too. Two new controls dissect this component. A target-geometry control, a synthetic predictor made of the true target plus noise calibrated to each decoder's word-level accuracy, shows that context tracking is not a by-product of word decoding and target geometry. A control that permutes predictions across runs from either the same or from different sessions shows that most of the observed context-tracking is not caused by an EEG recording session signature. Instead, context tracking mostly follows the text. A single EEG window therefore carries passage-level information that a contextual target can absorb. The results locate word identity in the early layers of the language model, discourse state in the deeper layers, and make the choice of target layer a design dial for EEG language decoders.
papers.summary: Building on earlier work that decoded words from 19-channel EEG recorded during silent reading, the authors train one decoder per layer of `Llama-3.1-8B` to see where EEG-decodable information sits in the model. Word-level decodability peaks in early layers and declines with depth, while **a context-tracking component that follows the text passage grows in deeper layers**. Even a decoder that sees a single 0.5-second EEG window tracks the passage. Controls show this is neither a by-product of word decoding nor a recording-session signature. The choice of target layer therefore works as a design dial for EEG language decoders.

papers.title: No-Regret Language Generation
papers.abstract: We introduce no-regret generation, which requires a generator to make a sublinear number of mistakes uniformly over all demonstration sequences and compatible target languages. We also formulate an agnostic variant that allows arbitrary demonstrations that may not be compatible with any languages. For both settings, we introduce tree-based mistake-forcing dimensions that exactly characterize finite-horizon minimax complexity and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for no-regret generation. Our characterizations reveal a rich spectrum of generation rates: up to constant rescaling, every admissible nondecreasing profile is attainable in both the realizable and agnostic settings. Finally, we connect generation complexity to online prediction: for language classes of finite Littlestone dimension \(d\), we obtain realizable mistake bounds of \(O(d\log(1+T/d))\) and agnostic regret bounds of \(O(\sqrt{dT\log(1+T/d)})\). The realizable bound is optimal up to universal constants.
papers.summary: The authors define no-regret language generation, in which a generator must make a sublinear number of mistakes for every sequence of demonstrations and every compatible target language. They also define an agnostic variant in which the demonstrations need not fit any language. New tree-based "mistake-forcing" dimensions exactly characterize the minimax complexity in both settings and show that essentially any admissible growth rate of mistakes is achievable. For language classes of finite Littlestone dimension d, they prove a realizable mistake bound of O(d log(1+T/d)), which is **optimal up to constants**, and an agnostic regret bound of O(sqrt(dT log(1+T/d))).

papers.title: Scalable long-range machine learning interatomic potentials with electrical response for atomistic material modeling
papers.abstract: Accurate atomistic simulations of materials under electric fields require long-range electrostatics and electrical-response modeling at length scales beyond the reach of conventional first-principles methods. Yet these capabilities remain difficult to reconcile with the scalability of machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs). Strictly local models enable efficient spatial parallelization but neglect long-range interactions, whereas existing electrostatic extensions introduce global dependencies that hinder distributed computation. Here, we overcome this limitation by analytically separating the long-range electrostatic forces and Born effective charges (BECs) into a global electrostatics calculation and strictly local derivatives of learned latent charges. This formulation preserves the spatial decomposability of equivariant MLIPs while enabling distributed evaluation of energies, forces, stresses, and BECs across different boundary conditions. Implemented as DPA4C-LR on the \texttt{nvalchemi} platform, the framework scales to 5.2 million atoms on four GPUs at approximately twice the computational cost of its short-range backbone. Trained on energies and forces, DPA4C-LR accurately infers BECs and reproduces the field-dependent infrared spectra of water. We further demonstrate its capabilities by recovering the characteristic slim polarization hysteresis of relaxor \ce{Pb(Mg_{1/3}Nb_{2/3})O3}, which is obscured by finite-size effects in smaller simulations; predicting a room-temperature field-driven ionic conductivity of $6.8 \pm 0.7$~mS/cm in amorphous \ce{Li_{0.9}NbO_{0.9}Cl_{4.1}}; and modeling interfacial thermal transport across Si/diamond interfaces with slab-corrected electrostatics. By combining long-range physics, electrical-response inference, and distributed computation, this framework extends predictive atomistic modeling toward device-relevant length scales.
papers.summary: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) that include long-range electrostatics usually lose the locality that lets them run in parallel across many GPUs. The authors separate long-range forces and Born effective charges into one global electrostatics calculation plus strictly local derivatives of learned latent charges. Implemented as `DPA4C-LR` on the `nvalchemi` platform, the model **scales to 5.2 million atoms on four GPUs at about twice the cost of its short-range backbone**. It reproduces the field-dependent infrared spectra of water and the polarization hysteresis of a relaxor ferroelectric, and it predicts ionic conductivity in an amorphous solid electrolyte.

papers.title: JAXtari: High-Throughput and Easy-to-Modify Arcade Learning Environment
papers.abstract: The Arcade Learning Environment (ALE) has been a cornerstone of Deep Reinforcement Learning research, providing a standardized benchmark for evaluating general agents. However, its lack of native support for object-extraction and environment modification restricts research into evaluating whether agents learn robust causal models or rely on brittle visual heuristics. Furthermore, the ALE's dependence on CPU-based emulation creates a significant bottleneck in modern GPU-accelerated training pipelines, limiting both experimental scale and iteration frequency. In this work, we introduce JAXtari, an open-source, high-performance reimplementation of Atari 2600 environments. By leveraging massive GPU parallelization, JAXtari allows PPO agents to finish training on 100M environment steps on a single A100-GPU in under an hour. Beyond speed, it provides object-centric observations and a flexible modification system, allowing researchers to, e.g. develop neuro-symbolic methods or discover novel shortcuts and subsequently train and adapt their agents rapidly, sometimes in only minutes.
papers.summary: The Arcade Learning Environment (`ALE`) emulates Atari games on the CPU, which bottlenecks GPU-based reinforcement learning, and it offers no easy way to extract objects or modify games. `JAXtari` reimplements Atari 2600 environments in JAX for massive GPU parallelism, so that **`PPO` agents finish 100M environment steps on a single A100 in under an hour**. It also provides object-centric observations and a system for modifying games, which helps when testing whether agents rely on shortcuts and when building neuro-symbolic methods.

papers.title: In Human Memories. Technology, Creativity and Self-Determination: An Ethical Proposal
papers.abstract: This research investigates the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in modern compositional practices, with a particular focus on two case studies: Convergence (2020/21) by Alexander Schubert, for String Ensemble and AI System, and In Human Memories (2024) by Francesco Vitucci, for four cellos and one electroacoustic player, whose installation was created by the Electronic Music School of the "N. Piccinni" Conservatory of Bari. The initial historical survey traces the evolving use of technology in composition, revealing how the search for new expressive possibilities has driven the development of technological tools through experimentation. The appearance of AI marks a fundamental shift: no longer just a tool, AI now poses questions and challenges to the composer. Engaging with AI becomes an exploration of an unknown entity, whose full capabilities are still largely undiscovered. This new interaction leads composers to confront AI not merely as a passive resource but as a participant in the creative process, outlining an ethical path to reclaim technology as a creative tool. In Human Memories reflects this dynamic, demonstrating how AI can serve as both inspiration and a driving force in shaping contemporary music.
papers.summary: Through two case studies, Alexander Schubert's `Convergence` for string ensemble and AI system and Francesco Vitucci's `In Human Memories` for four cellos and electroacoustics, the author examines how AI is changing musical composition. After a historical survey of technology in composition, the essay argues that **AI acts as a participant in the creative process rather than a passive tool**. It proposes an ethical path in which composers reclaim technology as a creative instrument.

papers.title: A Language-Informed Loss for Visual Generation
papers.abstract: End-to-end visual generation with pixel-space loss has recently achieved competitive performance without the need for learned image tokenizers. In this work, we study whether language-informed supervision can provide a richer training signal than pixel loss for visual generation. We introduce LILIE (pronounced "lily"), a Language-Informed and Lossless Image Encoder. LILIE is an invertible image transform trained such that a vision-language model can recover captions from noised features. The encoder uses a normalizing flow transformer trained jointly with a vision-language model via next token prediction. We then use the encoder to extract a simple language-informed loss for text-to-image generation. We train JiT models with LILIE loss, reducing gFD by 14 points (66.84 $\to$ 53.01) against a pixel-only baseline on the GPIC dataset. Our code, encoders, and generative models are available at https://suchiragarwal.com/lilie.
papers.summary: The authors test whether supervision informed by language can give pixel-space image generators a richer training signal than plain pixel loss. They build `LILIE`, an invertible image encoder based on a normalizing-flow transformer, and train it jointly with a vision-language model so that captions can be recovered from noised features. The encoder then supplies a language-informed loss for text-to-image training. Trained with this loss, `JiT` models **cut gFD from 66.84 to 53.01** against a pixel-only baseline on the `GPIC` dataset.

papers.title: An Efficient Approach to Beetle Damage Detection of Banana Using Deep Learning
papers.abstract: Visible surface damage of banana fruits by Basilepta subcostata (the banana fruit scarring beetle) can reduce their market value. Here, manual inspection of Banana fruits is subjective and difficult to scale. This study presents a lightweight framework based on YOLOv8n deep learning model for locating individual bananas and classifying their visible surface condition as healthy or unhealthy. The term beetle damage in the paper title is used operationally for the locally observed scar-like surface condition; the model does not identify a specific beetle species or biological cause. A custom dataset of 2,473 images containing 5,827 annotated banana instances was prepared from local-market imagery in Bangladesh. The reported experiment used an 80/20 protocol with 1,982 training images and 491 test images. A pretrained YOLOv8n model was trained at 640x640 resolution for 50 epochs with a batch size of 4. On the test partition, it achieved 81.36% precision, 74.30% recall, 77.67% F1-score, 87.04% mAP@0.50 and 59.33% mAP@0.50:0.95. A YOLOv8s comparison gave slightly lower F1 and mAP while using a substantially larger checkpoint. The YOLOv8n checkpoint occupied 5.96 MB and required 6.54 ms/image for inference on an NVIDIA Tesla T4. The results support YOLOv8n as a compact baseline for instance-level banana surface inspection within the studied acquisition conditions.
papers.summary: A lightweight `YOLOv8n` detector locates individual bananas and classifies their surface as healthy or scarred, the kind of damage associated with the banana fruit-scarring beetle. It is trained on a custom dataset of 2,473 images with 5,827 annotated bananas from local markets in Bangladesh. The model reaches **87.04% mAP@0.50** and a 77.67% F1 score. The 5.96 MB checkpoint runs at 6.54 ms per image on a T4 GPU, and the larger `YOLOv8s` scored slightly lower.

papers.title: TriRouter: Sparse-to-Dense Electrode-Space Routing for Robust EEG Motor Imagery Decoding
papers.abstract: Motor imagery brain-computer interfaces require reliable decoding from multichannel EEG, but practical acquisition often yields sparse or corrupted electrode montages. We propose TriRouter, an electrode-space routing framework with discriminative-preservation, mask-robustness, and latent-compensation paths. A validation-calibrated router uses observable channel availability to allocate path contributions, preserving complete-channel discrimination while increasing representation recovery under severe missingness. In BNCI2014-001, TriRouter outperforms standard public backbones and a dynamic-spatial-filtering corrupted-EEG baseline. It improves accuracy over the strongest corrupted-EEG baseline by 3.68, 4.02, and 6.46 percentage points at nominal 25%, 50%, and 75% missing settings, and remains effective under structured regional missingness and additional low-channel dataset evaluation.
papers.summary: Motor-imagery brain-computer interfaces often have to decode EEG from sparse or corrupted electrode sets. `TriRouter` combines three paths, one that preserves discriminative features, one robust to missing channels and one that compensates in latent space, and a calibrated router weights them by which channels are available. On `BNCI2014-001`, it **beats the strongest corrupted-EEG baseline by 3.68, 4.02 and 6.46 percentage points** at 25%, 50% and 75% missing channels. The gains hold under region-structured missingness as well.

papers.title: Beyond the Benchmark: Conditioning, Domains and Failure Modes of Qwen3-TTS
papers.abstract: Qwen3-TTS reports state-of-the-art zero-shot voice cloning, but its technical report leaves open how the model should be conditioned, how it behaves outside read speech, and how it fails. We characterise its two cloning interfaces, in-context learning (ICL) and X-Vector, against Chatterbox, XTTS-v2 and F5-TTS on read, meeting, emotional and air-traffic-control (ATC) speech, using eighteen objective measures, an LLM judge, a spoofing countermeasure and a listening test. Neither interface dominates: ICL clones timbre more closely from correctly transcribed references, X-Vector clones timing, and ICL degrades sharply when a short reference transcript is wrong. Domain explains four times more variance than system choice. Qwen3-TTS leads on intelligibility and pitch register but trails on prosody, and the objective measures rank systems differently from listeners. An off-the-shelf countermeasure flags its clones no more often than genuine recordings, and on ATC radio it fails for every system. Code and audio are released.
papers.summary: The authors probe `Qwen3-TTS` beyond its technical report. They compare its two voice-cloning interfaces, in-context learning (ICL) and X-Vector, against `Chatterbox`, `XTTS-v2` and `F5-TTS` on read, meeting, emotional and air-traffic-control speech. Neither interface wins outright, ICL degrades sharply when the reference transcript is wrong, and **domain explains four times more variance than the choice of system**. Objective metrics rank systems differently from human listeners, and an off-the-shelf anti-spoofing detector flags the clones no more often than genuine recordings.

papers.title: HardEval: An Execution-Verified Benchmark for AI-Driven Security Hardening and Compliance Remediation
papers.abstract: Implementing Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) controls remains a demanding operating-system administration task. Each natural-language security requirement must be translated into a precise and persistent configuration change. These changes span Secure Shell (SSH) configuration, authentication policy, audit rules, and kernel parameters. Existing benchmarks do not measure whether a model can perform this task on a live system. Code benchmarks evaluate isolated programs without persistent system state, while agent benchmarks largely focus on applications rather than operating-system configuration. In this paper, we introduce \textbf{HardEval}, an execution-verified benchmark for evaluating language-model-assisted security hardening. HardEval is built from Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 STIG controls that fail on an unhardened baseline system. Expert-written reference remediations and Open Vulnerability and Assessment Language (OVAL) checks serve as hidden ground truth for grading; they are never shown to the model, and each task states only the required security outcome while withholding the implementation. The model produces a Bash script, which is executed on a live virtual machine and graded from fail to pass using the corresponding OpenSCAP/OVAL compliance check. Evaluation of fourteen frontier and open-weight configurations reveals large and uneven capability differences across security domains. A recurring failure mode is plausible security code that does not satisfy the exact compliance condition. For four open-weight configurations, multi-run Wilson confidence intervals preserve the observed ordering. HardEval is publicly available.
papers.summary: Applying Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) controls requires turning natural-language security requirements into exact, persistent operating-system configuration changes, and existing code and agent benchmarks do not test this on live systems. `HardEval` builds tasks from `Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8` STIG controls that fail on an unhardened machine; the model writes a Bash script that runs on a live virtual machine and is graded by hidden `OpenSCAP`/`OVAL` compliance checks the model never sees. An evaluation of fourteen frontier and open-weight configurations finds large, uneven capability gaps across security domains. **A recurring failure is plausible-looking security code that does not satisfy the exact compliance condition.**

papers.title: Expressivity of IQP Feature-Map Quantum Kernels via Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces
papers.abstract: Quantum kernels are among the most promising methods in quantum machine learning, providing a natural way to embed data into high-dimensional Hilbert spaces via quantum circuits and capturing non-linear relationships in data. Their learning behaviour is governed by the function class they represent, which is formally characterized by the structure of the associated Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS). However, a theoretical characterization of this function class, and of how it depends on the choice of feature map and its hyperparameters, is still lacking. In this work, we focus on the Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial (IQP) feature map and derive a Fourier representation of the associated RKHS generators as finite sums of trigonometric functions evaluated on polynomially transformed input variables, with a finite set of accessible frequencies determined by the circuit construction and scaled by the bandwidth hyperparameter. This representation identifies three bandwidth regimes with qualitatively distinct expressive properties from localised, through multimodal, to periodic. Numerical experiments on synthetic datasets with controlled periodic and multimodal structure, across data dimensions and feature-map configurations, reproduce the three regimes in both supervised classification and unsupervised anomaly detection, benchmarked against a classical Gaussian kernel. These results make the relationship between expressivity and data structure explicit for IQP kernels: expressive power translates into a practical benefit only when the accessible frequencies match with the structure of the data, which provides a criterion for selecting the bandwidth when the periodic or multimodal structure of data is known.
papers.summary: The function class a quantum kernel can represent is formally described by its Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS), but how that class depends on the feature map and its hyperparameters has not been characterized. For the Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial (`IQP`) feature map, the authors derive a Fourier representation of the RKHS as finite sums of trigonometric functions over a fixed set of frequencies scaled by a bandwidth hyperparameter. This yields **three bandwidth regimes, localised, multimodal and periodic**, which experiments on synthetic classification and anomaly-detection tasks reproduce against a classical Gaussian kernel. The extra expressivity helps only when the accessible frequencies match the structure of the data, which gives a rule for choosing the bandwidth.

papers.title: Equivalence testing and run-count design for stochastic machine-learning experiments
papers.abstract: Claims that two training methods perform equally well often rest on a non-significant difference between two or three runs per method. We develop a protocol, with its power theory, for certifying practical equivalence in per-run metrics such as the AUROC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve). It rests on a two-level (seed x item) variance model separating between-run dispersion from item-level noise. Equivalence within a pre-specified margin is tested by two one-sided tests (TOST), equivalently by a confidence interval inside the margin; a two-level bootstrap covers composite statistics. A closed-form formula converts a margin and a target power into runs per method; its shifted-t refinement is calibrated against the realised two-level process. Simulations on a 270-cell grid and under non-Gaussian seed laws confirm the formula within its design-relevant range, from five runs per method. For four published runs of a joint energy-based model, the failure to certify equivalence was largely decided by design: with the variance calibrated to those runs, two per method certify with probability near three per cent, whereas certifying 0.01 AUROC at 80 per cent power needs twelve even under exact equality. A second case study on a thousand-seed CIFAR-10 zoo and the MultiBERTs checks the formula against real seed laws (within 0.05 in that range) and resolves comparisons that two or three runs leave undecided. In a two-stage design (pilot, then formula), our experiments suggest that an upper confidence bound on the pilot variance substantially reduces the undersizing seen with its point estimate.
papers.summary: Claims that two training methods perform equally well often rest on a non-significant difference between two or three runs each. The authors propose a protocol for certifying practical equivalence: a two-level (seed by item) variance model, two one-sided tests (`TOST`) against a pre-specified margin, a two-level bootstrap for composite metrics, and a closed-form formula for the number of runs needed to reach a target power. In a case study on a joint energy-based model, two runs per method certify equivalence with only about 3% probability, while **certifying a 0.01 AUROC margin at 80% power needs twelve runs even when the methods are exactly equal**. Checks on a thousand-seed `CIFAR-10` model zoo and `MultiBERTs` show the formula stays accurate on real seed distributions.

papers.title: VISTA: Steering LLMs with Latent User Values Inferred from a Few Survey Answers
papers.abstract: Personalizing a language model requires knowing what a person values, which stays largely consistent across tasks. Yet most methods either learn task-specific preferences or place the user's profile in the prompt, where models struggle to act on it. We introduce VISTA (Value-Informed Steering and Targeted Acquisition), which infers a latent profile from users' (full or partial) survey answers, and maps the profile through a hypernetwork to a user-specific steering intervention in a frozen LLM to select answer choices or generate free-text responses. Given the same evidence, VISTA matches or beats in-context profiles on synthetic preferences (Food2D), the World Values Survey (WVS), and PrimeX, without adding prompt tokens. To reduce the cognitive burden of completing full surveys, VISTA also chooses which questions to ask and when to stop: on WVS it stops after 6% of the questionnaire while retaining 94% of the full-history gain, where standard adaptive testing retains at most 42%. The dominant steering direction is an interpretable value axis on which VISTA places unseen users accurately. Our results point toward pluralistic alignment that adapts to individuals at deployable cost.
papers.summary: Personalizing a language model requires knowing what a user values, but most methods either learn task-specific preferences or put the user profile in the prompt, where models struggle to act on it. `VISTA` (Value-Informed Steering and Targeted Acquisition) infers a latent value profile from full or partial survey answers and uses a hypernetwork to turn it into a user-specific steering intervention on a frozen LLM. It matches or beats in-context profiles on `Food2D`, the World Values Survey (`WVS`) and `PrimeX` without adding prompt tokens. It also picks which survey questions to ask: on `WVS` it **stops after 6% of the questionnaire while keeping 94% of the full-history gain**, compared with at most 42% for standard adaptive testing.

papers.title: Blitz: Accelerating the Diffusion Modules of AlphaFold3 and Boltz-2
papers.abstract: Diffusion-based protein structure prediction models produce all-atom structures in about 200 denoising steps, and that cost has driven a number of few-step samplers. We present Blitz, a few-step distillation framework that uses a geometric noise schedule to distribute steps more evenly across noise scales, then learns those updates through multistep consistency training. Physical steering and target-free candidate selection help reduce the remaining geometric defects at inference. We apply Blitz to AlphaFold 3 and Boltz-2, reducing denoising from 200 steps to eight. Because published few-step results use different benchmarks and scoring procedures, we compare both distilled models with their teachers and other few-step methods under a common evaluation protocol covering structural accuracy, interface quality, ligand placement, and stereochemical validity. Blitz retains teacher-level structural accuracy, with AF3-Blitz outperforming all evaluated few-step baselines and exceeding its teacher on several accuracy metrics.
papers.summary: Diffusion-based protein structure predictors take about 200 denoising steps to produce an all-atom structure. `Blitz` distills these models into few-step samplers by combining a geometric noise schedule with multistep consistency training, and adds physical steering and target-free candidate selection at inference to fix remaining geometric defects. Applied to `AlphaFold 3` and `Boltz-2`, it **cuts denoising from 200 steps to eight** while keeping teacher-level accuracy under a shared evaluation protocol. `AF3-Blitz` outperforms every few-step baseline evaluated and beats its teacher on several accuracy metrics.

papers.title: Tool Recommendation for Multi-Step Agents: Finding Every Tool a Task Needs
papers.abstract: A multi-step agent task fails when a single tool it needs is missing, yet the tools an agent may need are too many to list: the roughly 8,200 tools on the platform we study have definitions that together exceed the context window of any model we evaluate. We present Tool Recommendation, a deployed system that gives an agent all of them, hundreds of times more than a typical MCP server exposes, through a fixed interface of three tools. It runs at the gateway between agent and tools, executing every call under the end user's own credentials and checking it against the user's consent for each service and the tools the agent may use. We evaluate it on both a public retrieval benchmark and billed end-to-end session cost. On ToolRet, Tool Recommendation places every tool a query needs in the top ten 57% more often than BM25, a lexical ranking that commercial tool search offers, and compares favorably with published systems up to nine times its size. In paired multi-step workflows, its first recommendation covered every required tool in 93% of Codex sessions, and against a fixed list of 100 tools it cut input tokens by 17% with Codex and 40% with Claude Code and the total bill in all 14 runs, by up to 40%, with no change in task completion.
papers.summary: A multi-step agent task fails if a single needed tool is missing, yet the roughly 8,200 tools on the platform studied have definitions too large for any model's context window. `Tool Recommendation` is a deployed gateway system that exposes all of them through a fixed interface of three tools, running each call under the end user's credentials and checking it against per-service consent. On the `ToolRet` benchmark it places every needed tool in the top ten 57% more often than `BM25` lexical search, and its first recommendation covered every required tool in 93% of `Codex` sessions. Compared with a fixed list of 100 tools, it **cut the total bill in all 14 runs, by up to 40%, with no change in task completion**.

papers.title: GLOBE: Evolving Structured Agentic Memory for E-commerce Product Optimization in Generative Search
papers.abstract: Optimizing product listings for generative search requires language agents not only to rewrite effectively but also to continually self-improve by retaining successful strategies across diverse categories. However, existing approaches often treat structured listings as free-form text, leaving effective strategies implicit in prompts, search trajectories, or rewritten outputs rather than accumulating them as a reusable agentic memory. To address this limitation, we introduce GLOBE, an agentic framework that drives continual self-improvement by storing optimization knowledge in an evolving handbook of explicit, field-scoped behaviors. In each episode, an Editor applies relevant behaviors and receives rank-based feedback, which a Reflector converts into behavior updates. Crucially for dependable execution in real-world settings, a Moderator removes redundant proposals, a Curator commits accepted changes, and consistently harmful behaviors are deactivated. This cycle transforms episodic feedback into a persistent, field-scoped optimization memory. Experiments show that structured behaviors outperform monolithic prompt optimization, while feedback-driven evolution and moderation further improve effectiveness and reduce downside risk. The learned behaviors also remain effective on unseen product categories, suggesting that agentic memory evolution supports interpretable and transferable product optimization.
papers.summary: Agents that optimize e-commerce product listings for generative search usually treat listings as free-form text and leave the strategies that worked buried in prompts or outputs. `GLOBE` instead stores optimization knowledge as an evolving handbook of explicit behaviors, each tied to a specific listing field. An Editor applies behaviors and receives rank-based feedback, a Reflector turns that feedback into updates, a Moderator removes redundant proposals, a Curator commits changes, and behaviors that keep causing harm are deactivated. **Structured behaviors outperform monolithic prompt optimization** and remain effective on unseen product categories.

papers.title: The Cognitive Cost of LLM Writing: A Reading-Time Comparison with Human Text
papers.abstract: Although linguistic differences between human-written and Large Language Model (LLM)-generated texts have been extensively studied, their implications for the cognitive effort involved in reading remain less explored. In psycholinguistics, reading time is commonly used as an indirect measure of cognitive processing effort. Building on this perspective, we investigate whether human-written texts and their LLM-generated rewrites exhibit differences in predicted reading time that may reflect differences in processing demands for readers. To this end, we introduce RoBERTa-RT, a model trained on human eye-tracking data to predict word-level reading times. We evaluate the model on both internal and external test sets, construct a paired dataset of 496 human-written articles and their LLM-generated rewrites, and apply RoBERTa-RT to compare their predicted reading times. Our findings show that LLM-generated rewrites tend to be shorter and have slightly lower predicted total reading times, while exhibiting higher predicted reading times per word. These differences are associated with systematic linguistic changes, including longer and less frequent words, greater lexical diversity, and higher contextual predictability. From a cognitive perspective, our findings suggest that LLM-generated writing may redistribute reading demands: reducing the amount of text to process while increasing the predicted processing effort associated with individual words. This highlights the importance of considering not only the linguistic characteristics of machine-generated content, but also its potential implications for human cognitive processing.
papers.summary: Studies of how LLM-generated text differs from human writing rarely ask how much effort it takes to read. The authors train `RoBERTa-RT` on human eye-tracking data to predict word-level reading times and apply it to 496 human-written articles paired with LLM rewrites. The rewrites are shorter and have slightly lower predicted total reading time, but **higher predicted reading time per word**, driven by longer and rarer words, greater lexical diversity and higher contextual predictability. This suggests LLM writing shifts reading effort from the amount of text toward the processing of individual words.

papers.title: Neural Expansion: A Unified Mechanism for How Deep Neural Networks Generalize
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks demonstrate remarkable generalization despite being highly over-parameterized, challenging traditional statistical learning theories. While several theoretical paradigms such as margin-based bounds, PAC-Bayesian analyses, and neural tangent kernels provide global explanations, they often lack mechanistic insight into how generalization emerges from training dynamics. We introduce Neural Expansion, a unified geometric framework that characterizes generalization through the expansion of directionally-selective ray coverage in the input space. Using Generalization Intervals (GIs), we quantify direction-specific regions around training samples where the model's predictions remain stable. Our extensive empirical studies across diverse architectures and datasets reveal that training leads to progressive expansion of ray coverage, particularly along directions with low Jacobian singular values. This mechanism helps explain a large fraction of correctly classified test inputs, adversarial examples, and even mislabeled or out-of-distribution samples through the geometry of ray coverage rather than instance-level memorization. By connecting input-space curvature to predictive behavior, our framework provides a mechanistic foundation that complements existing global theories of deep learning.
papers.summary: Global theories such as margin bounds, PAC-Bayes and neural tangent kernels do not show how generalization in over-parameterized networks emerges during training. `Neural Expansion` is a geometric framework that measures Generalization Intervals, which are direction-specific regions around training samples where the model's predictions stay stable. Experiments across architectures and datasets show that **training progressively expands this coverage, especially along directions with low Jacobian singular values**. The authors argue the mechanism accounts for many correct test predictions as well as adversarial, mislabeled and out-of-distribution cases without appealing to instance-level memorization.

papers.title: Recognizing Study Lineage Is Not Enough: Over-Crediting Same-Trial Evidence in LLM-Based Medical Verification
papers.abstract: Publication count is not study count. A model can identify shared trial lineage correctly in a direct task yet over-credit a second publication from the same trial when aggregating evidence. We evaluate this behavior in medical LLM verification using 14 source-audited clinical families and five model conditions. The families span provenance, clinical applicability, result direction, and composition; the provenance families provide the direct lineage tests. Recognition and aggregation are separate stateless calls, and repeated calls assess within-input stability. Across all three original provenance families, GPT-5.5 identifies the independent update in 10/10 recognition calls per family but over-credits the same-trial report in 5/5 separate aggregation calls per family. Selected Qwen3-4B and Ministral-3-8B conditions show the same cross-task contrast. A study-grouping instruction reduces GPT-5.5 over-credit from 4/5 to 0/5 in each later pure-provenance family. Other model conditions show mixed behavior, and rejected outputs limit several comparisons. The results identify a behavioral gap between elicited lineage recognition and evidence aggregation. The code and data artifacts are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/study-lineage-review-artifact.
papers.summary: In medical evidence verification, two publications from the same clinical trial should not count as independent evidence. Using 14 source-audited clinical families, the authors test recognition of trial lineage and evidence aggregation as separate calls. `GPT-5.5` correctly identifies the shared lineage in 10 of 10 recognition calls per family, yet **over-credits the same-trial report in 5 of 5 aggregation calls**, and selected `Qwen3-4B` and `Ministral-3-8B` conditions show the same gap. An explicit instruction to group by study reduced `GPT-5.5` over-crediting from 4/5 to 0/5 in later pure-provenance families.

papers.title: RedDarwin: Evolving Jailbreak Skills against Frontier LLMs
papers.abstract: Red teaming must continually adapt as frontier LLM safeguards evolve, yet existing approaches largely search for adversarial prompts or optimize within fixed attack procedures. We observe that even when an attack becomes ineffective, its underlying mechanisms can remain useful and can be revised or recombined to construct stronger attacks. Based on this insight, we introduce RedDarwin, an agentic framework that shifts the unit of jailbreak evolution from prompts and fixed attacks to executable attack skills. RedDarwin consists of 47 reusable base skills and autonomously revises, composes, executes, and selects them using target-model feedback, allowing successful discoveries to become building blocks for subsequent evolution. RedDarwin produces 65 evolved skills, improving 44 of 47 base attacks and increasing their mean attack success rate (ASR) on AdvBench from 18.8% to 47.3%. These evolved skills consistently outperform baselines on the held-out StrongREJECT and frontier LLMs unseen during evolution; with only 10 target-model queries, RedDarwin achieves 100% ASR on GPT-5.6-Sol, 92% on Claude-Sonnet-5, and 80% on Gemini-3.8-Flash. Analysis of the evolution trajectories further shows that strong attacks often emerge from novel combinations of reusable mechanisms rather than from individually dominant ones. We believe this paradigm can accelerate adaptive red teaming and inform stronger safeguards, creating complementary value for both safety evaluation and defense.
papers.summary: Existing red-teaming methods mostly search for adversarial prompts or tune fixed attack procedures, even though the mechanisms behind an attack that stopped working can often be revised or recombined. `RedDarwin` is an agentic framework that evolves executable jailbreak skills: starting from 47 base skills, it revises, composes, executes and selects them using feedback from the target model. It produced 65 evolved skills, raising the mean attack success rate (ASR) on `AdvBench` from 18.8% to 47.3%, and the skills generalize to the held-out `StrongREJECT` benchmark. With only 10 queries per target, it reports **100% ASR on `GPT-5.6-Sol`, 92% on `Claude-Sonnet-5` and 80% on `Gemini-3.8-Flash`**, and strong attacks tend to come from new combinations of reusable mechanisms.
